summary: The respondent was prosecuted under section 16(1)(a) of the Delhi Food Adulteration Act, 1954 for having committed an offence punishable under section 7(2) read with section 13(1) (d) of that Act. The trial Magistrate acquitted the respondent on the ground that he had not been able to prove that the sample contained any substance in the food and was adulterated. The High Court held that the respondent was guilty of having committed a contravention of article 14 of the Constitution, and that the prosecution was not entitled to rely upon the definition of ' adulteration ' under section 2(g) of Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word ' adulteration" in section 2 (g) means "a person who is in charge of a public nature". Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'tribly ' includes any substance which is not capable of being used for the purpose of human consumption or for the purposes of human life. [630B] 2. The word 'tubly ' means "any article which is capable of having been used for human consumption". It is a term of art and includes any article which has been used in connection with the human affairs. The definition of adulteration ' is wide enough to include a person who has been using it for human use or for any other purpose. [730C] 3. The meaning of the word "tribally" is not restricted to a person whose duty is to be performed by him. It is only when a person is in possession of a food and is found guilty of an offence under section 13 (1) readwith section 13, he must prove that it was used for any purpose other than that which is intended to be used for such purpose. The words "tubally" are not restricted merely to a particular article but also to a specified article. [779E F] 4. In the instant case, the respondent had been using the word `tribarily ' in section 3(1). He was not able to establish that he was in charge for any of the purposes mentioned in section 13. The prosecution has failed to prove the ingredients of the offence under the Act. [777E F; 880A] 5. In view of the fact that the definition is wide, it cannot be said that the expression 'toribly" is used in the context of the definition. [783B C] 6. The respondent was not guilty of any offence under any of these provisions. He was therefore guilty of the charge under section 3 (1). [777F G] 7. In order to attract the applicability of article 13, it must be shown that he has been in charge and has committed an act which is likely to cause a public nuisance or is likely thereby to cause such a nuisance. The use of the expression "turbarily" in the definition would not amount to a 'trically ' within the meaning of article 19(1), but it must mean that he is guilty of a contravention under any other law. [784E F, 880B] 7: In the present case, there was no evidence on record to show that the Respondent had been in possession or has been convicted for an offence falling under section 5(2). The prosecution failed to establish the ingredients mentioned in the Act and the trial Magistrate rightly acquitted him.

The appellant was convicted under section 16(1)(a) of the Bihar Food Adulteration Act, 1947. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced him to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the finding of the Sessions Judge that the appellant had committed a breach of the conditions of the licence was not correct. HELD : (i) The finding of fact recorded by the Sessions judge is erroneous. [408 D] (ii) The conviction and sentences are set aside. In the present case, the appellant was found guilty under section 7(1) (a) read with section 16 (1)(b). He was convicted for an offence under section 5(2) of that Act. [508 E F] (iii) The High court was right in holding that the evidence of the appellant did not establish that he had committed any breach of conditions of a licence. [608 G H] (iv) The presumption of possession is not weakened by the fact that the person who has been convicted is a tenant and the burden is on him to prove that he was a tenant. [709 F] In the instant case, there was no evidence to show that the shop in question was a "dealer" within the meaning of section 2(1). The finding recorded by both the courts below was not based on any evidence. [643 D] The appellant had failed to prove his possession and the presumption of the possession could be drawn only if he proved that he is a dealer.

The respondent instituted a suit for recovery of possession of the land in dispute on the ground that he was a tenant of the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the lease was not a lease within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1950. The High Court held that the tenancy was a lease and that the respondent was entitled to possession of it under the provisions of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The suit was not maintainable because the lease had been terminated by the appellant on the expiry of the period of lease. The lease was for a period of two years from the date of termination of the tenancy and the lease having expired, the respondent could not be evicted under section 2 (1). [657 H] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that there was no subsisting lease between the parties and the suit was barred by limitation. [658 A B] (iii) The respondent had not been able to prove that he had been a tenant for a long period of three years from that date. The respondent could, therefore, be evicted only under section 3(1). The High court was right in saying that the suit is barred by time. [757 C D] (iv) The lease having been terminated on the expiration of the term of the lease, the appellant cannot claim any protection under section 12 of the Transfer of Property Act. [788 A B]. (v) The finding of the High Court that the appellant was a lessee for a short period of five years from this date is not correct.

The assessee, a public limited company, was assessed to income tax under the Income Tax Act, 1961 on the ground that the income of the assessee had escaped assessment. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant and held that the Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income for the relevant assessment year. The High Court in second appeal held that since the IncomeTax Officer had not applied his mind to the question whether the income was liable to be assessed under section 10(2) of the Act, he could not have made a reference to the High Court under Section 256(1) of that Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High court erred in holding that the provisions of Section 256 (1) were applicable to the case and that the assessment proceedings were vitiated by non application of mind and that, therefore, the Incometax Officer had jurisdiction to make a reference under section 256(2). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred on the High Courts under Section 260(1)(b) is not confined to the powers of the High courts under Section 263(1). [630B] 2. The provisions of Sections 256 and 256 (3) are not exhaustive of the powers conferred by Section 263. It is only when the Income 'tax Officer has reason to believe that a particular income has escaped assessment, he may, after giving him an opportunity of being heard, make a report in writing which he considers necessary or expedient for the purpose of satisfying himself as to the correctness or otherwise of the information furnished and the reasons for such belief, pass such orders thereon as it thinks fit. [631C] 3. The powers conferred on a High Court by Section 256 are wide and have been limited to the power of the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution. It has been held that in view of the provisions contained in Sections 256(3) and 256(4), the Income Revenue Officer is not competent to make an order under Section 264(1), but he can, after considering the report of the Income assessment officer, make such orders as it considers necessary for the purposes of satisfying itself as to correctness or legality of the order. [731C D] 4. The jurisdiction conferred on High Courts by Section 260 is limited to those powers which are expressly provided in the Act and not otherwise. [781E F] 5. In the instant case, the HighCourt was right in holding the assessment proceeding vitiated by lack of jurisdiction or lack of territorial jurisdiction. [783C D; 784A B] 6. The order passed by the Income. Tax Officer is a final order under section 263(2), and the High 'Court has no power to make such an order. It cannot be said that the order passed in exercise of its powers under Section 261(1 ) (b) was not a final one. [784E F; 784B] 7. The question whether a particular document is a document or not is essentially a matter of judicial review and it is only if the court has to decide whether the document is an instrument or not, whether it is an order passed under Section 262(1); whether it can be said to be an order made under Section 252(2); whether the court can make such a reference. [831C E] 8. The expression "any order" in Section 261 (1)(a) of Income Tax, 1961 means any order made by the Commissioner under section 264(3). [784G H; 784E F].

The appellants were the daughters of a Hindu female. The first respondent was married to one K who died in 1943 leaving behind his widow and children. On the death of K, the first respondent executed a will bequeathing her property to K. The appellant 's mother executed a gift deed in favour of K on the ground that she had no right to alienate the property. The appellants were not entitled to any share in the property as they were not parties to the gift deed. The trial court held that the gift was valid and that the will was void. On appeal, the High Court held that K was not a party to the document. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the document was invalid because it was executed by K in favour Of the first appellant and that it was not executed by him. HELD : (i) The gift deed was valid as it was signed by K and his mother. It was therefore void. [630 B] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the deed was invalid as it did not contain any provision for the transfer of property to a Hindu male. The document was executed on behalf Of the second appellant and his father. The gift was made by K on behalfof the first and the mother. The deed was executed only after the death or the death, whichever is later. [730 B C] (iii) The document in question was not registered as a gift of property. It did not mention the name of the second respondent. The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that K had no title to the property and that he was entitled to the benefit of section 7(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. [774 D] (iv) The deed in question is a valid document and it did contain any specific provision for transfer of the property to another Hindu female and that therefore the gift could not be made by her.

The Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950 (Madras Act IV of 1951) was passed by the State Government under section 3(1)(a) of the Madras Hindu Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1959. The respondents were assessed to pay a tax on the amount of contribution payable to the temple. The respondent challenged the validity of the levy on the ground that the Act did not provide for the levy of the tax on any particular day. The High Court held that the levy was invalid because it was beyond the competence of the State Legislature under section 4(1) (a). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The levy was valid as it was within the competence and authority of the Government under the Act. [657 D] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the imposition was invalid as it had not been passed by a competent authority. The impugned Act did provide for levy of tax on certain specified day. It was therefore, valid. [757 G H] (iii) The impugned Rules were ultra vires and void. [781 A B] (iv) The provisions of section 4 (1)(b) of Madras Hindu Endowments Act are not ultra vires the Constitution. [783 D F] (v) The imposition of tax was invalid on the grounds that it was in contravention of the rules made under the Madras Public Religious Endowments Rules, 1959 and therefore the levy could not be sustained. [784 E G] (vi) The contention that the impugned Rules did not contain any provision for the imposition of a tax is wholly misconceived.

The appellant, a practising advocate in the Punjab High Court, was prosecuted for contempt of court by the respondents under section 5(1) read with section 7 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. The respondents filed an application before the High Court under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure praying that the proceedings be quashed on the ground that the appellant had not been given a hearing and that the order was passed without notice to them. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the contempt was not maintainable because the appellant was not given a personal hearing, and that there was no sufficient cause for the same. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application under section 7(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (i) The High Courts have no jurisdiction in the matter of issuing a notice to the respondents and that it is not open to the High Courts to issue a notice under section 9 of the Act. [755 F] (ii) The order passed by the High courts is not appealable under section 115 of the Criminal Procedure Code. It is only when an appeal is filed against the order, that the appeal is pending before the Supreme Court and the High 'Court has no jurisdiction. [771 C D] (iii) The appellant was given a right to move the High or the High High Court for quashing the proceedings in question. The order of the High Judge is appealable under sub section (2) of section 115. [761 F G] (iv) The appeal is not maintainable as it is filed within time.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1949. The conviction was confirmed by the High Court on appeal by special leave. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) Section 7 of that Act is a self contained code and does not apply to any enactment which has been repealed or replaced by the Central Act, 1950. (ii) Section 8 of the Act is an exception to the general rule that if a statute is repealed by the Act, it shall be deemed to have been repealed by that Act and the repeal shall not affect the validity of such a law. The provisions of the repealed Act are intended to apply to all enactments which have been enacted in the State of Punjab. (iii) Section 9 of the old Act does not make any provision for repeal of the new Act. (iv) Section 10 of the repealing Act is not an exception and must be deemed always to have retrospective operation. The saving provisions contained in section 7(1)(b) of the Amending Act are not intended to affect the operation of the saving provisions. (v) Section 11 of the amending Act does no doubt apply to a repeal which has already been repealed but it is only when the repealing statute is replaced by another enactment, that is, the repeal will not affect any validity of the repeal. The words "in respect of anything done or omitted to be done in pursuance of the provisions of this Act" are intended not to affect any invalidity of the earlier law. (vi) Section 12 of the General Clauses Act does only apply to cases where there has been a repeal and no repeal is made by the repealing enactment, but it applies to cases which have already been done or purported to be taken under the repealed statute. The repeal will take effect from the date of the commencement of the Central Ordinance. (vii) Section 13 of the , does not affect section 7 Of the General Clause Act.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the Karta of a joint Hindu family. The properties were sold by the respondents to the appellant and the respondents were divided into two separate properties. The decree holder filed an application for execution of the decree on the ground that the properties were not joint property and that the decree was not executable as it was passed without jurisdiction. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the compromise decree was a nullity and that it was not enforceable as it had been passed without authority. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The compromise decree is a nullity because it is passed without the authority of law. It is not necessary for the court to decide whether the compromise should be executed or not. [657 B] (ii) The High Courts have no jurisdiction to pass any decree in respect of the properties which were sold in execution of a decree. The compromise was not a nullity as it did not contain any provision for the execution of decrees. It was only when the decree is passed and the decree has been passed, that the court has power to pass such orders as are necessary for execution. [757 B C] (iii) The decree in question was a decree for money and not a decree which could be executed without jurisdiction and it was executable as a nullity. It does not contain a provision for execution unless it is shown that the property was sold by a person other than the manager of the joint Hindu Family. [779 E F] (iv) The terms of the compromise were not intended to be used in the execution proceedings, but only when it was executed without authority of Law. It could not be said that the parties had no power to execute the decree.

The respondent was a firm carrying on business in the Bombay State. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of certain sums due to him from the respondent. The decree holder claimed that the decree was not executable and that the respondent had no right to execute the decree. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the order of the trial court was not appealable under section 115 Code of Civil Procedure, and that it was not open to the respondent to execute it in execution of the decree, and the decree holder appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the rule of the High Courts is applicable only where a decree is passed against a company which has been wound up by the court or by an order of a court, and it is not open for the respondent, to execute such a decree in execution thereof. The rule of law is applicable to a case where a company has been dissolved by the Court or by any order of court, it cannot be said that the judgment debtor had no title to the property in question. The rules of law are applicable only when a company is wound up and the court has power to execute a decree against a person who has been declared as insolvent. The words "any order made under section 116 Code of Criminal Procedure" in the rule are not intended to be construed in their popular sense, but they must be read in their ordinary sense. It is well settled that the word "decree" in section 115 of the Code of civil Procedure means a decree which has become final and conclusive on the date of the order or the date when it was made. The expression "decree holder" in rule 2(1) of the Civil Procedure Code means a person whose name is entered in the register of creditors, and does not include a person against whom an application for execution had been made under the decree or order of any court, or where the decree has become enforceable by reason of the fact that he has been discharged from his liability to pay the debt. The word "judgment" in r. 2(2) of Order XXI of the Rules is not intended merely to include a decree for money which has ceased to exist and it must be construed as a decree, but also includes a decree passed against an person who had become insolvent. It would therefore be open to a party to apply for execution under section 117 Code of criminal Procedure to execute an order in execution. The application for the execution was not maintainable because the respondent did not file any application for executing it and he could not have filed the application for execute it, but only applied for execution.

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with the respondent for supply of electrical energy to the appellant. The contract was for supply and sale of electrical goods to the respondent. The contracts were for supply, supply and distribution of electrical materials. The respondent claimed that the contract was not for supply but for supply. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim on the ground that the contracts were not for work and were not a works contract within the meaning of section 2(g) of the . The High Court held that the transaction was for work, and that the agreement was for works and was not a contract for sale. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent was not liable to pay sales tax on the turnover of the respondent 's factory. HELD : (i) The contracts are for supply or sale of electricity but for work which is for the purpose of carrying out the work of the appellant and the contract is for work. [619 F G] (ii) The contract is a works contracts for supply to the assessee. It is not for the assessee to prove that the goods were supplied by him. The fact that the contractor was not the owner of the goods, does not make any difference in the price of the property. [720 A B] (iii) The agreement is for supply only to the contractor and not to the contractors. It cannot be said that the work was for the supply of electricity. The contractor is not a person who has supplied the goods. The agreement also does not contain any stipulation regarding the price or the price at which the goods are supplied. [779 C] (iv) The respondent 'residings were for the construction of the contract and the contracts did not contain such stipulation. The work was to be done by the contractor. The appellant was liable to sales tax under section 2 (g) read with section 3(1)(d) of . The contract provided that the works shall be completed within three months from the date of completion of the work. The terms of the contracts are not merely for the execution of the works and the work is to be completed by the Contractor.

The respondent was a dealer in the goods. He sold the goods to the appellant and the respondent was also charged under section 420 I.P.C. for having committed an offence punishable under section 409 I. P.C., read with section 34 I.p.C, read with sections 5(1)(d) and 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted the respondent on the ground that he was a benamidar in the transaction and that the transaction was not one of sale but was a sale within the meaning of section 5(3). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to try the case because the transaction did not amount to sale within section 5 (1) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that the transactions were not one for sale and therefore the transaction could not be said to have been a sale under section 5 of the Act. [737 D] In the instant case the transaction took place on the date when the transaction came into existence. It was only after the transaction had come into existence, that the respondent had sold the same to the complainant. The High court was in wrong in holding the transaction as a sale and not one under section 120B I. p.C.[737 E] In view of the fact that the complainant was a partner in the transactions it could not have been said that he had sold it to the respondent.

The petitioner, a private limited company, was employed as a clerk in the Southern Railway. The petitioner was appointed as a driver in the Northern Railway on March 31, 1982. He was also appointed as an Assistant Engineer in the Western Railway on April 1, 1982 and he was given a salary of Rs. 10,000 per month. On May 14, 1983, the petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the action taken by the respondents in not taking any steps to recover the amount from the petitioner. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had no locus standi to file the writ petition and the High court was right in dismissing the petition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner has a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. It is not necessary for the petitioner to establish his case before the Court that he had no right to claim any compensation or damages. [702C] 2.2 The petitioner is entitled to claim compensation in respect of the loss caused to him by the accident and the loss suffered by him on account of the negligence of the staff of the Southern Railways. It has been established that the staff have a right to recover from the employees of the Northern Railways. The petitioners are not entitled to any compensation for the loss sustained by them on account Of negligence or misconduct of the officials of the Western Railways. [781D] 3.1 In the instant case, the respondents have no locus to file writ petition in respect thereof. They have a fundamental rights under Article 14 of the constitution. The respondents are not bound to pay any compensation to the petitioner for the damage caused to them by the negligence or breach of their duties. [783E F] 3:2 The petitioners have a statutory right to seek redress against the action of the respondents. It cannot be said that they have a locus standi in respect whereof the petitioner has no locus, title or interest to file any writ petition. They are entitled to ask for relief against the acts of their officers and servants. [784E F; 784A] 3 :3 The petitioner 's claim is based on the principles laid down by this Court in Union of India vs M. P. Sharma & Ors., ; , followed. In the circumstances, the petition is dismissed. [777F] 4:4 The petitioner shall be entitled to the compensation for loss sustained on accountof negligence or negligence of their staff.

The appellants were holders of land in the State of Bombay. They filed applications under section 47(1) of the Bombay Land Revenue Act, 1901 for restoration of possession of their lands. The Tribunal dismissed the applications on the ground that the application was barred by limitation as it had not been filed within time and that the applications were barred by time. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the provisions of section 47 (1) were applicable to the case and that, therefore, the application for restoration was barred under section 48(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD: The Tribunal has no power to review its own order on the question whether the applications filed by the appellants were barred under the Act. [657 H] The High Courts have not properly exercised their jurisdiction in dealing with applications under sections 47 and 48 of the Act and the Tribunal has rightly exercised its discretion in dealing the applications under the provisions. [757 A B] In the present case, the Tribunal had no power under section 49(1), to review the order on merits. The application for review was not barred by the limitation prescribed by section 48 (1). [658 F G] The Tribunal had jurisdiction to review an order of the Tribunal and it could not have exercised its jurisdiction in deciding the applications made by the appellant under section 46(1)(a) because, the applications for restoration were filed within the time fixed. [625 A B]. The Tribunal was right in holding that the Tribunal was not competent to review any order passed by it on merits as it did not exercise its power under the Code of Civil Procedure.

The appellant was the Mahant of a temple. He had been appointed as a trustee for the temple and he was appointed as an agent of the deity. The suit was decreed by the trial court on the ground that the temple was not a public temple within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. The High Court held that the suit was not maintainable because it was not one for the purposes of the Act and that the award was bad in law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as it was a public institution within the definition of section 3(1)(a) of that Act. HELD : (i) The question whether the temple is a public or private property within the scope of the section does not arise in this case. [782 C] (ii) The High Courts had no power to entertain a suit as the property was not an 'public temple ' within the ambit of section 1(1). [785 D] (iii) The award was not bad because it did not contain any provision for the institution of a suit and that it was one for which the temple belonged. It was therefore not necessary to decide whether the suit had been filed in the Court or not. [774 C E] (iv) The finding of the High Courts on the question whether a particular temple is an 'private temple ' is correct. [764 D] In the present case, the temple had been established by the deity and it was established that the property belonged to the deity in the temple. It did not belong to the temple nor was it a public religious institution within its meaning. The question of the temple being an 'Public temple ' does not depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The temple was a private temple within its scope.

The appellants were charged with contempt of Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal and directed that the appellants be removed from service. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court committed an error in holding that the charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the charge was not established beyond reasonable doubts. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The charge is proved beyond doubt and the charge is not proved beyond any reasonable doubt. [775G] 2. The appellants are guilty of contempt of court. They have been charged with the contempt of the Court. They are guilty by a Court of law. They were guilty of gross misconduct. They cannot be punished for contempt of courts. [771C D] 3. The charges are proved beyond all reasonable doubt, and they are not proved to be guilty of any contempt of Courts. [761F G] 4. The allegations in the charge are not established by the appellants. They must be held guilty of misconduct. [751G H; 771A B] 5. The appellant is guilty of professional misconduct. He has been convicted for contempt. He was sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and a fine of Rs. 500/ . The High Courts have not committed any error in taking the view that the allegations are proved. [781G] 6. The contempt of Judges is not established unless there is a prima facie case against the appellants, nor is it shown that the appellant was guilty of such misconduct. The Court has to be satisfied that the offence is proved. If the High Courts are satisfied that there is no prima facie evidence against the appellant, they are entitled to punish him for contempt under section 7 of the Contempt of Courts Act.

The appellants filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell the properties in dispute. The arbitrator passed an award on March 31, 1983 and made an award in terms of section 30(2) of the , which was signed by the parties. On July 1, 1983 the Registrar of the High Court granted a certificate under section 30 of the . The appellants filed an application for stay of the proceedings before the High court. The High Court dismissed the application on the ground that the award was not signed by them and that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to pass the order in terms thereof. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Judge erred in holding that the order passed by the Registrar was a nullity because the award did not contain any provision for the filing of an application under section 29 of the Act and that there was no provision for filing an application before the arbitrator, and that since the award had been signed by both parties, it could not be said that the proceedings were vitiated by non compliance with the provisions of section 29(2). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed under section 31 of the is a nullity and is liable to be set aside on the grounds that the application was made within time. [795B] 2. The award in question was signed on behalf Of the parties and it was not a nullity. It was therefore a nullity, because the arbitrator did not act as an arbitrator. [77C D] 3. The Registrar had no power to grant stay of proceedings before him. He could not have granted the certificate under Section 30(1) of , but he could not do so. [76D E] 4. The power of the Registrar to grant a stay of proceeding is not absolute and it cannot be said to be an order of nullity. [75G H; 77A B] 5. The Court has no jurisdiction in the matter of granting a stay under section 28 of the Arbitration Act, 1940. It is well settled that the power of a court to grant interim stay does not extend to the exercise of its inherent powers. The discretion conferred on the Registrar by Section 30 is discretionary and it is only when the court exercises its power to do so, that the court has no power under section 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [ 771C] 6. The jurisdiction of the Court in granting a temporary stay does extend to cases where there are exceptional circumstances or where there is exceptional circumstances which may warrant such a conclusion. [782B C] 7. In the instant case, the award in respect of the properties was signed and verified by both the parties on behalf and the same day. The appellants had not filed any application for interim stay. They were therefore entitled to stay of execution proceedings before it. [791F G] 8. The question whether the order of the arbitrator was a valid one or not is no longer res integra. It cannot be disputed that the Registrar had power under Section 29(1)(a) to grant an injunction against the appellants in respect thereof. [802C D, F] 9. In view of the fact that the parties have been given an opportunity to file their objections and if they so desired, the order granting interim stay cannot be sustained.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that he had no right to continue in possession of the premises and that the appellant was not entitled to continue the tenancy. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was not a licensee within the meaning of section 2(1) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High Court held that the agreement between the parties was void as it was not an agreement for lease and that it was a contract for sale. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The agreement was void because it was one of the conditions mentioned in section 2 (1) of that Act which provided that the tenant shall be entitled to remain in possession until he has been evicted from the premises. The appellant had not been able to prove that the lease was a lease and therefore the respondent could not be evicted. [657 H] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that section 2 of the Act did not apply to the facts of the case. The agreement did not contain any provision for the termination of the tenancy by the tenant. It was merely an agreement which was a condition precedent to the termination or termination of his tenancy. [757 H; 758 A] (iii) The appellant was entitled to be in possession when he had been evicted. The suit was therefore barred by section 2 and it was open to the respondent to contend that the contract was void.

The appellant, a student of the respondent college, was prosecuted for having committed offences under section 16(1)(d) read with Section 16(2) of the . The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the findings recorded by the Enquiry Committee were perverse and that the finding recorded by it was based on no evidence or that the same was vitiated by any error apparent on the face of record, and that there was no material before the High court to justify its conclusion. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have erred in interfering with the findings of fact arrived at by the enquiry committee. [702D] 2.2 In the instant case, the High Courts had not properly appreciated the evidence and come to a different conclusion on the basis of which the conclusions were based. The High court was right in holding the findings arrived at without any material before it. [777F G] 3.1 In the absence of any material to justify the conclusion reached by the High courts, the finding of fact recorded by them are not vitiated by error apparent or on the record. [781E F] 2:2 The High Power Committee has rightly held that the conclusions arrived at were perverse. It is well settled that the decision of the Enquiry committee must be based on some material before a court which is not an appellate authority and it cannot be said that the conclusion arrived at was perverse. [783G H] 3:3 In the present case, there was nothing to show that the enquiry officer had acted in accordance with law or that there were any error of law apparent on record. The findings recorded are based on a material before him. It has not been shown that the Enquiry Officer acted in violation of principles of natural justice or that it was vitiated due to some error apparent from the face. [784E F; 784A] 4:4 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that the report of the enquiry Committee was based upon no evidence. The conclusion arrived by the Board on the material before them cannot be sustained. [802D E] 5:5 The High power of interference under Article 226 of the Constitution is not a matter which can be gone into in an appeal or revision under Article 136 of the constitution. It does not mean that the Court has to exercise its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitu tion. [ 784B C] 6:6 In the case of a person who is found guilty of misconduct, the Court must satisfy itself that the evidence was reasonably and bona fide. The Court cannot interfere with the finding arrived at on the ground that the charges were proved. [788E F]. 2:7 The High 'Court has not properly exercised its jurisdiction in interfering or interfering with an order of dismissal passed by a subordinate authority. It can exercise its power under Article 32 of the Consti tution only if it is satisfied that the case was bona fide and that no reasonable person could be said to have acted in contravention of the provisions of the Act. [789E F, 784A B] 2 :7 The Court has not exercised its discretion properly or with a view to finding out whether the findings are perverse or not. It cannot interfere under Article appellate jurisdiction unless it is shown that there is some material on record which would justify its conclusions. [773G H; 784B D] 3 :8 In the circumstances of this case, no interference is called for in the order of the High 'court. The appeal is dismissed.

The appellant, a firm of the respondent, was charged with offences under sections 120 B and 420 I.P.C. for having committed an offence under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted all the accused on the ground that they were guilty of criminal misconduct and that the prosecution was not competent to take cognizance of the offence under sections 161 and 165 I. P.C., but convicted them for having abetted the commission of an offence punishable under section 161 read with Section 5(2) (d). The High Court, in appeal, held that the conviction of the appellant on the basis of the evidence of a witness was not justified. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had no jurisdiction to take cognisance of the offences under section 165 I .P. C., and that there was no evidence to show that the offence was committed by the appellant in furtherance of his official duty, and that he was guilty of an act which was done with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the public interest. HELD: (i) The conviction of a person under section 4(1) (a) readwith section 5 of the Act is not justified because it is not proved that he had abetted the offence, and the prosecution has failed to prove that he abetted the act which is done with the intention of causing such acts. [707 D] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant was guilty under section 6(1), read with s 5(3) (b). The conviction must be based on a presumption that he committed an act punishable under sections 165 and 165I.P., and not under section 7 of the .

The appellant Bank, a Bank, was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar and sugar. The respondent bank had taken over the goods to the Bank. In the course of its business, the Bank had taken the goods for sale. The Bank also took over the consignment. The appellant Bank filed a suit against the Bank for recovery of the amount due from it. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the Bank was not entitled to recover the amount from the respondent bank. The High Court held that the bank was not liable to pay any amount due under the contract and that the appellant Bank had no right to recover it from the Bank, and that since the Bank did not take over the consignments, the appellant bank was entitled to enforce its liability against the respondent Bank. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The suit is not maintainable because the Bank has taken over a consignment of sugar in the course Of its business. It is only when the goods are sold and delivered to the bank, the amount becomes due under a contract. [601B] 2. The question whether the Bank is entitled to realise the amount by way of security or otherwise does not arise for consideration in this Court. [702C D] 3. In view of the provisions of section 45 of the Indian Contract Act, the High Court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit on the ground that it was not maintainable. [781E F] 4. The expression "security" is defined in section 2(e) of the Contract Act as meaning "security". It means security for the purpose of securing the equitable distribution and availability of goods or for securing the availability of such goods or securing the due performance of any contract, express or implied, to be performed by a person who has been appointed to act under the terms of an agreement or contract. The words "security", in section 45 are not defined in the Contract Acts. [783B] 5. In order to attract the applicability of section 46 of the Act, it is necessary to take into account the various clauses of the contract which are relevant for the purposes of the present case. The terms of the said clause are: (i) "security for the due date" means security; (ii) " surety" means a person whose principal or interest in the goods has been entrusted with the custody of the bank and includes any person who is appointed to perform the duties of the surety; (iii) " sureties" means an agent, manager, secretary or other officer of the Bank; (iv) " bond" means the security for securing securing the proper performance of the obligations under the Contract. [784E F].

The appellant was the holder of a village in which he was appointed as an Assistant Commissioner. He was appointed to the State of Madhya Pradesh by the Government of India under section 3(1) of the Act. The appellant was appointed on the basis of a notification issued under section 4 of the Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals and Alienated Lands) Act, 1951, which provided that "the holder of an estate shall be entitled to receive from the State Government all arrears of land revenue and cesses payable by him in respect of such estate or tenure as may be prescribed. " The appellant claimed that he was a hereditary holder of the village and was not entitled to any share in the estate. The trial court held that the appellant was a holder of his estate and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant had been appointed on a permanent basis by the State under section 5(1)(a) of Act, and as such he was entitled to the share in it. [657 D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the respondent was not an hereditary holder, because, the appellant had no right to receive the land revenue from him. The High court was wrong in holding the appellant 's suit. [757 G H] (iii) The respondent was a tenure holder and was entitled only to receive it from the Government. [779 D E] (iv) The grant of the estate was not a permanent one, because the appellant did not hold any land as defined in section 2(1).

The respondents were the descendants of a Hindu undivided family. They claimed that they had no right to hold property in the joint family properties and that they were entitled to succeed to the estate of the deceased. The trial court held that the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of the rule of primogeniture, as they were not members of the joint Hindu family. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that there was no custom in the family law and that the rule was applicable only to the members of a joint Hindu Family. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the rules of prim primogenciation were not applicable to the case because they were governed by the Mitakshara law, and that, therefore, the rule could not be applied to the respondents as they had been governed by Mitakshara law. HELD : (i) The rule of lineal primogenogeniture was not applicable in the case of a member of a family. [657 H] (ii) The rules of lineal lineal prim prim primitiveiture were not intended to apply to members of joint Hindu families, and therefore, they could not have been applied to members thereof. They were governed under Mitakshara law and not by Mitakshara Law. [757 A B] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the custom of primitive primogen primogen descent was applicable to members belonging to a family, and the rule did not apply to them as they belonged to a joint family. In the present case, the respondents had been recognised by Mitakshara Mitakshara law but were governed only by Mitakshara laws.

The appellants are manufacturers of cotton fabrics. They were manufacturing cotton fabrics and they were also manufacturing cotton yarn. The appellants claimed exemption under the Notification No. 175/83 dated 1st March, 1982. The Assistant Collector rejected their claim on the ground that the cotton fabrics manufactured by them were not excisable goods as defined in section 2(1) of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said Notification and also the validity thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants were entitled to exemption under Notification No 175/84 dated 1.3.1982. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the notification did not apply to cotton fabrics as defined therein in section 3(1)(a) of Central Excise and Salt Act, 1922. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Courts have rightly held that the said notification did apply to the cotton fabric manufactured by the appellants. [799B] In view of the fact that the impugned Notification No 176/83 was applicable to cotton yarn, it cannot be said that the same was applicable only to cotton fabric and not to cotton cloth. [781C D] The High court has rightly held in favour of the appellant. [783D] The notification dated 1th March, 1983 is applicable only where cotton fabrics are manufactured by a manufacturer or manufacturer or producer or manufacturer. It does not apply merely to cotton cotton fabrics which are manufactured after the commencement of the Act. The said notification cannot be extended to cotton textiles as defined under section 2 (1) (a).

The petitioner, a private limited company, was granted a permit under section 68 of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 for the transport of passengers from Uttar Pradesh to Uttar Pradesh. The Regional Transport Authority issued a notice under section 80 of the Act calling upon the petitioner to show cause why the scheme should not be cancelled and published in the Gazette. The petitioner filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying that the scheme be cancelled. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the petitioner was entitled to the permit as he had been granted a stage carriage permit under the Act. The revision petition preferred by the petitioner against the order of the trial court was also dismissed. In the writ petition filed by the State, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Court erred in quashing the scheme and directing the Regional Transport Authorities to issue a notice to the petitioner under section 81 of the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1976. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme is not an administrative act but an administrative function. It is a quasi judicial function. The jurisdiction of the High Courts are limited to the question whether the scheme is in conformity with the provisions of the statute or not. [799B] 2. The power of the State Government under section 79 of the is not confined to the jurisdiction of civil courts. The powers of the Civil Court are limited only to the powers of civil court and not to the power of civil Courts. It cannot be said that the power conferred by the Act is confined to those powers which are expressly provided in the statute. [771C] 3. The High Court was right in holding that section 81(3) of the Road Transport Corporation Act, 1956 is a self contained code and does not apply to the proceedings before the civil court. [762E F] 4. The provisions of sections 80 and 80 of Code of Criminal Procedure are intended to be construed strictly and in consonance with the scheme. It has been held that the jurisdiction conferred by section 81 is confined only to those matters which are specifically provided in a statute. The Act does not contemplate any procedure for the trial of suits or proceedings before civil courts, but it does not provide for any procedure to be followed by the civil courts and the civil Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain such applications.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in a case which was not investigated by the police and that the prosecution had failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the appellant was guilty of an offence under section 161 Indian Penal Code and section 5 of the Act. The sanction given by the Government of India under section 6(1) of Prevention of Anti Corruption Act is not a bar to the prosecution of the appellant. The order of sanction is not in accordance with law and must be set aside. The appellant was rightly convicted on the basis that he was falsely implicated. The conviction of the accused under section 4(2)(d), read with s. 5 (1) (d) of Act is therefore illegal. The prosecution case was that the sanction given to him by the Inspector General of Police was not a valid sanction and the sanction was not in conformity with law. The fact that the Inspector had been prosecuted for an offence punishable under section 165 Indian Penal code, does not make any difference between the two conditions mentioned in section 5 and the one which is required to be satisfied before the order of conviction can be made. The question whether sanction given under section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a valid one or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The object of the sanction is to secure the ends of justice, and if it is found that there was no evidence to show that the accused had been guilty of any offence punishable with imprisonment for life, it would be open to the Court to examine whether the sanction granted by the Director General of police was a valid or not. The test which the High Court has to determine is whether the prosecution has proved its case beyond all reasonable doubt and if so, whether the accused has been guilty or not, whether he has been falsely involved in any other offence.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had been convicted by a court of competent jurisdiction in respect of an offence committed by him while acting as a public servant, and that the sanction granted by the Government of India under section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act was not valid. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the prosecution had failed to establish that the appellant had been guilty of any offence punishable with imprisonment for more than three years and that he was not entitled to be prosecuted under section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, because, in the absence of a sanction granted under section 6(1), the sanction given by the government of India was not invalid. HELD: (i) The sanction granted to the appellant under section 4(1)(a) of Prevention of Anti Corruption Act is valid and must be set aside on the grounds that it was not necessary for the prosecution to establish a case against him. [707 D] (ii) The High court had rightly held that the sanctioning authority had acted in accordance with the provisions of section 5 of the Act, and the sanction accorded by the Central Government under section 3(1). [708 G H] (iii) The appellant was not guilty of an alleged offence. He was therefore entitled to the benefit of section 165. [774 D E] (iv) The prosecution had not established that the Government had acted mala fide or that it had acted with reasonable diligence in acting as required by section 5 (1). The sanction given under section 7(1 ) is valid.

The respondents were the tenants of a building in which they were the owners. The appellant landlord filed an eviction petition against the respondents on the ground that the respondents had not been evicted from the premises and that the appellant was not entitled to any protection under section 14(1)(e) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. The appellate authority dismissed the appeal holding that the landlord was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(h) of that Act. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that section 14 of the Act is applicable only where the landlord has been evicted by the landlord and the tenant has been dispossessed by the tenant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding against the appellant. [730C] In the instant case, the respondents were not entitled for protection under the Act. They are not entitled either to any relief or reliefs. [771D] The High Courts have rightly held that the premises in question were not a building within the definition of 'tenant ' and therefore they cannot be evicted from it. [764C D] In view of the fact that the landlords had been dispossessed, the landlord is entitled to protection under sections 14(l)(e). [774F G] The respondents are not tenants within the scope of section 14. They have been dispossessed in accordance with the provisions of the Rent Act.

The respondent was a mortgagee of land in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of possession of the land on the ground that he had no right to hold the land as a tenant under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The decree holder contended that the respondent was not entitled to hold land as defined in section 2(e) of the U .P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the land was not a 'estate ' within the meaning of section 2 (e) and therefore the respondent could not be held to be a ' jagir ' within section 2. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the definition of 'estate" in section 3(e)(i) of U. P. Consolidation Act, 1952 is wide enough to include land which is not a "estate ' and therefore, the respondent cannot be held liable to pay compensation under section 2 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The definition of "estate" is wide in its amplitude and it is not possible to hold that the word 'estate is wide. [630 B] (2) In view of the definition given in section 4(e), the respondent must be held entitled to compensation under the Act as he was a ' inam ' within meaning of the expression "estate". The definition does not include land as understood in the definition. It is only when the word is used, that is, the sense in which it occurs. [730 B C] (3) In the instant case, the definition is wide and it cannot be said that the term 'estate was not defined in the Act or in any other law for the time being in force. The definition is clear enough to cover land as used in section 5(e).

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 302 and 201 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the date of occurrence, the deceased had gone to his shop in a jeep and he was seen by him at about 10.30 p.m. when he was returning home, he saw the appellants coming out of the house of one K.M. Thomas, who was standing near the shop of the deceased. The deceased was taken to the hospital where he was declared dead. He was examined under Section 313 Cr. P.C. and was put up for trial. The Trial Court convicted the appellants under Sections 304 Part I and 201 IPC and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction of the appellants and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellants were guilty of the offence under Section 302 read with section 34 IPC. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction of all the accused under Sections 201 and 201 is set aside. [701D] 2. The appellants are convicted under Section 304 Part II IPC and they are sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for two years. They are sentenced under Section 201 readwith Section 34 IPC to undergo R.I. for one month. [771G H; 772A B] 3. The offence under Sections 307 and 201 of the I.P.C., is not proved beyond reasonable doubts, but it is only when the accused has been convicted under section 201 read alongwith Section 34, IPC that he had committed the offence of murder. [763F G] 4. In the instant case, the prosecution has failed to establish the charge against the appellants beyond reasonable reasonable doubt. The evidence of PW 1, who is an eye witness to the occurrence, clearly shows that he was a member of the unlawful assembly and he had seen the accused at about 11.30 P.M., when he reached the shop in question. He had also seen the appellants at about 12.30 a.m., when the deceased was returning from his shop, he noticed the appellants going to his house and saw them coming out. The other accused were also present there. They were also seen by PW 1 at about 6.00 p.M.; PW 2, who had seen him at the time of occurrence. He has stated that he saw them near the place of occurrence and saw the appellant coming out from the shop. He did not know the appellants when the incident took place. The fact that PW 1 was present at the scene of occurrence is also not established by the evidence of PWs 2, 3 and 4. [753G H] 5. In view of the above, the conviction under Section201 read with Sections 201 IPC is set set aside and the sentence of imprisonment for three years is maintained. [781F G; 771A B C] 6. The appeal is allowed.

The assessee company was carrying on business in India. The assessee company had entered into a contract with the foreign company for the supply of certain documents and payments made to it by the foreign Company. The foreign company paid royalty at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per annum from the foreign companies. The Indian Companies Act, 1913, was enacted to provide for the payment of royalty in respect of certain amounts received by the assessee from foreign companies and to make payments to foreign companies within a period of six months from the date of receipt of the notice. Section 5(2) of the Income Tax Act provides that where any income is received by an assessee under a contract, the amount shall be deemed to have been received in India for the purpose of computing the taxable income. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the foreign exchange was not a receipt within the meaning of section 5(3) and therefore the Indian Companies (Amendment) Act, 1969 did not apply to the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the Indian companies were not entitled to the deduction under Section 10(2). On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that since the foreign currency was received in British India, it could not be said that the income was received by a foreign company and therefore it was not taxable. In the appeals before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the amount received by it from foreign company was not liable to be included in the taxable turnover under Section 5 (2) because the foreign receipt was received outside India for purposes of computing its taxable income under Section 4(3). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "income" in section 2(a) of that Act means income received by any person from a foreign Company and not from a person who is resident in India or outside India. It includes income received from a company which is resident outside India and not outside India but from a non resident in British Indian. [630E] 1.1 The expression 'income" has been used in the context of the word "income". In the context, it is clear that the expression "Income" means income derived by an individual or other person from any source which is directly or indirectly received by him from a source which has been received by his own source and not by way of income. [730E F] 1:2 The word "profits" in Section 2(b) of this Act includes income derived from any sources which is wholly or indirectly made out of the income of an individual, whether resident or outside Indian. In other words, it has been defined in the Act to mean income received or received by way Of income. It means income accruing from a sources which are directly or substantially in the nature of income and not in British British India. [779E F; 830A] 1 :3 The expression used in section 5 (1) is wide enough to include income derived therefrom for purposes other than those mentioned in section 4(2), but it does not mean income from a business which is carried on by the company or outside of India. In this context, the word 'income ' has been given a wider meaning and it cannot be said to have any application to the case of the appellant that the receipt was not received in Indian. The word 'profits" used in Section 5 of the Act means profits derived from business which are carried on in British Pakistan or outside British India and includes income from such business. [783E F, 830B] 1.(a) In the instant case, the foreign bank had received royalty at a rate of RS. 1.5 per annum and it was only when the foreign foreign company had received the amount from foreign Company that it was received as a source.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction but acquitted him on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in the murder of one of the accused. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The evidence of a witness is not corroborated by any other evidence. It is only when it is corroborated by some other evidence that the witness has been falsely implicate in the crime. [657 H] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the evidence of an accomplice is not admissible under section 114 of the Evidence Act. [757 B] (iii) The conviction of a person who is charged with murder is not based on any rule or practice which requires that corroboration should be given to the testimony of a accomplice unless it is shown that he has been wrongly convicted by the trial court. [783 C D] (iv) In the present case, the evidence was corroborated by other evidence and the High Court had rightly held that the appellant had been guilty of murder. [784 G H] The evidence in this case was not corroborated with any other material except the statement of a approver. [781 B] The conviction under section 34 is based on some other material. It cannot be said that the testimony given by the approver was not admissible in evidence unless it was corroborated in material particulars. [777 D] In the instant case, there was no evidence to show that the approver had been wrongly acquitted by the High court. The appellant was therefore guilty of the murder. The conviction was based on a solitary statement which was corroborated with some other circumstances.

The appellant was a public servant. He was charged with offences under sections 161, 165 and 165 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court convicted him on the ground that he had been in charge of a public office and that he was not liable to be prosecuted for an offence under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The appellant was not a public officer within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. He could not be convicted on the basis of his conviction under section 5. [657 H] (ii) The word "public servant" in section 5 means a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the State or of any other State, and includes a public servants. It is well settled that a public authority must be deemed to have been in existence when it is established that he is employed by the Government or of a local authority. The word 'public servant ' has not been defined in the Act but it is used in the definition of "public servants" in the Indian Code. [757 H; 758 A] (iii) The expression "public office" in sub section (1) of section 2 means a public place and includes any office or office which is held by the State Government or local authority, and does not include a public service. [779 B C] (iv) The definition of 'public servants ' in section 2(a) of that Act is wide enough to cover all public servants employed in the State. It means a post held by an officer who is appointed by the Central Government or the local authority under the Act, and it includes any other office which has been held by him for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the said Act. [777 C D] (v) The words "public place" in clause (b) of sub section 2 are wide enough and include a post in connection therewith or incidental to the affairs thereof. It does not mean any office which can be held by a public body.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the Bombay Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1958. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment for six months. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case because the provisions in the Act did not apply to a case where the provisions were not complied with, and that the procedure prescribed by the Rules was not followed. HELD: The High court was right in holding that the rules were not mandatory and that they contravened article 14 of the Constitution. [657 F] In the present case the appellant had been convicted under sections 5(2) and 5(3) of Act. The provisions of section 5 (1) are not applicable because the procedure laid down by the rules was not complied in as much as the procedure for the trial of an offence is followed. [757 F G] In view of the fact that the appellant was found guilty under section 3(2), the High Court was right to enhance the sentence and reduce the sentence. [781 A B] The provisions in section 5 are not mandatory, because they are not complied by the procedure provided in the Rules. [783 C D] The procedure prescribed for trial of a offence is not followed because the rules are not directory. [784 E F] The appellant was therefore entitled to be convicted under the Act. [777 A B].

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death for life. The High Court acquitted the accused of all the charges. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not corroborated by the medical evidence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) The evidence of eye witnesses is not consistent with the innocence of the accused and the High Court had rightly convicted them under section 201 read with s.34 I. P.C. [601 D] (2) The High court was right in holding that the prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [702 G H] (3) The conviction of the appellants under section 304 Part 1, I.A., is not sustainable because the evidence given by the eye witness is consistent with his innocence and it is not necessary for the High court to examine the witnesses in order to find out whether they were interested in the prosecution case or not. [781 D] In the instant case, the evidence was corroborated by some independent evidence of a doctor who had examined the deceased. The medical evidence did not show that the deceased was injured in the occurrence and he was taken to hospital for treatment. The doctor who conducted the postmortem examination stated that the injuries were caused by a sharp edged weapon. The prosecution has not proved its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubts. [783 D] The High Courts have rightly convicted the appellants of all charges under section 34, I .P. C., and the conviction of them under s 201 readwith s. 34 I P. C.

The appellant was tried for the murder of one of the accused and convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that they were members of a unlawful assembly, and that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the conviction of the appellant under section 307 read with s 34 I P.C. was not sustainable in law because it was not proved that he was members of an unlawful assembly. The charge against him was not established beyond reasonable doubts and therefore the conviction could not be sustained. The offence of murder is one of murder, and the accused must have been acquitted on the basis of the evidence adduced by the prosecution. The conviction of a person under section 34 is based on circumstantial evidence. It is well settled that in an appeal against acquittal, the High Court should not interfere with the order of acquittal unless it is shown that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused was members or that he had been guilty of the offence. In the present case, the evidence of the prosecution witnesses showed that the appellant was members and that he knew the accused as a result of which he was attacked by the deceased. The evidence of P.Ws. 2 and 3 clearly established that they knew the persons who were members or the members of the unlawful assembly at the time when the incident took place, and therefore, the conviction under section 326 read with sections 34 I I. P. C., is not sustainable.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of goods, was assessed to customs duty under the Customs Act, 1962 on the basis of the invoice value of the goods. The petitioner filed an application before the Collector of Customs for revocation of the licence and for refund of the amount paid by him. The Collector rejected the claim holding that the petitioner had not been able to prove that the goods were imported in India and that the assessment was illegal. The revision petition filed by the petitioner against the order of the Collector was dismissed by the Appellate Authority. In the writ petition, the petitioner contended that the order passed by the Collector under section 11(1) of the Act was without jurisdiction and as such the order was not liable to be set aside. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "imported goods" in section 11 (1) means goods which are imported into India or exported outside India. [703F] 2. The word "immediate goods" is used in the context of the words "immediately goods" and not in the sense that they are imported in the course of inter State trade or commerce. It is well settled that the expression "in respect of goods" means goods imported into a local area, but does not include goods which have been imported into another local area. [781G] 3. The words "in any other case", in section 12(1), are wide enough to cover all kinds of goods which were imported into the local area and not to be imported into or exported out of India. They are used in a local areas, but do not include articles which have already been imported by the importer. [783G] 4. The term "immovable goods" has been defined in section 2(g) of that Act as meaning goods which had already been cleared from the customs area and which were exported out thereof. It means goods brought into the customs areas or which are not imported into any local area or which have not been imported in a particular local area but which have actually been imported for the purpose of export. [784G] 5. The meaning of the word "exported goods", in the definition of "impecially goods" as given in section 3(1)(a) is to include goods brought within the customs limits or which were not imported in any local areas or where there has been no such entry in the customs records, but are imported for purposes other than those specified in section 13(2). [783A] 6. The definition of 'immovable property" in Section 2(h) is wide enough and it includes goods which may be imported from a local Area or which had not already been exported out. [777E F] 7. The scope of the expression `immediate ' means goods that are imported from any local Area, but not for purposes of export, and the words `immovable ' have to be construed in their popular sense. [779A B] 8. The use of the term "in relation to goods" would mean a mere change in the law or fact which may have been passed by an authority competent to do so. [773B C] 9. The object of the legislature is to provide for the levy and collection of customs duty on goods brought in the local areas and to provide that the levy shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by the rules made under this Act.

The respondent was the owner of a property in suit. The appellant sold the properties to the respondent on the ground that they were not entitled to any share in the property. The sale was confirmed by the Collector and the sale was set aside by the Revenue Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The sale of the properties was void as it was not a mortgage but a mortgage. It is not a sale within the meaning of section 2(1)(c) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. [408 D] (ii) The respondent had no right to claim any share or interest in the properties. He was entitled to claim the share or interests in the suit. But he could not claim any interest in that property. [509 G H] (iii) The appellant 's father was a minor and his father was not entitled under section 7(1) of Bombay Land revenue Code. The respondent was not liable to pay any debt due to him by virtue of the sale. He had no title to the properties on the date of the mortgage. [609 G] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that the sale of a share or a interest in it was void because the sale did not amount to a mortgage within the definition of 'family ' in section 2 (1)(d). The sale could be set aside on the grounds that the transaction was not one for the purpose of the Act.

The petitioners were convicted under section 161 read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The petitioners filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order of the High Court. The main contention raised by the petitioners was that the petitioners had not been given any opportunity to cross examine the witnesses examined by them. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the order passed by the Committee was without jurisdiction and that the Committee had no power to issue a notice to the petitioners for their examination in accordance with law. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The Committee has not given any reasons for its conclusion. The report of the Committee is not based on any material or evidence. [775B] 2. The order passed under section 5 (1) (d) is a non speaking order and it cannot be said that the report of a Committee is without jurisdiction. It is only when the Committee has given reasons for his conclusion, that the opinion of the committee is not in accordance therewith. [77C D] 3. The Court has to see whether there are sufficient grounds for proceeding against the petitioners or not. If the Committee finds that there are reasonable grounds for holding the inquiry, it would be open to the Committee to issue notice to all the witnesses who have been examined by the prosecution. [76G H; 77A B] 4. The power of the Court under section 6(1) is discretionary and has to be exercised judicially in accordance only with the provisions of the Act. [75F G] 5. In the instant case, the Committee did not give reasons for holding that there were sufficient grounds to hold the inquiry. It had given reasons in support of its conclusion that the witnesses were not available to meet the charges against them. The reasons given by the committee are not germane and relevant to the proceedings. [78F G; 77B] 6. In view of the fact that the Court has recorded reasons for the conclusion, it is not possible to hold that there was sufficient ground for holding a inquiry.

The petitioners were carrying on business in the State of Rajasthan. They were assessed to tax under the Rajasthan General Sales Tax Act, 1948. The petitioners challenged the validity of the levy and collection of tax on the ground that the tax was not a tax within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act. The High Court held that the levy was a tax in respect of goods which were used for carriage by road or rail. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The levy is a tax under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and not a fee within the competence of the State Legislature. [655 H] (ii) The Act does not provide for any tax on goods which are used for transport by road and rail. It is only when the tax is levied, that is, the tax payable under Entry 49 of List I would be a tax on passengers which are carried on in the course of inter State trade or commerce.
