[755 H; 758 A] (iii) The tax is a fee for the carriage of goods and not for the purpose of carrying on any other business. It does not include a tax which is levied by the State Government under Entry 52 of List III. [779 C D] (iv) The imposition of tax is one of the two items mentioned in section 2 of the Rajasthan Act, but it is only where the tax has been imposed and collected, that the amount of tax has to be paid by the owner or person who pays the tax under entry 54 of list II. [777 C D; 858 A B] (v) The State Government has no power to impose a tax for the purposes of carrying passengers in the goods. It cannot be said that the imposition is one which is imposed on the owner of the goods and, therefore, it is not a levy within the definition of section 3(g). [777 D F] (vi) The impugned Act does neither contravene article 14 nor article 19(1)(f) of Part III of the Constitution. It merely imposes a tax upon passengers which have been used for the transport by rail or rail and that it is a levy under Entry 51 of List 11.

The appellant company was a registered society. The appellant company, a registered firm, entered into an agreement with the appellant for the supply of raw materials to its employees and the workmen were required to pay the same within one month from the date of the award. The workmen filed an application before the Labour Court under Section 33C(2) of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for reinstatement on the ground that the workmen had not been given any opportunity of being heard in the matter and that the appellant company had failed to comply with the provisions of the Act. The Labour Court held that the termination of services was illegal and void as it was not a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the employer was entitled to reinstatement on ground of victimisation. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the order of the Labour court was bad in law because the workmen did not comply with any mandatory provisions of law and that they were not given an opportunity of hearing before terminating their services. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of termination is a punitive one and must be set aside on the grounds of victimisation and unfair labour practices. [782B] 2. The employer has to satisfy himself that the workman was guilty of victimisation, unfair labour or unfair trade practice. It is not necessary for the employer to satisfy itself that the discharge of the workman is due to victimisation or improper labour practice but it is only when the workman has been given an adequate opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken. [77C] 3. The Tribunal has to consider whether the termination was justified on the basis of victimisation in the light of the principles laid down by this Court in M/s. Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs Their Workmen, ; , referred to. In the instant case, the appellant Company had not complied with the requirements of law. [76C] 4. The award of the Industrial Tribunal is set aside and the matter remanded to the Labour Appellate Tribunal for fresh disposal on merits.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of the eye witnesses, who were not examined by the prosecution, was inadmissible in evidence as they had been cross examined by them before the court. HELD: (i) The evidence of a witness is admissible in evidence only when he is examined by him and his statement is recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [630 B] (ii) The High Courts should not have relied upon the evidence in support of the prosecution case, because it was not possible to accept the evidence on record as a whole. [730 C D] (iii) The conviction of the accused under section 201 read with s.34 of the Evidence Act is unsustainable. [771 B] In the instant case, the evidence given by the eye witness was inadmissible and the High Court had rightly held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [764 D] In view of the fact that the accused had been examined before the Court, it cannot be said that he had been falsely implicated in the crime. [751 C] (iv) The prosecution has not proved its case and the conviction of accused under s 201 readwith s. 34 of Evidence Act was unsustainable. The evidence given in support thereof is admissible only when the accused is examined before him.

The appellant, a mortgagee of the mortgaged property, was in possession of the properties. The mortgage deed provided that the mortgagor would pay to the mortgagee a sum equal to the amount due under the mortgage and the balance shall be paid by him to the mortgagor. The mortgagee filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the plaintiff was entitled to redeem the mortgage on payment of the entire amount due from him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The plaintiff was not entitled to any relief under section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act. [632 D] (ii) The suit was barred by limitation. The suit is therefore barred by time. [733 E F] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the suit was not barred by the limitation. [781 A B] (iv) The defendant 's case that the mortgage was a mortgage and was not a mortgage, was not correct. The plaintiff had no right to redeem it on payment thereof. [783 D F] In the present case, the mortgage deed was executed in favour of the plaintiff and the mortgagee was entitled only to redeem. [784 G] (v) The mortgage was not one for the purpose of the suit. It was a loan advanced by the mortgagor to the defendant. The mortgagor had no interest in the mortgaged properties. Therefore, the suit is barred by section 53. [833 E H] (vi) The question whether the plaintiff could claim any relief on the ground that he was entitled under section 54 of the Act. The High Courts were right in not holding that it was a debt advanced by him and that the defendant had no locus standi to sue for redemption. [777 D F].

The appellants were appointed as Executive Engineers in the State of Karnataka. The State Government issued a notification dated 30th April, 1985 inviting applications for appointment to the post of Executive Engineer (Civil) and the appellants were selected by the Public Service Commission. The appellants challenged the said selection on the ground that the selection was vitiated because of the absence of any material before it. The Tribunal dismissed the application holding that the appellants had failed to prove that they had failed in the written test for the post. Aggrieved, the appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by the High court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants were not entitled to any relief as claimed by them. They had failed before the Tribunal to prove their case. [775F] 2.2 In the instant case, the selection of the appellants was vitiated on account of non compliance with the mandatory provisions of the Rules and the rules. The High Court has rightly held that the State Government had acted in violation of the mandatory provision of the rules and the Rules. [77G H; 77A B] 3.1 In the absence thereof, the State Govern ment had acted arbitrarily and without any material on record. [76B C] 2:2 The appellants have failed to establish their case before the High Courts. They have not been able to prove the case of the appel lants. [75G H] 2 :3 The State Governme nment has acted in breach of the statutory rules and there is no violation of any statutory rule or any statutory provision. [ 771A B, D] 3:4 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it cannot be said that the High candi was not justified in quashing the selection made by the State.

The appellants were tried for offences under sections 302, 201 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted them under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The High Court acquitted all the accused persons on the ground that they had committed murder of one of the co accused persons. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the evidence of the eye witnesses is not reliable and the evidence has been corroborated in material particulars. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution case is that the deceased had gone to the house of the appel lants and had gone there with the coaccused persons. He was a member of the family of the deceased and he had no motive for the murder of the two co accused. It is not possible to accept the evidence as reliable. [782C] 2. The evidence of eye witnesses cannot be accepted as reliable unless it is corroborated in any material particulars or by other evidence. The fact that they were seen at the time of occurrence, does not make the statement admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act. [771G H; 782A B] 3. The conviction and sentence of the appellants are set aside. They shall be released forthwith if they are not required in any other case. [764C D] 4. The appeal is allowed. The appellants are acquitted of all the charges. They are on bail. Their bail bonds stand discharged.

The appellants, who were workmen of the respondent company, challenged the award on the ground that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to fix the wage structure in respect of the appellants. The Tribunal held that the appellants were not entitled to any dearness allowance as it was a matter of discretion and that the dearness allowance should be fixed at the rate of Rs. 250 per month. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal had erred in fixing the wage scales in respect Of the appellants and the dearness allowances should be given to the workmen of their own choice and not on the basis of the formula laid down by the Tribunal. (ii) The appellants were entitled to the dearness Allowance as it existed before the Tribunal, and they were entitled only to the same scale as it stood before the amendment of the award. (iii) The dearness allowance was a fixed wage structure which had been fixed at Rs. 150 per month and not at the rates fixed by the tribunal. (iv) The basic principle of fixing the wages in respectof the appellants was that the workmen should be paid dearness allowance at the same rate as it prevailing before the date of the reference, and that this principle was applicable only to those employees who were employed on a particular day. (v) The fact that the wage scale fixed by tribunal was not fixed at any time during the relevant period would not make the difference between the wages payable to the appellants in respect thereof. (vi) The workmen of an industrial concern should be entitled to dearness allowance for the period they had been employed on the same day and not with reference to the date when the Tribunal took into account the fact that it was fixed at a higher rate than what was fixed by it. (vii) The wage structure fixed by Tribunal in respect whereof the appellants had been working on a different day would be a fixed minimum of Rs 250 per year. (viii) The wages payable for the appellants should be taken into account while fixing the dearness and not the rates which were fixed at different rates. (ix) The award of the Tribunal was based on the assumption that the appellant was entitled to a higher wage than what they had actually worked on a similar day. The workmen in respect to whom the appellants claimed that the wages should be calculated at the lower rate. (x) The tribunal had erred by fixing the basic wage structure as it prevalent before the reference and that there was no justification for fixing the minimum of the dearness. (xi) The Industrial Tribunal had not properly considered the question whether the workmen were entitled in respect only to their wages. (xii) The High Court was right in holding that the tribunal had wrongly fixed the basic wages at the higher rate as the appellants did not have any case for fixing a basic wage.

The appellants, who were the mortgagees of agricultural lands in suit, filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the mortgagee had no right to redeem the mortgage; (ii) the mortgagor had no title to the property; (iii) the mortgagees were not entitled to redeem them, and (iv) the mortgagors were not liable to be ejected under section 14(1)(c) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. HELD : The High Court was in error in holding that the mortgagee was entitled to a decree for redemption. [619 F G] In the present case the mortgagees had no interest in the property and they were entitled to the benefit of section 14 (1)(d). The appellants were not therefore entitled to any relief under section 15(1) (c) because they were not parties to the suit. They were not impleaded as parties to a suit. [719 F] In view of the fact that the mortgagees did not have any interest in their property, it was not necessary for them to implead the appellants as parties. The High court had rightly held that the mortgagors had no locus standi to file the suit because they had no rights to redeem it. [779 G H] The High Courts were right in holding on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties that the mortgages were not a mortgage and that the appellants were entitled only to the relief under the Act.

The respondent company was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton fabrics. The respondent company had its factory at Kanpur and its factory was situated at Kanpur. The Sales Tax Officer, Kanpur issued notices to the respondent under section 11(1) of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 for the period from 1st April, 1966 to 31st March, 1966. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notices on the ground that the sales tax authorities had wrongly assessed the turnover of the respondent company under section 4(1)(a) of U. P. Sales tax Act, 1947 and that the turnover was liable to be taxed under the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Sales Tax Authorities had wrongly applied the principle laid down by this Court in M/s. Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs State of Orissa, ; , followed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show that the respondent had not been assessed under section 3(1). Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (i) The High Courts have wrongly applied its principle in M. Hindustan Iron and Steel Ltd., vs State, ; and that it is well settled that the word 'manufacture ' has a wide connotation and includes any process of manufacture or sale. [601B C] (ii) In the instant case, the respondent was assessed under the Sales tax law for the year 1966 67. The sales tax Authorities had rightly applied its mind to the question whether the goods were liable to tax under the provisions of the Act or not. [702C D] (iii) The word 'process ' is defined in section 2(1), which includes a process of manufacturing, processing and processing. It means any process incidental or ancillary to the carrying on of the business of the assessee. The word "manufacture" has been used in the Act as meaning "any process incidental to the carried on by the assessee". [703D E] (iv) In view of the fact that the goods are not liable to sales tax under section 2 (1)(b), it is clear that the expression 'processing ' means any processes incidental or consequential to the carry on of a business. [781E F] (v) The definition of "manufacture ' in section 3 (1) (a) has been given wide meaning and it includes all process incidental thereto. It is not possible to accept the contention that the words used are merely descriptive of the nature of the activity which is carried on.

The appellant, a sugar factory, was employed in the respondent Mills. The respondents were dismissed from service by an order dated December 31, 1950. The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for damages and damages on the ground that they had been dismissed from services under the U.P. Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1952. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under the Act. The High Court in appeal reversed the order of dismissal and directed the appellant to pay a sum of Rs. 1,000/ as compensation for the loss caused to the respondents. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the Labour Appellate Tribu nal was not an order of discharge simpliciter but an order made under section 33(2) of the Act and therefore the order could not be sustained. HELD: (i) The order of the Labour Tribunal is a final order of transfer and not a mere order of termination simpliciter. It must be held to have been made by the employer in exercise of his statutory powers under the statute. [408 C] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the impugned order was an order which could be set aside on the grounds that it had been made without jurisdiction and that the transfer was not a discharge simpliciter. The fact that the employer had no power to dismiss the employee does not make any difference between the two conditions of service and the one which is applicable to him. [416 D] (iii) The appellant was dismissed from the service under the order dated January 31, 1951. The order passed on December 31. 1950 was an administrative order and it could not have been said that the respondents were not entitled for any relief.

The appellant, a private limited company, was incorporated under the provisions of the , and the Employees ' Provident Funds Act, 1952. The appellant was a public limited company carrying on business in the manufacture of tea products. The Employees ' State Insurance Corporation issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Act to the effect that the contribution payable by the employees to the Fund shall be paid to the employees within three months from the date of the notification. The respondent, who was a private company, challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was not a 'public limited company ' within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of that Act and that the provisions contained in the Act were ultra vires the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under article 226 of the Constitution, and that it could not be said that the Act was a 'private company ' as defined in section 2 (1) (d). Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is a self contained code and does not contain any provision for the levy of contribution on the employees of the Corporation. It is a well settled principle of interpretation that the legislature has to take into consideration the provisions in the statute and the scheme framed thereunder. [703 B] 2. The object of the legislation is to provide for the payment of contribution by the employers to the fund. The purpose of the enactment is to ensure that the employees are not paid any contribution or contribution to the Provident Fund. It has been enacted with a view to ensuring that the contributions are made in accordance with the provisions and regulations made thereunder. The scheme is intended to provide the payment for the benefit of the employees who have been employed by the employer. [774 C D] 3. The State Government has not given any reasons for its decision. It was not open to the legislature to say that the scheme is a 'Public limited company" within the definition of section 1(1). [704 B] 4. The provisions contained therein are ultra vires and void. [764 C E] 5. The objects of the statute are to provide a fund for the establishment of an industrial undertaking. It does not provide for any other purpose. The legislature has also given reasons for the decision. [754 D F] 6. The Legislature has not made any provision in the scheme which is ultra vires or void. The power conferred on it by section 3 (1)(c) is a statutory power and it cannot be said to be an executive power. It can only provide for a fund which is not a "public limited Company" within its ambit. [ 774 D] 7. The expression 'Public company ' in the definition has been used in the context of the scheme. The word 'public company ' means any person who is employed by or under the Central Government or State Government or a local authority. It cannot be held that the expression 'public purpose ' in section 3 of the is not intended to include a fund. [784 C] 8. The definition of 'Public purpose ' has been given wide and comprehensive meaning and it does not mean any other object which may be achieved by the Act. [794 D E] 9. The question whether the appellant is entitled to the benefit under the Act is one of fact and law.

The petitioners are workmen of the respondent State. Their services were terminated by the Labour Court on the ground that they have been retrenched in accordance with the provisions of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1985. The petitioners challenged the validity of the termination order before the High Court which dismissed their writ petition. In this appeal it was contended for the appellants that the termination of their services is illegal and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence on record and has rightly held that the petitioners are entitled to be reinstated in service. [775G] 2.2 In view of the fact that the workmen have been paid their wages for the period from 1st April, 1988 to 31st March, 1988, they cannot claim any benefit of the said Scheme. The High Courts have not properly considered the evidence and has wrongly held that there is no material on record to show that the workers are retrenched in pursuance of the order of the High court. [771C] 2:3 In view thereof, the High Courts should have taken into consideration the fact of the case and come to a conclusion that the work of the petitioners was not satisfactory. The Labour Court has rightly found that the respondents were not entitled to any benefit under the Scheme. [762F G] 3.1 In view, the order passed by the High courts is set aside and the writ petition is allowed.

The plaintiffs were the owners of a tea estate in which they had been granted a lease of certain properties. The defendants claimed that they were entitled to the benefit of section 7(1) (a) of the Bengal Land Revenue Act, 1901, and that they could not claim any right or title on the basis of the sale deed dated March 31, 1937, and as such they were not entitled to any relief under section 7. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had no right or interest in the property. On appeal by the defendants, the High Court held that the sale was void because it was a mortgage of certain immovable properties and that the defendants were entitled only to the benefits of section 8(1)(a) (i). In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence on record to show that the defendant had any right to the property in question. The sale deed did not mention the names of the plaintiffs and the defendants as their legal representatives. It was only after the death of the defendant that the suit properties were sold by the plaintiffs to the plaintiffs, that they had no interest in it. [408 D] In the present case, the plaintiffs were entitled under section 8 (1) of Act, to the extent of the right or ownership of the property and not as a mortgage. The High court was wrong on the ground that the plaintiff had no title to the properties.

The appellant was tried for the murder of one P.W. 1, a village worker in the State of Andhra Pradesh and convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that the evidence of P.Ws. 2 and 3 had not been properly recorded by the Magistrate. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The provisions of sections 5(1)(a), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not applicable to cases where there is a conflict between the provisions of section 145 Cr. P.C. and the provisions in Chapter XVIII of the code of Criminal procedure, 1898, as they apply to cases which have been tried by the Sessions Court under sections 147, 148, 149, 302 read together with section 149, I. P., and section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, are not attracted to cases covered by the provisions Of section 145(1) of that Code. (ii) The High Courts in the present case had no jurisdiction to try the accused for the offence under sections 148, 147, 149 and 302 readwith section 34, I P., as they were not tried by a Magistrate under section 145 (1) (a), Cr. The provisions Of sections 5 and 6 of the Act are not intended to be used in the interests of justice and it is only when the trial court has recorded its reasons for doing so that the accused may have been prejudiced, the High Court was right in holding that the provisions contained in section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code were not applicable. (iii) The procedure prescribed by sections 5, 6 and 7 of the Evidence Act, 1872, as it stood before the amendment of the Constitution, is not a mandatory provision for the trial of an accused person. (iv) The power to try an accused under section 147, I .P., is not intended in the interest of justice, but only when there are two distinct and separate trials, one by the same Magistrate or the other by the different Magistrates. (v) In the present cases, the trial Court had recorded its findings on the basis of which the High Courts had recorded their reasons for holding that there was a conflict of opinion between the two courts in respect of the accused persons. The trial court had not recorded any reasons for coming to the conclusion that the prosecution had failed to establish that the witnesses were interested in the case and that the statements made by the witnesses before the Magistrate were inadmissible in evidence. (vi) In view of the provisions relating to the procedure prescribed under section 162(1), Cr., the High court was right, in holding, that the trial had not taken into consideration the statements recorded by them before the police.

The appellant was a public limited company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling tea. The respondent, who was a factory owner in Bombay, applied to the State Government for permission under section 5A of the , to establish a factory for the purpose of running its factory. The State Government refused to grant permission under s.5A of that Act. The appellant filed an application before the District Magistrate under section 6A of . The District Magistrate rejected the application and directed the State to issue notice to the respondent. The High Court held that the appellant was not a public company within the meaning of article 12 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the District Judge is set aside and the appellant is directed to submit a report in respect of the proposed action taken by it under section 7A of , and the State shall take steps for the removal of the nuisance caused by the respondent 's factory. [733 D] (ii) The District Judge was not justified in issuing notice to respondent. [771 C] (iii) The appellant had no locus standi to file a petition under article 32 of the constitution. The District Court was therefore right in holding that the State had no jurisdiction to issue a notice to him. [761 D] In the present case, the District Court had not given any reasons for issuing the notice to it and the High Court was wrong in holding so. [781 C E] (iv) The State had not taken steps to remove the nuisance from the factory. It is only after the report of the State was submitted that the District judge had no power to issue the notice under section 4A of Act.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 135 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890. The trial court convicted him under section 5(1) (a) read with section 5 (2) (b) of the Act and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The appellant was not a railway servant within the meaning of section 2(g) of that Act. He had no right to use any goods in his possession. The fact that he had purchased the goods did not make the entry in the register of documents showing that the goods were used for the purpose of carrying out the business of the railway. [601 H] (ii) The High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was a railway employee within the definition of section 3(g). [602 A B] (iii)The fact that the railway had purchased goods from the railway did not amount to an entry in register of goods. The railway authorities were right in holding the railway property as a railway. The High court was wrong, in holding so. [701 C D] (iv)The appellant could not be said to have used any goods for carrying out any business of railway. He was therefore entitled to the benefit of section 5 of the . [603 B] In the present case the railway authorities had taken a view that the Railway was not liable to pay the penalty under section 4(1)(a) of Act. The appellant could have used the goods for the purposes of carrying on any business. He could not therefore be said in possession of the goods.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellants tenant on the ground that he was in possession of the premises and that the appellants were not entitled to any protection under section 14(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tenancy was not terminated by the respondent landlord and that since the tenancy had been terminated by a notice under section 13(2) of Act, the appellants could not be evicted on the grounds mentioned in section 14 of the Act. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to protection under Section 14(3)(e). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of the Rent and Eviction Act were applicable only to a case where the tenancy has been terminated, and that even if the tenancy is terminated by notice under Section 13(1) of that Act, it would be open to the landlord to evict the tenant from the premises. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The definition of 'tenant ' in section 2(e) is wide enough to include a person who has been let out for residential or non residential purposes and not for personal use. [703B] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent had been in occupation of the suit premises as a tenant under the provisions contained in Section 14 of Act. He was in occupation since 1964. The appellants were in occupation till 1964. They were in possession since 1964 when he was inducted into the premises by the appellants. The tenancy having been terminated on the basis of the notice under the Act, they could not claim protection under the Rent & Control Act. [771C] 2:2. The respondent landlord had no right to evict her tenant from any premises. The appellant 's father was in exclusive possession of a shop and he was entitled only to the benefit of the provisions as contained in section 13 (1) (e). The appellants are not entitled for protection under Article 14(l)(e), because she was in continuous occupation till 1965 when he became a tenant. [764C] 3:2 A landlord who is in possession after 1964 cannot claim protection against eviction on the strength of the tenancy. The right to recover possession is a statutory right and it is not open to him to invoke Article 14 of that Article. [754F G] 4:3. Section 13 (2) (f) of Rajasthan Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 provides for termination of tenancy by notice in writing of his intention to terminate the tenancy if he has been in continuous possession till 1965 and the tenant is not entitled under any other law. The expression 'tenant" in section 3(1), therefore, cannot be construed as a statutory tenant. It is well settled that a person can be evicted only on the death of the landlord or his heirs. [744C D] 4.3 In the present case, there was no dispute about the tenancy between the appellants and the respondent. The relationship between the parties was not disputed by the appellant. The question whether the tenancy in question was terminated by giving notice under sub section (1), is a matter of right. It cannot be said that the tenant had been inducted into possession after 1965 when the tenancy took place. [734F] 4(a) In the absence of any statutory provision, the relationship between landlord and tenant can not be said to have been terminated in view of the definition contained in sub section 2 (e), as it stood at the relevant time, is a question of fact. The tenant has no right or title to the premises after 1965.

The appellant, a private limited company, was incorporated in the State of Bihar. The Board of Directors of the appellant company had been established under the Bihar Electricity Supply Act, 1948 and the Board of Trustees had been constituted under the Act. The appellant contended that the Board had no power to frame any scheme for the purpose of the Act and that the scheme was not a 'scheme ' within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1964. The Tribunal rejected the contention on the ground that the State Government had no authority to frame the scheme. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to frame a scheme for its employees and that it was not open to the Board to frame an industrial dispute which could be raised before the Industrial Tribunal under section 10 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The scheme is a 'Scheme '. It is a scheme which has been framed by the State Legislature. The scheme does not provide for any machinery or plant for the management of the undertaking. [795 D] (2) The Board had power to make regulations in respect of the employees of the company and it was open to it to frame rules for the regulation of the business of the industrial undertakings. It has been established that the employees were not entitled to any gratuity or bonus under section 2 (g) (i). [796 G] (3) The State Government has power to fix the rates of wages and other conditions of service of employees in respect thereof. The State Board had also power to impose such conditions as it thought fit. It was open for the Board not to frame regulations for its own employees. [77 E F] (4) The Tribunal has no jurisdiction under section 11 of the , to frame schemes for the establishment of a new industrial undertaking. The Industrial Tribunal has not given any reasons for its conclusion.

The respondent wife filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for maintenance against her husband, alleging that she was not willing to live with him and that she had been living separately. The Magistrate passed an order directing the appellant to pay maintenance at the rate of Rs. 500 per month. The appellant filed an application before the Magistrate under section 488 of the Cr. P.C. for restitution of conjugal rights. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the respondent was not a 'wife ' within the meaning of Section 125 of Cr.P.C., and that the order passed by the Magistrate was not justified. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in interfering with the order of the Magistrate. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of maintenance is a nullity and the order made by the High court is liable to be set aside. [702B] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent had not been living together for more than three years. She was not in a position to live separately for more or three years and that there was no reason why she should not be treated as 'wife" within the definition of Section 3(2) of the Act. [774C] 2:1 The order passed under section 494 of the Criminal Procedure Code is set aside and the Magistrate is directed to proceed with the application for restitution. [764E F] 2 :2. In the facts and circumstances of the case, it cannot be said that the appellant was not living separately for a long period. It is well settled that the husband has been living in a different manner for more and less than three decades. The husband has to live together for a period of two years. [754F] 2(a) In the present case, there was nothing on record to show that the wife had been residing separately for several months. The respondent had also not been able to live in the same house for more so long. The wife has also not shown any reason why he should not live with her husband for more. [754E F; 759A] (b) In view of the fact that the parties have not been residing together for several years, it is not possible to hold that the marriage was not valid. [758B C] 2.(a) The order under section maintenance is set at naught and the appellant is directed not to live again for more more than two decades. [759F] (c) In case of any dispute between the parties regarding the maintenance, it will be open to the Magistrate to proceed further with the matter in accordance with law. [761E F]. (d) The respondent has not been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order under Section 488 of Cr., P. C. and the High Courts have committed an error in interfering in the order. [763A] 2 (a) It is open to a Magistrate to take into consideration the evidence adduced by the parties before it, if he finds that there has been any such cruelty or harassment as may be prescribed by law. The question whether the respondent has been residing with him for more, than three months does not arise. [762E F: 759A B] (e) In a case where the husband is living separately, the Magistrate has to take note of the circumstances in which he is living and if he found that there is no such cruelty, he may order the maintenance to be made at the same rate as the prevailing prevailing prevailing in the locality.

The appellant, a local authority, was the owner of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. The State Government granted permission to the respondent to construct buildings on the land in question. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the said lands and claimed that the said land was not a 'public purpose ' within the meaning of article 31A of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the land was a public purpose ' and that the respondent was entitled to possession of it under the provisions of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High Court held that the lands were not 'public purposes ' within article 31 A of the Constitu tion. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended: (1) that the suit was barred by limitation as the suit had been filed in the year 1948 and the suit having been filed beyond the period of limitation prescribed under section 3 of the Act, the suit could not be dismissed on the ground that the plaintiff was not entitled to any possession of these lands; (2) that there was no evidence to show that the Government of Gujarat had obtained permission from the State Government for constructing buildings on land in the city of Ahmedabad and that it was not necessary for the Government to establish that the defendant was a 'Public purpose '. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The suit was filed beyond time. [775F] 2. The plaintiff was entitled only to possession over the said property. The Government of Bombay had obtained sanction from the Government for construction of buildings on lands in question and not for constructing houses on land. The grant of permission by the State Govern ment was not in accordance with law. The sanction was not given by the Government. [771C] 3. The title to the suit property is a public interest and it cannot be said that the State was entitled under article 31 B of the Consti tution. [762F] 4. The question whether the plaintiff had obtained the permission from Government for erecting buildings on his land in dispute or not is a question of fact. The decision of the Government in this regard is final and binding on the parties. [751G H; 771A B] 5. The claim of the plaintiff that the defendants were entitled to the possession of certain properties was not barred by time. The defendants had not produced any evidence to prove that the property was a private property within the scope of article 32 of the constitution. [781F G] 6. The defendant was in possession of some lands in dispute and he was not liable to be evicted from the suit land. He was therefore entitled to recover possession of those properties from the plaintiff. [791G] 7. The plea that the title to these lands was a personal property within article 32 is not tenable because the Government had obtained consent from the Central Government for acquiring the said properties and the same was not taken into consideration by the Court.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 161 and 165 of the Indian Penal Code, for having committed an offence punishable under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The prosecution case was that on the date of the incident he had gone to the Railway Station at Jaipur in connection with a railway station at Jaipur and that he had been employed by him as a clerk in the Railway Department, and that on his return he was found guilty under section 161 read with sections 5(2) (d) and 5(3) of Prevention of Anti Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 165 read with s. 165 of Indian Penal code but acquitted him. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. Section 5(4) of that Act is a general provision and it does not apply to a public servants within the definition of "public servant" in section 2(d). The words "public servants" in s.5(1) (e) are wide enough to include public servants. The word "public" in the context of the expression "public". In the present case, the appellant had been appointed by the Railway Administration under the authority of the Chief Commissioner and was not an officer of the Government of India. He was therefore a public officer within the scope of section 6(1). The word 'public servant ' is wide enough in its ordinary sense to include servants who are employed by them as a clerks in the railway station. The expression "Public servant" has been used in the definition in section 5 and it is not necessary that the word "Public Servant" must be given a wider meaning.

The Respondent No. 1, a tenant of the land in dispute, purchased certain property from the Respondent No 2 and sold it to the Appellant. The Respondent No 1, who was the owner of the said property, filed a suit for recovery of possession of the same. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the sale deed dated March 31, 1977 was not valid and the sale was void as it was not executed by the Respondent Nos. 2 and 3. The Appellant preferred an appeal before the District Judge, Amritsar. The District Judge dismissed the appeal holding that since the sale in question was not registered under the Punjab Excise Act, 1914, the sale of the property could not be held to be valid. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the Appellant and set aside the decree passed by the Trial Court. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the Respondent that the said sale deed was not a registered sale within the meaning of section 2(e) of the Punjab Preemption Act, 1913, as amended in 1976 and that the Respondent had no right to recover possession of any property from him under the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of "sale" in section 2 (e) is wide enough to include a sale by a person who has been declared to be a purchaser for the purpose of recovery of money due from him and not as a purchaser. [615B C] 2. The expression "sale of property" in sub section (1) of section 3 of the East Punjab Preparations Act, 1934 is wide and it includes all sales by way of sale or purchase of any immovable property. It is well settled that the word "sale ' in sub clause (e), of section 4 of the General Clauses Act means a sale which is not registered as a sale within a meaning of the provisions contained in the Act and not a sale under the Act, but a sale effected by a purchaser on behalf or for the benefit of the person who is declared to have been a purchaser under the general law of the State. [715D] 3. In view of the language used in sub clauses (e)(i) and (f), of clause (g) of sub section 1 of section 6 of the Central Provinces and Berar Sales Tax Act, 1947, it is clear that the expression "any sale" in the said sub clause would include a transfer of property which is registered as an instrument of sale. [783B C; 784A] 4. The word "transfer" in clause (f) of subsection 1 of Section 3 of Act means an instrument which is intended to be registered as one of the modes mentioned therein and not an instrument for sale. It does not include a mortgage by way or sale. The words "any transfer of any movable property" are wide enough and it cannot be said that the words "other than a transfer" in Section 3(e)(ii) of Act are wide and they are intended to convey the intention of the legislature to give effect to the intention.

The appellant, a displaced person, was the owner of certain lands in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The respondent acquired the said lands for the purpose of acquiring the same under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Collector issued notice to the respondent under section 9(1) of the Land Acquisi tion Act, on the ground that he had no right to claim compensation under the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice and also for quashing the notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notice was not issued within the period prescribed by section 9 (1) and that the Collector had no jurisdiction to issue the notice on the basis of the evidence adduced before him, and that there was no valid reason for issuing the notice under section 8(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notice under Section 9(2) is not a mere formality but is a mere device to defeat the object of the Act which is to protect the interests of the displaced persons from the property and to prevent abuse of the process of Court. [630B] 2. The proceedings before the Collector are quasi judicial in character and it cannot be said that the proceedings before him were quasi judicial. It is not necessary for the Collector to issue a notice under the provisions of the . [631C D] 3. The mere fact that the respondent had no locus standi to file the return does not make any difference between the two proceedings, namely, the proceedings in which the proceedings were taken and the proceedings are quasi criminal. [732D E] 4. In the instant case, the Collector was not competent to issue notice under sections 9(3) and 9(4) of Act. He had no power to issue any notice under that section. The order of the Collector is therefore, set aside.

The appellant was elected as a member of the Maharashtra Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. on the ground that he had been disqualified for being chosen as a members of the society under section 7(1) (a) of the Act, and that he was not qualified to be chosen as an elected member. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the election of the appellant on the grounds that the appellant was disqualified under section 13(2)(b) of Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the disqualification under section 14(1)(a) was not one for being elected as member of a society under the Act and that the order of the State Government dated 30th April, 1987 passed by the State Govt. cancelling the election was illegal and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions in view of the provisions contained in section 13 (2)(a), (b) and (c) of Act, which were applicable to a society registered under the Maharashtra Co operative Societies Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not disqualified for having been chosen as member under section 3(3)(b). [775G] 2.2 In view of section 13 of the Bombay Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 1987, the appellant could not be said to have committed any breach of the conditions of his membership. [776A B] 3.1 Section 13(4)(a)(i) is applicable only where a member has been disqualified under sub section (2) or sub section(3). The appellant cannot be said that he has been duly elected as an election member under sub sections (1) and 13 of Act. [771B C] 3:2 In the instant case, the order passed by State Govt., cancelling the appellant 's election was not in accordance with law. The order of District Registrar dated 30.4.1987 is therefore illegal and invalid. [761C D] 4:3 The appellant could be said only as an authorised member under the provisions of sub section 1 (a). He had been duly disqualified for holding the post of a member under Section 13 (1)(b), (c). He was not entitled to be elected as such. [751G H; 771C] 4.2 The appellant has failed to prove that he is disqualified under the provision contained in sub section 2(a) or (3) of Section 13 of Maharashtra Coorg Societies Act and, therefore, he could not have been duly nominated as an agent of the Society. [781G] 5:4 In view thereof, the High Courts were right in holding that since the appellant had been elected as the member under clause (b), sub section 3 of the Cooperative Societies Rules, 1960 was applicable to the appellant.

The respondent was a Government servant. He was charged with having committed an offence under Rule 5 of the Maharashtra Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The respondent was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been compulsorily retired by the State Government. The State Government issued a show cause notice to the respondent for his compulsory retirement. The order of compulsory retirement was challenged before the High Court in writ petition. The High Court held that the respondent had committed an error in not awarding him compulsory retirement and directed the State government to pay him compulsory pension. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of compulsorily retiring the respondent from service was bad as it had been passed without giving any opportunity to the State to show cause against the proposed action. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned order of premature retirement is not in accordance with law and is liable to be quashed on the grounds that the State has no power to impose compulsory retirement on the respondent. [782B] 2. The Government servant who had been dismissed from the service by way of punishment cannot be said to have committed an act which is prejudicial to the interest of the public or any other person. The action taken against him was not in conformity with law. [771C D] 3. The disciplinary authority has power to pass compulsory retirement only on the basis of the report of the enquiry officer and not on the report submitted by the enquiry Officer. The power to retire a Government employee is not absolute or unfettered. It is only when it is found that the Government servant has been compulsorily compulsorily retired, the order passed by the Government is in accordance therewith. [761C] 4. The authority concerned must have given reasons for its conclusion and the disciplinary authority should have given an opportunity to showcause against the action proposed to be taken.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they had been in occupation of the premises under section 3(1) (a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1947, as amended by Act No. 1 of 1954. The appellants contended that the order passed by the District Magistrate was not a nullity because it was made without jurisdiction and that the District Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. The District Judge dismissed the suit holding that the appellants were in occupation since 1953 and that they were in possession of the shop under section 4(1)(a) (i) of Act No, 1 of 1955. On appeal by the respondents, the District Judge held that the appellant was not entitled to a decree for eviction on the grounds specified in section 3 (1) of . The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that section 3 of the Act was ultra vires and that it was not applicable to the case because the appellants had failed to establish that they have been in possession since 1953, and that as the respondents were in actual occupation of their premises under the provisions of the Rent Act, the order of the District judge was not valid. The appellant contended that section 4 (1)(b) of 'the Act was void as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the appellants did not establish that the respondents had been using the premises for a public purpose and that therefore the order was bad in law. Held, that the High court was right in holding that sections 3(2) (c) and 4 (3) of , were ultra vires the provisions Of section 3 and that section 5(1), as amended, did not apply to the facts of the case. The order passed under section 6(1 ) (a), was a nullity and therefore the appellants could not be evicted on the basis of the provisions contained in section 4 of the .

The appellant, a member of the Indian Administrative Service, was convicted by the Additional District and Sessions Judge for offences under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., read with Section 34 I .P. C. The High Court dismissed his petition on the ground that he had no jurisdiction to try the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of suspension passed by the Chief Justice of India, in exercise of powers conferred under Article 226 of the Constitution, is not a judicial one and is therefore illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of dismissal passed by him is not an administrative one and does not constitute a judicial function. It is only when it is shown that the Chief Minister or the Chief Secretary or the Governor of the State has acted in accordance with the rules of natural justice that he has no power to dismiss the case on the basis of the evidence adduced before him. [782C D] 2. The Chief Justice, in exercising his powers under Article 227 of the constitution, is entitled to act as a court of appeal and not as a Court of appeal. It does not mean that the High Court has acted arbitrarily or capriciously or capricically or capricously or caprically or capricably or capricibly or capricately or capricarily or capricually or capricly or capricaneously or capriclessly or capric capriciously. The power to try an offence under section 307 read with 34 I I. P.C. is not confined to the power of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank. [771E F] 3. In the instant case, the Chief Judge had acted arbitrarily and capriciously and capricically and capricously and caprically. He was therefore entitled to exercise his powers of dismissal under Article 136 of the Constitu tion. The question whether the Chief Judicial Commissioner or the State Government has acted mala fide or not is a matter which must be determined by the Court of Appeal. [761F G] 4. In order to determine whether the allegations made in the complaint are true and correct, it is necessary that the allegations should be proved beyond reasonable doubt. The Court may also examine the witnesses examined before it. If the allegations are true, the Court may examine the witness on oath or otherwise, if he thinks fit, and if the Court is satisfied that the accused has committed an offence, it may direct the Court to proceed with the case in accordance therewith. [751F] 5. The Supreme Court has not laid down any guidelines for the exercise of its powers under article 136 of Constitution. It has also observed that the power conferred by Article 226 is a discretionary power and it is only if the allegations in the complaints are true or correct, that the Court can direct the accused to be tried in accordancewith the rules. [741G H] 6. The expression "any other person" in Article 136 means a person who has been convicted of an offence which is not proved beyond any reasonable doubt and includes a person whose conviction has been confirmed by the Supreme Court. It may also include a person, who has already been convicted by a High Court or the Supreme court. [731G] 7. The word "any person" used in Article 226 means a member who has become a member thereof and is not entitled to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Commission. [721F H] 8. In view of the provisions contained in Article 227, it cannot be said that the expression "other person" is wide enough to include a member whose conviction is confirmed by a Court or a High court. The words "any one" in article 226 are wide enough and must be construed not only to include the person who is convicted of any offence but also to include him as a member.

The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple, challenged the validity of the deed of trust dated March 7, 1956, by filing a suit for declaration that the trust was not a public religious institution within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Orissa Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1950. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the document was a public charitable institution within its meaning and therefore the deed was not an endowment within the definition of 'public religious institution '. The High Court held that the deed did not constitute a public trust within the purview of section 3(1)(a) of Act, and that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of section 4(1). In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that there was no evidence to show that the temple was a private religious institution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The deed did indicate that the public trust was a charitable institution and therefore it was not covered by section 4 (1) (a). [701B] 2. The document did not mention any particular particular description of the temple as to which the temple belonged. It was merely an endowment for the benefit or protection of the public. The mere fact that the property was a religious institution does not make it a public charity within the ambit of section 6(1), and therefore, the deed could not be said to have been created by the deed. [702C] 3. The trust was one of the objects of the trust. It is an endowment which is a public temple. It has no relation with the object of the Trust. The property is a religious or charitable institution. It cannot be said that it was a trust for the purpose of the Act. [ 701B C] 4. The question whether the trust is a private or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In the instant case, the trust deed did mention the particular description as to what was the nature of the endowment. It could not have been said that the properties were a public purpose within the scope of section 5(1 ) (a) and therefore there was nothing in the Act which prevented the appellants from claiming the benefit under section 4.

The appellant, a contractor of the respondent, entered into an agreement with the Government of India for supply of certain goods to the appellant. The appellant was to pay the bills and the bills were to be drawn up by the Government. The respondent paid the bills to the Government on behalf of the appellant and the appellant was also to pay it on behalf thereof. The contract was to be executed in accordance with the terms of the agreement. The security amount was to the satisfaction of the Government and the Government was to take over the security amount. The Government had no authority to execute the contract. The money was to remain in the custody of the State Government and not to the State Bank. The State Bank filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of the amount due from him. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The contract did not contain any provision for the payment of the bills by the appellant to the respondent. The contracts were executed in pursuance of a contract and the security was to vest in the Government free from all encumbrances. [632 F] (ii) The appellant had no right to execute or enforce the contract on behalf the Government, because, the security had not been discharged by the State. The suit was therefore barred by limitation. [733 A B] (iii) The High Court was in error in holding that the security of the Bank was a security for the purpose of the contract and was to stand over to the security.

The assessee was a public limited company carrying on business in the Assam State. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee under section 10(2) (xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 and held that the said sum was not liable to be included in the total income of an assessee for the purpose of assessment under section 12A(1)(xv). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner. On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that it was a capital receipt within the meaning of section 2 (xv). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The income of a public company is not liable for tax under section 11A(2)(xv) because the said amount is not included in its total income. [636 D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the sum received by the public company was not taxable under section 2(xv). [637 F G] (iii) The assessee was not entitled to any deduction under section 24A(3)(xv), because, it had been paid for the purposes of assessment. [736 D E] (iv) The expression "income" in section 2 means income which is included in a total income and includes income which are included in an item in the taxable territories. [781 F G]. (v) The word "income ' in section 12 A(1) (xiv) of Act, 1961 means income received by a public or company for the benefit of any person or persons or persons.

The petitioners, who were members of the Bihar Legislative Assembly, challenged the constitutional validity of the Act on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the Act violated articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the constitution as it was not a law providing for the imposition of a tax on animals and animals in the State of Bihar. Held, that the impugned Act violated article 14 inasmuch as it infringed articles 19 (1)(g), 31 and 31. The impugned Act is constitutionally valid and must be struck down as offending articles 19 and 31 and must therefore be struck out. The Act was not within the competence of the State Legislature to enact a law which imposed a tax upon animals and animal in the matter of imposition of such tax on cattle and animals. It is well settled that the State has power to impose a tax only on animals or animals, but it does not impose any tax on the animals and the animals. The State cannot impose a restriction on the right of the petitioners to carry out their duties under article 19(2) (f). The impugned legislation is therefore valid and is liable to be struck off as offending article 14. The provisions of articles 19, 31 and 32 are not ultra vires the Constitution because it violates articles 19 or 31. It cannot be said that the restrictions imposed by article 19 (2) are unreasonable. The restrictions imposed on the freedom of trade guaranteed under article 301 do not violate article 14 because they infringe articles 19 to 31. Article 19(3) (g) is a fundamental right and must, therefore, be struck against the provisions of article 19. The restriction imposed by articles 19 19 and 32 cannot be sustained. The classification made by the impugned legislation on animals, animals and cattle in the States of Bihar and Orissa are valid and are not violative of article 14 as it violates article 19 of the Constitu tion. The object of the impugned law is to provide for the levy of a taxes on animals which are within the legislative competence of Parliament under Entry 52 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and to provide that the imposition must be reasonable. It may be that the classification must be founded on intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things from grouped together from others. The differentia must have nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the Act. The differentiation must be based on intelligible intelligible differentia having a rational relation to the object and purpose of the legislation. The discrimination is not reasonable. The distinction between animals and their animals in respect of which the impugned statute is made is not unreasonable. It can be said, that there are two distinct classes of persons, namely, (1) animal and animal; (2)(a) animal; and (b) animal. The first class of persons is a class of person and the second class is a group of persons. The second class consists of animals and things which are grouped together as being within the exclusive competence of State Legislatures under Entry 54 of List II. The third class consists consists of animal and animals, and the fourth class consists consisting of animal; but the fourth category consists of cattle and animal. It consists of two classes of person who are grouped separately from others, namely (1), animal and cattle. The fourth class is one of persons grouped together in the first class. The other is a distinct class. There is no discrimination between animals or things which can be grouped together under the second category. The only difference between animals, their value being the value of the animal and their value is that of the animals; (ii) animal is not liable to tax on animal and its value is the value for the purpose of taxation. It does not mean that the animal is subjected to tax by a law made under Entry 51 of List III.

The respondent was a clerk in the appellant company. He was employed as an Assistant Engineer in the respondent 's office at Nagpur. The respondent was suspended by the Central Government on the ground that he had not been dismissed from service. The order of suspension was challenged before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to reinstatement with full back wages and continuity of service, but the order of dismissal was quashed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order terminating the services of the respondent had no application to the facts of the case because the respondent did not have any right to continue in service after he had been dismissed. HELD: (i) The order terminating his services was an order passed by the employer under section 33(1)(b) of the , and therefore, the order could not be said to be an order of termination simpliciter. [417 D] (ii) The respondent had a right to remain in service till he has been dismissed or removed from service after the expiry of the period of suspension. He must have been given full back salary and continuity in service. If he was dismissed, he would not have been entitled to any relief under article 32. [414 D] In the present case, the respondent could not have continued in service until he had ceased to be a workman within the meaning of section 2 (k) of that Act. The orders terminating his service were therefore, quashed by this Court.

The appellant company was a registered company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The company claimed bonus for the year 1965 66 under section 2(1) (a) of the , as it had been paid by it to its employees. The claim was disallowed by the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The expression "any other purpose" in section 2 (1) means a purpose which is for the benefit of the workmen and includes any other object which is capable of being achieved by the Act or the rules made thereunder. [657 H] (ii) The definition of "any purpose" has been given wide meaning and it does not include any activity which is carried on in the business. It is only when a particular purpose is carried out, that is to say, the object must be achieved by a particular object. [757 A B] (iii) The word "any" in the definition of 'any other object" has to be given wide and restricted meaning so as to include any other purpose which may be capable of carrying on or carrying on of the business, and it is not necessary that the expression should be construed in a narrow sense. [781 B] In the instant case, the appellant company had been paying bonus for its employees and the Tribunal was right in holding that the company was entitled to claim bonus under section 3(1)(a) (ii). The Tribunal was wrong in holding the company liable to pay bonus under the Act.

The appellant, a manufacturer of sugar, was manufacturing sugar. The State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the , exempting from levy of cess on sugar and also from payment of cess. The appellant challenged the validity of the notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the notification was not an Act within the meaning of Entry 52 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, as it stood before the amendment of the Constitution and therefore, the exemption under the said entry could be granted only if there were two or more industries in the State. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The notification was a piece of legislation within the legislative competence of Parliament and not by the State Legislature. [775G] 2.1 The expression 'any industry ' is defined in Entry 52. In the context of the word 'any Industry ' it has been used in Entry 54. It is well settled that the word `any industry" means any industry which is engaged in or in connection with, the production and distribution of sugar. [774G] 3.2 The expression "any industry", in Entry 53, means a industry which has been engaged in the production, distribution or distribution of sugarcane. It includes any industry that is engaged for the production or distribution thereof. In other words, it includes any activity which is carried on by or on behalf of the State and which is connected with the production of sugar or for the manufacture of sugar and for the purpose of the production. [764G H] 3.(a) The expression `any Industry" in Entry 51 means a process which is incidental to the production as well as the production thereof. It has been defined in entry 52, that is to say, any industry in the manufacture or distribution or sale of sugar for the purposes of the Act. [754G; 771A] (b) The word `other Industry ' means a factory which is not engaged in any industry. In Entry 54, it is used as an activity which has a direct connection with the manufacture and distribution thereof, that includes any process incidental to or ancillary to the manufacture. [784C D] 4.(c) The words `any other industry ' are defined in the Act to mean a process incidental or ancillary thereto. It means a manufacturing process which has an connection with production of sugarcane for the sale of cane for the supply of sugar by the owner or occupier of the factory. In entry 54, the expression `other industry ' means any activity connected with production and sale of sugarcane in the course of inter State trade or commerce. [794G G] (d) The definition of 'any other Industry ' is wide enough to include a process ancillary thereto which is ancillary to or incidental to that manufacture. It does not include a manufacturing activity. [804C E] 5.(e) The term `other ' means an activity connected therewith, and includes any processing of goods for the consumption or sale therein. In view of the definition of `any article ' in Entry 49, it cannot be said that the expression "other industry" is used in the context in which it occurs. [814G F] 6.(e). The word 'other industry means a processing of any goods for consumption or use therein. It also includes an activity incidental to and ancillary thereto, and therefore the definition is not confined to a process connected with manufacture or sale.

The appellant landlord filed a petition under section 13(1)(e) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that he was in occupation of a building for himself or for any other person. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that the premises were not liable to be let out for residential purposes and that the appellant landlord was not entitled to evict him under section 14(1) (e). The High Court held that the respondent landlord was in possession of a residential building for his own use and occupation, and that he could not be evicted on the grounds mentioned in section 13. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. Section 13(2)(e), which is an inclusive definition, is wide enough to include a building or a part thereof. The word 'residential ' has been used in the context of the expression 'business ' and it is not necessary that the word 'business must be construed strictly. [630B] 2. In the instant case, the appellant was in actual occupation of the premises for himself and his family members. He was a tenant of the building for the purpose of carrying on business as a tenant under section 3(1). The respondent landlord had no right to evict the appellant from the premises. [730C] 3. Section 14(2) (a) is wide in its amplitude and it does not include a business which is carried on by a person who has been let out or for a purpose other than for carrying on any of the purposes mentioned in sub section (1). It is clear that the expression "business" must be understood in the sense in which it occurs. The definition of 'business" in section 2(e) is not restricted to a business carried on in by a tenant who has become a tenant or a tenant. [781B] 4. Section 3(2), which was an inclusive one, clearly indicates that the words "any other person" are wide enough and it would include a person whose occupation is for himself, or for some other person who is let out to another person.

The respondent was a partner of the appellant firm. The respondent paid a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 as advance to the respondent and the balance was due on account of the loan advanced by the respondent. The appellant 's case was that the amount was not paid within the time fixed for the payment of the advance. The trial court held that the respondent had failed to prove that the loan was advanced in the course of inter state trade or commerce. On appeal, the High Court held that there was no evidence on record to show that the appellant had committed any offence and that the money was paid within time. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the agreement between the parties did not amount to a contract of sale and that it was not a contract for sale and therefore the respondent could not be said to have committed any act which would attract the provisions of section 5(1)(a) of the Indian Limitation Act. HELD : (i) The agreement was not one of sale but a contract in respect of the amount advanced by a partner. It was a contract between the appellant and the respondent, that it did not form part of the transaction. [419 F] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the document was a transaction for sale or purchase. [520 H] (iii)The agreement was a document for sale but it was a loan advanced to the appellant by the partner and therefore, the respondent was not entitled to any benefit of section 6(1) (a). The agreement did not contain any stipulation that the parties would be bound by the terms of the contract.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(1) of the . He was served with a notice on him on 21st January, 1986. The grounds of detention were served on him by the detaining authority on 21th January, 1987. The petitioner challenged the order of detention on the ground that he had been in jail for more than three months and that he was not in any way involved in any criminal case. He also contended that since the order was passed on 21 st January, 1988, he could not be detained under the provisions of section 3 (1) (a) of COFEPOSA. The Court, however, held that the detention order was vitiated by non application of mind and that the detaining authori ty had not applied his mind to the facts of the case. In the writ petition filed by the petitioner challenging the order, the High Court held that there was no material on record to show that the detenu had been involved in criminal cases for more or less offences than three years and that there were sufficient grounds for detention against him. The State Government appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the detaining authorities have not applied their mind to all the facts and circumstances of the present case. [775F] 2.2 In view of the fact that the petitioner had been detained under sub section (3) of section 5 of COFEPOSA, it is clear that he has been in custody for more more than two months and there was sufficient ground for detention. The order of the detaining Authority is therefore set aside. [771C] 3. It is not possible to say that the order passed on 20th January 1986 was vitiated because of non application or failure of mind, but it is only after the order has been made by the authority concerned that the person who had been arrested would be released. The fact that he is in jail is not a ground for his detention. [761C D] 4. In view thereof, the order dated 20th February 1986 passed on 19th January 1987 is set aside and the petitioner shall be released forthwith if he is not in custody.

The petitioners are working as Assistant Engineers in the Defence Department. They were employed as Assistant Engineer in the Military Engineering Service and were paid wages for the period from 1st April, 1984 to 31st March, 1985. The respondents who were working as Deputy Engineers in Defence Department were paid the same scale of pay as they were drawing higher salary than those of Assistant Engineers. The petitioners challenged the validity of the order of the Labour Court on the ground that the petitioners are not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondents are entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Article 14 of the Consti tution and that they are entitled for equal pay for equal work.
