Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled only to the benefits of the scheme of the Defence Services Rules, 1985 and not to the extent of their entitlement to the same benefits as they have been working in the same department. [795B] 2.2 The respondents are not paid wages on the basis of the pay scale of Assistant Engineer. They are entitled under the scheme to the higher salary for equal works. [774C D] 3.1 In the instant case, the petitioners were employed by the Military Department and they have no right to claim any relief in the matter of payment of wages for equal Work. The fact that the petitioner has been working as a Assistant Engineer does not make it clear that the employees are entitled on the same pay scale. [764C E] 3.(a) The petitioners cannot be denied the benefit under Article 14 because they have not been paid wages in the earlier years. They have also been paid the salary for the last two years. Their claim is based on the principle of equal work and equal work, that is, equal work for equal workers. [754G H] (b) The respondents cannot be allowed to claim the benefit as they are not being paid wages by way of pay scale or otherwise. They cannot claim any protection under Article 16 because they are denied the same benefit.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer issued notice on the assessee under section 34(1)(a) of that Act and served a notice on him under section 148 of the Act calling upon him to show cause why he should not be assessed to tax for the assessment year 1945 46. The assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the notice was invalid because it had been issued by the Income tax officer, and that the notices were not served on him within the time prescribed under section 147(1) of his Act. The High Court in appeal took the view that the assessee had no right to file a return under section 16(2). Held, that the provisions of section 148(1), as amended by the Indian Finance (Amendment) Act, 1950, were not applicable to the case because it was issued after the expiry of the period prescribed for filing the return. The notice was not served within the period specified in section 147 and the notice could not be served on the person concerned. The proviso to section 147, as amended, did not apply to a case where the assessee was not given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The words "in respect of any income chargeable to tax under this Act" were used in the context of the expression "in relation to any income or profits chargeable to income or gains chargeable to assessment for that year". The words 'in respect thereof ' were used by the legislature in section 148, as it stood before the amendment. The word "in regard to any tax" was used in section 149(1). The words used in sub section (2) were used only in the sense of "in connection with any income and profits chargeable under this section". The expression "for any purpose other than the purposes of the Income Tax Act, 1961, did refer to a notice issued by a Hindu Undivided Family. The expression 'in relation thereto" was not intended to include a notice which could be served within one year from the end of the assessment for the year 1945 47. The section does not say that the words "for the purpose of the income or any profits chargeable in respect of which the return relates to the assessment years 1945 46 and 1946 48 were used as meaning "in the case of a Hindu Joint Family". The word 'person ' in sub s.(2) was used by section 148. The legislature intended that the expression 'person" should be construed in its ordinary sense, but it did not say anything more than the words 'for any purposes other than those mentioned in sub sections (1), (2), (3) and (4). The word,person ' occurring in sub cl.(2), was used to mean a person who has been assessed to assessment under this sub section. The language of the section is clear enough to include an individual who has not been assessed for any income tax or profits or gains under the Act. It does not contemplate that the person who is assessed to the tax should be assessed in respect thereof, but only one person who was assessed and the other person who had been assessed must be deemed to have been assessed as such. The object of the legislature was to give a clear indication that the income chargeable for any assessment year under this subsection was not liable to be assessed on the basis of the return filed by him within one month from the date of the notice, and it was only after the period mentioned in section 146(1A) had expired. The Legislature intended that if the Income ' Officer was satisfied that the return was not properly served within a reasonable time, he should have issued a notice to the assessee requiring him to pay a sum of Rs.

The petitioners are the employees of the respondent Bank. They are the members of the Board of Directors of the Bank. The petitioners were elected to the Board by the Central Government under section 10(1) of the Act. The Board of directors of the bank, after considering the objections raised by the petitioners, decided to appoint the petitioners as their agents. The Central Government issued a notification dated 30th April, 1985, inviting applications for appointment of the petitioners on the ground that they were not qualified to be appointed as their agent. The said notification was challenged in this Court by way of Writ Petitions before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the petitioners were not eligible to be considered for appointment as their services were terminated by the Board under section 11(1). Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board is a body corporate and it has its own power to appoint any person as its agents. It is an authority of law to make rules for the regulation of the affairs of the public. [703F] 2.2 The Board may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint any persons as its agent. But the Board may appoint such persons as it thinks fit. The scheme of the Scheme is not a statutory one and it is only an executive act. It has no power to make any rules for appointment or appointment of any person. [774F] 3.1 In the instant case, the Board has been constituted under section 12 of the . The Board has no authority to appoint such person as it considers necessary to do so. The object of the scheme is to provide for the constitution of a committee and to make provision for the appointment of persons as agents. [764F G] 4.2 In the absence of any statutory provision, the Central Govern ment may appoint any other person as the agent. [754G H; 771A B] 5.3 The Board cannot be said to have acted in a manner which is not permissible under the Act and the Rules. [784F H] 6.4 In the present case, there are no statutory rules for recruitment of persons by the Government. The impugned notification is not an executive order. It does not provide for any delegation of power to the Central Govt. The power conferred on the Central Gov ernment under section 3(1)(a) of that Act is a statutory power and it cannot be challenged in any court. [ 771C] 6.(5) In the circumstances, the impugned notification dated 29th April 1985 is quashed and set aside.

The respondent assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61 under section 34(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner and directed the appellant to pay a sum of Rs. 2,000 as penalty. The respondent preferred an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal which held that the amount of penalty was not a tax but a tax on income and that the Appellate Authority had no jurisdiction to pass orders under section 35(1). In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the order passed by the Appellate Com missioners was not appealable under section 66(2) of Act. HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the power conferred on the Appellate Tribu nal to pass an order under section 36(1), is a judicial power and it is not open to the Appellate Commissioner to pass such orders as he thinks fit. [657 H] (ii) The power of the Tribunal to pass any order under the Act is a discretionary power and the High Court has no jurisdiction in passing an order on the application for stay of proceedings pending before it. [757 A B] (iii) The Appellate Tribunal has no power to pass a decree under section 37(1)(a). It is not correct to say that the powers conferred by section 35 are wide enough to include the power of a Tribunal to grant stay of proceeding pending before the Tribunal. The power conferred by the statute is discretionary and it cannot be said that the discretion conferred on an Appellate Tribunal is not a judicial function. [783 C D] (iv) In the present case, the Appellate Board had no power under section 38(1 ) to pass the order under sub section (2). The High Courts have no jurisdiction under section 39(1); and the Appellate Court has rightly held that it was not open for the Tribunal in passing the order.

The respondent was appointed as a Sub Inspector of Police in the District Jail, Kanpur. He was promoted to the post of Sub Inspector on December 1, 1953. The respondent filed a complaint against him under section 161 I.P.C., alleging that he had committed an offence under section 409 I. P.C. and that he was not given any opportunity to cross examine him. The Magistrate held that the respondent was guilty of an offence punishable under section 420 I. p.C, and that the order of dismissal passed against him was illegal. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the Magistrate in exercise of its powers under article 226 of the Constitution. HELD : (i) The order of the High court is not a judicial one and must be set aside. [657 H] (ii) In the present case, the respondent had been given an opportunity to examine him before he was appointed. He did not avail himself of the opportunity to rebut his evidence. He had also failed to produce any material on which the order was passed. The order was therefore, illegal and void. [757 H; 758 A] (iii) In view of the fact that the charge sheet was submitted against him, the High Courts were right in holding that the charges framed against him were not proved. [779 B C] (iv) The High Courts had no power to interfere under article 136 of the constitution.

The appellant was appointed as a Medical Officer in the Health Department of the Government of India on April 1, 1971. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Surgeon in the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on May 14, 1972. The appellant was promoted as a medical officer in the Department of Health. On June 29, 1972 he was promoted by the Ministry on the basis that he was entitled to be considered for promotion to the higher post of Medical Officer. He challenged the promotion of the appellant on the ground that his promotion was not based on any rule or order made by the Central Government under article 309 of the Constitution and that the appellant was entitled only to be promoted as Assistant Surgeon on the date when he was appointed in the said Department. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the promotion was based on a rule or Order made by it under article 311(2) of the Constitu tion. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant 's promotion to higher post is based on an executive order and not on any statutory provision. It is well settled that in a case where a person has been promoted as Medical Officer he cannot be considered to have been promoted to higher posts unless he has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action. [710E] 1.2 The appellant, who was appointed to the Indian Administrative Service on April 14, 1971, was not entitled to any promotion in the post which he was holding earlier as Medical Officers. He could not be promoted to that post because he had been given an opportunity of being heard. [771C D] 1:3 In the instant case, the appellant ' was promoted on May 15, 1972 and his promotion to that higher post was based upon a rule made by him under article 310(2). The appellant could not therefore be considered as having been promoted on April 13, 1971 when he had already been promoted. [761C] 1 :4 In the absence of any statutory rule or direction in this regard, the promotion to which he belonged was not on the same footing as that of a person who was promoted earlier on May 16, 1972 when he joined the Indian Medical Service on May 13, 1972, and his seniority was determined on the footing that he had not been promoted earlier. [751G H] 1.(a) The appellant has been denied promotion to a higher post on April 15, 1971 because he was not given any opportunity of hearing. He is entitled to have his representation considered by him in accordance with law. [781C E] (b) The promotion to lower post is governed by the rules made under article 235 of the constitution and it cannot be said that he has not been given any chance of being promoted on the grounds that he did not possess the requisite qualification for promotion as Medical officer. [791G] 1(c) The High Courts have rightly held that the promotions to higher grade were based on some rule or orders made by them under article 233 of the Consti tution. [741F G] (d) The promotions to lower posts are based on the principle of seniority and not upon any statutory rules. [731G F] 1 (e) The post of Health Officer is a separate cadre and it is governed only by the Rules made under Article 309 of India. It cannot be held that there was no rule or practice in the Indian Civil Service which could be said to have come into existence on April 19, 1972 as the appellant had not passed the requisite test for promotion. [721G G] 2(e) In the present case, there is nothing in the rules which can be said with regard to the appellant having been appointed as Medical Assistant Surgeon prior to May 14.

The respondent, a displaced person, was the owner of certain lands in the State of Punjab. The respondent claimed that he had no right to hold the land as a tenant under section 3(1) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The Collector held that the respondent was entitled to hold land as an occupancy tenant under the provisions of the Act and that the land was not liable to be declared as an agricultural land. The High Court upheld the view of the Collector. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Act did not provide for a ceiling on holdings in the hands of displaced persons and that section 3 (1) was ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as the Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: The High Courts were right in holding that the provisions contained in sections 3(2), 4(1)(a) and 5(1), are ultra vires Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitu tion. [730C] (i) The Act is a self contained code which provides for ceiling on land holdings. It does not provide any guidance to the State Government or the Collector in fixing the ceiling area. The Act has been enacted with a view to preventing the displaced persons from holding land as tenants under the Act. The object of the legislation is to prevent the displaced person from holding agricultural lands as an occupant under the Punjab Land Tenures (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1947. [771G] (ii) The provisions contained therein are ultravires the Constitution and are void.

The appellants were the descendants of a Zamindar in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The Ruler of the erstwhile State of Gwalior, was appointed as a guardian of the land and the Government of India by notification dated March 1, 1950, issued a notification under section 4 of the Abolition Act declaring that the estate of the Zamindar shall be held by him as an evacuee property. The appellants filed a suit for declaration that the order of the Ruler was invalid because the Government had no power to make any order in respect of the estate which was vested in the Ruler and that the appellants were entitled to claim compensation under section 6 of the Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the Government was competent to make an order in regard to the estate as it stood before the Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950. The High Court held that the Ruler had no authority to make a law for the management of the estates and that he was entitled to compensation under the Act because the Ruler did not exercise his powers under section 3 of the Administration of Proprietary rights (Estate, Mahal and Alienated Land) Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had no jurisdiction to make such an order. HELD : The order of a Ruler is valid because the order made by the Ruler is invalid because it is not in accordance with law. [619 F] (a) The order made under section 5 of the Consolidation Act is valid and must be set aside. [720 A C] (b) The High court was right in holding that a Ruler could make an appointment to the State Government as a result of his death, because he had no such power. [779 D E] (c) The appellants were not entitled to any compensation under any law for their estate. They were entitled only to claim the compensation under that law. The order was made in accordancewith law and not by the High court.

The appellants were the tenants of a premises in Bombay. The respondent landlord filed an application under section 13(1) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the notice was not served within the time prescribed by section 13 (2). The trial court dismissed the application holding that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 13 were applicable only where the landlord had tendered the rent and tendered the same in accordance with the provisions contained in section 13 of the Act, and that the tenant was not entitled to any protection under section 14(1)(a) (i). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that section 13 was applicable only when the landlord tendered the amount in accordance therewith. [782B] In the instant case, the notice served on the appellants was not a valid notice within the meaning of section 14 (1)(b) (ii). The notice served by the appellants did not contain any provision for the payment of rent and the notice sent to them was not accompanied by any such provision. [77C D] In view of the provisions in section 12(2), the respondent landlord could not be said to have tendered the entire amount in compliance with the requirements of section 12 (1) of that Act. The notice was served on him within the period prescribed by the section and the appellants were not entitled for any protection as contemplated by section 14.

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the Indian State. The respondent company had its registered office at Calcutta and the respondent company, acting under the provisions of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was appointed as a managing agent of the company. The appellant company was incorporated in India with the object of promoting the company to the detriment of the shareholders of the respondent Company. The company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling goods for the purpose of carrying on its business. It was also registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, that the respondent had a right to carry on the trade of the appellant company in respect of the shares held by it. The Income tax Officer rejected the contention of the assessee that the managing agent was not a "person" within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Act and that the appointment of the managing agents was invalid as the managing agency had no power to appoint any person as managing agent. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the appellant was a "company" within section 2 (6) Of the Act, and that it was not an "person". On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Tribunal held that there was no "person", within the definition of "person ". Held, that in view of the provisions contained in section 2 of the Income tax (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, the managing director could be appointed as managing agents only if he had a power to make appointment of any person other than the managing Agent. The managing agent could not be appointed by the managing managing agent merely because he was a managing director and that he was not entitled to carry out his duties under the Act.

The respondent was appointed as a Junior Engineer in the Mysore State Electricity Board. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Executive Engineer on March 31, 1956. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated March 31. 1956 passed by the Government of Karnataka. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was entitled to be considered for promotion to the cadre of Junior Engineers and that he was not entitled to any relief under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ peti tion. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High court was in error in holding that there was no provision for the Board to make a selection for promotion of Junior Engineer and that the Board had power to make any selection for the post. [417E] (1) The Board has power to frame rules for recruitment to the posts of Junior Engi neers, Assistant Executive Engineers and Assistant Executive Officers. The Board is not competent to frame regulations for promotion in the cadre. The rules are framed under section 3(2)(a) of the Mysore Electricity Supply Act, 1948. [414C] (2) The High Courts have no jurisdiction in entertaining a writ peti tions. [416E F] (3) The power conferred on the Board by section 3 is not confined to the power to prescribe the method of recruitment and promotion of junior Engi cers. The power to fix the method for recruitment is limited to the powers to be exercised by the Board in respect of the posts which are held by it.

The petitioner, a police constable, was arrested on the spot and he was remanded to judicial custody. He was released on bail by the Additional District Judge, Cuttack, on the ground that he had no right to claim compensation for the injuries sustained by him in the incident. The petitioner filed an application before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of the impugned order of detention and also prayed for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to release the petitioner from custody. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the impugned orders were not justified on the grounds that the petitioner had no locus standi to file the present petition. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The impugned order is liable to be quashed and set aside. [730F] 2.2 In the instant case, the petitioner was arrested by the police on the basis of a report lodged by him under Section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He had no personal knowledge about the incident and he had also been involved in the commission of the alleged offence. The police did not examine any witnesses to prove that the incident was committed by the petitioner or his family members. The question whether the petitioner could claim compensation on account of the injuries suffered by him was not a matter which would be covered by Article 32 of the constitution. [771G] 2:3 In the present case, there is no evidence to show that the injured person had sustained any injury in the occurrence. The fact that the deceased was taken to hospital and he died on account thereof cannot be said to be an offence under Article 21 of the Constitu tion. [782A B] 3:4 The petitioner has not been able to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. He is entitled to compensation for injuries sustained in the alleged incident. [791G H; 79A] 4:5 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it cannot be held that the petition under Article 32 was maintainable.

The petitioner, a member of the Indian National Congress, was convicted for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the High Court. The petitioner challenged the order of the High court on the ground that the petition had been filed in the Supreme Court and the petition was not maintainable. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petition must be dismissed. [775F] 2. The writ petition is dismissed. There can be no doubt that the petitioner has a right to move this Court for relief under article 32 of the Constitution. It is well settled that the right to approach this Court is not an absolute right but it is only when the person who seeks to move the Supreme court is informed that he will have to move his own case and ask for an order from the High Courts. [771C] 3. The right to apply for a writ of habeas corpus is a fundamental right which has been conferred on the citizen by article 21. It cannot be said that the person seeking to move an application for a Writ of habeas Corpus is not entitled to move any other Court for the enforcement of his fundamental rights under article 19(1)(g) of the constitution. [762C] 4. The expression "law" in section 2(a) of this Act means a law providing for the right of freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by article 19 (1)(f). [773F G] 5. The word "law " includes any law providing or authorising the exercise of any power conferred on it by or under any law for the time being in force. It does not mean that the expression "public order" is used in section 3(a), and the expression must be construed in a sense which has to be given its widest amplitude. [753F] 6. The words "law ' includes any order made by or on behalf of the State Government or any other authority empowered under the Act.

The appellant, a surety of the respondent Bank, was appointed as a Receiver in the United Khasi Hills District. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of the amount due to him from the appellant. The appellant contended that the attachment order was illegal and void because it had been passed by the Court of Wards under section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree and directed the respondent to pay a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ as damages for loss caused to the appellant in the course of his business. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the attachment was illegal because the attachment had been made by the court of Wards; (ii) the order of attachment was not legal and valid; (iii) the decree passed by a Court of wards under section 54 of the Act was not liable to be set aside. HELD: The attachment was in contravention of the provisions of section 53, and therefore the attachment could not be set off against the respondent 's claim. [601 F G] In the instant case the attachment did not amount to an order passed by any Court of law under the Act. The attachment had not been made against the Bank. Therefore the attachment must be held to have been illegal because it was passed in contravention with the provisions contained in section 53. [702 A B] (iv) The attachment could only be set out against the person who has been appointed as Receiver and not against the surety.

The appellants were dealers in sugar. The Sales Tax Officer, Sales tax, U.P., issued a notice to the appellants under section 3(1) of the Uttar Pradesh Sales Tax Act, 1948 for payment of sales tax on the sale of sugar. On appeal by the appellants, the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the sale was not liable to be taxed as it did not amount to sale within the meaning of section 2(6) of that Act and that the sales were not exigible to sales tax under the Act. The High Court in revision held that there was no sale within section 3 (1) (a) of Uttar Pradesh Act, which was a law relating to sales of sugar and therefore the sale could not be taxed under the provisions of the Act as it was not a sale within that meaning. In appeal by special leave, HELD : The sale in question was not exigible for sales tax because the sale in respect of sugar was not one of sale within cl. (a). [775 B] The sale of goods is not liable for sales Tax under the Uttar Bharat Act. It is a sale which is not exigible under the Sales tax Act. [776 C D] The definition of "sale" in section 2 (6) (b) of U. P. Act, does not include sale within any meaning of that expression. The definition is wide enough to include sale of a commodity or goods. It does not mean sale which has been subjected to tax under a law for the time being in force.

The appellant was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him by the State Government on December 13, 1986. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his detention. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of detention was not made within the period of three months from the date of detention and that the appellant had been detained under section 3(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the grounds of his detention were vague and indefinite and that there was no material before the detaining authority to justify the order for detention. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the High court is not a speaking one but a reasoned one. It is only when the Advisory Board has considered the report of the Advisory board that the detenu had been in jail for more than three months and that he was likely to be released on bail. [775B] 2. The detaining authority must have regard to the nature of the offence, the circumstances of each case, the nature and seriousness of the crime, the manner in which it is committed and the period during which the detention has been made. If the Advisory Boards are satisfied that there is sufficient cause for not making a reference to the Advisory body, the Court would be justified in directing the detention of the detenu. [771C] 3. The expression "may" used in section 3 (2) means the date on which the order is made and the date when the order was made. It does not mean that the period for making a report under sub section (3) of section 3 has to be taken into account. If there are sufficient cause, the detention order cannot be said to have been made within three months. [761C D] 4. The word "may ' means the day on which it was made and not the date from which the report is made. [751G H; 771A B] 5. In the instant case, there is no material on record to justify that the detention was made within two months of the order. The appellant had not been released on the ground of his being in jail. He has not been given any opportunity of making a representation against the order and the fact that he had been released after three months of his release would not make him liable for detention under section 7(2). [764C] 6. In view of the fact, the High Courts have taken into consideration the report made by the Advisory Com missioner and the report submitted by the Board on December 12, 1986, it is clear that the State has not considered the representation of the appel lant. The State Government has not given any reasons for its order to enable the appellant to make a reference under section 8(2), as required by sub section 3 of section 7 of the .

The petitioner, a retired Judge of the High Court, was appointed as an arbitrator. The petitioner filed an application under section 34 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940 for setting aside the award on the ground that the award had been made in contravention of the provisions of the Act and that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to entertain the application. The respondent contended that the petitioner had not committed any error in making the award. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the agreement was not signed by the petitioner and that it was not a signed document, and that there was no arbitration agreement between the parties. The High Court held that the petition was not maintainable because the petitioner did not know the contents of the agreement and had not filed any objection to the award, and therefore the application was not barred under section 30(2) of the Arbitration Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the arbitration agreement was signed by a person who had signed the document and that he had signed it. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The award was signed in contravention with the provisions contained in section 30 (2) and the arbitrator was not competent to entertain it. [795B] 2. The arbitrator had jurisdiction to try the application on the basis of the arbitration clause. The agreement was executed by a party who had entered into an agreement with the petitioner, and the award was made in breach with the consent of the parties, and there was nothing to show that the parties had signed them. [77C] 3. The question whether the arbitrator has jurisdiction to decide the application under Section 34 of Arbitration Act is not one of fact. It is well settled that the Court cannot entertain a suit on the grounds mentioned in section 20(2). If the award is signed by an arbitrator, it is open to the court to decide it on the merits. [76G] 4. The jurisdiction of the Court under Section 30 (1) is not limited to the jurisdiction of a civil court. It has been held that there is no arbitration clause in the agreement between two parties and the same can be invoked only by the arbitrator, and if the award does not contain any arbitration clause, it cannot be said that the proceedings were vitiated by fraud or collusion. [75G] 5. The Court cannot decide a dispute on the question of jurisdiction. It would be open to an arbitrator to decide whether there was a arbitration agreement or not. [74C D] 6. In the instant case, the petitioner has not filed his objection to his appointment as an Arbitrator. He had signed in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law and he had also signed it in contravention thereof. The petition was therefore barred under Section 29(2), and the application for setting up of a new arbitrator cannot be entertained. [73C] 7. In view of the fact that the respondent had signed on the agreement, and since there was an arbitration clause which was signed on behalf and the petitioner was not entitled to raise the plea that he was not bound by the arbitration proceedings.

The appellants, who were the partners of a firm, filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of possession of certain properties. The respondent contended that the decree was not executable as it was passed in execution proceedings and that the respondent had no right to execute the decree. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the mortgage was not executed within the time fixed by the Court. The High Court held that the mortgagee 's right to sue was a conditional one and that it was not an absolute one and therefore, the decree could not be executed in execution of the decree because the mortgagor had no vested interest in the mortgaged property. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the mortgagor 's rights to sue were extinguished by reason of the provisions of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the decree passed in his favour was not a conditional order. [657 D] (ii) The expression "any person" in section 47 means a person who has been dismissed or removed from service under the Act, and includes any person who is dismissed or removal from service. In the present case, the mortgagee had no interest in any property. Therefore, the High Court was right in directing the respondent to execute a decree in his name. [757 D F] (iii) The words "any other person" occurring in section 48 of the Act are wide enough to include a person whose rights were extinguished and not an assignee or assignee.

The appellant was the adopted son of one G, who was a Hindu undivided family. The respondents were the sons of G and his wife. A suit for partition was filed in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Tirupathi against the appellant on the ground that the appellant had no right to maintenance under section 3(1)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates Act, 1953. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondents were not entitled to maintenance as they were not in possession of the properties and that the property was not liable to be partitioned. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that section 3 (1)(b) of Act did not apply to the case because, the respondents had no title to the property and that they were entitled to a decree for partition. HELD : The High Court was right in holding the respondents ' possession of their properties as joint family property. [612 D] In the present case, the appellant was not in actual possession of his properties. He was not entitled under section 4(1) (a) to maintenance. [713 F G] The High Courts were wrong in holding on the basis that the transaction was a gift and was not a gift within the meaning of section 3 of Act. [774 D] The appellant was a minor and was therefore entitled to the benefit of section 4 (1) of Hindu Succession Act. The High court erred in taking the view that the transactions were not a transfer within the definition of 'family ' in section 3.

The respondent, a widow of the appellant, was a nominee in the Life Insurance Corporation of India. The respondent had paid the amount to the appellant on account of the death of her husband. The Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 148(2) of the Act calling upon the respondent to show cause why the amount should not be recovered from her husband for non payment of the amount due under the policy. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notice on the ground that the notice was barred by limitation as it had been issued after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed under section 147(2). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent had not complied with the requirements of section 148 and that the amount could not be recoverable from her. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The notice was not barred by time as it was issued after expiry of three years from the date of the notice. [795D] 2.2 In view of the fact that the appellant had paid a sum of Rs.3,50,000 to the respondent on account thereof, the notice under s 148(1) was not valid and the notice could not have been issued within three years of the accrual of the cause of action. [774E] 2:3 The notice under sec. 148(3) is not barred because it was served on the respondent after the period prescribed by section 147 (2). It is only when the notice is served on him that he has paid the sum due under a policy, the amount can be recovered only for non compliance with the provisions of section 147. [764F] 2(a) The notice issued under secs 148(5) is valid and it cannot be said that the income of the respondent was not liable to be included in the notice as contemplated by section 148 (1).

The respondent, a resident of the State of Madhya Pradesh, was the appellant in the appeal. The respondent filed an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for setting aside the abatement of his appeal on the ground that the period of limitation prescribed by section 5(2) of the Act had expired and the period prescribed by the Act was not extended beyond the period specified in the proviso to section 5 (2). The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court, HELD: Section 5(1) of that Act is a substantive provision which provides that no appeal shall lie from any order passed under the Act except on an application made by the appellant or his pleader for the purpose of obtaining a decree against him in respect of any matter specified in section 5. The words "any order" occurring in section 4(2), are wide enough to include an order passed in appeal under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [637 D] In the present case, the period for which the appellant had applied for setting off the abatement was extended beyond a period of three years from the date of the application and not from the time when the application was made. The period prescribed in section 6(2)(a) is two years from that date. The limitation prescribed under section 6 (2) is, therefore, within the meaning of section 5 and not within the period mentioned in section 7(2). [638 G H] In view of the provisions contained in section 3(1), the period during which an appeal has been filed is three years after the date on which the application for setting it aside was made and the time prescribed under that section is, thereafter, extended beyond one year from the commencement of the Amendment Act.

The appellant, a private limited company, was carrying on business in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The respondent No. 1, who was running a bus under the name and style of "Machhi Nagar" was appointed as a driver by the District Magistrate, Jhansi, to carry out the provisions of the U.P. Motor Vehicles (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The appellant was permitted to run his bus under section 68(1)(b) of the Act on payment of prescribed fee. The Regional Transport Authority, Jhansi passed an order directing the respondent No 1 to carry on the business in question within a period of one month from the date of the order. The State Government issued a notification under section 67(2) of U. P. Motor Vehicle (Regulation and Eviction), Act, 1947, which was published in the Gazette on May 3, 1986. The said notification was challenged by the appellant before the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent had no power to issue a notification for carrying out the purposes of the said Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Regional Transport Officer had no jurisdiction to issue the order under section 66(2)(b). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Regional Authority had no jurisdic tion to issue such a notification. [703F] 2.2 The Regional Commis sioner had no authority to issue any such notification. The power of the Regional Authority was not vested in it by law and the order passed by the Regional Com missioner could not be challenged on the ground that the said notification did not apply to a private company. [771C] 3.3 The Regional Committee had no competence to issue or issue the said notifications. The Act does not provide for any delegation of power to the Regional Committee. It is only in respect of the matters enumerated in section 68 (2) (b). The Regional Officer has no jurisdiction under section 64(2), and therefore, the order of the District Authority was liable to be quashed. [761C D] 4.4 In the instant case, the Regional Officer had not given any reasons for holding that the appellant had no locus standi to issue it. The order passed in favour of the respondent was set aside by the High court and the matter remanded to the District Court for fresh disposal on merits.

The appellants were convicted under section 5(1) of the Punjab Security of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1960. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment for a period of two years. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the offence under section 3 (2) of that Act was not committed by the appellants and that the provisions of section 5 (1) were not applicable to them because they were not in conformity with the provisions Of the Act. HELD : The offence under the Act is a criminal act and it must be proved that the offender had committed an offence under that Act. [637 D] In the present case, the appellants were found guilty of offences under section 4 (1). They were convicted for the offence of theft of coal from their possession. The conviction was therefore not justified. [738 G H; 739 A B] The offence of criminal breach of trust is a serious one and it cannot be said that the act was done by the appellant in furtherance of his common intention. [781 D F] In view of the provisions contained in section 5 of the Act, the prosecution must prove that the appellants had committed the offence. [783 E G] The prosecution has not proved that there was any breach of the trust. The appellants were therefore guilty of an offence punishable under section 6 (1), read with section 7(2) and section 7 (3). [781 A B].

The respondent company was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of cloth and cloth. The appellant company had entered into an agreement with the respondent for the sale of cloth, and the appellant company agreed to pay the same to its employees. The agreement provided that the remuneration payable by the employees shall be paid to the employees who were not entitled to any remuneration under the terms of the agreement. The respondent was a partner in the firm. The Income tax Officer held that the services of the employees were not liable to income tax as they had been rendered service for the purpose of earning profits and gains from the business of the appellant. In appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the Tribunal held that there was no transfer of the services to the respondent and that the transfer of services was not a transfer of service but a transfer which was made in pursuance of the contract. The High Court answered the question against the Revenue. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The agreement was not an assignment of service and was not one for consideration as it was made on behalf of the respondent. (ii) The remuneration payable to the employee under the contract could be said to have been received by the assessee from the company. (iii) The payment of remuneration in respect of the service rendered by him to the appellant was a transfer within the meaning of section 2(22)(vi) of the Income tax Act, 1922. (iv) The payments made by the respondent to the appellants were not for consideration and could not be said as an assignment for consideration. (v) The income from the sale proceeds received by it from the appellant were not taxable under the Indian Income tax (Investigation Commission) Act, 1961. (vi) The services of a person who was not entitled under the agreement to receive remuneration in lieu of service rendered to him could not have been included in the taxable income of the assessee. (vii) The transfer of an employee from one company to another is not a sale within the definition of 'business ' in section 2 (22)(iv). (viii) The amount received by a person on behalf or on behalf, was not liable for income tax under the Act. (ix) The amounts received by him as remuneration could not, therefore, be said not taxable in view of the provisions of section 3(23)(vi).

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellant on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in the murder of his wife, and that the evidence of the witnesses was not corroborated by any other evidence. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the confession made by the deceased before her death was inadmissible as it was not voluntary. HELD: (i) The confession is admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act. It is a statement made by a person who has been given a confession and is admissible in evidence under section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act, and is not admissible under any other law. [657 H] (ii) In the instant case, the confession was voluntary and it was inadmissible under section 26 of the Act. The confession was admissible under the provisions of section 27. [757 A B] (iii) The statement made before the police was admissible in a substantive form. It was not admissible as evidence under any law. The statement was admissible only to corroborate the maker of the confession and it is admissible only if it is corroborated by other evidence or by other material. [625 D E] (iv) In view of the provisions contained in section 27, the statement made after the police had been examined, must be held to be voluntary. [557 A C] (v) The High court was right in holding that the statement was inadmissible in evidence and not admissible in law. It could not have relied upon the confession as it is voluntary. The question whether the confession is voluntary or not depends on the facts of each case.

The appellant was appointed as a General Manager in the Life Insurance Corporation of India. He was suspended from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from service by an order dated March 31, 1973. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of termination and for quashing the order dated April 1, 1973 passed by the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, Delhi. The Single Judge held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order terminating the services of the respondent was invalid because the appellant had been appointed as General Manager and was not a workman within the meaning of Section 2(oo) of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in holding that the impugned order was invalid inasmuch as it was passed by an authority competent to do so. [795B] 2.1 The appellant had no right to claim any relief on the basis of the impugned orders. The impugned order is not a law within the ambit of Article 12 of the Constitu tion and cannot be challenged in a court of law. [774C D] 2:2. The appellant was a General manager and was appointed by the Central Government under Rule 3 of the Rules. He had been working as General Managers in the Department of Insurance. He continued to work as General manager till he retired from service. He could not be said to have been appointed on probation for a period of two years. He did not hold any post in the Bank and was therefore entitled to claim relief under Rule 4. [764C] 2 :3. The order terminating his services was passed without giving him an opportunity of being heard. The termination of service of the employee was illegal because he had not been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action. He has no right or right to be heard in the matter. The power conferred on the authority under Rule 5 is not absolute and it is only when the authority is satisfied that the employee is guilty of misconduct or misconduct, that the services are terminated without giving any opportunity of hearing to him. [754G H] 2(a) The order of the Single Judge was set aside by the Division Bench in appeal and the writ petition filed by the appellant before this Court was dismissed. The Division Bench also held that since the appellant has been dismissed for misconduct, he is not entitled for any relief. [784C E] (b) The impugned orders are quashed.

The Orissa Excise and Salt Act, 1947 was enacted to provide for the grant of licences to retail vendors in respect of certain specified areas. Section 3(1) of the Act provided that no person shall sell or otherwise transfer any liquor or intoxicating drug except with the previous sanction of the State Government. The State Government issued a notification under section 4(2) of that Act, which was published in the Gazette on May 15, 1971. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification was not valid and could not be enforced against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the State had no power to issue a notification in respect thereof, and that the impugned notification was invalid as it was issued without authority of law. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The High Courts were right in holding that section 3(2)(a) of Act did not apply to the grant or renewal of licences under section 3 of the Excise Act. [775G] (2) The notification dated May 15 1971 was valid and had no retrospective effect. It was therefore invalid for the reason that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to issue the notification in question. [771C D] (3) The State had not issued any notification under the Act, and the High court had rightly held that the said notifications were ultra vires the State Legislature. [762D] (4) The decision of the High courts was correct. It is well settled that the power to grant licences under sections 3(3)(a), 4(1)(a)(i) and 5(2), are not subject to any restrictions imposed by the Act. In the instant case, the State has no authority to issue such a notification. [753F] (5) The impugned notification dated June 15, 1972 was valid as it had been issued without the previous approval of the Government. It could not have been issued in respect whereof the State was bound to grant the licences under the Excise and Taxation Act. The notification did not contain any provision for the issue of a notification which was issued after the expiry of the period of licence. [783F G] (6) The power to cancel or suspend the licences is subject to the restrictions imposed in section 3. It cannot be said that the Government had no authority under the statute to issue any such notification. The impugned notifications were therefore valid and must be quashed.

The appellant was charged with murder under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to death. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The evidence of the eye witnesses is not consistent with the innocence of the accused and it is not safe to rely on the testimony of a witness who has been examined in this case for corroboration. [657 H] (2) There was no evidence that the deceased had seen the appellant 's house at about 8 p.m. or that he had seen him at the time when the murder took place. The evidence is not sufficient to prove the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. [757 B C] (3) The High Court was in error in holding that the evidence of a eye witness is not corroborated by any other evidence. [781 D F] (4) There is no evidence on record to show that the accused had seen his house at 8 p p. m. or about 8 P.m., and that he knew the accused at the relevant time. The High court was in wrong in holding the appellant guilty of murder under s.302 read with s.34 of the Evidence Act. [783 D] (5) There are no evidence to show the guilt against the accused beyond reasonable doubts. The circumstances relied upon by the prosecution are not consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt but also with the guilt. [784 G H] In the present case, the evidence was corroborated by some other evidence and it could not be said that the appellant had seen a person at the scene of murder.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The land in dispute was acquired by the appellant under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for construction of a building on the land. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the scheme and the award of compensation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the scheme was not a 'public purpose ' within the meaning of section 2(1) (d) of the Act, as it stood at the relevant time. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the land in question was a public purpose and therefore the land was not covered by the expression "public purpose" within the definition of 'public purposes ' as defined in section 2 (1) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The scheme was a private purpose and it could not be said to be a public object within the scope of the expression 'public utility '. [630B] In the instant case, the land is covered by a scheme which was in existence at the time when the scheme came into force. The scheme itself did not fall under any of the clauses of section 3(1). The appellant had no right to claim compensation for the land acquired. The question whether the land could be said or not was not one of fact and law. [730C] In view of the provisions of section 23 of the Land Acquisi tion Act, the High court rightly held that the appellant was entitled to claim the compensation under section 23(1)(d) on the ground that it was a 'Public purpose ' as contemplated by section 23 (1).

The appellant was the adopted son of one B. The testator died in 1938 leaving behind his widow and two daughters, who were the adopted sons. The appellant claimed that he had no right to claim any share in the properties. The High Court held that the testator had no power to make a gift under section 8 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and that the will was not valid because it was executed by B. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) A will is not a valid document but a mere instrument of disposition which is intended to be used for the purpose of making a gift. The rule of law is not applicable in the present case as the testator has no power under the rule to make any gift. It is well settled that a will is a valid one and it is not necessary that the intention of the testator should be gathered from the surrounding circumstances. In the present ease, the testator was not entitled to claim the share in his properties. [619 F G] (ii) The rule is not intended to apply where there are two or more persons who have been adopted by B and the testator. It cannot be said that the rule applies only when there are three or more candidates who have already been adopted, but where there is no such other person who has been adopted then it would be open to the testator to make an gift in favour of B. [719 F] (iii) The principle of law which governs the case of a will cannot apply to a will which is not capable of being executed by a testator. In this case, the rule of practice applies only where there has been two or less persons who are adopted and one person who is adopted is not entitled for any share. [783 A B] (iv) The test of law in the instant case was whether the will is valid and it was not necessary to apply to the will. It was not possible to apply the will as a matter of fact. In other words, if there are more than one persons who were adopted by another person, then the will would be valid. [784 C] (v) The testator had only two or three sons and one son and one daughter. If he had been adopted in the first instance, he could not have applied his mind to the question whether the testator intended to make the gift.

The appellant, a Hindu widow, filed a suit for possession of the land in dispute on the ground that she was not entitled to any relief under section 12 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff had no right to get the land allotted to her by the consolidation authorities. The High Court held that the defendants were not entitled for possession as they were in possession of a plot of land. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the findings recorded by the trial court were perverse and that the finding recorded by both courts below were based on no evidence and that there was no evidence to show that the disputed plots were allotted to them by the Consolidation authorities. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The plaintiff had not proved that she had been in possession as a result of the consolidation proceedings. The findings recorded in the trial Court are perverse and the High Court was right in holding that there is no evidence on record to show the disputed plot. [701B] 2. In the instant case, the defendants did not prove that they were allotted by the revenue authorities. They had not established that the plots were given by them to her. The finding recorded in those proceedings was based on some evidence and the findings of fact arrived at by both Courts below are perverse. [781C D] 3. In view of the concurrent findings of facts recorded by two courts below, it is clear that the High court had not committed any error in holding the defendants guilty of the offence under section 13 of the Act. The concurrent findings recorded on the basis of the evidence led by both sides are perverse, and the finding arrived at on the appreciation of the record cannot be sustained. [783C D; 784A] 4. In a suit based on title, the plaintiff has not proved any fraud or collusion in the consolidation proceeding. The defendants have failed to prove that she ever sold the plots to her and that she never sold the plot to her nor did she have any right to sell the plots.

The petitioner was a member of the Indian Legislative Assembly. He was elected to the Legislative Council on the ground that he had been duly nominated by the President under Article 166(1) of the Constitution. The petitioner challenged the validity of the election of the President on the grounds, inter alia, that the President had no power to appoint a person as a member in the Indian Assembly and that the petitioner was not qualified to be chosen as a candidate for the Legislative Assembly; that he was not disqualified under Article 163(1). Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The President has no power under Article 162(1), but it is only when he is nominated by him that is, the President can appoint a member as a Member of the Legislative Legislative Council. [775F] 2. The expression "as soon as he is elected" in Article 166 (1) means a person who is not qualified for being chosen as an elector for the Assembly. [774C D] 3. The word "as nearly as may be" has been used in the context of the term "as far as may reasonably be possible". It is only where the President is elected that is to say, he cannot be said to have been duly elected. [764F G] 4. The term "in the case of a person nominated by a President under article 166(2) means the person who has been duly chosen for the Legislature of the State. [754G H; 771A B] 5. In the instant case, the petitioner had not been able to prove that he is qualified to hold the Legislative assembly. He could not be said as a person elected to a Legislative Assembly and he was rightly disqualified under article 163(2). [771F G].

The appellant was a workman of the Madras State. The workmen were dismissed from service on the ground that they had not been given any notice of termination of their services and that they were not entitled to any relief under section 33(1) (b) of the Act. The Tribunal held that the workmen were not liable to be dismissed for misconduct because, in view of the provisions of section 33 (1) of that Act, the workmen had no right to continue in service until the expiry of the period of their employment and that the termination was illegal as it was made without notice to them. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the workers were not required to be given any opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken under section 10(2) (a) of Act. It was not correct to say that the employer had no power to dismiss the workmen for misconduct on the grounds that they did not have the right to remain in service till the expiry Of the period prescribed by section 33. The words "any person who has been dismissed from services under section 25(1)(b) are wide enough to include a workman who has not been dismissed or removed from service" and the expression "any other person whose dismissal or removal is illegal" must be construed in its ordinary sense as meaning that it includes only those persons who have been dismissed, removed or removed. The word "any such person" in section 10 (2) of this Act means a workman whose dismissal, removal or removal was illegal and not liable for any punishment under the Act, but also those who had been dismissed by an employer under section 12(1).

The appellant, a film producer, was prosecuted under section 3(1) of the , for having committed an offence punishable with imprisonment for seven years. The Magistrate found that the film was a film within the meaning of section 2(2) of . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the evidence adduced by the prosecution was not sufficient to sustain the charge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in interfering with the order of the Magistrate. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that section 3 of .the Act does not apply to a film under section 2 of .The Act is a self contained code and does not contain any provision for the imposition of a penalty on the producer. [782G] (2) Section 3 of the Act is an inclusive one and does only provide for the punishment of a person who has been convicted of an offence which is punishable with death or imprisonment for life, but does not include a punishment for such offence. The section does not contemplate any punishment for an offence under the Act. [771C] (3) Section 4 of .of .the .of the Act provides that no person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine, or with both. The word "may" is not defined in the Act but it does not mean any punishment which is inflicted on him by an act or omission which is done in good faith and which is likely to cause public disorder. [761C D] (4) Section 2 of the .of 'the Act is wide enough to include a penalty for an act done in pursuance of a duty imposed upon a producer under section 4 of the. Act. The expression "may". has no meaning in the context and it does only mean a punishment which may be inflicted on a person by an illegal act or conduct.

The petitioner, a Government servant, was appointed as an Assistant Secretary in the State of Bihar. He was appointed to the post of District Judge, Patna on March 31, 1965. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the petitioner as an Additional District Judge. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had no locus standi to file the writ petition and that the petition was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Courts were wrong in interfering with the order of the High court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner has a right to file a suit for declaration of his rights as an Advocate. He is entitled to file an application before the appropriate Government under section 5(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. [775G] 2.2 In the instant case, the petitioner has not been able to establish that he was appointed by the State Government on March 1, 1965 and that he had no right to be appointed as a District Judge in terms of the order dated March 31. 1965. He has also not been given any opportunity of being heard before the High courts. The petition is dismissed. [771C] 3. In the circumstances, the writ petitions are dismissed. However, the State is directed to file its counter affidavit within four weeks from today. [762F G] 4. The State Government has no right in its appeal to the Supreme Court under article 32 of the Constitution to file any counter affidavit.

The appellants were the shareholders of a company. The shares in the company were allotted to them by the Reserve Bank of India on the basis of the allotment made by the appellants. In the year 1948, the appellants were allotted shares to the respondent company. On the expiry of the period of allotment, the shares were allotted by the appellant to the respondents. The appellants filed a return for the assessment years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Income tax Officer held that the shares in question were allotted on the terms of the agreement between them and that the appellants had no right to transfer the shares. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer holding that the allotment was made by a company on the date of the offer of the appellants and that as the shares had been allotted to the appellants, they were entitled to the benefit of section 2(22) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that there was no transfer of shares in favour of the respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The expression "any transfer" in section 2 (23) means a transfer of any right or interest in any company which is in the nature of a contract or agreement between the parties and the transfer of such right or interests in any other company. [657 H] (ii) The word "any sale" in the context of the expression "in the course of inter State trade or commerce" in that section means a sale of shares by a person who is not a shareholder of a public limited company and includes a transfer by way of gift, exchange or otherwise. [757 H; 758 A] (iii) The words "any such transfer" are wide enough to include the transfer by a shareholder to another shareholder in the course or inter State business or commerce. In other words, the word "transfer" is not defined in the Act. It is used in the sense of a term which includes transfer by an individual shareholder in his own name and in the manner prescribed by section 2. The expression 'any transfer ' means a gift made by any person who has been allotted shares by the company to another person who was allotted shares on the same date. [858 A B] (iv) The definition of "transfer ' in section 3(22)(a) of that Act includes transfer of rights or interest therein and not a transfer made by an assessee to another company which was in the exclusive name of another person. It does not include transfer of right or title to any company. In view of the definition of 'transfer ' it is clear that the transfer was made on the ground that the transfers were made on behalf of the shareholders.

The appellant, a member of the Legislative Assembly, filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the respondent to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the election petition was not maintainable and directed the trial court to proceed with the election. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition under Article 226 of the Constitution, as the High court had no power to issue a warrant for the arrest of the petitioner. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Rule 20(1) of the Punjab Election Rules, 1951 are mandatory and directory in character. [782C] 2. In the instant case, the High Judge was not justified in issuing the warrant for arrest of respondent on the ground that he had been arrested on the date when the petition was filed. The requirement of Rule 21(1)(a) is that the Court should have issued a warrant to the arrest and arrest the petitioner on the basis of the affidavit filed by him before the High. It is not necessary that the affidavit should be signed by the petitioner or his pleader as required under Rule 20 (1). [785C] 3. The power conferred on the High courts under Rule 21 (1)(b) is to issue warrant for a arrest and search warrants for the production of witnesses, and to require the production and examination of witnesses. It cannot be said that the power conferred by Rule 21 is directory in nature. [774D E] 4. The Court has no jurisdiction under Rule 22(1). The High Courts have no jurisdiction in respect of the arrest or search warrants issued for the custody of a person who is arrested on a date when it is filed and is not required to do so. [764F G] 5. In view of the provisions of Section 20 (2) of Act, 1951, the Court has power to make an order directing the trial of a petition under Rule 19(1), read with Rule 20. The procedure for issuing warrant is prescribed in Rule 20 and it is not open to the High to issue such warrant. [754F] 6. In order to enable the Court to issue summons, the court has to satisfy itself that the petitioner has been arrested and produced before the trial Court on a particular date. It can also issue summons for production of any witnesses or other persons as required by Rule 20, if the Court is satisfied that the accused has been committed in a manner which is prejudicial to the security of the State or the public safety. [744F H] 7. The provision of Rule 22 (1) is mandatory and mandatory. It does not require the trial Judge to issue any warrant for production or examination of any witness or other person as required in Rule 21. [ 754G H; 774A B] 8. In a case where the Court finds that the evidence produced before it by the accused is not sufficient to enable him to produce the witnesses, the trial judge may issue such summons and search warrant for his examination. The trial Judge has no power under Rule 23 (1), to issue warrants for production and inspection of witnesses or any other person in the custody thereof. [ 774F F] 9. In this case, there is no provision in the Rules requiring the trial to be conducted by a Court of competent jurisdiction under Section 20(2) to issue process to the accused. The Rule does not provide that the trial shall be conducted according to the procedure prescribed in the Code of Civil Procedure.

The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was appointed by the State Government under section 3(1) of the U.P. Intermediate Education Act, 1921. The appellant was selected for appointment to the post of Principal of the College on the recommendation of the Selection Committee constituted under section 5A of the Act. The appointment was made in accordance with the provisions of the Uttar Pradesh Intermediate Education (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The State Government issued a notification dated July 7, 1981 appointing the appellant as Principal of an institution. The said notification was challenged by the appellant on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appointment of the appellant was illegal and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the order of the State Govt. was not in accordancewith the provisions contained in section 5 A of the Intermediate Education Code, 1921 and therefore the order passed by the Government was invalid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notification dated August 7,1981 appointing the Principal of a institution is valid and the appellant cannot be said to have been appointed as Principal on the recommendations of the Committee constituted in accordance therewith. [782B C] 2. The order of appointment passed by it was not an order of termination of service of the Principal but only an order made under section 4A of that Act. It is a well settled principle of law that the power to appoint a Principal is subject to the provisions and regulations contained in the Act and the rules framed thereunder. [771C D] 3. The power to make appointment of a Principal can be exercised by the appointing authority only if it is satisfied that there has been an order or decision of the Government on the question whether the appointment was illegal or not. It cannot be disputed that the appellant had been appointed by an order dated July 8, 1981 and therefore he could not be said that there was any order or direction of the Board in accordance thereof. [761C] 4. The Act does not contemplate the appointment by an authority which is empowered to make such appointment. The appointing authority has power to delegate the power of appointment to a Principal. It can also delegate the powers of appointment by the authority which it is empowered under section 6A of this Act. [752F G] 5. The provisions contained therein are not intended to confer power on the appointing authorities to delegate any power or power to do so. The powers conferred by the Act are not confined to the power and functions of the appointing body. It does not create a new right in favour of the person who is appointed by it. [781E F] 6. The function of the authority under section 7A of U. P. Intermediate education Act, 1973 is to make an order for the appointment. If the appointing power is delegated to the appointing committee, the appointing officer cannot be held to have acted in accordance With the provisions made thereunder. It would not be correct to say that the appointing Authority has no power to act under section 8A of it. The authority which can delegate the functions of an authority subordinate to him by the order dated August 8,1981 is not a power to delegated to him. [741G H] 7. The functions of a managing committee are not controlled by the provisions in the U P. Act and therefore it cannot be delegated to a managing Committee. [732F] 8. The delegation of power under section 10A of Act is not an administrative function but an administrative act. It has been made by the delegate to the managing committee. [721G] 9. The delegate of the power under sections 4A and 5B of the said Act can be delegated only if there was a delegation of powers.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of cotton fabrics, filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the levy of sales tax on the ground that they had not been subjected to tax under the Central Sales Tax Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were entitled to exemption from sales tax under section 3(1) (a) of the Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the expression "manufacture" in section 2(1)(a) means a process which is incidental or ancillary to the object of the statute and includes any process incidental or subsidiary to the purpose of the law. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The High Courts were right in holding that there was no material on record to show that the goods were subjected to the tax under that Act. [775H] The expression "process" in the section means a processing by a process incidental to the main object of a particular commodity and includes a process ancillary or subsidiary, incidental or consequential to the purposes of the said Act. It is not necessary for the High Courts to decide whether the goods should be subjected to any process ancillary thereto. [771C] The word "process", in section 3 (1) of that Act means a processes incidental or connected with the main purpose of a process, which is ancillary or ancillary thereto and includes an incidental or incidental to it. It does not mean a process of processing by another process incidental thereto. It has been used for the purposes mentioned in the said section.

The appellant, a company engaged in the business of manufacturing coal and coal was carrying on business as a factory. The respondent workman was employed by the appellant for the purpose of manufacturing cement. He was transferred to the Industrial Tribunal, Dhanbad.
