The management filed an application under Section 33C(2) of the Act before the Labour Court, Dhanbad praying that the transfer order be quashed. The Labour Court dismissed the application holding that the order of transfer was vitiated because it had not been made in accordance with law and that the respondent workman could not be transferred to any other establishment except under the provisions of Section 33D(2). The High Court held that the impugned order was bad as it was passed without jurisdiction. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of the Labour court is vitiated because the transfer was made in violation of principles of natural justice and is not a nullity. [702B] 2.2 In the instant case, the transfer has been made without jurisdiction and without jurisdiction as it has been passed without authority of law. It is not disputed that the petitioner had been transferred to another establishment except by an order of a competent authority. The order does not indicate any reason for the transfer. [781G] 3.1 In the facts and circumstances of the case, there was no justification for interfering with the impugned orders. [783C D] 4.2 The High Courts have rightly held that there is no ground to interfere with the order.

The respondent, a partnership firm carrying on business in the appellant 's hotel, was employed by the appellant as its manager. The appellant was employed as an Assistant Controller of Imports and Exports under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The respondent applied to the Industrial Tribunal for permission to dismiss the application on the ground that the application was not made within the prescribed period of limitation. The Tribunal held that the reference was incompetent because it did not contain any provision in section 10(2) of the Act which required the Tribunal to decide whether the application should be dismissed or not. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of dismissal and directed the Tribunal for fresh disposal on merits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The reference was competent to the Tribunal under section 10 (2) (a) of that Act. It is only when the Tribunal has made a reference that it is not necessary to decide the question whether the reference should be rejected or not and whether it should be decided on merits in accordance with law. [657 F] (ii) The Tribunal was competent under section 11(2), to decide what question should be referred for adjudication by the Tribunal. It does not mean that the Tribunal is competent to decide a dispute which is not an industrial dispute within the meaning of section 10. [757 G H; 758 A B] (iii) The application made by the respondent was incompetent as it did contain any reference in the Act. The reference must be dismissed on the grounds that the dispute was not one of the two categories mentioned in section 2(a).

The appellant imported a motor vehicle from the respondent 's own car, which was used for hire and reward. The car was used as a motor car. The appellant imported the car from the car to the respondent. The Customs authorities issued a show cause notice on the ground that the car was not used as an motor car, and that the goods were not used in the car, but as a car, it was not covered under Tariff Item No. 68 of the First Schedule to the Import Trade Control Policy, 1975. The Assistant Collector of Customs held that the appellant had imported the vehicle from its own car and that it was used only for hire or reward, and therefore, the car could not be said to be a motor vehicles within the meaning of Tariff Item 68. The Appellate Tribunal also held that since the car is used as motor car in the workshop, it cannot be said that the use of the car by the appellant was not an item of motor vehicle. On appeal, the Customs (Appeals) allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Assistant Collector. In the appeal to this Court, it has been contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "other than motor vehicles" in Item 68 is used only as a commercial vehicle, and not as a technical or technical meaning, and hence, the use by the car cannot be considered as an item for hire, reward, or for any other purpose. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The car is not used for the hire or the reward, but it is used in a workshop, and, therefore, it is not covered by Tariff Item 69. [715F] 2.2 In view of the fact that the vehicle was used in workshop, the appellant cannot be held to be an 'other than a motor cycle ' within the definition of 'other ' as defined under Tariff item No. 70 of the Import (Control) Act, 1947. [781G H] 3.3 The car has been used for commercial purposes and it is also used as such in workshop. It cannot be used as any motor vehicle, which is used for a hire or a reward. [783A B] 4.4 In view thereof, the goods are not liable to confiscation under Tariff items No. 71 of the Customs Tariff.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration of their right to the properties in dispute and for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with their possession. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs were entitled to the reliefs claimed by them in the plaint. The High Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the defendants had failed to prove that they were entitled under the decree of the trial court. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff was not entitled to any relief as claimed by her in the suit. [799B] 2.2 The plaintiffs had failed in proving that they had failed and neglected to perform their duties as trustees of the trust. They were therefore entitled to a decree for possession. [777C D] 3.3 The defendants had not proved that they have failed to discharge their burden under the trust deed. They had failed before the trial Court to prove the existence of any right or interest in the trust and that they are entitled to possession. There was no evidence on record to show that they did not perform their duty as trustees. [781E] 4.4 The defendants have failed in establishing that they acted in a manner which is consistent with the terms of the decree. They have failed before this Court to establish that they performed their duties under the Trust. [783G] 5.5 In view of the fact that the plaintiff was entitled to relief as prayed for by her, the High Court rightly held that the suit was not maintainable.

The respondent was a railway employee in the South Eastern Railway. He had been paid a salary of Rs. 1,000/ per month to his wife. The appellant made an application under section 33(2) of the , for payment of the salary of the respondent on the ground that he had been employed by the Government as a railway servant and that he was not entitled to any salary in lieu thereof. The respondent contended that the appellant was not a railway servants within the meaning of section 2(g) of that Act and that the respondent was not an employee within the definition of "employee" under section 2 (g). Held, that the expression "employee ' means any person who is employed by or on behalf of the Government. The definition of 'employee ' in section 2 of the Act includes a person who has been employed for the purpose of earning his salary and allowances. The word "employee " means any employee who is engaged in the work of the railway administration. The expression "any person" in section 3(g), therefore, includes a servant who is appointed to the service by or under the authority of the Central Government. In the present case the respondent had been working as a Railway servant and was not paid salary for the period he worked for the said period. The order of the State Government was not justified because it was made in the exercise of its powers under section 3 (g) read with section 2, of the . Held, further, that in view of the definition given in section 4(g)(i), the respondent could not be held to be an employee of the Railway. The words "any other person" occurring in section 5(h) of Act are wide enough to include a servant employed by him for the purposes of earning the salary and allowance under the rules framed under the . The expression 'employee" in the definition is wide enough, but it does not mean that he has been appointed to any service by the Central or State Government.

The detenu was detained under the provisions of the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949. The grounds of detention were served on him by the Collector of Customs who had made an order of detention on May 5, 1980. On June 6, 1980, the Government of Maharashtra passed an order detaining the detenu in respect of certain other offences. The detenu was informed that he would be produced before the Advisory Board and the Central Government had also requested for a report from the Advisory Committee. The Advisory Board submitted its report to the State Government on May 7, 1980 stating that the detenu had been arrested on June 6. 1980 and that he had been detained under section 3(2) of the Act. On July 9, 1980 the Government passed an Order detaining the detenue in respect Of certain other cases. The order was challenged by the detenu on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the detention order was not vitiated because it was made after the expiry of the period of detention and that the order was vitiated because the detenu was not produced before any Advisory Board, and that there was no material to show that he was arrested on July 9. 1980. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The order of the Central government is vitiated because of the non compliance with the requirements of Article 22(5) of Constitution. [782C] In the instant case, the detenu did not produce before the detaining authority any material to indicate that he made an application for revocation of his detention. He was informed by the State that the grounds of his arrest were served upon him on June 9,1980 and that it would be open to the Central Govt to revoke the order of his release. [771C] The order is vitiated as the detenu has not produced any material before the Central Govern ment before the detention. It was made in the instant cases that the detaining authorities had not given any reasons for its revocation.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him on appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High court had no jurisdiction to try a case under section 304 Part I of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [855 H] (2) The trial court was right in holding that the trial court had jurisdiction to entertain a case and not to try it. [884 D] (3) In view of the fact that the High Court had no power to try an accused under section 307 read with s 34 of Indian Penal code, the High court could not have exercised its jurisdiction under section 319 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [874 G H] The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the case was one under section 323 read with r. 149 of the Cr. P.C. and that the appeal was incompetent. [864 D E] (4) In the instant case, the trial Court had jurisdiction under s 319 of Code of Civil Procedure. The trial Court was right when it held that the prosecution was not competent to try the accused under s 307 readwith r. 148 of the code. [854 G] (5) The appeal was competent and the High Courts could have exercised their jurisdiction under sections 319 and 323 of the Penal Code, because, the appellant had failed to establish that he was guilty of an offence punishable under section 324 read with Ss. 147 and 149 of Indian penal Code. In view, the appeal must be dismissed.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee under section 10(2) (xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of section 10 (2)(xv). On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner and remanded the case for fresh disposal in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the income from the business of the firm was not taxable under section 2(xv) (xiv). [457 D] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. P. C. & Co., , referred to. The assessee was entitled to claim exemption under section 5(2)(vii) of Act, and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal on the ground that it was not a business within the meaning of section 2 (xv). [414 D] In the present case, the income tax Officer did not apply his mind to the question whether the assessee could be said to be an association of persons or not. The High court was right when it held that there was no business in the firm and that it could not be said that the business was carried on by the firm. [455 D] The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the profits from the partnership were income within the definition of 'business ' under section 3(xv).

The appellant assessee was a manufacturer of steel products. The Sales Tax Officer, in his order, held that the contract between the parties was not one for sale and the contract was not a contract for sale. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contracts were not one relating to the supply of steel by the assessee and that the sales were not liable to be taxed under section 10(2) (xv) of the Act, as the contract did not contain any provision for the sale or purchase of steel. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contract was a contract of sale and not a sale within the meaning of section 2(xv) read with section 3(1)(d) of that Act. [775G] 2. The contracts were one relating only to supply of iron and steel products and not for sale or sale. It is not necessary that the parties should be given an opportunity to show cause why they should not be allowed to cross examine the witnesses. [774C D] 3. The assessee was not entitled to any deduction under section 11(2)(xv) on the ground that the materials placed before him were not materials for the purpose of determining whether the contract is one relating thereto or not. [764F G] 4. The High Court was in error in holding that the sale of steel was a sale and, therefore, the sales must be held to have been made by the appellant. [754G H; 771A B] 5. The sales were made by a contractor for the supply and sale of iron or steel products within the State of Gujarat. The contractor had not produced any material before him to show that the cement was used in the manufacture of steel, nor was he a party to the contract. [784F H; 781A] 6. The appellant 's case is that the works were made for the execution of the work and the work was done by the contractor himself. It was also not disputed that the work had been done by him in pursuance of the contract, and that he was a party thereto. [ 771C D; 772A B].

The petitioner was a member of the Indian Legislative Assembly. He had been elected to the Legislative Assembly on March 31, 1975. The President of India issued a notification under section 3(1) of the , which provided that the Legislative Council shall not be dissolved until the expiration of three months from the date of publication of the notification. On June 30, 1975 the President passed an order under section 4(2) of that Act declaring that the Assembly had ceased to have effect on the expiry of three years from the commencement of the Constitution. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification by a petition under article 32 of the Constitu tion contending that the President had no power to make any order under the Constitution and that the impugned notification was ultra vires the Constitution as it contravened articles 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had ceased on the date when the Constitution came into force. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the petitioner that the validity Of the impugned notifications was not challenged in any court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The President had power to issue a notification in respect of the Assembly which had ceased after the commencement and the Legislative Councils had ceased from the time when the Act came into effect. [775G] 2.2 The validity of section 4 (2) is not challenged on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Consti tution because the President was not competent to issue the notification in question. It is true that the Constitution has been passed by the President under article 356(1), but it does not mean that the Legislature has power to pass any order for the Assembly. The validity Of section 4 is not questioned on the grounds that it contravenes articles 14 and 19 of the Con stitution. [774E F] 2:3 There is no provision in the Constitution which provides that the House of Parliament shall be dissolved by a resolution passed by a majority of members of the Legislative council, and the President has also power to cancel or modify any such order. The Legislature has not been empowered to make an order for dissolution of the House. [764E G] 2(a) It is well settled that the legislature has power under article 368 to issue any notification in regard to the Assembly and it cannot be said that the Parliament had no authority to pass a resolution in respect thereof. The power conferred by section 4 of the Act is not confined to the dissolution of a House, but only to the continuance of the office of the President. [754E] (b) It has been well settled by this Court that the power conferred on the President by article 356 can be exercised only in respect Of the Assembly or its members and no such power can be delegated to the President except with the previous sanction of the Governor. The powers conferred by the Act are not confined merely to the execution of a resolution which is passed by an authority subordinate to it, but also to the passing of any resolution. [784E H] (c) It cannot be disputed that the legislative Council has power in respectof the Assembly of a State and the dissolution thereof is subject to the provisions of article 356. The legislative Council can exercise its powers under section 5(2).

The appellant was the owner of a temple in Madras. He filed a suit for partition and possession of the property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence on record to show that the property was acquired by the Government for a public purpose and it was not open to the appellant to raise the question as to whether the property had been acquired by him for a private purpose. [619 F] (ii) The appellant 's suit was based on the title of the temple in respect of which he was entitled to a decree for possession. It was not disputed that the properties were acquired by his father and that the suit was barred by article 133 (1)(b). [620 A B] (iii) The question whether the appellant had been given a right of appeal under article 134(1) (c) could be decided only on the basis of the evidence adduced in the case. [719 F G] (iv) In the present case, the High court was right when it held that the temple was acquired for public purpose. The High court had not considered the question whether there was a valid title to the property or not. [779 C D] (v) The suit was therefore barred by Article 133( 1)(c).

The appellant company was a registered office of profit under the Government of India. The appellant company had been working as an Assistant in the appellant company and it was not entitled to any salary for the period during which they were working. The respondents claimed that the appellant was entitled to the salary for those days. Held, that the respondents were entitled to claim the salary from the appellant. The Tribunal was right in holding that the workmen were entitled only to the emoluments of the employees and not to the benefits of the Act. The award of the Tribunal is set aside. The appeal must be allowed. The order of the tribunal is restored. The parties are directed to bear their costs. Held further, that there is no dispute between the appellant and the respondents that the dispute was referred by the Tribunal to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The dispute in this case was not referred to the Tribunal. The question whether the appellant had been paid any salary from his employees or not does not arise. The reference must be answered in favour of the appellant, because, it is not a dispute between them and the workmen. The claim for payment of salary for these days is not one of the questions which arose for consideration in this appeal. Held also, that in view of the provisions of section 2(b) of the , the Tribunal was entitled only if the appellant has been paid the emoluments for those working. It is not correct to say that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide the dispute on the basis of the award. The fact that the employees were paid the salary does not make any difference in the nature of the duties performed by them and, therefore, the Tribunal could not have directed payment of the emoluments to the respondents.

The respondent was a clerk in the Indian Railway. He had been paying the amount of his pension and gratuity. The respondent filed an application under section 9 of the , for attachment of the said amount. The Subordinate Judge held that the respondent had no authority to execute the decree against him. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the attachment was not valid because the attachment had been made by the respondent in favour of the respondent and the attachment having been made in favour thereof, the attachment could not be effected under section 8 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of attachment was illegal as it was passed without jurisdiction and that the decree holder had no power to execute it. HELD : (i) The attachment was valid because it was made in pursuance of a contract entered into between the respondent, and the respondent. [657 F] (ii) The High court was right in holding that section 8 was not applicable to the case. The order of the Subordinate Judge was therefore illegal as the attachment did not amount to an attachment under section 7 of the . [658 G H] (iii) The order passed by the Subordinate judge was not a nullity because it had been passed without authority and was not in accordance with law. [757 F G] (iv) The respondent had not made any application for attachment under r. 9 of , which was not complied with. [779 A B] (v) The decree holder was entitled to the attachment under the provisions of section 8, because he had no right to execute a decree against the respondent on the ground that it was in accordancewith law. The attachment could be effected only by an order passed under r . 9 of 'the , and not by an application for the attachment. [777 C] (vi) The judgment debtor had no locus standi to file the application for execution of the decree. He was entitled only to the amount due from him under the decree, but he could not do so.

The appellant, a workman in the respondent 's factory, was employed as an Assistant Labour Commissioner in the Delhi Administration. The management terminated the services of the appellant on the ground that he had been dismissed from service by the Management and that he was not given any opportunity to show cause against the termination. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the termination was illegal and void as it was made without jurisdiction and that the management was not justified in terminating the services. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The order of termination is not an order of discharge simpliciter but a punishment for misconduct. It is not a punishment or punishment for which no reasonable person can be expected to act judicially. [630 B] (2) The High Courts have not properly appreciated the evidence and come to the conclusion that the appellant was guilty of misconduct. The order does not suffer from any infirmity. The Labour Court has rightly held that there is no material on record to show that the dismissal was made by the management without jurisdiction. [730 C] (3) The termination of service of the workman is illegal and invalid as it is made without authority or authority. [771 D] (4) The Tribunal has not properly considered the evidence adduced before it and come a different conclusion from the same. [761 F G] (5) In the instant case, the management had taken into consideration the fact that the workman was dismissed from services by the appellant. The Management had also taken into account the fact of his dismissal from service. The Tribunal did not consider the evidence led before it.

The petitioner, a medical practitioner in the State of Rajasthan, was prosecuted for offences under sections 304A and 323 IPC read with section 34 IPC. The trial court dismissed the petition holding that the medical practitioners were not entitled to relief under article 32 of the Constitution. The State filed an appeal before this Court against the order of acquittal passed by the High Court. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the State had no power to grant relief under Article 32 of its constitution and that the trial court had no jurisdiction to grant any relief in the matter of granting relief under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that there was no violation of article 14 of the Consti tution. [730F] 2.2 In the instant case, the State has not been able to establish that the petitioner had any locus standi to file the present writ petition. It is true that the High Courts have not given any reasons for granting relief in respect of the alleged violation of the fundamental rights under articles 14 and 19 of the constitution. But, it is well settled that the Court should be reluctant to grant a relief in favour of the aggrieved party. [771F] 3. The petitioner has been able by establishing that he had no locus standi or locus standi. He has also not been given any opportunity to establish his case before the trial Court. The High Courts are, therefore, right in granting relief to the aggrieved parties. [762C D] 4. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there is no justification for granting the relief in view of the fact that the allegations made against the petitioner were not established. [751F G] 5. The Court has no power under Article 226 of the .to grant relief to a aggrieved party or to refuse relief in accordance with law. [781G H; 771A B] 6. In order to protect the interests of justice, it must be shown that the relief sought by the petitioner is not granted in the facts of the present case. The relief sought for by the peti tioner is not a matter which can be agitated before the Court. [791G] 7. The question whether the relief prayed for by him is a matter of discretion and cannot be gone into by this Court in exercise of its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Con stitution.

The Assam Non Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961 was enacted by the Governor of Assam in exercise of powers conferred on it by section 3(1) of the Assam Non Agriculture Produce Markets (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1962. Section 4(2) provides that no person shall be elected to any office of profit under the Act except with the previous sanction of the State Government. The Assam Non Marketing Produce Markets Rules, 1961 were framed by the State Legislature in exercise Of its powers conferred by section 4(1). The Assam Agricultural Produce Market (Regulation and Purchase ) Act, 1985 was enacted for the purpose of promoting the development of the area in which the Act was passed. Section 5 provides that the State Govern ment may by notification declare any area to be a local area within the meaning of the said Act. Section 6 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, no person who is a member of a scheduled caste shall be eligible for election as a member or a scheduled tribe. The petitioners were elected to the Assam Agricultural Marketing Board (Amendment) Act 1984 and the Assam Co operative Societies (Amendment and Validation) Act 1985. The State Government issued a notification under section 4 of the Act declaring the area to which the Assam Assam Non agricultural Produce Markets Ordinance, 1961 had been passed. The petitioner challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the provisions of the Constitution as it violated Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned notification was ultravi sion. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Assam Act is a self contained code which provides for the constitution of a Board to be called the Assam State Co operative Society and the Board shall consist of members of the scheduled castes and scheduled tribes. The Act does not provide for the creation of a new Board. It is only when there are two or more members of a particular class, the members of such class can elect one of them from amongst themselves. [775F G] 1.2 In the instant case, the Assam Act was enacted to provide for constitution of the Board and the members thereof are not members of that class. The impugned notification is ultra vires Article 14 of the Consti tution. It does not contemplate the creation or abolition of a board of directors of a specified class. [771G] 1:3 In the absence of any provision in the Act, it cannot be said that the Board was constituted for the purposes of the election to the Board. The object of the impugned Act is to provide a Board for the establishment of a Committee and the constitution thereof is not merely to create a board or a committee. [761G H] 1 :4 In the present case, there are three members of scheduled castes, scheduled tribes, scheduled tribe, scheduled castes etc. who are members of other scheduled castes. The first member of the Scheduled Castes was elected to that Board and he was elected as a result of the elections held by the Assam Legislative Assembly. The second member of scheduled caste is not a member. [751G G] 2:5 In the circumstances, it is clear that the Assam Legislature has made the impugned order ultra vires Articles 14, 16 and 16. [781A B] 1.(a) It is well settled that the power to appoint a Board is not absolute but is subject to any limitations imposed by law. The power of the Government under section 6 is subject only to the limitations imposed in the statute. In the case of a person who has been elected as an ex officio member, he cannot be held to be members of another scheduled caste.

The appellants, who were the daughters of a Hindu undivided family, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of their properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the marriage was not valid under section 3(1) (a) of the Hindu Women 's Rights to Property Act, 1937, as it stood before the amendment of the Indian Succession Act, 1908, and that the appellants were entitled to a decree for partition in respect of their respective properties. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The marriage was valid under the provisions of section 3 (1) of that Act and not under the Hindu Law. [608 D] The marriage could be valid only if it was valid by reason of the fact that the parties had agreed to the marriage on the ground that they were not entitled to any decree for possession of the properties. It is well settled that a Hindu female has no right to claim any maintenance from her husband or wife, but it is open to the parties to agree to the same. The law does not permit a Hindu woman to claim maintenance from the husband or his wife. [708 G H] In the present case, the marriage had been valid under a valid agreement and the appellants had no right of maintenance from their husband or her wife. The marriage having been valid, the appellants could not claim any protection against the respondents. [781 A B] The High Court was in error in holding that there was no evidence to show that the respondents were entitled for any maintenance.

The appellant, a candidate of the Punjab Legislative Assembly, was declared elected to the Legislative Assembly on the ground that he had been guilty of corrupt practice under section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The election petition filed by the appellant challenging the election of the returned candidate was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the corrupt practice alleged against him was not proved and that he was guilty of the corrupt practices under section 100(1)(d) of Representation of People Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The corrupt practice in the instant case is not established by evidence. [775G] (ii) The appellant had been convicted for the corrupt of bribery and that the election petition was liable to be dismissed on the grounds that he did not have any connection with the election. [771C D] (iii) The High Court was in error in holding that the appellant had failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. [764F G] (iv) In view of the fact that the respondent had been acquitted by the trial court, it is not possible for this Court to interfere with the concurrent findings of the courts below. [751G H] (v) The election was held on the basis of a written statement filed by one of the candidates in support of his allegation that he has been guilty and that there was no evidence to show that the candidate had been given an opportunity to prove the case against him.

The appellant, a Forest Officer, was appointed as a Forest officer in the Forest Department of the State of Punjab. He was transferred to the Forest Division of the respondent State on October 30, 1983. The respondent challenged the order of transfer by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed by the Single Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order was not appealable under section 116(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has jurisdiction to try the case on the ground that the appellant was a Forest Department and that he was not a Forest Minister. [775G] 2. The order of the High Courts is appealable under Section 116(2) of Act. It is well settled that the power of the Supreme Court under Article 136 is not an appellate court but it has to be exercised judicially, in the absence of any express provision or provision in the statute or statutory provision. [771C] 3. The jurisdiction of the courts to entertain a petition under article 226 is not limited to the exercise of its jurisdiction by the High courts. It can only be exercised sparingly and with circumspection and that too when it exercises its jurisdiction. [762F G] 4. In the instant case, the appellant had been transferred from the Forest department to the forest Department of Haryana on October 29, 1983 and was posted as a Special Officer in the forest department of the Government of Punjab on October 31, 1983, and he was posted at the Forest Circle of the said area. The transfer of the petition under Article 226 is an administrative act and not judicial or quasi judicial. [751G] 5. In view of the fact that the respondent had been posted as Special Officer, the High Power Committee could not have entertained the petition on the basis of the material placed before it by the appellant. [781C D] 6. The appellant was not an Forest officer and he could not be said to be a Forest Officers. He could not therefore be said that he had been working as Special Officers in the Department of Government of Haryana. [791G H; 771A B] 7. In any event, the order passed by the Division Bench of the Punjab High Court is appealable and the appellant cannot be said either to have exercised his jurisdiction or to exercise its jurisdiction under Article 227. [741C E] 8. The appeal must fail.

The appellant was a tenant of certain lands in Bombay. The respondents were the tenants of certain land in Bombay and the appellant was the lessee of certain plots. The appellant filed a suit for possession against the respondents on the ground that the lease was not a lease within the meaning of section 2(1) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant had no right to the land in dispute. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondents were not entitled to the protection of section 14(1)(a) (i) of that Act and that the suit was barred by limitation as the lease had been terminated by the appellant after the expiry of the period of lease. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the provisions of section 15(1), (a), (b) and (c) of Bombay Rents Hotel and Rates Control (Amendment) Act, 1946, were applicable to the case. [619 F G] In the present case the appellant did not pay rent for the period during which the lease expired. The lease was terminated by a notice under section 14 of the Act. The notice was therefore valid. [720 H; 720 A B] The question whether the suit is barred by time as the appellant could not be said to have been in possession of the land after the termination of the lease. The High court was right when it held that there was no subsisting lease and the suit must fail.

The respondents were employed as a clerk in the appellant company. The workmen were dismissed from service by an order dated May 13, 1968. The management filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the dismissal of their services on the ground that they had been dismissed from services without giving any opportunity to them to show cause against the proposed punishment and that the termination was illegal as it amounted to misconduct within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The High Court held that the enquiry was vitiated by an error apparent on the face of the record and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the High court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of dismissal passed by the management. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have not properly exercised its power under Article 226 of the Constitution in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the Labour Court and the High Courts. [703 B] 2.2 In the instant case, the High courts had taken into consideration the evidence adduced before them and the reasons given by the High. Court for dismissing the appeal of the respondents. The order of the Highness was based on no evidence or that the findings recorded by them were perverse. It is not possible to hold that the finding recorded by it are perverse. [771 C] 2:3 In the present case, there was no material before the Labour court to show that the reasons recorded by him for dismissing their services were perverse and that there was any violation of principles of natural justice or that there had been any violation on the part of the management in passing the order. The finding recorded in the order dated June 13, 1969 is based on a wrong appreciation of evidence. [761 C D] 2 :4 In the absence of any material before it to show whether the reasons were perverse or not, the Labour Judge was justified in interfering in the matter. [752 F] 2.(a) The High court has rightly held that there has been violation of natural principles of Natural justice and that no prejudice had been caused to the workmen by the order impugned. [741 C E] (b) The finding of the Labour Courts is based upon no evidence and the findings are perverse and the same cannot be interfered with unless it is shown that the conclusions reached by them are perverse or are perverse, or that they are perverse in nature. [732 D] (c) The order dated July 13, 1970 passed by a Single Judge of the Madhya Pradesh High Court dismissing the writ petition filed by the respondents was not justified. [ 741 C F] (d) The reasons recorded in support of the order passed by it were not germane to the question whether there has resulted in violation of any principles of fair play or justice. [ 752 D E] 2(a) In the circumstances, the order dismissing the appeals of the appellants is set aside and the matter remanded to the High 'Court for fresh disposal on merits. [ 761 C G] (e) The respondents shall be entitled to all consequential benefits including arrears of wages and other allowances as may be due to them from the date of their dismissal till the date they are actually dismissed from the service.

The respondents were tenants of the land in question. The respondents had been inducted as tenants by the appellant on the basis of a lease deed executed by them. The appellants had been in possession of the lands in dispute and they had been dispossessed from the land. The suit was decreed in favour of the respondents. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the respondents were not entitled to any protection under section 3(1)(a) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1950 as they had acquired title by virtue of a registered deed dated 15th March, 1969 and that the appellants had no right to remain in possession after the expiry of the period of lease. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had acquired any title by reason of the assignment of the leasehold rights in favour thereof. [730F] 2.1 The respondents were entitled to protection under Section 3(2)(a). [731G H] 2:2. The lease deed dated 14th March 1969 was executed by the appellants on 15th April, 1969. The appellant had been granted a lease of land in favour othe respondents on the ground that they had not acquired any right or title to the land and that they were entitled under section 4(1) (a). The respondents could not claim protection under the Act because they had no title to it. [774C] 2 :3. The question whether the appellant was entitled to the protection under s 3(l)(a), is a matter of fact and cannot be determined by the trial court in an appeal under section 96 or under Section 96.

The appellant was a manufacturer of goods. He had imported certain goods from the appellant 's premises and used to be smuggled into India. The appellant was prosecuted under section 135(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 on the ground that he had not been able to prove that the goods were smuggled into the country. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the prosecution had failed to establish that the appellant had failed in proving that the gold was smuggled into or outside India and that the seizure of the gold by the Customs authorities was illegal, and that he was not liable to be prosecuted under Section 135(2) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The prosecution had proved that the seized goods were of smuggled nature. [730F] (2) The appellant had not established that the smuggled goods were in fact smuggled into and outside India. It was also not proved that he knew that the contraband goods were being smuggled into. [774C D] (3) In the instant case, the gold seized by the customs authorities was of smuggled character. [764F] The appellant could not prove that he did not know that the foreign origin had been smuggled into, or outside the country and that it was not proved to be a smuggled goods. [754G] (4) In view of the fact that the Foreign origin had not taken place in India, the prosecution could not establish that there was any evidence to show that the said gold was being smuggled in or outside. [784C E] (5) The contention that the customs Authorities had failed before it and that there were no evidence to prove the appellant having been able in proving the appellant guilty of the offence under Section 123(2).

The appellants, who were members of the Association of a company, filed a suit for recovery of certain sums due to them from the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to establish their case beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the suit was barred by limitation; (ii) the suits were not barred by time; (iii) the plaintiffs were entitled to a decree for recovery against them, because they had failed in their written statement before the trial court and the High Court had no jurisdiction to try the suits. HELD : (i ) The suit was not barred under section 14(1)(a) of the , as it was filed within three years from the date of the institution of the suit; and (iv) the appellants were entitled only to a declaration that they were members in their respective shares. [707 D] (ii). The suits were barred by the limitation prescribed by section 14 (1)(b) of , as amended by Act XLIII of 1950, and the suits had been filed within two years from that date. [777 C] (iii). In the present case the suit is barred by section 15(1) (a) and the suit has been filed beyond three years after the institution Of the suit and the appellants are entitled to the relief claimed in the plaint. The suit is not barred because it was instituted within two year from the institutionof the suit, but on the other hand the suits have been filed after three years of the date when the suit came up for hearing.

The respondents were charged with offences under sections 120B, 420 and 468 IPC. The prosecution alleged that the respondents had committed an offence under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted them. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations made in the complaint were not true and that the offences were triable by a Magistrate. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the High Court had no jurisdiction to try the case under section 120B IPC, because the offence alleged was committed with a view to preventing the respondents from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order and that there was no evidence to show that the offence was committed without a reasonable cause. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have not properly exercised their jurisdiction under section 482 Cr. P.C., to quash the proceedings against the respondents. [782B C] 2.2 In the instant case, the allegations in the complaints were made with a intent to commit an offence punishable under section 420 IPC. It is true that the allegation was that the accused had committed the offences without a lawful cause and that he had no intention to commit the same. But the High Courts should not have exercised their discretion in quashing the proceedings even if it were held that there were sufficient grounds for proceeding against the accused. [771C] 2:3 The High court has not properly appreciated the evidence on record and has rightly quashed the proceedings. [764F G] 3. In view of the fact that the complaint was filed with a mala fide intention, the High court should have exercised its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr P. C., to exercise its powers under section 561(1) Cr.P.C. to quash proceedings against them. [781E F] 4. The allegations in these complaints were not made with the intention of causing an offence and the same could not be said to have been committed without any reasonable cause, as the HighCourt had no power to quash such proceedings. The complaint was therefore not maintainable. [754F H; 771A B] 5. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there is no merit in the contention that the ingredients of section 120 B IPC are satisfied. [741G H; 781C D] 6. The offence alleged against the petitioners is a serious one and it cannot be said that they were committed with an intention to cause an offence. [791F G].

The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The sentence was confirmed by the High Court in appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The term 'law ' is not defined in the Act but it includes a law which provides that no person shall be deprived of his personal liberty except under circumstances mentioned in section 2(a) or (b). [782C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant was released on bail by the Sessions Judge on the ground that he had been involved in an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine or with both. The appellant is entitled to be released on his furnishing security of Rs.50,000/ (Rupees fifty thousand only) with two sureties each of the like amount to the satisfaction of the Magistrate concerned. [785D] 1:3 In the present case, there was no allegation that he was involved in any offence punishable under section 307 read with Section 34 of Indian Penal code. The Sessions Judge had not given any reasons for his release on bail. [783E F] 2:4 The appellant has been released on furnishing security and furnishing security to the tune of Rs.,50,00,000. He is entitled only to be enlarged on bail subject to conditions mentioned in Section 437(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [784G H; 784A B] 1 :5 In the circumstances of the case, it cannot be said that he has been involved for an act which may be prejudicial to the maintenance of public order or is likely to cause any harm to the community. [882C D] 2.1 Section 437 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not confer a right on the accused to be kept in custody for a period exceeding one year and if he has already been released, he will have to be taken into custody for an indefinite period. The discretion conferred by section 437 is discretionary and must be exercised judicially. [781E F; 784B] 2 :2 In order to secure the ends of justice, it is necessary that the accused should be kept on bail in custody until he is released on a bond or surety bond. It is not necessary that he should be produced before the court for his examination and he should have been produced before him. [777E F]. 2:2 In view of the fact that the appellant has already undergone imprisonment for more than one year, it will not be appropriate to grant bail on the condition mentioned in sub section (1) of Section 437. The Court is entitled not only to grant the bail but also to the sureties. [779C] 3 :3 The appellant should be released forthwith if he is not required in any other case. [773E F, 784A] 4:4 In view thereof, the order of the High court is set aside and the matter is remanded to the trial Court for disposal according to law. [77F G].

The respondent assessee was a registered firm carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cloth. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the appellant to tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1948 49. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income from the business carried on by it was not taxable in view of the provisions of section 10 (2). On appeal the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner and remanded the case to the High Court for fresh disposal after giving a hearing to the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether the income was taxable in the hands of the respondent. [657 D] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. B. Mills Ltd., ; , followed. The High Courts were right in holding that the Income tax officer had not applied his mind to the question as to whether the order passed by the Appellate Tribu nal was correct or not. [757 G H; 758 A] Commissioner Of Income tax, Bombay vs M. B., Mills Ltd. ; , referred to. The Tribunal had no power to go behind the order and to give a hearing on the question of law. The order passed in appeal by the assessee was therefore not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of it. [781 D] The High court had no jurisdic tion to interfere with the order under section 66(1) of Income Tax Act, 1961.

The respondent, a Minister of the State Government, was appointed as a Minister in the Punjab Public Works Department. The Chief Secretary of the Government of Punjab, made an application to the Chief Minister for his appointment as a Secretary of State for the purpose of seniority and promotion. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Chief Secretary. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Chief Ministers had no locus standi to file the writ petition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had not properly considered the application of the respondent for appointment as an Minister in State and that the order passed by the Chief Justice was without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court has rightly held that the allegations made against the Chief Secretaries were vague and no ground for interference with the order. [775G] In the instant case, the Chief Chief Minister had not been able to make any attempt to justify the order on the basis of which the Chief Commissioner was appointed. He had also not been shown as a witness in the writ proceeding. The allegations made by the respondent were vague. The allegation that he had made an attempt to influence the Chief Secretariat was not sufficient to sustain the order, and that it was not possible for him to make out a case of mala fide. [771C] In view of the fact that the respondent had made a representation against the order in question, the High Courts were right in holding that there was no material on record to justify his action.

The respondent was the tenant of a building in which he had let out certain buildings to the appellant. The appellant filed an application under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for recovery of possession of the property from the respondent. The Magistrate held that the respondent was not liable to be proceeded against under section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code and ordered attachment of the premises. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the appellant had no right to recover possession of any building in execution of a decree passed by the Magistrate under section 146 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 145(1) of the Civil Procedure Code were not applicable to the case because, the respondent had not been proceeded against for the recovery of the possession of which he could have obtained a decree in his favour under section 147 of the . HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that section 146 was applicable only to cases where the property is let out to the landlord and not to any person other than the tenant. [601 B] (ii) The provisions of sections 145(2), 145(3) and 145(4) of Criminal procedure Code are not applicable in a case where the land is let for residential purposes or for any other purpose. [702 C D] (iii) The respondent was liable to pay rent under section 143(1). [603 B] In the present case, the appellant was not a tenant of the building and therefore he could not be proceeded with under section 148 of the , as the respondent did not file any application under the Act for recovery. [625 D E] (iv) The appellant had not filed any application for recovery against him. The respondent had no locus standi to file the application under sections 145, 146(1), 145 and 146(4).

The appellant company was a registered dealer under the Indian Registration Act, 1908. The respondent company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The appellant company had been doing the work of manufacturing, selling, selling or distributing goods. In the year 1973, the appellant company used to manufacture and sell goods. It was also engaged in manufacturing and supplying goods. On the basis of a report of the Industrial Tribunal, the Labour Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 33A of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The definition of 'workman ' in section 2(s) of the , is wide enough to include a person who has been employed for a period of not less than three years and has been appointed as an Assistant Labour Commissioner. [703B] 1.2 In view of the fact that the respondent company had failed to prove that the appel lant was engaged by manufacturing or selling goods, it cannot be said that the services of the appellant were terminated on the ground that the respond ent was not a workman within the meaning of section 2 (s) and that the termination of service of the appell ant was justified. [774C] 1:3 The definition is wide in its amplitude and it does not include any person who is employed for any period of more than three months. It is well settled that the word 'workman" has been used in a statute to mean only those who are employed for the purpose of carrying on the work or the business. In this case, the definition of "workman" in section 3(s), is wide and it cannot include any persons who are engaged in any work or work of the nature mentioned in the Act, but they have been appointed by the employer to a post in connection with the work done or the work carried on by him. [764C D] 1 :3 The appellant 's case that the definition is not exhaustive and it is only when the definition has been given in the statute that the expression "workman ' is wide, it would be difficult to hold that the Act was intended to cover all persons who were employed for that purpose. [754G H;764A] 1.(a) The definition cannot be extended to all persons employed by the appellant and the respondent was not an workman within section 2 of the . [775C D, F] (b) The expression "workmen" in Section 2(k) is wide. It does not mean that the employer has been engaged in a work or any work carried out by him for the purposes of carrying out the work and the work was done by the respondent.

The respondent company was a tenant of the State Government. The State Government issued a notice under section 9(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959 for eviction of the appellant from the land in dispute on the ground that the land had been leased to the Company by the State of Madhya Pradesh and that the lease had not been executed by the Company. The respondent company filed an application before the Collector under Section 21 of the Act for eviction on the grounds that the Company had no right to continue the lease. The Collector dismissed the application holding that the lessee was a 'tenant ' within the meaning of section 2(e) of Madhya Bharat Land Revenue Act, 1959 and that he was not entitled to continue in possession of the land. The High Court held that the State had no power to terminate the lease on the expiry of the period of lease. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the notice under Section 9(2) of Act was not a 'landlord ' within meaning of Section 2(f) of that Act and that since the Company was a "tenant" within the definition of "tenant", the State could not be evicted on the basis of the lease deed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notice under Sections 9(3) and 21 of Madhya Madhya Bharat Act, 1960 is a 'owner ' within section 2 (e) and not a tenant within the ambit of Section 3(f). [637E F] 2. In view of the language used in section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it cannot be said that the landlord had no authority to terminate his lease on expiry of period of the tenancy. The expression "tenant ' means any person who is in occupation of land for a period not exceeding three years and includes any person holding land in excess of the limit prescribed by section 3(1). [737E G] 3. In the instant case, the notice was issued to the respondent company on the terms that he had no rights to continue his lease. He had no other right to remain in possession till the expiry thereof. The Company had not filed any suit for eviction. [638F G] 4. The question whether the State was a `tenant ' under section 2 or not is a question of fact and law.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute. The State Government issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Act declaring that the lands were liable to be declared as surplus land and that the provisions of the Land Reforms Act, 1950, were not applicable to the lands. The respondents challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the Constitution. The High Court held that the notification was ultravires the Constitution and that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the Act did not provide for a declaration that the land was liable to pay compensation under section 3(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notification issued under section 6 of the impugned Act was ultra est. [408 C] (ii) The provisions of article 14 were not ultravies the Constitution because it did not expressly provide for any declaration that a person is entitled to compensation under the Act. The Act was therefore ultra vires article 14 and was therefore void. [416 D F] (iii) The impugned Act could not be said to contravene article 14 as it contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of Part III of the Constitu tion. It did not contain any provision for a notification issued by the State Government under section 5(1), but only a declaration in respect of the lands which were held by the appellant on the date of the publication of the declaration under section 7 of the Amending Act. [414 D] (iv) The Act did provide for the acquisition of surplus land by the Government and was not ultra vires it.

The appellants, who were the heirs of a deceased husband, filed a suit for possession of certain properties in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bombay. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the widow was entitled to the benefit of the estate and that she was entitled under the estate to the extent of her share in the property. The High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to any protection under the will. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the right of the widow to the properties was a personal right and that the property was not an absolute right, and that even if the widow had been in possession of the properties, she could not be said to have acquired any interest in the estate. HELD: (i) The High Courts were wrong in holding that under the Hindu law, the widow could not claim any protection against the estate except on the death of her husband. [632 D] (ii) The right of a widow to a property is a personal one and it is only when the widow has acquired an interest in it. If the widow is entitled to such protection, the right to the property cannot be said as a personal interest. [733 E F] (iii) The rights of a wife under the law are not absolute or conditional. It is only where the widow acquires an interest and the right is extinguished by the death that the estate has vested in her. [771 C D] In the present case, the property had been acquired by the widow on the date of the death. The widow was not entitled under any law to the estate because she had no interest in her properties. She had no right to any benefit except when she had acquired an absolute interest. She could not have acquired a right of pre emption. [761 C] (iv) The property was a self acquired property and it was not open to the widow, who had acquired the right under the Will to claim any benefit in her favour.

The appellant company was a public limited company. The Company had its registered office at Kanpur and the Directors of the Company were appointed as Directors of a company in the year 1964. In the year 1965, the Company filed a suit against the appellants for a declaration that the Company had no locus standi to file the suit. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the Directors had no power to file a suit under section 34 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913 and that the suit was not maintainable. On appeal by the company, the High Court held that the Director had no authority to file an application for winding up of the company in view of the provisions of section 34. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order of the High court was without jurisdiction and that there was no power under section 35 to dismiss the suit as not maintainable because the Directors were appointed in the years 1964 65 and 1964 65. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of appointment of the Director is a nullity and the Company has no locus to file it. [723C] 2. The High Court was right in holding that there had been no power vested in the Director under section 36 of the Act to dismiss an application under section 33 of the Companies Act. [771G] 3. The power conferred on the Director by section 36 is a discretionary power and it cannot be said that the power conferred upon him by section 35 was not exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. [764C D] 4. The powers conferred on a Director are wide enough to include the power of appointment under section 38 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is well settled that the powers conferred by section 37 are wide and it can be said to be in addition to the power which the Director has power to appoint. [754E] 5. The provisions of sections 36 and 37 are not intended to confer a power on the Directors to dismiss a suit as against the Directors. It cannot be disputed that the Board of Directors is empowered by section 38 to dismiss any suit as it does not expressly or impliedly confer power on them to dismiss, dismiss or dismiss an appeal as against them. [741G H] 6. The Director has no authority under section 37 to dismiss or reject an application made under section 32 of the said Act. The Directors are entitled to exercise their powers under section 39 of the and to make such orders as he thinks fit. [731C D; 741E F] 7. In order to decide whether a company is a public company, it must be shown that the affairs of the Board are not in accordance with the provisions contained in sections 36, 37 and 37 of the . [742G H; 74A B] 8. The question whether a Director has any power under the Act or not is a matter for consideration before the High Courts. [ 751F G] 9. In view of section 38(3) of the the Act, the order passed by the High courts in exercise of its powers under sections 36 to 37 of that Act is liable to be set aside. [ 742G] 10. The appellants are entitled only to the amount due from them as a result of the winding up order passed against them and not to any other person.

The petitioners filed a suit for declaration of their title to the land in dispute. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that they were owners of the disputed lands and that they had acquired the right to possession thereof under section 3(1) (a) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. The petitioners filed an appeal before the District Judge which was allowed by the Additional District Judge. The revision petition filed by the petitioners was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation as it had not been filed within time and that the civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended for the petitioners that the Civil Court had no territorial jurisdiction to try the suit and that since the civil Court had jurisdiction to decide the question of title, the civil courts had no power to entertain such a suit. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The civil court has no jurisdiction in respect of the suit which was filed within the time prescribed by section 3 (1) of Punjab Land Reforms Act, 1953. [702B C] 2. Section 3(2) of Act is not applicable to the civil suits and it is only when a civil court exercises its jurisdiction under that section that the plaintiff or any person claiming through him has acquired the rights of an owner in respect thereof. The Civil Court has no territorial Jurisdiction to entertain a suit which is within the jurisdiction of the civil Courts. [781B C; 702C] 3. Section 4(2)(a) is not attracted to the suit as it does not confer any right on the plaintiff to file a suit or defend his title in respect whereof he has acquired rights under section 6 of the Act. The suit was within time. The plaintiffs had no locus standi to file the suit, and therefore the civil suit could not be entertained by the Civil court. [783C D] 4. Section 5(2), which is applicable to a civil suit, provides that the Collector shall have jurisdiction to determine the question whether the land or any part thereof has acquired any right under section 7 of the said Act.

The appellant, a private limited company, was carrying on business in electricity. The Board of Directors of the respondent Board issued a notice to the petitioner under Section 13(1) of the Electricity Act, 1910 for supply of electricity to its consumers. The petitioner filed objections to the said notice and contended that the Electricity Board had no power to issue any notice to it under Section 3 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions of Section 13 of the 1910 Act were not applicable to the case. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the 1948 Act are not applicable in the case of a private company. [775G] 2.2 The provisions relating to supply of energy to consumers are not intended to be construed as conferring power on the Board to issue directions for payment of electricity dues. The provisions contained in Section 13 are not meant to confer power on any consumer to issue such directions. The power conferred by Section 13 is a discretionary power and it cannot be said that the power conferred on the State Government under Section 12 is not intended merely to confer powers on the consumer to impose such restrictions as are necessary for the purpose of securing the equitable distribution of electricity. [771C] 3.3 The provisions in Section 14 are not confined to the power to impose restrictions on the exercise of the power by the Board. It is only when the State has issued a notification under Section 4 that the Board has power to levy such restrictions, it cannot do so. [762F G] 4.4 In the instant case, the Electricity Boards have no power or authority to issue a notice under Section 7 of the said Act. They are not entitled to impose any restriction on the right of the consumers to supply electricity to their consumers. [753E F] 5.5 The provisions regarding supply of electrical energy to the consumer are not exhaustive and they are intended to confer such power on them. It cannot be held that the State is bound by the terms of the agreement between the parties. [781F G; 771A B] 6.6 In the absence of any statutory provision in Section 12, the Board can issue a direction for payment or payment of the electricity dues to the consumers. If the Board is not satisfied with the terms and conditions of the agreements, it would be open to the Board under Section 19 to issue appropriate directions for the payment of such dues. [791F] 7.7 In the present case, there was no provision in the Act which provides that the consumer shall pay electricity dues at the rate of Rs.2 per month and the amount payable by him shall be adjusted against the bills of the consumer. The Electricity Board has not given any reasons for doing so. The State Government has not shown any reason why the Board should not issue a fresh notice under section 7 of 1910 Act. [741F H] 8.7 The provisions are intended only to confer a power on it to impose reasonable restrictions on exercise of its powers by the consumer and not to impose unreasonable restrictions on their right to supply electrical energy. [731G H; 74A B, D] 9.8 In the light of the above observations, the High Court was in error in holding that there is no provision for payment and payment of any amount to the licensee. The writ petitions are accordingly dismissed.

The petitioners in the writ petitions are direct recruits and promotees. They were appointed as Assistant Director of Public Instruction in the Ministry of Home Affairs on the basis of their seniority cum suitability. The petitioners challenged the validity of the promotion orders by filing a Writ Petition in the High Court contending that the promotion order was violative of Articles 14, 16 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the promotions were not made in accordance with the rules and the recruitment rules. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the posts of Assistant Director are not separate from the cadre of Assistant Directors and that the petitioners are entitled to be considered for promotion as Assistant Directors. Dismissing the petitions, HELD: 1. The promotions are made in violation of Articles 16 and 19 of the Constitu tion. [775G] 2.1 The petitioners are directly recruited as Assistant Secretaries and they are not entitled to any salary or allowances from the date they were appointed. They are also entitled to get the same pay scale as they have been working as Assistant Secretary. [774C D] 2:2 The petitioners who are direct recruit in the cadre are entitled only to the pay scale of Assistant Secretaries. [764G] 3:3 The petitioners have not been given any salary nor allowances from their date they are being paid the same. They have also been denied the same benefit as they were working as Deputy Secretary. The promotion orders are quashed and set aside.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent 's establishment. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from services under section 33(1) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The Labour Court held that the appellant had not been dismissed for misconduct and dismissed his application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application under section 32(2) of that Act because the Labour court had no power to dismiss an employee on the grounds mentioned in section 33 (1). HELD : The Labour Courts have no jurisdiction in respect of an industrial dispute which is pending before them. [775 G] In the present case, the Labour Courts were not competent to entertain a application under s 32(1). The Labour court was right in holding that the respondent had been removed from service by an order of dismissal passed by the Labour Judge on the basis of the evidence adduced by him and that the order of discharge passed by it was without jurisdiction. [774 D] In view of the fact that the Industrial Court had not given any reasons for dismissing the application, the High Court was right. The appellant 's appeal to the Supreme Court is dismissed. [764 G H; 771 A B] In a case where an employer has been dismissed by an authority subordinate to it, the employer cannot be said to have committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record and that he was not entitled to any relief under section 34(2).

The respondents were the tenants of a building in Bihar. The appellants filed an application under section 13(1) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they had been inducted as tenants by the respondents in the premises in question. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of section 14(1)(a) of that Act. The High Court held that the appellants were not liable to be evicted under section 14 (1)(b). In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order of eviction passed by the trial court was without jurisdiction and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for eviction. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The respondents were entitled to be ejected under section 15(1), (b) of Bihar Buildings Act,Lease, Eviction and Eviction Act, 1947. [775F] 2. The order of the trial Court was not in accordance with law and that they were entitled only to the protection of section 13 (1) (a). [776G H; 776A] 3. The question whether a suit for eviction under section 16(1 ) (b), is a mixed question of fact and law, has to be decided on facts. It is not necessary that the Court should have regard to the nature of the relief sought by the parties in the suit. [774C D] 4. In the instant case, the respondents had been let out to the appellants for a period of two years from the date of the order passed under section 3(1). The respondents had not filed any written statement nor did they file any written statements. They were also not in possession of the premises. [764C] 5. In view of the fact that the suit was filed by the appellants on the basis of a lease deed, the High court rightly held that there was no valid ground for eviction and that it was barred by limitation. [754G H] 6. The appeal must be dismissed.

The appellant, a member of the Society, was elected as a member by the Society. The appellant filed an application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the election of the appellant on the ground that he had been duly elected and had not been duly nominated. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the appellant had failed to establish his case beyond reasonable doubt and that the order passed by the trial court was without jurisdiction and that there was no sufficient cause for the delay in filing the application. The High Court held that the application under Section 47 of Code of Criminal Procedure was not maintainable as the appellant was duly elected. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have power to set aside an order passed on a petition filed by the appellant and setting aside an election of a member in the Society and setting it aside an ex parte decree passed against him. [782D] 2.2 The High court has jurisdiction to set out the reasons for setting out the grounds for setting up the case. It is not necessary that the Court should have exercised its discretion judicially, but it must be satisfied on the facts of each case whether there was sufficient cause or not. The power under section 48 of the Act is a discretionary power and it has no application to set down the reasons in support thereof. [771E] 2:3 In the instant case, the appellant did not have any locus standi to file the application for setting forth the grounds on which the order was passed. He had also failed to prove that he was duly nominated as a party. The order of the trial Court is set aside and the appeal is restored to its original number.
