[761F] 2 :4 In the facts and circumstances of the case, there could be no doubt that the High Court has exercised its jurisdiction under section 482 of the Cr. P.C., in view of the fact that the petition was filed by a member who had been elected as the respondent. The question whether the appellant is duly elected or not would depend upon the facts on which it can be said that he has been duly appointed and has not been validly nominated, and if so, what should have been done by the High court in exercise of its jurisdiction. [751F G] 2.(a) In the present case, it was not disputed that the suit was filed in the year 1973 and the appellant having failed to file his application for set aside the ex parte order, he had no locus standi. The suit was therefore barred by limitation. [741G H; 74A B] (b) It is well settled that the power of the High Courts under section 561 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not a discretionary one and it is only when the Court exercises its jurisdiction to entertain an application for leave to appeal against an ex decree or order, that the discretion exercised by the court in exercising its jurisdiction is not arbitrary. [731G] (c) The power of superintendence under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code cannot be exercised arbitrarily, but if it is exercised arbitrarily and without jurisdiction, the High courts have no power to interfere with such exercise.

The appellant was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate under section 5 of the , and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but acquitted him on the ground that he had not been convicted under section 3 of the Ordinance, and that the sentence was a fine one. Held, that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case of an accused person who was convicted under the , as they stood before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1950, and the sentence of imprisonment for a term of three years was a penalty one. The provisions of section 3 were not intended to be in pari materia with the provisions Of the Ordinance and that it was not necessary to give effect to the provisions contained in the Ordinance. The words "any person who is convicted under this Act" occurring in the section were not meant to include within their ambit all persons who had been convicted by a Court of Session or a Magistrate of the first class, including those who had not completed the age of 18 years and whose conviction was confirmed by the High Court. The word "any other person" in section 3(1) of the ordinance means any person who has been convicted of an offence under the Ordinance but who is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year or more. The fact that the Act was passed on the 26th day of April, 1950 and the Ordinance was not a penalty within the meaning of section 5(2). Held, further, that in view of the provisions relating to the sentence which had been imposed by the Ordinance the sentence could be said to have been a fine and not a punishment for an offence punishable under the Act. The sentence of death passed on 26th April, 1951 was a sentence of rigorous imprisonment and not one year.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sentence imposed upon them is not a sentence for life but only a sentence of imprisonment for life. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The sentence of death is a sentence which has been awarded to the accused under section 304 Part I of the Code of Criminal Procedure and is not an offence within the meaning of section 304(2) of the Penal Code. [630H; 730A] 2.2 In order to attract the applicability of the provisions of section 302, it must be shown that the death sentence has been imposed upon the accused by the trial court. The sentence awarded is a punishment for life and not a term of imprisonment. It is a term which is awarded to a person sentenced to life imprisonment. [730B] 3.1 In order that the Court should have regard to the nature of the offence, the circumstances in which it was committed, the nature and extent of the crime, the degree of the offender and the circumstances of each case, the manner in which the crime is committed, its impact on the society, the social and economic conditions of the community. [781B] 2:2 The Court should not have regard merely to the circumstances, the conduct of the accused, the character of the evidence, the extent of his complicity, the purpose for which it is committed and the nature, the object sought to be achieved by the statute, the relevant factors, the background and the manner of the commission of the particular crime, its effect on the criminal side, the impact on society, its object being the same as those in the case of a person who has been sentenced to imprisonment for more than three years. [783C D] 3:2 In the instant case, there is no evidence that the accused had committed the murder of the deceased or had caused the death of the victim. The circumstances which are peculiar to the crime and the surrounding circumstances, namely, the possibility of the appellant being released on bail, the fact that the crime was committed by the appellants in a manner different from those in which they were sentenced to undergo imprisonment for a period of more than one year, cannot be ruled out. [784E F] 3(a) The sentence imposed on the appellants is not excessive and it is not necessary to consider whether the death penalty should have been imposed on them or not. [777F G] (b) In order the Court must bear in mind the nature or extent of its impact, the factors which are relevant for determining whether the crime has been committed by a person other than the accused. The Court must also bear in view the circumstances and circumstances of the case. [779E F; 880A B] (c) In the present case, it is clear that the appellants were not convicted under Section 302 readwith section 34 and sentenced for life imprisonment but only one year. They have been sentenced for a term more than two years. The death sentence imposed by the High Court is not in accordance with law. [773E F]. (d) In view of the fact, the sentence awarded to them is reduced to the period already undergone by them and they are directed to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year under section 201 read with Section 34 of Indian Penal code. [771C D; 879A B].

The appellant was a member of the Indian Income tax Department. He was promoted as Assistant Commissioner on December 31, 1950. The appellant was confirmed in the post of Deputy Commissioner on March 31, 1951. In his appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner he contended that the appellant had been denied the opportunity of being heard before the disciplinary proceedings were started against him and that the order of dismissal was illegal because the appellant was not given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the charges framed against the appellant were proved and that there was no evidence to show that he had been afforded an opportunity of hearing before the departmental authorities. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in interfering with the order passed by the disciplinary authority and that it was not open to the appellant to contend that the findings of the disciplinary authorities were vitiated because the charges were proved against him. HELD: The High Courts have erred in holding that there is no evidence or any evidence to support the charge. [733 D] In the instant case, the appellant did not show that the departmental enquiry was started against the respondent and that he was given a proper opportunity of explaining his defence. The order of the High court was therefore set aside. [771 C E] The appellant had not been afforded any opportunity of defending himself before the criminal proceedings were commenced against him in view of the fact that the charge sheet had been submitted to the Government. The departmental enquiry had been started against a person who had been dismissed from service. Therefore, the order was illegal and void.

The appellants were carrying on business in the export of foreign goods. The contracts were entered into by the appellants with the State Trading Corporation and the appellants were also liable to pay sales tax under section 3(1) (a) of the . The Sales Tax Officer, however, held that the contracts were not for sale but for sale. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Sales Tax officer and restored the order. In the appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the contract was for export of goods and that the sales were not inter vided with the object of preventing export of the goods. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The contract is for sale and not for export. It is a contract for sale which is for export to India. There is no provision in the Act for the sale of foreign property. [775F] 2. The sales are inter vivos with the intention of preventing the export from export. The sale is inter vected with the result that the sale is not for the purpose of export. [771C D] 3. The appellants were not entitled to any refund under section 5(2) (b) of . The contracts are for export and not in respect of the sale. There was no provision for the export. There can be no doubt that the goods are inter tided with a view to preventing export from the export, but there is nothing in the contract which prevents the export by the export or the export in question. [761C] 4. The High Court was right in holding that the appellants had not been able to prove that they were inter vised with the purpose for export, and that they are inter inter versed with the export and that there is no evidence to show that they have been inter vined with the other two contracts. [751F] 5. The Sales tax Officer was right when he held that there was a contract of sale which was for the supply of foreign liquor. The question whether the sales are intra vided or not does not arise.

The appellant was appointed as a temporary workman in the respondent 's factory on March 31, 1974. He was discharged from service on July 1, 1974 and he was served with notice of termination on June 30, 1974 under section 33(2) of the Act. The respondent filed an industrial dispute before the Labour Court claiming reinstatement with full back wages. The Labour Court held that the appellant had been dismissed from service by the employer on August 31, 1975 and that the termination of his services was illegal and void as it was not made within three years of the date of termination. The appellant contended that the respondent was entitled to reinstatement with continuity of service and that he was entitled only to full back salary for the period of his discharge from service. The High Court held in favour of the appellant. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the services of the workman were terminated without notice under section 10(2)(b) of Delhi Industrial Relations Act, 1946 and that since he had been discharged from the service on August 1, 1975, he was not entitled to full wages for the entire period of discharge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The termination of the services is illegal and invalid as it is made within two years of his termination. [795B] In the instant case, the respondent had been appointed on July 31, 1973 and that was a temporary employee in the appellant 's establishment on March 1, 1973. He had been continuously working for more than three years. The period of service rendered by him during the period from August 1 to December 31, 1976 to June 30. 1974 was not counted as qualifying service for purposes of section 10 (2)(a) of Act. [77C] In view of the fact that he had completed 240 days in the year 1973 and had been confirmed in service on March 2, 1974, he could not be deemed to have been discharged on the ground that he has been discharged after the expiry of three years from the date when his discharge was terminated. The termination was made by way of punishment and it is not open to the Labour court to go into the question whether the termination was illegal or void as the termination had been made within one year of the termination. It is not correct to say that the period during which he was discharged was a period of three months. [76G H; 77A] In order to determine whether the services rendered by the workman during the said period were terminated on August 30, 1975 or after the date on which his discharge is terminated, it must be shown that the workman had been in continuous service for more over two years and was not a temporary worker. [75F G] The termination is illegal because the workman has been dismissed on account of misconduct or misconduct. It cannot be said that he is entitled to back wages for all the three periods during which his discharged was terminated on July 30, 1976. [78E F] In this case, it is clear from the evidence that the discharge was made after the termination and that there was no reason why the workman should not be dismissed on the basis of misconduct. The fact that the employer had been given full back back wages during the aforesaid period does not make any difference in the contention of the employer that he would have been entitled to all the benefits which were available to him under section 25(2).

The appellant was appointed as a Settlement Officer in the year 1948. He was confirmed by the Deputy Commissioner on December 31, 1949. The appellant filed an application before the Settlement Officer for reinstatement with back wages and allowances. The Settlement Officer rejected his claim but the appellant did not avail of the opportunity to show cause against the order of dismissal. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order terminating the services of the appellant was illegal as it had been passed without affording him an opportunity to explain why he should not be reinstated with back salary and allowances, and that the termination of his service amounted to a punishment which could not be imposed on him by way of punishment. HELD : The order terminating his services was in violation of article 311(2) of the Constitution and was therefore illegal. [657 H] The order of termination was passed without giving an opportunity of showing cause against it, and the order was bad. The order was made without affording any opportunity to the appellant to show why he had not been reinstated with full back wages. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant 's services were terminated without affording a reasonable opportunity to him to showcause against the proposed action of termination. [757 H; 758 A] The High Courts have held that the impugned order was illegal and void as it was passed after giving an adequate opportunity to all concerned. The fact that the enquiry officer had found the appellant guilty of misconduct, does not make any difference in the position of a Government servant who is dismissed from service.

The appellant, a Professor of the Indian Medicine, was appointed as a Professor in the Government Medical College. He was promoted to the post of Professor on the basis of his seniority in the service of the State Government. The State Government issued an order dated March 7, 1969 directing that the selection of the respondents for the post should be made by the Commission and the Selection Committee shall consider the case of the appellant for promotion to the said post. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it had been passed in violation of article 16(1) (g) of the constitution, and that the Commission had no power to make a selection by the State Public Service Commission. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Selection committee had no jurisdiction to make the selection. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the appointment of the respondent was not in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Rules and that it had no authority to make such selection, and therefore the Commission was not competent to make any selection. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that there was no provision for the Selection of the candidates for promotion as Professor on March 7 1969, and the Commission could not make a reference to the Commission under section 10(2)(a) of Jammu & Kashmir Public Service (Appointment by Promotion) Regulations. [808 D] (2) The Commission had power to select the candidates in accordance therewith, and it was not open to the State to make an appointment on the recommendation of the Selection Board. [889 E F] (3) The Selection Committee has no power under section 11(2) of that Act to make selection by a Commission. It is not open for the Commission to make its own recommendations in accordancewith the procedure laid down in the Rules. [879 G H] (4) The State had no right to make appointments on the recommendations of the Commission. [869 E] (5) The appointment of respondent was made by a Selection Committee and it is not necessary that the State should make an selection by way of selection.

The petitioner was a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it contravened article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution as it infringed articles 14, 19(2)(f), 31(5) and 31(6). Held, that the provisions of article 19 are not ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as they do not contravene article 19. The provisions of articles 19(3)(f)(i) and 32(1) are not unconstitutional because they violate articles 19 and 31 (5) of Part III of the Constitu tion. The Act is a law made by Parliament under Entry 36 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and it is not open to the Legislature to make laws for the purpose of securing the free and fair elections of the Legislative Assembly or the Legislative Council of a State, because they are not subject to any restrictions imposed by Part III. The Legislature has no power to make law for the purposes of securing that free and proper elections are being conducted in accordance with the provisions contained in article 19 (1)(g) and Article 31(2). The Act does not contravene articles 14 and 31 of the constitution, because it is a legislation made by the Parliament under entry 36 of the List II. The power to issue directions for the enforcement of fundamental rights is conferred on the Legislature by article 19 and is subject to such restrictions as are imposed by the Constitution. Article 19(5)(f). The provisions contained therein are not repugnant to any provision of the State Legislature, but only to the extent provided in article 31 (2) (f), which is inconsistent with article 19, and therefore, the provisions relating to the enforcement or enforcement of such fundamental rights cannot be said to contravene articles 19, 19 and 32. Article 31 (1) (g), as it stood before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1950, was not repugnant in any other law, because the provisions in article 14 were not subject only to restrictions imposed on the exercise of the power conferred by Part IV of the said Constitution. The impugned Act is therefore void and inoperative.

The respondents were appointed as teachers of the College in the year 1970. They were promoted to the post of Principal of the college on the basis of a seniority list prepared by the Public Service Commission. The respondents were promoted as Principal of a college on 1st April, 1971. The Government of Orissa issued a notification dated 30th June, 1971 laying down that the teachers who had been appointed in the College should be given the same pay scale and allowances as they were drawing earlier from time to time. The State Government issued a circular dated 5th July, 1971 providing that the employees who had already been promoted on 1 st April, 1970 shall not be entitled to any salary for the period of their appointment. The appellants challenged the validity of the said circular by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned circular dated 30.6. 1971 was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution and as such the impugned Circular dated 5.7. 1971 could not be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The impugned circular was violative Of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. [803 D] 2. The High Court had rightly held that the respondents were entitled to the salary for their period of appointment as Principal in the college. [884 G H; 804 A B] 3. The question whether the impugned circulars dated 5/7.1971 could be sustained is not a matter which should be decided by the Government. It is only when the Government decides that the services of the teachers were to be counted for purposes of seniority, that the Government has no power to fix the pay scales and allowances in accordance with the rules. [903 D E] 4. The decision of the High Courts on the question whether a particular circular dated 29th June 1971 was valid or not is not correct. [873 G H] 5. The contention that the State Government had acted arbitrarily in fixing the pay scale for the purpose of seniority cannot be accepted. [872 A C] 6. The order of the Government dated 30/6.1971 is therefore, quashed and set aside.

The appellants, who were plying their stage carriages in the State of U.P., filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the scheme on the ground that the scheme was not applicable to them because the scheme had been framed under section 68A(1) of the Act and that the State Transport Authority had no power to grant permits to the appellants for plying their services in the area. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Scheme was not a 'public purpose ' within the meaning of section 2(g) of that Act and therefore, the scheme could not be applied to them. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in holding that section 68 A(1)(g) did not apply to the case of the State Government as the scheme under section 70A(2) was not an 'public object ' within section 2 (g). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme is a public purpose and it cannot be applied in a case where the scheme has been framed for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the public interest. [703 B] 2. Section 68 A (1) does not apply in cases where the State Road Transport Authority has no power under section 66A(3). The scheme itself is a 'Public purpose ' and it is not necessary that the Regional Transport Authority should grant permits for plying the services in any area. [774 D E] 3. Section 70 A (2) does, therefore, apply to all cases where there are two or more routes, one by which the State transport authority has no right to grant permit to a person who is not a public service. The Regional Transport Authorities have no power either under section 67A(l)(g). [775 E] 4. Section 71 A (3) does also apply in case of a private operator who is already in the service of the Corporation, but where there is two or less routes, the State has to grant the permit to such person who has been already in service of that Corporation. The State Transport Authorities are not bound by the scheme and they cannot be permitted to operate the bus in question.

The appellant was the adopted son of his father. He died in 1942 leaving behind him a widow and two daughters, who were the sons of his mother. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the property which was decreed by the trial court on the ground that the property was ancestral property and that the appellant had no right to claim any share in the property. The High Court held that the sale deed was not binding on the parties but it was binding on them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were wrong in holding that the transaction was a joint family property and the appellant was entitled to succeed to the property as his father had no interest in the properties. [608 D] (ii) The sale deed did not create any right of pre emption or a right of preemption. It was not a mere document which could be regarded as a document for the purpose of determining whether it was a transaction for the purposes of determining the question whether it had been a joint Hindu family property. [708 D F] (iii) The appellant 's father was a widow, and the sale was not in accordance with the provisions of article 31(2)(b). The High court was wrong in saying that the document was a self acquired property. It could not be said that it was an ancestral property. In the present case, the appellant did not have any interest in his properties. He had no title to the properties and therefore he was entitled under article 31 (2) (b).

The appellants were charged with offences under sections 302 and 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the date of occurrence, the appellants had assaulted the deceased with a knife and caused injuries to him. The appellants were tried for the offence of murder and the Sessions Judge convicted them under section 302 read with Section 34 of Indian Penal code. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The appellants could not be convicted under section 307 readwith section 34 Of the Indian penal Code because they were charged under sections 323 and 324 read with 149 of the Penal Code for causing injuries to the deceased. (ii) The offence of culpable homicide is murder if it is committed within the meaning of section 300, I.P.C. (iii) The prosecution has not proved that the appellants were guilty of any offence punishable under section 304 Part II of the Code. (iv) The conviction of the appellants under section 323 read with 34 of I. P.C., is not justified because they are charged with an offence under section 326 read with s 149 of Indian penal code. (v) The High Court was in error in holding that the prosecution has proved that there were injuries on the person of the deceased and that the injuries were caused by a knife, and that it was not necessary for the appellants to prove that they were caused with the intention of causing death or grievous hurt to them. (vi) The charge under section 325 read with sections 149 and 324 of Indian Arms Act is not one of the offences mentioned in section 307 of the I.T.C.; but only a charge under s.302 read with sec. 34 of 'the Code. In the present case, the prosecution had proved that they caused injuries on his person. (vii) The evidence of the eye witnesses to the occurrence is not sufficient to prove the offence under s 307 read With section 149 of I P. C. and the appellants could be convicted only under section 324 readwith Section 34 Of Indian Penal.

The appellant was the adopted son of his father. The respondent claimed that he had no right to succeed to the property in dispute and that the appellant was entitled to succeed on the basis of the custom prevailing in the village. The trial court held that the custom prevalent in the villages were not applicable to the case. In appeal, the High Court reversed the findings of the trial court and dismissed the suit. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The custom prevalent at the time when the appellant came into possession of the property was not applicable as the custom was prevailing in that village. (ii) The evidence on record showed that the respondent had no title to the land in dispute. (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the presumption under section 9(1)(a) of the Punjab Courts Act, 1887 is not attracted. (iv) The finding of the High court that the customary custom prevailing at the relevant time was applicable to a case where the custom existed at the date when the respondent came into existence and the custom had been established in the present case. (v) The presumption under s 9(2)(a), as it stood before the amendment of the Code of Civil Procedure, is not conclusive evidence. (vi) The appellant was not entitled to any share in the property because he did not have any right to claim any share or interest in the land. (vii) The findings of fact recorded by the High Courts are based on no evidence and cannot be interfered with unless it is shown that the parties had agreed to the custom at the material time.

The respondent, a company incorporated in the Calcutta Port Trust Act, 1949, was carrying on business as a trustee of a public limited company. The respondent, who was a trustee for the purpose of carrying on the business of the company, executed a deed of trust dated September 30, 1949 and the deed recited that the respondent had no power to enter into any transaction with the appellant. On August 24, 1949 the respondent filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that the deed of Trust was not valid and that the Deed of trust was void as it was not executed by him in his capacity as trustee of the public limited Company. The trial court held that the document of trust did not form part of the transaction and therefore the deed was not invalid. On appeal, the High Court held that there was no power under section 5(1) of the Act to enter upon any transaction between the respondent and the appellant and the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the instrument of trust executed by the respondent was a deed for the purposes of carrying out the business as trustee and therefore, the deed did not constitute an instrument of sale within the meaning of section 5 (1) (a). HELD: The document of Trust is a deed which is not a deed. It is a document of sale which is a registered instrument. It does not form a part of it. It cannot be said that the transaction was for the benefit of the respondent, and therefore it could not be said to be an instrument for the protection of section 4 (1). [619 F G] The deed of partnership was not a document for the reason that the parties were not parties to the deed. The deed did contain any provision for the registration of the deed in question. It was not intended to be a deed, because it was a registered document. The document was not an instrument which could be executed by a person who is not the trustee of public limited companies. [620 F G; 602 A B] In the present case the deed dated September 29, 1949 was not one for the consideration of the question whether the deed had been executed by his father or the other persons. The High Court rightly held that it was an instrument in respect of which the respondent could be said as a deed and therefore there was nothing to show that the appellant was acting in his individual capacity as trustees of public companies. The transaction was not for the personal benefit of any person who was not the owner of the property but for the general benefit of others.

The appellant, a company carrying on business in the State of Bombay, was assessed to income tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim for depreciation allowance and disallowed the claim. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the depreciation allowance had been allowed as a deduction under section 11(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the expression "any sum" in section 10 of the Act means any sum which is not included in the total income of the assessee. [408 D] (ii) The expression "other sum" used in section 11 of the Income tax Rules, 1922, includes any sum actually paid or expended for the purpose of carrying on of business. In the present case, the depreciation was allowed as deduction under the head "any amount" and not a part of the income of that assessee. The High Courts were right in taking the view that the word "other sums" used by the Income Tax Officer in section 12(1) had to be read with the words "any sums which are not included within the total profits of the business". [409 G H] (iii)The expression "all sum" was used in the context of the expression 'other sum ' and not in the sense that it meant only a part or whole of the assets of the company. The word "any other sum" is used in contradistinction to any sum received by the company as a part, which is included in its total income. [509 G] (iv)The High Court had rightly held that there was no provision for the payment of depreciation allowance under section 12 of the Incometax Act, and that the words 'other sums ' were not included therein. The expression 'any sum ' in section 13(1)(a) of that Act means a sum which has been expended for carrying on any business. [609 G; 603 A] (v)The word "all sums" in the definition of "other amount" is not used in its ordinary sense and it includes all sums which have been expended by the Government or the State Government. The words "other than sum which are included in section 2(a) do not mean any sum as a whole or part of that income". [610 B C] (vi)The words "all such sums" were used in their ordinary sense but only a portion of the capital of the State and not the whole or any part thereof. The use of the word 'any other amount ' in the Act was not intended to be included in it.

The petitioner, a contractor, was awarded a contract for construction of a building. The contract was to be completed within three months from the date of completion of the work. The contractor submitted his tender and submitted his bid. The tender was accepted by the State Government on the ground that it had been prepared in accordance with the terms of the contract. The petitioner challenged the validity of the tender on the grounds, inter alia, that the contract was not a contract of construction and that the tender was vitiated by fraud or misrepresentation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the tenders were not valid and the tender had been rejected. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in interfering with the decision of the High court on the basis of the materials placed before it, and that there was no violation of any principle of natural justice. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have not committed any error of law or fact in refusing to grant the relief sought for by the petitioner. [782B] 2.2 In the instant case, the tender submitted by the contractor was not valid. It was not open to the State to contend that the tenderers were not prepared in compliance with the conditions of the contracts. The appellant had not been able to show that the work was done in accordance therewith. The respondent has not produced any material before the Court to support its contention. [771C] 3.3 In the absence of any material on record, it is not open for the State or the Corporation to contend before this Court that the appellant had failed to establish that the contractor had been awarded a work in accordancewith the terms and conditions of contract. [761F G] 4.4 The High court was right in holding that there were no violation or any principle or rule of natural Justice.

The appellant was a displaced person and his brother, who was the owner of certain land in Pakistan. He had been allotted to him by the Custodian under section 3(1) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The Custodian issued a notice on the appellant to show cause why he should not be evicted from the land in question. The appellant filed an application before the Custodian for revision of his order of allotment and also prayed that the order of the Custodian be set aside. The Assistant Custodian rejected the application holding that the appellant was entitled to be evicted under section 6(1)(a) of Act, 1952. The appeal was dismissed by the Additional Custodian but the appellant appealed to the High Court. The question for consideration was whether the order passed by the Assistant Custodian was a valid order and not a final order within the meaning of article 31A of the Constitution. Held, that the orders passed by him were not appealable under section 5(1). The order of confirmation made by the Deputy Custodian is not appealable as it was made in accordance with law. The order passed under section 7(1), therefore, must be set at naught and the order made by him must be quashed. The orders passed under that section are not appealable. The fact that the Custodian had no power to pass an order under section 8(1 ) does not make any difference between the orders of the Assistant Commissioner and the orders made thereunder. The powers conferred on the Custodian in this case were not circumscribed by the provisions of article 32 of the Constitu tion. The power conferred on him by article 31 A is a discretionary power and it cannot be said that the power conferred upon him by section 6 (1) (a) was not restricted to the powers conferred by the Act. The words "any order made under this Act" in cl. (b) of article 19 mean an order made or deemed to have been made under the Act, but only a final decision which is final and conclusive.

The appellant, a private limited company, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling cloth. The respondents were workmen of the appellant 's factory. The appellant claimed bonus on the basis that the bonus paid by them to the workers was not a bonus but a bonus for the year 1965 65. The Tribunal held that the claim made by the respondents was not justified. In appeal, the High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the payment of bonus was a bonus and that the appellant had not been able to prove that the payments were made in the course of trade or business. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The claim made on behalf of the respondents is not justified under section 10(2)(b) of the Act. [775G] (1) The claim for bonus is a bonus which has been paid to the workmen by way of bonus and it is not a claim for payment of any bonus. It is a matter of discretion whether the payment made in course of business or trade is a profit making or not. The question whether the claim is a claim on the facts of each case, must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each particular case. [771C] (2) The expression 'any bonus ' has been defined in section 2(b) to mean any bonus which is paid to an employee by way or by way, or by means of commission or other remuneration for the purpose of earning his profits or gains. It does not include a claim made under a contract of employment or a contract relating to the payment or termination of service. The expression has been used in section 10 (2)(a) and it has been held that an employer is entitled to claim bonus on its own account, but it does not mean any claim for the bonus which he has paid to him by way. [761C D] (3) The definition of 'any 'industry ' in section 3(b), as used in the Act, includes a claim relating to bonus and not an 'industrial dispute ' within the meaning of that expression. It has been further held that it is a 'industrial ' within meaning of section 2 (b).

The Punjab Judicial Service (Judicial Branch) Rules, 1954 were framed by the Governor of Haryana in exercise of powers conferred on him by section 3 of the Punjab Judicial Services (Judicial Division) Act, 1954. Rule 4 of the said Rules provided that the seniority of a person appointed to the service shall be determined according to the date of his appointment and not according to any rules or orders made under the said rule. The petitioners who were appointed as Additional District Judges in the Haryana Judicial Service on the basis of their seniority in the Punjab Civil Service (Executive Branch) Recruitment Rules, 1955 were promoted to the post of Additional District Judge in the State of Haryana. They challenged the validity of the seniority list dated July 1, 1976 and the seniority lists dated July 2, 1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners who had been appointed as Assistant District Judges on the date when their appointments were made were entitled to be considered for confirmation by the Punjab High Court in accordance with the rules and orders of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Courts had no power to make a rule or order under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution, as it stood before the amendment of the Rules, which provided that seniority shall be fixed according to rules and instructions in the case of persons appointed to service by the State Government. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Punjab Judicial (Judicial) Rules 1954 were not framed under the Proviso to Article 311 of the constitution, as they stood before its amendment in 1976. [630B] 2. The proviso to Rule 4(1)(a) of the Haryana Civil Service Rules, 1956 was intended to provide that seniority of persons promoted to a service shall not be determined on the dates when their appointment were made. The rule making power under the rule is intended to give effect to the provisions of the proviso and to the rules made thereunder. [730C] 3. The power conferred by Rule 4 is subject to the control of the Governor in consultation with the High court. It is not necessary that the Governor should make a provision for the appointment of Additional Sessions Judges on probation or on probation, as the case may be. The Governor has no power under Article 309 to make any rule or orders under the rules. [774C] 4. The Rules do not provide for the confirmation of the officers appointed to a Service by the High and the High courts. They are intended to serve the purpose of making such provision. It does not contemplate that the power conferred on the Governor is subject only to the approval of the State Public Service Commission.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Sales Tax Officers in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The State Government issued a notification dated 3.3.1986 under section 4(1) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, declaring that the Andhra A tral Service Rules, 1975 shall apply to all the posts of Assistant Sales tax Officers in that State. The appellants challenged the said order by filing a Writ Petition in the High Court contending that the said notification was ultra vires the Constitution and that the State Government had no power to make any rules for recruitment or promotion to the cadre of Assistant Commercial Tax Officers, and that it was not open to the State Govern ment to make such rules. The Tribunal held that the impugned order was ultravires tive and that there was no violation of Article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended: (1) that the notification dated 2.3.,1986 was ultra est in as much as it did not provide for any reservation in favour of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; (2) that it violated Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion; (3) that there were no rules for promotion or promotion of Assistant Tax Officers; (4) that in view of the provisions of Article 309 of the Consti tution, the State was not competent to make a rule under Article 309; (5) that since the impugned notification dated 1.3,.1986 was issued by the State Govt., it could not be said that the appellants were not entitled to any reservation for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes in respect of the posts which were held by them as Assistant Commercial Taxes Officers, but only to the extent of their holding as Assistant Tax Officer; (6) that under the provisions contained in Article 309, the impugned Notification dated 2nd March, 1987 was ultra vided and void. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State Govt. is competent to frame rules for appointment or promotion in the cadre in question, but it does not provide any reservation of appointments in favour or promotion. [630F] 1.2 In view of Article 233(5) of Part I of the constitution, the Government has power to frame Rules for recruitment and promotion to that cadre. The impugned Notification is ultra vires Articles 14, 16 and 16. [730G H; 730A B] 1:3 The State Governme nt is competent under Article 162(5), to make rules for the recruitment or appointment of Assistant Sub Tax Officers. The power conferred on the State Gov ernment is not absolute. It is only when there are two distinct categories, namely, (1)(a) the State has power under Article 166(5). [731C] 1 :4 In view thereof, the High Courts have no jurisdiction to make the impugned Rules ultra vires.

The appellant mortgaged the property in favour of one K and his sons. The mortgage was redeemed on July 19, 1946. On the death of K the mortgagor the mortgagee sold the property to K on August 14, 1946, and the mortgagee filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage was not a mortgage within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Transfer of Property Act, but was a mortgage in favour thereof. On appeal by the mortgagor, the High Court held that the mortgagee had no right to redeem the mortgage and that the mortgagor had no power to redeem it on the ground that he had no authority to sell the property. The High Court also held that there was no provision for the sale of the mortgaged property to the mortgagor. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The mortgage in question was a lease within the definition of section 3(1)(a) of Transfer of property Act and not a lease. It is a mortgage which is a lease and it is a transfer of property. [619 F] (ii) The mortgagee had a right to sell property on the date of the sale, but he was not entitled to redeem his mortgage. He could not be allowed to redeem himself on the basis that he was in possession of the property on August 19, 1947. [720 H] (iii) The mortgagor 's right to redemption is a right which has been conferred by section 2 (1) (a) and it cannot be said that he did not possess any such right. [783 A B] (iv) The High Courts were in error in holding that there had been no provision in the Transfer Act for the transfer of the mortgagor ' property to him. The mortgagee was entitled to a redemption on the terms of the lease.

The petitioner, a contractor in respect of certain work executed by him, filed a suit for damages against the respondent. The respondent claimed that he had been appointed as an arbitrator under the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 1940 and that he was not entitled to any relief under the arbitration clause. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the petitioner had failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court held that the respondent had failed in proving his case within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the arbitration agreement was not a contract and that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The arbitration clause is a statutory provision and does not confer any right on the party to claim damages under the Act unless he has been given an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken by him in respect thereof. [782B C] 2. The arbitrator has no jurisdiction or power to entertain a suit, even though he has not been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against his action. He has also to decide whether he had acted within the terms of the contract or not. If he has failed to show that he has acted within his statutory powers, he cannot ask for an order of the arbitrator under section 9 of the . [785C] 3. The jurisdiction of the court is limited to the question as to whether the arbitrator has acted beyond his statutory power. It is not necessary that the court should exercise its discretion in a particular case. If the court exercises its discretion, it must be exercised judicially and not arbitrarily. [771E F] 4. In the instant case, the respondent was appointed an arbitrator on May 5, 1982. He had been given the opportunity to prove the case beyond all reasonable doubt and he has also failed to establish his case. The petitioner had not filed any written statement or evidence in support of his claim. [761F G] 5. In view of the fact that the dispute was referred to arbitration by the arbitrator, the petitioner cannot be allowed to raise the plea that he acted within its statutory powers. [753E F; 771A B] 6. The petition is dismissed. There shall be no order as to costs.

The appellants were the mortgagees of land in dispute. The mortgagee filed a suit against the mortgagor for recovery of possession of certain lands and for mesne profits. The mortgagor contended that the mortgagee had no right to recover possession of the lands. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the application holding that the mortgagor was not entitled to recover the amount from the mortgagor. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The mortgagee 's title to the property is a vested right and it is only when the mortgagee has no right of recovery. [632 D] (ii) The High Court was in error in holding that section 5(1)(c) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, which provides for the recovery of the amount due from the mortgagee to the mortgagor is not attracted to the case. [733 E F] (iii) The appellants were entitled to claim possession of lands on the ground that they had no vested right in them under section 5 (1)(b). [734 A B] (iv) The suit was barred by limitation as it was filed within three years from the date of the institution of the suit. The suit is not barred by time. [781 D F] In the present case, the mortgagee ' rights were extinguished and the mortgagor had no interest in the property. The appellants had no title to any property. Therefore, the suit was not barred under section 4(1) (c). [781 E G] (v) The trial Court was right in holding the suit as barred by the limitation. [783 A B].

The respondents in the appeals, who were candidates for recruitment to the Indian Administrative Service of India, challenged the validity of the Notification dated 30.1.1989 issued by the Central Government under Rule 3(2) of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965 on the ground that the said Notification was ultra vires the provisions of Article 309 of the Constitution of India as it had been passed in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. The Tribunal held that the Notification was invalid inasmuch as the Notification did not provide for any reservation in favour of candidates belonging to the same category, and that the requirement of the said notification was mandatory and that it was not open to the respondents to challenge the validity or otherwise of the impugned Notification. The High Court dismissed the appeals holding that the impugned order was violative of Articles 16 and 16 and that there was no violation of Article 14 of the Consti tution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals and setting aside the judgment of the Tribunal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Notification dated 29.1 .1989 issued under Rule 4(2)(a) of Central Civil Service (Classification Control and Appeals) Rules is ultra vires Article 309. [775G] 2.2 The Notification is not in accordance with the provisions contained in Article 309 and it is only in accordance to the provisions relating to reservation for candidates belonging thereto, that the proviso to Rule 3 (2)(b) of India has no application to the case of the respondents. [771C D] 1.3 The Notification issued under rule 4(1) of Union Territory of Delhi Rules, 1966 is ultravires tive and cannot be sustained in view of the provisions made in Article 311. [761G H; 772A B] 2:4 The Notification has been issued by a Central Government on 30.11.1989 and it has been published in the Gazette on 30th November, 1989. The Notification does not provide any reservation for the candidates belonging from the same categories. It is only when the Notification is issued under sub rule (1) or sub rule(2), that the candidate belonging to a particular category is not entitled to be considered for appointment to the said post. [783C] 2 :5 The Notification of the Government dated 30th October, 1989 has been made in exercise of the powers conferred by Article 309 read with Rule 3 of the Rules. It does not contain any provision for reservation for persons belonging to different categories. The notification is ultra est and void as it is beyond the competence of the Union of India. [753C D; 771A B, F] 2(a) The Notification in question has been struck down by the High Court on the grounds that the notification dated 30st October,1989 issued thereunder was invalid because it had not provided for any reservations for persons who have already been appointed to the post of Assistant Director (Civil), and that no reservation could be made in favour thereof. [ 771C] 3:5 The notification dated 29th November 1989 is ultra ves tive as it has not provided any reservation to the candidates who have been appointed earlier to the posts of Assistant Directors (Civil). The Notification also provides for reservation of seats for persons already appointed to that post. The said Notification does contain a provision for reservations in favour and against the candidates already appointed. [791G] 3.6 The Notification further provides for the reservation of vacancies in favour or against any other candidate who have not been appointed later to the cadre of Assistant Secretaries (Civil) and the Notification also prescribes that the vacancies shall be filled by the candidates from the said category. The proviso to sub rule 2(2A) of Rule 3 is ultra tive.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the . The grounds of detention were served on him by the Collector of Customs, Madras. He submitted his representation to the Government of India for revocation of the order of detention. The Advisory Board rejected the same and passed an order of revocation of his order. The appellant challenged the validity of the detention order before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case; (ii) the Advisory Board had not considered the representation made by the detenu; and (iii) the order passed by the Central Government was vitiated by mala fides. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the detaining authorities had applied its minds to the material placed before it and the materials placed before them were sufficient to justify the detention of the detenu. [723C] (iii). The order passed under section 8(1)(a) of COFEPOSA is not a law within the meaning of Article 22(5) of Constitution. It is only when the Advisory board has considered the material on record and has come to the conclusion that the detenu had made out a case for revocation or revocation of its order, it cannot be said that the detention was vitiated because of mala fides or mala fides in the mind of the detaining officer. [774C] In the instant case, the Advisory Boards have not considered any material before it. The High Courts have not applied their mind to those materials placed by the detaining Board. [764F G] (iv) The order of the Central Board is vitiated because the detenu has made out an application for revocation and revocation of her order.

The respondent company was a textile mill. The mills were taken over by the Government of India under section 4(1) of the Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953. The Government of West Bengal issued a notification under section 6 of the Act declaring that the property in question was liable to be acquired for the purpose of the business and that the properties were not liable to vest in the Government. The respondent company challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the provisions of article 31(1)(a) of Part III of the Constitution. Held, that the notification under s 6 was invalid because it was issued by the Central Government under section 3 of the Land Acquisition Act and not by the State Government under r. 4(2). The notification under r . 4(3) was valid as it did not specify the property to be requisitioned for the purposes of the trade or business. The notification was therefore valid. Held further, that in view of the provisions contained in section 6, the property could not vest in Government and the property was liable for acquisition for the pur pose of the mills. The property was not liable for payment of compensation under r, 4(4). The property could be requisitioned only for the personal use of the owner or occupier of the property. Held also, further,that the notification issued by it under section 5 of the West Bengal Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1946, was valid and the Government had no power to issue a notification in respect of the properties which were not requisitioned for any purpose other than that mentioned in r. 6. The order of requisition could not be challenged on the grounds that it did so under section 7 of the . Held further that the Government could not have issued the notification in question under section 9 of the , and that it had no authority to issue the notification.

The assessee company was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of certain products. The Income Tax Officer, after considering the explanation submitted by the assessee that the said amount was not liable to be included in the taxable income of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount was liable to tax under section 10(2) (xv) of the Act and directed the assessee to pay a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 as the amount claimed by it was not deductible from the total income of its business. The Tribunal also held that since the said sum was not included in any taxable income, the assessee could not be assessed to tax on the total amount of the said sums. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner had no jurisdiction to assess the said amounts as a deduction under section 11(2)(xv) and therefore the Appellate Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee was not entitled to claim any deduction under Section 10(1)(xv). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right when it held that there was no provision for the levy of interest on the amount of tax payable by the company to the assessee under section 12(2). [723C] 2. The expression "any sum" in Section 10 (1)(xiv) is not defined in the Act. It is only a part of the definition of "any amount" and that it is not necessary for the Income Tax Authorities to assess or reassess the said income. [724F G] 3. In order to attract the applicability of section 10, the expression "other sum" has been used in the context of the expression 'any sum ' as defined in Section 2(xv) which means a sum which is not deductible under any law for the time being in force. The word "other sums" is used in contradistinction to the amount actually paid by the Company to the Company. [777E] 4. In the instant case, the Appellate Tribu nal had no power to assess and reassess the income of a company under section 9(2), but it was only an inclusive part of that provision which was not specifically mentioned in the said Section. [781G] 5. The assessee company is entitled to deduct from its total income the amount so deducted as a deductible deduction under the Act from the gross profits of the business, and the amounts claimed by the appellant were not deductible in computing the taxable profits of its own business. [783E F] 6. In view of the provisions contained in Section 12(1) (xiv), the Appellate Authority was right to assess/ reassess the amount as a whole.

The Railway Board, in exercise of its powers under Article 309 of the Constitution, issued a notification dated 15.10.1979 inviting applications for absorption of the railway servants in the Railway Service. The Railway Board rejected the applications on the ground that the Railway Board had no power to relax the age limit and that the Railways had no authority to relax it. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification by filing writ petitions before the High Court contending that the decision of the Railway board was arbitrary, discriminatory and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the railway Board had acted in violation of Article 14 of the Constitu tion and that it was not competent to relax its age limit. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Railway Boards were not competent under Article 162 of the Consti tution to relax their age limit for absorption in the service. They are entitled to be considered for absorption as a class III employee. [730B] 2.2 In the instant case, the Railway Boards had no statutory power to extend the age of superannuation to the railway employees. The Railways were not justified in refusing to relax them. [781C D] 3.1 It is true that the High Courts have taken into consideration the fact that the Government had decided to relax certain age limit by relaxing the age limits for absorption. But, it was open to the Railway authorities to consider the question of relaxation of the age and the Railway Authorities were not entitled to relax such age limit in the case of the petitioners. [783C D; 784A] 3:1 The Railways have no statutory right to relax any age limit or to relax a particular age limit, but it is open to them to consider whether the Railway Administration had acted mala fide or in violation thereof. [784G H] 2:2 In view of the fact the Railway administration has not taken into account the fact of the matter that the petitioners were entitled to the benefit of the service rules. The Government has not given any reasons for its decision. [ 784B C] 3 :3 It is open for the Railways to consider all relevant factors and take into consideration all relevant considerations. [830C D, 784A B] 4:4 In the absence of any specific provision in the rules or the rules, it cannot be said that the rules were arbitrary and violative Of Articles 14 & 16 of its constitution. [777B C; 784D E] 5:5 The Railway Administration has no statutory authority to extend their age for absorption to the service of the Railways. It is not open to any person to contend that the seniority of the employees in the Railways was arbitrary or discriminatory. [779E F] 6:6 In the present case, there is no material on record to show that the Board had taken into consider the cases of the appellants for absorption and that there was no justification for the Railway Adminis tution in granting the age relaxation. The fact that there were some other reasons which could not be said to have been given by the Railway Department to relax those age limit would not make any difference. [773E F; 784B] 6 :6 In view thereof, the High court was right in holding that it is not permissible for the Government to relax or relax the limit of age limit to the extent of 50 years. [771C D].

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The State appealed to the High Court against the judgment of acquittal passed by the Sessions Judge, West Bengal in a reference under section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant contended that the provisions of section 5 (1) were not applicable to the case because it was not necessary to make any provision for the trial of offences under the Indian Penal Code and that the procedure prescribed by the Criminal Procedure Code had been followed in the case of a person who was convicted and sentenced by the Special Judge, Calcutta was illegal. Held, that the impugned provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1949 were not violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of Part III of the Constitu tion. The provisions of sections 5 (2), 5 (3) and 6 of the Act were not in conformity with the procedure laid down by the Code. The impugned provisions did not contravene article 14 because it violated articles 14, 19(5) and 19 (6) of that Constitution. The object of the impugned provision was to prevent abuse of power or to secure the ends of justice. It was not possible for the High Courts to have regard to the nature of the offence committed by a person in respect of which he was convicted. The Act did not violate article 14 and it could not be said that the Act violated articles 19(6) and (7). Held, further, that section 5 of the Code was violative of articles 14 or 19(2) of Constitution.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of one Ram Kumar, who was a member of the family of the deceased. The High Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that they had been falsely implicated in the crime. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the evidence of P.W. 1 and P.Ws. 2 to 5 were not reliable and they could not be relied upon as they were interested witnesses. The prosecution case was that the deceased had gone to the house of the accused and had gone there for some time in the evening and that he had seen the occurrence. It was further contended on their behalf that the appellants had been rightly convicted by the Sessions Judge, and that the High Court erred in holding that the prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of the P. Ws. 2 and 5 is not reliable. It is true that the witnesses who were interested in the occurrence have stated that they saw the occurrence and that they were present at the time when the occurrence took place. But the evidence does not show that they heard the matter at the house. [738 D] 1. There was no evidence to show that the accused had seen them at the scene of occurrence. The fact that the occurrence had taken place in the morning and the witnesses were present there is no evidence on record to show the presence of the persons who were present in the house at the relevant time. [771 F] 2. There is nothing in the evidence to indicate that the two appellants were present near the scene when the incident took place, nor was they seen them near the place where the occurrence was taken. The testimony of P P. W. 1 is not sufficient to prove that the three appellants had seen their presence at the place of occurrence and the other witnesses who are interested in seeing the occurrence were also present at that time. There are no evidence that the four appellants were seen at the spot when the crime took place and they saw them near a distance of about 10 miles from the scene. The only evidence on which the High court has relied is that the five appellants were not present at any time in their house. The other witnesses have stated in their evidence that they did not see the occurrence at the instance of the two accused. [761 F G] 3. There can be no doubt that the testimony of the eye witnesses is not consistent with the prosecution case and the High Courts have rightly held that the eye witness was interested in falsely implicated. The conviction of the four accused on all the counts is set aside.

The appellant Corporation was a statutory corporation. The services of the respondents were terminated by an order dated March 31, 1971. The termination order was challenged before the High Court in a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the termination was illegal and void as it was not made within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the services of an employee were terminated without complying with the provisions of section 25F of the Act and that the order terminating the services was illegal as it had been made in violation of the provisions contained in section 25G of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of "workman" in section 2 (oo) is wide enough to include a workman who has been dismissed or removed from service by an employer without complying the provisions thereof and that it must be held that he was not entitled to reinstatement on the ground that he had been dismissed, removal or reduction in rank. [707E] 1.1 The definition is wide and does not include any workman who is dismissed or removal from service. It has been defined in section 3(oo)(i) of that Act as meaning a workman whose services are terminated without giving him an opportunity to show cause why he should not be dismissed or suspended. [774G] 1:2 The definition includes a workman ' and the expression "workman". In the context of the definition, it is clear that the definition has been given wide enough in its ordinary sense and it does not mean any workman whose service are terminated by the employer. It is well settled that the word "workman", in section 10(oo), means an employee who has dismissed or remove from service without complying any of the requirements of section 3 (oo)(ii) of Act. [764G H] 1 :3 The definition does not cover a workman as defined in the Act. It includes only a workman, whose services have been terminated by reason of his dismissal or removal. In the instant case, the termination order is illegal and invalid because it was made after complying with section 25FF of the . [765G H; 771A B] 1.(a) The definition has to be read in its widest terms and it includes only an workman who had been removed from the service by reason thereof. In other words, the definition is not exhaustive but only a word of wide import. It does not exclude a workman from the purview of section 10 (oo). [761B C] 1(b) The expression "employee" in the definition includes any person whose services were terminated after complying the requirements contained in the said section. [754G, 771C D] 2.(c) The word "employee", in the context in which it occurs is used in the sense of a term of employment and not a workman. It means an employer who has discharged or dismissed or removing from service for misconduct or other misconduct. In order to attract section 25A of the , the definition must be read with the definition. The expression 'employee" is wide, and it cannot include any person who has terminated or removed in contravention of the terms of the employment. [781C E] 3.(d) The words "workman ' means an workman whose termination has been terminated after giving him a reasonable opportunity to explain his conduct and conduct. It may be that the employer has discharged the burden of proving that he has discharged his duties as a workman on the basis of the record of the case. [791F G] 4.(e) The High Courts have not correctly interpreted the definition in section 9(oo).

The assessee, a dealer of goods, was registered under the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1948. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the application on the ground that the sales were not inter vided and inter vected. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes. The Assistant Commissioner held that the sale was inter vined and inter inter versed and inter tained inter vivos. The Tribunal, however, held that there was no transfer of goods in the course of inter inter State trade or commerce within the meaning of section 2(f) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the Sales Tax officer had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and that the order of the Assistant Commissioner was erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The sales were inter victed and inter State sales within the definition of "sale" in section 2 (f) as it stood at the relevant time. [782B] 2. The sale was intra vided inter vider and inter state sales within that meaning. The High Court was right in holding that the assessee was not a dealer within the scope of the expression "sale". [785C D] 3. The order of assessment is set aside and the Sales tax Officer restored the order to the extent of the tax payable on the sale. [771D] 4. The question whether the sales are inter voven or inter State sale within the ambit of section 5(2) of Act is not a question of law.

The appellant was a director of the respondent company. The Directors of the company were prosecuted for offences under sections 420 and 471 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, and section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that the Directors had not been authorised to make payments in respect of the shares held by them as a result of which they were invested in securities and that the company was guilty of criminal breach of trust and cheating. The trial court convicted the appellants under section 420 read with sections 34 and 5(2)(d), and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the directors had no authority to make payment in respect thereof as a matter of course, and that they were not authorised to do so under section 5 (1)(e) of that Act. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the statements made by the Directors were inadmissible in evidence because they were admissible in evidence. [737 D] In the present case the statements were admissible as evidence in evidence and the statements could not be used for any purpose other than those mentioned in section 5 of the Act. The statements were not admissible under section 10 of the Evidence Act. [771 C E] The High Courts had rightly held that the statement made by Directors was inadmissible in law because it was not admissible in law as evidence. The High court was right, in holding, that the entries made by them in the books of account and the entries were inadmissible under section 11 of the .

The appellants were appointed as Deputy Superintendents of the State of Gujarat in the State. They were promoted to the Indian Administrative Service on the basis of their seniority and promotion. The State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1956, which was published in the Official Gazette on May 1, 1957, for the purpose of filling up the posts of Deputy Superintendents. In pursuance of this notification the State Government made an order dated July 7, 1957 appointing the appellants as Deputy Secretaries to the State Governments and the Central Government. The appellants were promoted as Deputy Commissioners of the States. They challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that the State had no power to make any order under section 6(1)(a) of that Act in view of the provisions of article 309 of the Constitution, and that the impugned order was not valid. Held, that the appellants were entitled to be appointed as Assistant Secretaries to State Governments only on the recommendation of the Commission. The order was made by the State Govern ment under section 7(1). The order made by it was in accordance with law and the rules framed thereunder. The Central Government had no authority to make such an order. The impugned order did not contain any provision for the appointment of the appellants on the recommendations of the Commis sioner. The power conferred on the State under section 8(1), read with r. 5, was not confined to the appointment and promotion of the appellant as Deputy Secretary to the Government of India. The expression "any other person" in r. 6, means a person who is appointed to the Central or State Governments. The word "other person" used in r, 5, did not include any person who was appointed to a State service on the date of his appointment and was therefore entitled to continue in the service till he attained the age of 55 years.

The petitioners who were dealers in cotton seeds, challenged the validity of the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1968 (Act No. III of 1968) on the ground that they were not entitled to exemption under section 3(1)(a) of the Act. The High Court held that the sales tax authorities had no power to levy tax on the sale of cotton seeds and that the provisions of section 3 (1)(b) of Act No. IV of 1968 were ultra vires the State Legislature, and that they could not be said to have contravened article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the impugned Act was violative of article 14 inasmuch as it did not provide for any tax on sale of goods in the course of inter State trade or commerce, and therefore, the provisions Of section 3 were ultravires. HELD: (i) The impugned Act is a colourable legislation and is not hit by article 19(1) (a). It is not open to the legislature to impose a tax on sales of cotton seed which are outside the purview of article 19. [630 B] (ii) The provisions of the impugned Acts are ultra vires articles 14, 19(2)(b), 31 and 31 of the Constitu tion. [731 C D] (iii) The Act is not violative of articles 14 and 19(3). It does not provide any tax for sale of a cotton seed within the meaning of article 301. [774 E F] (iv) The contention that the Act was ultra vires article 14 is not correct.

The first respondent, who was the owner of a suit properties, filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage. The first respondent contended that the mortgage was not binding on him and that the mortgagor had no right to redeem the mortgage in view of section 3(1) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, which provided that where the mortgagee has failed to pay the debt due from him under the mortgage, he shall be entitled to redeem it. The trial court held that the mortgaged property was not a mortgage within the meaning of section 2(2) of that Act and that as the mortgagor was not entitled to any relief under the Act, the mortgagor could not claim any relief in respect of the mortgaged properties. On appeal by the first respondent the High Court set aside the decree and remanded the case for fresh disposal on merits. The High Court held that since the mortgagee had failed to discharge his debt due to him under section 3 (1) he was entitled to a decree for redemption, and that he could not be allowed to redeem such mortgaged property. In appeal by special leave it was contended that in view Of the provisions of section 4(1), the mortgagor is entitled to get a decree against the mortgagee on the ground that he had failed in his capacity as a mortgagee, and the mortgagor 's right to redemption is extinguished only if he has failed in the capacity of a mortgagee. HELD: (i) The High Courts were not justified in holding that the mortgagee was not liable to pay any debt due under the mortgages. [682 C] (ii) The mortgage was a mortgage by conditional sale and it was not open to the mortgagor to redeem his mortgaged property on the date of redemption, but only a mortgage. It is not open for the mortgagor either to redeem or to redeem a mortgaged property after the redemption is over.
