[782 D] (iii) The mortgagee 's liability to pay a debt due by him under a mortgage is extinguished when he has paid the debt. If the mortgagee is entitled, he cannot be allowed the benefit of section 5(1). [785 E F] (iv) The mortgagor ' right to recover the debt is extinguished if he fails in his presence and the creditor pays the debt within the time prescribed by section 4 (1). The mortgagor has no right or title to the property. He can claim any benefit under the decree for recovery of the debt, but he cannot claim any protection under the decrees for redemption.

The appellants were the tenants of a cinema premises. The respondent filed an application under section 14 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 for eviction of the appellants on the ground that they had been in possession of the premises as a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the suit was not maintainable because the suit had been filed by the respondent under section 13 of the said Act and that the appellants were not entitled to any protection under section 12 of the Rent Act. In appeal, the High Court held that the respondent was a tenant in respect of the suit premises as defined in section 2 (1) (a) of that Act and the suit having been filed within the period of limitation prescribed by the Act, the appellants could not be evicted from the suit property. The High Court also held that there was no bar to the jurisdiction of the civil court to entertain a suit for eviction on the grounds specified in section 13. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of the Maharashtra Rents, Hotels and Lodging Houses Rates Control (Amendment) Act, 1954 were not applicable to the suit as they had not been made parties to the proceedings before the civil Court. HELD: The High Courts have jurisdiction to entertain the suit in view of the provisions contained in section 12. [619 F] In the present case, the suit filed by respondent was not a suit within the time prescribed by section 13 and therefore the suit could not have been dismissed on that ground.

The appellant was a director of the respondent company. The respondent, who was a managing agent of the company, was appointed as a managing director of a company under section 12 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. He was appointed by the company on the basis of a resolution passed by the Board of Directors of the Company. On the death of his father the appellant was appointed to the post of managing director. The appellant was also appointed as managing director in the company. In the year 1957, he was appointed a managing partner and was appointed on the same terms and conditions as were applicable to him. He continued to hold office till the date of his appointment. On December 12, 1957, the respondent filed a suit for declaration that the appointment of the appellant as managing agent was illegal and void. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had ceased to be a director within the meaning of section 12 and that the respondent was not entitled to any relief under section 18. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The word " managing" in section 12 means "any person who is appointed as such by the Central Government or State Government". It does not mean "any other person who has been appointed as an managing director" and it includes "any company which is appointed by a Central Government". [682 H] (ii) The words "any such person" in the section are wide enough to include "any persons who are appointed as the managing director". It is not possible to say that the word "other person" has been used in the Act. The words 'any person whose appointment is made by a company, do not mean any person who was appointed or appointed as director. [693 A] (iii) The expression "anything done or purported to be done under the Act" in sub section (1) of section 18 means "all persons who were appointed as directors" and not "any one". It has been defined in the statute that "any act done or purporting to be in pursuance of a direction given by the Court, shall be deemed to have been done or taken under the provisions of the Act". The word 'other person ' is used in section 18 and it does not include "other persons" as defined in that section. [793 B C] (iv) The proviso to sub section 2 of section 19 of the , which makes a provision for appointment of an managing partner, does not make any difference between the words "other than those who were holding office under the Central or State Governments". It only means "other things done or intended to be performed" and that is, therefore, the word 'any other thing done or done in pursuance thereof. [783 D F] (v) The definition of "other" in clause (a) of sub section 1 of section 2 is wide enough and it has been held by this Court in M/s. B. P. Co., Ltd. vs The State of Bombay, ; , followed.

The appellants, who were the partners of a firm, filed a suit for eviction against the respondents on the ground that they were in occupation of the premises in question. The Trial Court dismissed the application holding that the partnership was not a partnership within the meaning of Section 2(1)(d) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The High Court held that the firm was not an unregistered firm within the definition of the term 'business ' as defined in Section 2 (1)(e) of that Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants were not in occupation for more than three years and they were not entitled to any protection under the Rent Control Act. [775H] 2. The respondents were not tenants within the purview of Section 3(1) (d) read with Section 2 of the Act. They were not liable to be evicted on the grounds that they had been in occupation by virtue of the provisions of Section 13(2)(e). [776G H] 3. In view of the fact that the appellants were in possession of the shop in question, the High Court was right in holding that they could not be evicted under the provisions contained in Section 13 (2) (e) readwith Section 2. [77H] 4. The appellant 's case is that the premises were not a business within the ambit of Section 12(1). The respondents had been inducted as a partner of the firm and therefore, they could be evicted only under the terms of the partnership deed. [76G] 5. In the instant case, the appellants are in occupation since the premises was not in their occupation for a long period. They have been inducted by the firm on the basis of the rent receipts issued by them. The Rent Control Authority has rightly held that they did not become a partner within the scope of Section 14(2) read alongwith Section 13 of the Rent Act. The order of eviction passed against the appellants is set aside and the appeal is restored to its original file.

The Andhra Pradesh Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 was enacted by the State Legislature with a view to provide for the acquisition of land for the purpose of the Act. Section 3(1)(a) of the said Act provided that the provisions of the Hyderabad Land Reforms Act, 1972 shall apply to all lands held by the Central Government or any local authority in the State. The Act was amended by Andhra Pradesh Act No. 1 of 1976 which came into force on April 1, 1976. By a notification dated May 5, 1976 the Andhra Pradesh Legislature passed an Act providing for the compulsory acquisition of the land for a public purpose and for matters connected therewith. Section 4(1) provided that in respect of any land held by a person other than a member of a family or a member thereof, the provisions relating to the compulsory purchase of such land shall apply only to such land as may be specified in the notification. The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling & Regulation) Amendment Act, 1975 was enacted with a object to provide that the acquisition for any purpose connected therewith shall be deemed to have been made by the Government or local authority under section 4(2). Section 5 provided that no person other except a member or a family of a member shall hold land in excess of the ceiling area specified in section 4. The appellants who were members of the family filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned Act on the ground that they were not members of a Hindu undivided family and that the impugned legislation was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act was violative Of article 14 and was therefore violative of articles 14 and 19(1), (g) and (g). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned Act is a self contained code and has no application to the present case. It is not possible to hold that the Central Legislature had intended to provide compulsory acquisition for a limited purpose or for matters incidental thereto. [630B C] 2. The State Legislature was competent to enact the impugned law in view of the provisions contained in section 3(2) and the Act which came to be enacted with retrospective effect from April 1. 1976. The Central Legislature could not make any provision relating to compulsory acquisition, but it could not do so by reason of the fact that the State legislature had intended that the land should be held for a specified purpose or that the ceiling areas should be deemed for a period not exceeding one year. [730C] 3. The provisions contained therein are in pari materia with section 4 and the provisions in the Act are in addition to those contained in sections 4(3) and 5 of the Andhra Act. [781E F] 4. Section 6 of the Land Reforms Amendment Act is intended to give effect to the provisions made in the impugned Acts. The object of the amending Act is to provide a compulsory acquisition to the members of an undivided family for a certain period not less than one year, and to provide the compulsory acquisitions for a particular purpose or purposes connected therewith, and for that purpose, it would be necessary to give retrospective effect to such provisions. [783E F; 784A] 5. The legislature has intended to make a provision relating only to compulsory purchase in respect thereof. It was not possible for the Parliament to provide any compulsory acquisition by the Union of India or the State Governments. [784F G] 6. Section 7 of the Central Act is in pari with section 3 of the General Clauses Act, which provides that no land shall be held by any member or member thereof except a person who has been declared as a member under section 5. It also provides that if any land is held for any specified purpose, the State Government may make an order providing for compulsory acquisition.

The workmen of the respondent company were employed in the appellant company. The workmen were dismissed from service on the ground that they had not been given any opportunity to show cause against their dismissal. The management filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal and for quashing the order. The High Court held that the workmen were guilty of misconduct and that the order was bad because it was passed without giving an opportunity to them to showcause why they should not be dismissed from services. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of discharge was based on a wrong appreciation of evidence and was therefore illegal. [657 H] (ii) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to pass the order in question because it did not give an opportunity of showing cause against its dismissal. It was open to the management to show that the workman had been dismissed from employment. But, if the management did not comply with the requirements of section 33A of the , it could not be said that there was any violation of the principles of natural justice. [757 H; 758 A] (iii) The workmen had no opportunity to prove their case and the order passed by the Tribunal was bad. The Tribunal was therefore right in holding that the dismissal was illegal because, the workmen had been given an opportunity for showing cause. [859 B C] (iv) The management did have the power to dismiss the workmen on the grounds of misconduct or inefficiency. It could not, therefore, be said to have exercised its discretion arbitrarily and without giving any opportunity of being heard to them.

The appellant, a Professor of the University, was appointed as a Principal in the University. The Selection Committee recommended the names of the candidates for appointment to the post of Principal. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the selection and appointment of the respondents. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Selection Committee had no power to appoint the respondents on the ground that the selection was vitiated by mala fides or mala fides. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Selection Committees are not empowered to appoint a Principal as a result of an enquiry into the merits of the case and the suitability of the candidate for appointment is not made in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [775G] 2.2 The Selection committee has power to make appointments on the basis of merit, but it does not have power to do so. It is only when the Selection Committees have power under section 16(1) to appoint an officer or a person appointed by the Selection Board that the appointment should be made in conformity with the Act and the Rules. [774C] 3. The selection committee has no power either to make any appointments on a particular basis or on the recommendation of the Selection Commis sioner. It does not, therefore, follow that the Committee is empowered to make such appointments on any particular basis. [764F G] 4.1 In the instant case, the Selection Boards have power in making appointments on different dates and there is no provision for appointment on the same basis. The Committee has no authority to make a selection on the said basis. It cannot be said that the appointments were made in violation of the provisions contained in section 16 (1) of the . [765G H] 4:2 In the absence of any provision for making appointments, the selection is vitiated by non compliance with the mandatory provisions of section 16 of the , and the rules are not ultra vires. The appointment of respondents on different posts cannot be made without following the procedure prescribed in the Act or the Rules as laid down in the Rules and the Regulations. [754G H; 771A] 5:3 In the present case, there is nothing to show that the appellant was appointed by Selection Committee on the recommendations of the selection committee. The appointments were not made without complying with the statutory provisions of law.

The petitioners, who were owners of certain lands in the City of Bombay, applied for permission to construct a building on the land in question. The Municipal Commissioner issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Act declaring that the proposed construction was not necessary and that the building would be required for a public purpose. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court which held that the construction was necessary for a private purpose, and that it was necessary to do so under section 5(1)(a) of that Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The impugned notification was not valid as the construction had been completed on March 31, 1964. The construction was completed on April 1, 1964 and the building was required for the public purpose and it was not open to the Municipal Commissioner to issue a notification in respect of the proposed constructions. [808 D] (ii) The construction had already commenced on March 30, 1964, and the construction having been completed within the period of three months from the date of the publication of the notification under s.4(1). [809 G H] (iii) The petitioners were not entitled to any protection under article 19(1), (g) of Constitution. They had no right to challenge the validity or legality of the construction on the ground that it had been made without complying with the provisions of section 5A of the . [807 D] In the present case, the construction in question was completed within three months of the date on which the construction commenced. The notification under sec.4 (1) was issued on April 31, 1966 and the petitioners were entitled to protection under articles 19(2), 19(3) and 19(4).

The appellant, a resident of Pakistan, was allotted to the Government of India in Pakistan. The Union of India, by its letter dated December 8, 1960, requested the Government to make an award on the basis that the Indian territory of Pakistan was not a territory within the meaning of article 31A of the Constitution. The Government of Pakistan made an award under section 6 of the , which provided that the Union of Pakistan shall be deemed to have been formed in India and that the said Union shall be entitled to the compensation payable by the Union for the period during which the Union was formed. In the meantime, the Indian Independence Act, 1947 came into force. The Indian Independence (Amendment) Act, 1948 came into effect on January 1, 1948. By section 2 of the Act, the Government was empowered to make a award in respect of any territory within India and the Union shall not be entitled, except with the previous sanction of the Central Government, to the extent provided by the said Act, to be made applicable to such territories. The appellant challenged the validity of the said award on various grounds. The High Court held that the award was invalid because it was made in respect Of territory within Pakistan and that it was not an order made under section 3 of the Indian Reorganisation Act, 1913, as it stood before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The award was valid and could not be challenged on the ground that it did not contain any provision in the Indian Constitution which was a part of the territory of India. [657 H] (2) The Indian territory was an integral part of India and it was therefore not an integral parts of India within the territories of India as defined by article 31 A of the Consti tution. [757 B C] (3) The Union Government could not make a reference under section 10 of the . [658 F G] (4) The expression "any territory" in article 31(A) means an area within the territory which is comprised in the territory and includes an area included in the territories which are comprised in that territory. [781 D E] (5) The word "any other territory" used in article 32 of the Constitu tion includes an areas within the territorial limits of India or any part thereof.

The appellant mortgaged the land in favour of the respondent. The mortgage deed was executed on May 19, 1943, and the mortgage deed recited that the mortgagor had paid Rs. 1,000 to the mortgagee on July 31, 1944, and that the mortgagee had not paid the amount due under the mortgage. The mortgagee filed a suit for recovery of possession of the mortgaged land on the ground that the mortgage was void as it was not executed within the period of limitation prescribed by section 13(1) of the Transfer of Property Act. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the plaintiff had failed to prove that the mortgaged property was a 'property ' within the meaning of section 2 (g) of that Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The mortgage was not a 'goods ' within section 2(g) Of the Transferof Property Act and therefore the mortgagor could not be held liable for the payment of the amount. [601 B] (ii) The mortgagee had failed in proving that the suit property was an 'property" within the definition of section 3 (g). The mortgage did not create a right or interest in the mortgaged properties. The mortgagor had failed, therefore, to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. [702 C] (iii) The plaintiff had not proved that the mortgages were executed on July 19, 1944 and that he was entitled to recover possession of it under section 13 (1) (g), because, the mortgage in question was a mortgage within the contemplation of the Act. [781 D F] (iv) The suit was barred by limitation as it did not contain any provision for the time being in force. The plaintiff could not prove that he had paid the entire amount due to him under the mortgages.

The appellants were employed as a casual labourer in the Bombay State. The appellants were engaged in the business of transport and transport service. They were paid tax on their vehicles. The said amounts were collected by the appellants from the employees of the appellant company. The amount was collected by them from the appellants under section 3(1) of the Maharashtra Sales Tax Act, 1959. The amounts were received by the employees from the appellant Company. The appellant company challenged the levy of tax on the ground that the amounts were not liable to be taxed in view of the provisions of section 2(g) of that Act and that the said amounts could not be taxed under the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the expression "any person" in section 2 (g) means any person who is engaged in any business or profession or vocation but does not include a person who has been engaged in such business or vocation and includes any person engaged in an activity which is carried on by him in connection with his business. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "other person" used in section 3 (1) means persons who are engaged in a business or occupation of any goods or services or both. It does not mean that persons engaged in that business or avocation do not include persons engaged by him. [703F] 2. Section 2(h) of this Act defines "any other person" to mean persons engaged on the business or calling for any information relating to the business, profession or occupation. The definition is wide enough to cover persons who were engaged on a business and profession. It is not possible to define the expression 'other person ' in section 4 (1). [704F] 3. Section 3(h), which defines "other persons" to include persons employed in any industry or undertaking. The word "any" is wide and it does not cover persons engaged for carrying on any business. It cannot be said that the definition of "other than persons engaged as a temporary labourer" in the Act is wide. [771C] 4. Section 4(h)(i) of Bombay Act, which defines 'other persons ' to mean person who are employed in an industry or a undertaking. It also includes persons engaged under any other law for the time being in force. The words "any persons engaged or engaged in" in sub section (1), which is in pari materia with the definition, are wide enough and it cannot be construed as including persons engaged directly in the said business.

The appellants, who were the owners of a cinema theatre, filed an application under section 3 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1916 for grant of a licence to the respondent No. 1 for running a cinema house in the State of Madhya Pradesh on the ground that they had been granted a licence by the State Government under section 4(1) of the Act and that the respondent Nos. 2 to 5 were not entitled to any renewal of their licence. The appellants contended that the grant of the licence was arbitrary and violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the licensing authority had no power to grant the licence, and that it was not open to the State Legislature to issue a notification under section 6 of the said Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the licensing authorities were not competent to grant a licence in favour of the appellants. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the licence granted by the District Magistrate was arbitrary, and violative Of article 14. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The grant of licence is a matter of discretion and cannot be challenged on any ground whatsoever. It is not open for the State to issue an order under section 5 of the . [799 F] 2. The licensing authority has power to refuse a licence if it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for not granting the licence. If the licensing authori tys order is based on some extraneous considerations, it would be open to him to challenge the validity of the grant. [701 A B] 3. The State Government has no power under section 7 of the and the licensing Authority cannot refuse a grant of an licence in respect of a particular cinema house. It can issue a writ of mandamus directing the State or the State, to grant it. If there is any violation of article 19, the order granting the license must be set aside. [771 B] 4. The power conferred on the licensing officer under section 8 of the is not absolute and cannot extend to a licence granted in favour or for a licence issued in favour thereof. It has no authority to grant an order of renewal unless it is shown that there is sufficient cause to justify the grant, and if the licensing or the local authority refuses to grant such a licence, the licensing court would be justified in refusing the grant on the grounds specified in section 7. [761 C] 5. The order granting a licence is not arbitrary and must be quashed. [752 B] 6. The validity of an order passed under section 10 of the can only be challenged by a person who has been granted the licence in his favour or by any other person, if he is satisfied with the conditions mentioned in section 8, that there are sufficient grounds for refusing the licence to grant him a licence. [741 C D] 7. The contention that the order passed by the licensing and local authority granting the licences was arbitrary is not tenable. It cannot be said that the State has no jurisdiction to issue the same. [732 B C] 8. The fact that the appellants had been given a licence under section 9 of the does not make any difference in the position of the licensing, or the licensing order passed thereunder, is not a ground for refusing a licence on the basis of which it can be granted. [721 D E] 9. The question whether an application for grant was made by a licensee under section 11 of the , is a question of fact and cannot arise in the present case.

The plaintiffs entered into a contract with the respondent for mining of coal in the area of the appellants. The lease was to expire on January 1, 1957. The appellants were granted a lease of the land in favour of the respondent. On June 30, 1957 the respondent wrote a letter to the appellants stating that the lease was not renewed and that the appellants had no right to renew the lease. The appellant replied that the letter was not signed by the appellants and that it was not a valid document. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of contract. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the agreement was not binding on the parties. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The agreement was void because it was executed in the presence of the parties and the appellants were entitled to renew it. [657 H] (ii) The document was a valid one and the same was not an instrument of contract and could be acted upon by the parties at all. [757 B] (iii) The letter was signed by both the parties but the same did not form part of the document. It was not in dispute that the respondent had no authority to renew its lease. [781 D F] (iv) The appellants ' plea that the contract was not valid and the suit was barred by res judicata. [783 C] (v) The High Court was right in holding that the document was not executed at all, because it did not contain any provision for the grant of a lease. It could not be said that the parties were bound to act upon the terms of the contract. [784 D F].

The appellants were prosecuted under section 5(1) of the Bihar Sugar (Control of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution alleged that the sugar was sold by the appellants to the State Government for sale of sugarcane in the State of Bihar and that the appellants had no locus standi to file a complaint against them. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of section 5 (1) were not applicable to the case because, the Act did not apply to the cases where the sugar sold was purchased by the appellant for sale or purchase of sugarcane. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Act was ultra vires the Constitution and that it violated article 14 of the Constitution as it contravened articles 19(1)(f) and 31(2) of Part III of the Constitu tion. HELD : (i) The provisions of the Act were not ultra vires article 14 because, in view of the provisions contained in section 5 of the Prevention of Foodgrains Act, 1955, the appellants could not be prosecuted under the Act. [408 D] (ii) The Act was not ultravires the Constitution inasmuch as it violated articles 19 and 31 of the constitution. It was therefore void. [416 E F] (iii) The impugned Act was violative of article 14. [414 A B] (iv) The appellants were rightly prosecuted under article 14, because, they had no right to file any complaint against the sugar in the manner prescribed by the Act and that they were not entitled to any protection under article 19(2)(f).

The appellants, who were dealers in sugar, challenged the order of the State Government dated March 5, 1977 and the State Govt. issued a notification dated May 7, 1977 exempting the industries from payment of sales tax on the sale of sugar to the extent of Rs. 1,50,000/ per annum from the date of its issue. The appellants contended that the State government had no power to grant exemption under section 3(1) (a) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957 and that the notification dated March 7, 1978 was not applicable to the case in hand. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government had no authority to grant the exemption from sales tax to the appellants. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order dated March 3, 1977 was not a law within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) and that it was not open to the State to issue any notification under section 4(1). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government had power to issue a notification under Section 4(3) (b) of Karnataka Sales tax Act, 1958. [782B] 2. The order dated April 7, 1979 was not an order of exemption from payment or sales tax. It was open to it to the Government to issue such a notification. [771C D] 3. The power conferred on the State under section 5(3)(a), is subject to the conditions laid down in sub section (2) of Section 4 of the Act. The Government has no power or authority to issue the said order. It is open to any person aggrieved by an order made by the State, to file a writ petition before the High Court. [761C] 4. The notification dated April 8, 1977 issued under section 6 of the Mysore Sales Tax Rules, 1957 was not in force at all. The said order was not challenged by the appellants in the High court. [753F G] 5. The appellant had no right to challenge the said orders on the ground that it did not contain any provision for granting exemption from tax to a person who has been granted exemption under Section 3(2) (c). [764C D, F] 6. The contention of the appellant that the power conferred by section 4 of Karnataka Act was not available to them and that there was no provision in the said Act which could be made applicable to them is not tenable. [781F G; 771E] 7. The question whether the State had no jurisdiction to issue an order under Section 6 of Karnataka General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1969 or not would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death for the offence of murder and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The High Court acquitted all the accused persons on the ground that they were not members of a unlawful assembly, and that they had been falsely implicated in the crime. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the appellants were not entitled to any benefit under Section 34, I. P.C., and that the conviction of the appellants was illegal. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution case is that on the date of occurrence, the deceased was a member of a assembly and he had been convicted for murder of one of the accused. The appellants were members of the unlawful assembly. They were not armed with any common object or intention to kill the deceased. The common object of the assembly was to commit an offence punishable under Section 304 Part I I.p.C.; that the prosecution case was that on a date when the occurrence took place, the accused attacked the deceased and caused injuries to him. The evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 is corroborated by the medical evidence. The medical evidence clearly establishes that the deceased had been assaulted by the appellants with the common object. [775F] 2. The offence under Section 201 I. p.C is not murder but it is culpable homicide amounting to murder. It is a case of culpable homicide. The intention of the legislature is to cause death in the ordinary course of nature and to cause injury to the deceased if such act or omission causes any injury to any person. [771G] 3. In the instant case, the appellants had been charged with having committed an offence under section 201 I.,P. C. The conviction of all the appellants is set aside.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, purchased certain property in the name of his wife and two daughters. The Income Tax officer issued notice under section 34(1) of the Act to the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 on the ground that the transfer was effected by a registered instrument or by an instrument which was not registered in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee filed his return of income for the years 1964 65 and 1965 66. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim holding that the transaction was not one of transfer but was one of sale and that the property in question was a transfer within the meaning of section 2(15) of that Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee had no right to transfer the property under section 22(2)(a) of Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1964. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that there was no transfer within section 22 (2)(b) of Act and that it was not a transfer in the present case. The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. In the appeal to this Court on behalf of the assessee it was contended that the sale was effected with a view to bringing about an asset or property which is not registered under section 2 (15) (a). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The transfer of property by a Hindu Undivided Family is one of the transfer and is not a sale within the definition of the expression in section 2 of the Income tax act. It is only when it is effected with an intention to bring about an income or property that is to be taxed under section 23 (2) (b). The transfer is effected by an agreement which is registered as a transfer. [637 D] 1.2 In the instant case, the transfer of the property was effected in accordancewith the provisions contained in section 22 and not with the intention to bringing it into existence any asset or properties which are not registered. It was only when the transfer is made by an unregistered instrument or a registered document, that the transferor has no right or title to the property. The transfer was made by a deed of transfer and the transfer in question is effected in pursuance of the said agreement. [737 D F] 1:3 In the present ease, the sale of the house in question had been effected with the object of bringing about a change in the ownership of the wife and children. It could not be said that the intention was to bring an asset into existence at the time when the property is sold. The fact that the wife or children were not registered would not make any difference. [781 D F; 838 A B] 1 :4 In the case of a transfer, the assessee has no option but to bring it into the existence any income or properties in question. It cannot be said to have been effected by the transfer. The sale was made with the result that the income or assets were not sold at the instance of the transferor. [838 A C] 1.(a) In the facts and circumstances of the case, there is no evidence on record to show that the transfers were effected in contravention of the provisions Of section 22. [783 D F]. (b) The transfer in pursuance thereof was effected after the transfer took place. It may be that the transferee has a right or interest in the property which he has acquired under the provisions and the transferor is not entitled to any benefit whatsoever. In such a case, it cannot be held that section 22 of the income tax Act had no application to the facts of the present cases.

The appellant was charged with the offence of selling adulterated food to a Food Inspector under section 16(1) (a) read with section 5(2)(d) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case was that the appellant had purchased the adulterated food from one person and sold it to another person. The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge for having committed an offence under section 7(1)(d). He was also convicted under section 8(2) (d) readwith section 5 of the Act. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove that the adulterated article was adulterated and that the offence was committed in contravention of section 7 (1) read alongwith section 5 (2)(e). HELD: The prosecution had not proved that the food was adulterated. It is true that the Food Inspector had not examined the appellant as a witness but he did not examine him as a witnesses. But, it is true, that the evidence of the complainant was not corroborated by any other evidence. But in the present case, the Food Inspectors were not examined as a defence witness. The Food Inspector was not examined and the prosecution could not be said to have proved that there was no evidence to show that the sample was adulterated article. [619 F G] In the instant case, it was not established that the milk was adulterated or adulterated article, because, the appellant did not produce any evidence to prove the charge against him. The High Court was right in holding that the quantity of the food which was adulterated was adulterated as no evidence was produced by the prosecution to show what was the quantity which was consumed in the sale of the adulterated articles.

The appellant was a clerk in the office of the Municipal Board, Jabalpur. He had been dismissed from service on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to defend himself against the order of dismissal passed by him. The appellant filed a suit for setting aside the order and for a declaration that he was entitled to be reinstated in service with effect from the date of his dismissal. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled only to the benefit of the order, but dismissed the suit on the grounds that the order was not passed by the Collector, Jabalpur, and that the period of limitation prescribed under section 115 C.P.C. had expired on the date when the order came into force. The High Court in revision held that since the order had been passed by a competent authority, it could not be said that the suit was barred by limitation. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court was right in holding that the dismissal of the suit by the District Collector was not justified on the basis of the decision of the High court in Ram Krishna Dalmia vs State of U.P., ; and that since there had been a failure to comply with the order within the period prescribed under the Act, the order could not have been passed against him. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the District Magistrate was not a nullity because it was passed by an authority subordinate to it. [795B] 2. The District Collector had no jurisdiction to pass the order on the appellant 's dismissal. He could not pass the decree in his favour. [774C D] 3. The appeal must be dismissed. [764F] 4. In the instant case, the High Courts have held that there was failure to exercise the power of the State Government under section 116 C. P.C., and that it was not open to the appellant to challenge the order passed by it on the same grounds as were available to him in the appeal before the Collector. [754F G] 5. The question whether the High courts had jurisdiction to entertain the suit or not is a matter of fact to be decided by the competent authority. [784C E] 6. In view of the fact that the State has no power to pass an order on an application made under section 151 C.p., and the High 'Court has rightly held that it had jurisdiction in the matter.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the sole proprietor of a joint family. The properties were divided into three parts: (1) the properties were sold by the father to his wife and (2) the appellant 's mother had no right to sell the properties. The trial court held that the appellant was not entitled to any decree for partition in respect of the properties, but only a decree for possession was passed on the basis of the valuation of the property. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the valuation was not based on the valuation and that the value of the lands was not the proper consideration for determining the question whether the valuation should be determined on the ground that the properties had been sold by a father to another person, and that if the valuation had been determined on a proper consideration it would have been open to the appellant to raise the question as to whether the value fixed by the trial court was correct. HELD: (i) The High Court erred in holding the valuation as not based upon the valuation. [608 B] (ii) The appellant ' contention that the property sold by him was a joint Hindu family and that it was not open to him to raise this question at all, because, the valuation could be determined only on the assumption that the price fixed by him had been correctly determined on his basis. It is true that the trial judge has found that the respondent 's father was a minor and that he was not a minor. But it does not mean that the court should have held that there was no question of any consideration for the valuation, but it must be shown that the parties had agreed to the valuation on the footing that the sale was in accordance with the valuation fixed by it. [708 C] (iii) The trial judge was wrong when he did not consider the valuation at all. [781 D F] (iv) The court should not have held the valuation to be a proper one and must not have allowed the appellant an appeal to the High court.

The appellant filed a suit for the recovery of certain amount of money and for mesne profits. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the valuation of the suit was not proper, but the High Court in revision held that the value of the decree had to be determined on the basis of the valuation made by the District Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were wrong in holding that section 115 C.P.C. could not apply to a case where the valuation was made by a District Judge, and that the District judge had no jurisdiction to pass an order under section 115 D.P., Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as it did not have jurisdiction to try the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) The High Court was wrong in taking the view that the provisions of section 115 B.P, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, were applicable to a proceeding under the U.P . and that no such power could be exercised by the High court in revision under section 116 D. P. Act. [795 F] (2) The jurisdiction of the District Court is not confined to a matter which has been specifically referred to in sub section (1), but it does not include a matter covered by sub section(3). [796 G H] (3) In the instant case, the High courts were wrong. They had no power to pass any order under the Act. The District Court was right in holding the valuation as per the provisions contained in sub sections (1A), (2B) and (3D) of section 116 C. P., Code.

The respondents were owners of the land in question. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the acquisition proceedings on the ground that the land was not acquired by the State Government under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and that the acquisition was illegal as it was not for the State to acquire the land. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondents were not entitled to any relief in respect of the acquisition of the lands. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondents are owners of a land which is not required by the Land Acquisi tion Act, and the acquisition is for the public purpose of the State. [601B] 2. The acquisition of a property under section 6(1)(a) of that Act is not for public purpose but for public purposes. [702C] 3. The land in dispute was acquired by a State Government on the basis of an agreement between the parties and the Government. The possession of the respondents was taken over by the Government on January 1, 1976. The Government had no authority to acquire it under section 5(1). [603E F] 4. The State Government is not entitled for any relief under article 226 of the Constitution. [613F G] 5. The writ petition is dismissed. [599A B] 6. The appellant 's remedy in respect thereof is a statutory right and the High court has no jurisdiction to entertain the petition.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that the building was constructed by the State Government in accordance with the provisions of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the construction was completed within the period of limitation prescribed under section 13(2)(b) of the Act. The High Court held that the landlord had failed in proving that the constructions were completed within a period of three years from the date of the institution of the suit and that the suit was barred by time. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that since the building had been constructed after the expiry of the period prescribed under the Act, the landlord could not be evicted on the basis of the provisions contained in section 13 (2)(a) of Act and that since there was no evidence to show that the buildings were completed beyond a period within the meaning of section 13 of the said Act, it was not open to the appellant to contend that the decree for eviction passed by the trial court was erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions contained under section 12(2) (b) are mandatory and the High Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain a suit on the grounds of limitation. [775B] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant landlord had not proved that the premises were completed after the institution Of the suit. The suit was filed within three years of the date when the suit for ejectment was filed. The period of two years prescribed under sub section (2) of section 12 is the period during which the suit has been instituted. [77E] 2:2 In the present case, there was a dispute between the parties regarding the construction and the building in question. The appellant landlord did not prove that it had completed three years ' period within which the decree was passed. The question of limitation does not arise for consideration in this appeal. [76G H; 77A] 2 :2 In view of the fact that the respondent landlord had filed a civil suit, the High court erred in taking the view that the plaintiff had failed before the trial Court and the suit having been instituted within three months of the filing of the civil suit the appellant was entitled to raise the question of jurisdiction. [75F] 3:3 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that the disputed construction was complete after the date on which the building became available. The respondent landlord could have raised the question as to whether the construction had been completed within three year of the commencement of the proceedings. [78B C] 4:4 In view thereof, the suit filed by the appellant for eviction was barred under section 14(2), and the decree passed by trial court is set aside.

The appellant, a contractor of the respondent company, entered into an agreement with the Government of India for construction of certain works in the State of Bihar. The contract was to be executed by the Governor of Bihar on the terms and conditions mentioned therein. Under the agreement the Government had to make a reference to the arbitrator appointed under section 8(1) of the Act. The arbitrator appointed the appellant as the arbitrator. On the question whether the arbitrator could have made an award in respect of the works in which he was appointed, HELD : (i) The arbitrator was not competent to make the award. The award is not a judicial one and it is not binding on him. It is not open to the Government to make an award under section 7(1). [619 F G] (ii)The arbitrator could not have made any reference to arbitration in respect thereof. The words "any dispute" in section 8 are wide enough to include a matter which is referred to arbitration. The word "court" in the Act means a court of appeal and it includes a court or tribunal. It does not mean a court. [620 H] (iii)The award is a judicial order and it must be read as a whole. The language used in section 7 is wide enough, and it cannot be construed as a judicial instrument. [719 F] (iv)The words "court of appeal" are wide and the word "Court" has to be given its widest meaning. It may include a court which has been appointed under the Act and not a court subordinate to it. The expression "court " means a tribunal subordinate to the High Court. [783 A B] (v)The word "any matter" in sub section (1) is wide and it does not include any matter which can be referred to an arbitrator. It cannot be said that the words "other disputes" are capable of being referred to the arbitration.

The respondent, a Public Works Department, was charged with offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and Section 5(2) read with Rule 7 of the Prevention and Corruption Rules, 1947. The respondent pleaded that he had been in service of the State Government as a result of which he was transferred to the State of Punjab. He also alleged that he was not in service at the relevant time and that he would be entitled to pension under the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court dismissed his petition on the ground that he did not have any right to claim pension under Rule 7. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The respondent was a public servant within the meaning of Article 311(2)(b) of the Constitution and as such he was entitled to be retired from service. He was not entitled to any pension under rule 7. [702D] 2.2 In view of the provisions contained in Rule 7, the High court was right in holding that the respondent was not a public employee within the definition of Article 21 of the Constitu tion. The High Court was right when it held that the impugned order of discharge passed by the State Govern ment was illegal and void. [781G] 3.1 In view thereof, the impugned orders of discharge were quashed. [783E F] 4.2 The respondent is entitled to claim the pension under Rules 7 and 8 of the Civil Procedure Code on the basis that he could not be retired at the time when he was posted in the State. [784G] 5.3 In view Of the provisions made in Rule 8, the respondent is also entitled to get the benefit of the said rule.

The respondent company was a limited company. The respondent company, a limited Company, was incorporated in the year 1949 and its shareholders were declared elected to the general public. In 1951, the respondent company filed returns of income for the assessment years 1950 51 and 1950 51. The Income tax Officer held that the shares of the company were not liable to tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but the High Court in appeal reversed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the expression "any company" in section 2(g) means a company which is not a limited limited company and includes a company, and that the word "any other company" used in the Act must be construed as including a company as defined in the Indian Companies Act. HELD: (i) The expression "other company" has been used in section 10 of the Act to mean a company incorporated in India. It is not necessary that the words "any person" should be interpreted in their ordinary sense and it would be sufficient if they were intended to be construed in their popular sense. [408 D] (ii) The word "other companies" in the context of section 10 must be read as including any company which has been incorporated in a statute or an instrument of association or body of individuals, but that is not enough to include a company in its ordinary sense. It would be enough if they are intended to have a limited purpose and object. [508 D F] (iii) The words "other persons" in sub section (1) of section 2 must be interpreted as including the company which was incorporated under the Indian Act.

The appellant was a dealer in the goods sold by him to the respondent. The appellant made an application under section 66 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947 for the purchase of certain goods from the respondent and the latter refused to accept the same. The respondent contended that the appellant had no right to sell the goods to the appellant as he was not a dealer within the meaning of section 2(1) (d) of the Act. Held, that the word "dealer" in the definition of "dealer", in the context of the words "dealer ", is wide enough to include a person who has been appointed by the State Government under the Act and that the expression "dealer " includes any person who is engaged in the business of buying goods from one person to another. The word "sale" in section 2 (1) of Bombay Sales tax Act, 1948 means a person whose principal place of business is situated within the definition. It is not necessary that the person who was appointed by him should be a dealer and not a person engaged in any business of selling goods from another person to others. The expression "sale " includes a person carrying on the business as a dealer. The words "any person" in sub section (1)(d) are wide enough, but they must include only persons who were appointed by them to another person. The definition is wide and it cannot be said that the intention of the legislature was to exclude persons who had been appointed to another company or persons who have been appointed as such.

The respondent was charged with an offence under section 161 I.P.C. for having committed a criminal breach of trust and for having abetted the commission of the offence, he was convicted by the Special Judge under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The respondent contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to try the case because it did not decide the question whether the respondent was guilty of any offence punishable under section 165 I. P.C., and that the respondent had committed a breach of the trust or of any rule of law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "any offence" in clause (d)(i) of section 5 of the Act means an offence which is punishable with imprisonment for life or with fine or with both. It does not mean that the word "any other offence" has been used in the context of the definition of "any act done by a public servant". The expression 'any act committed by a Government servant" in section 5 is wide enough to include acts done by him in pursuance of his duties and functions. [630 B] 2. The words "anything done or purported to be done by any public servant" are not defined in the Act. It includes acts done in pursuance thereof. In the context, it has been held that the expression "other offence" is used in section 161(1) of that Act. [730 B C] 3. The word "every act done or purporting to be performed by a person in pursuance whereof he was not liable to any punishment under the Act, and therefore, the expression 'other offence ' has been defined in section 2 (d). In the present case, the respondent did not commit any offence under the Indian Penal Code. [830 B D] 4. The High Court was right in holding that the words "other offences" in the definition are wide enough and it could not be said that the appellant had committed an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with imprisonment. [931 C E] 5. The question whether a public officer is guilty of a criminal offence under clause (e) of sub section (1) (a) of Section 5 of that Code must be determined on the facts and circumstances of each case. [430 B F] 6. The definition of 'any other act done in furtherance of the duties or functions of a public office" in sub section(1), is wide and it includes acts performed by any person in respect whereof he is not liable for any punishment. [532 D E] 7. The term "other act done" in Section 5(2) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 means an act done with the consent or connivance of a Government official. It is well settled that the definition must be given its ordinary meaning and it is not necessary to refer to acts done with a view to preventing the commission thereof from being committed by public servants. [511 B C; G H] 8. The object of the expression in clause 2(d) is to prevent the commission or any act done under a public duty. It must be shown that the act was done with an intention to cause the public servant 's property or that he had no such knowledge or knowledge as would have caused him a loss to the Government. [ 511 B C, G H; 516 A] 9. The mere fact that the public officer was not guilty of an offence does not make it a case of criminal breach. It may be that the Government servant is guilty and he is liable for punishment under clause 2 (a). [533 D E F] 10.

The petitioners who were working as casual labourers in the Railways, had been appointed to the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil) in the Railway Administration on ad hoc basis. They were absorbed in the Indian Railways and were absorbed by the Railways. The petitioners challenged the validity of the order of absorption in the Central Administrative Tribunal, which held that the petitioners were entitled to be absorbed in service as casual labourer in the same department. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the Railway Board had no power to make any rules for the purpose of recruitment and conditions of service of temporary employees. Allowing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Railway Board has no power under the Rules to make rules for recruitment and condition of service in the Union Territory of Delhi. [703E] 2.2 In the instant case, the petitioners have been absorbed in a particular department. They are entitled to get absorption in that department. Their services were regularised by the Railway Adminis tration on ad temporary basis. The Railway Administration has no authority to make such rules for regular employment of temporary labourers. [781E] 3.3 In the circumstances, the Railway administration is directed to consider the cases of the petitioners for absorption in service and to take appropriate action in accordance with law within a period of six months from the date of receipt of this order. [783G H; 784A B] 4.4 The Railway Administ tration shall make regular appointments on ad permanent basis. If the Railway adminis trate is directed not to fill up any vacancy, it will be open to the petitioners to claim absorption in a suitable post.

The appellants, who were members of the Association of Cotton Mills Ltd., filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the notification issued by the Central Government under section 4(1) of the , on the ground that it contravened articles 14 and 19 (1)(g) of Part III of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notification was invalid as it violated articles 14, 19 and 19 of the Act and that the provisions of the bye laws were not ultra vires the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notification issued under section 3(1)(a) of that Act did not contravene article 19(1), because it contravened article 19 (2) (g) and (h). The notification was valid as it infringed articles 14 or 19 (3) (f) and the provisions Of Part III were ultra vires. [630 F] (ii) The provisions of section 4 (1) (a) and section 4 of the Bombay General Clauses Act, 1904, are not ultravires. The provisions Of section 4 are not in conflict with article 19 and they are void as it contravened the provisions contained in Part III. [730 G H] (iii) The power to issue a notification under section 6(1 ) (a), is not confined to the power of the Central Legislature to make laws for the regulation of trade, commerce or intercourse. It is only when the power is conferred by the Act, that power can be exercised in respect of matters enumerated in Part IV. [781 A B] (iv) The powers of the State Legislature are wide and they cannot be restricted to those powers which are expressly provided in the statute. The power conferred by section 6 (1), therefore, must be confined only to the powers of a Central Legislature.

The assessee company was a private limited company and its shareholders were assessed to income tax under the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer held that the assessee company had not been assessed to wealth tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50 but it was also held that there was no income from the assets of the company. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. In the appeals before this Court, on behalf of the Revenue, it was contended that the High Court had erred in holding that the income from which the dividend was payable was not taxable under section 2(6) of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1956, and that the amount of compensation paid by the company to the shareholders was not liable to be included in the total income of the assessee. HELD : The High Court erred in taking a contrary view. [775 B] In the instant case, the income tax authorities had wrongly held that it was not a revenue receipt but a revenue receipts and that it could not be said that there were no income for the year 1948 49. [771 C D] Commissioner of Income Tax vs M/s. P.M. Pulp & Paper Mills Ltd., ; , followed. The High Courts had wrongly applied the principle laid down by this Court in Commissioner of Wealth tax, Bombay vs M. P., P. V. section Ramanujam and Co. Ltd., [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, referred to.

The respondents were prosecuted for offences under sections 5(1)(d) and 6 of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961. The prosecution alleged that the forest produce was used by the forest officials in the State of Kerala and that the timber was used as a raw material for the purpose of manufacturing the goods. The trial court acquitted all the accused persons but convicted them under section 5(2)(d). The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the trees were not used as raw materials for the purposes of manufacturing it. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the Forest Officer had no jurisdiction to try the case and that he was not a 'person ' within the meaning of section 2(d) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The forest produce is used as an raw material in the manufacture of goods and therefore, it cannot be said that the word 'person" has been used in the definition of "person '. [630B] 2. The definition of 'person in section 2 (d) means a person who carries on business or personally works for the manufacture or sale of goods or for any other purpose whatsoever". It is not necessary to refer to the definition as defined in section 3(1) of that Act. The word 'Person ' has been defined in the Act and it is not intended to include a person whose activity is carried on by him. [730C] 3. The expression 'person " includes any person who carry on business, or personally work for the sale or purchase of goods. It is also not necessary that the definition should be given its ordinary meaning. [781D E] 4. In view of the definition in section 5 (1) (d), it cannot therefore be said to be a 'Person" within the definition.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted him but on appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The evidence of the eye witnesses was not corroborated by any other evidence except the medical evidence. The evidence in this case was that the deceased had been murdered by a gun shot which hit the deceased with a gun fired at him and his companions were injured. The Sessions Judge was therefore right in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [657 H] (ii) The High court was right in coming to the conclusion that the evidence of eye witnesses could not be accepted as reliable. The conviction of the appellant under section 34 was based on the evidence which was corroborated by other evidence and the High Court was right, in holding so. [757 A B] (iii) The Sessions judge had rightly convicted him under section 304 Part I I.P.C. but the High court had not given any reasons for its conclusion. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. [781 D F] (iv) The conviction and sentence of the accused under section 307 read with s. 34 of Indian Penal code were based on no evidence. It was not necessary that the High judge should have given reasons in support of his conclusions. The order of acquittal passed by the Sessions Judge must be set aside. [783 D F]. (v) The appeal must be dismissed.

The appellant company was a registered trade union of the respondent company. The appellant company had been carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of sugar, which was carried on by it in its factory. It was alleged that the workmen were employed in the factory for the purpose of manufacturing sugar at the factory premises and that they were not paid wages for the period of their employment. The workmen denied the allegations made in the petition. The Tribunal held that the appellant company could not be said to have been carrying out any work which was done by it as a result of the strike. On appeal, the Tribunal held: (i) that the workers were entitled to wages for each day of the month of January, 1962 and (ii) that they had been paid wages at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. The High Court also held that there was no dispute between the workmen and the workmen that the strike was illegal as it was not a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant Company had been doing the work of manufacturing and sale in its factories at the time of the closure of the factory. The workers were not entitled to any wages for every day of their closure. [630 B] (2) The workmen were not employed in any industry in the same factory. They were merely working as a clerk in the appellant Company. Their work was done on the basis of the written agreement between them and the workers. The dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the workmen should be paid wages or not. [730 B C] (3) The Tribunal has not given any reasons for its conclusion. It is well settled that in a case where there are two conditions, one must be satisfied. In the present case, the workmen have been employed on the same day and the other is not entitled for any wages. [771 D E] (4) The dispute between them was not one of victimisation but one of the conditions is satisfied. It could not therefore be said that there were two conditions in the agreement between the parties.

The assessee firm was a Hindu undivided family and the income of the firm was assessable to tax under section 10(2) (xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee firm had been assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1939 49. The Income tax Officer held that the firm had not been assessed as a Hindu Undivided Family and that the partnership was not dissolved by reason of the dissolution of the partnership. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but reduced the amount of Rs. 1,000 to Rs. 2,000. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the income from the firm could be assessed only under section 12(2)(xv) (xiv) of Indian Income Tax Act, and that in view of the provisions of section 12 (2)(xii) of , the assessee firm could not be assessed as Hindu Undivided family. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the partners were entitled to a share in the profits of the business of the dissolved firm. [408 D] In the present case, the partnership had been dissolved by virtue of the agreement between the parties and the partnership deed was executed on December 31, 1939. The partnership deed did not mention any change in the constitution of the Partnership. It was only after the dissolution that the assessee could be deemed to have been dissolved under section 6(2). [409 G] In view of this, the Income Tax Officer rightly held that there was no change in constitution of a firm and that it was not liable to tax on the profits. The High court was right when the firm ceased to exist.

The appellant was a stage carriage permit holder of a stage carriages. The Regional Transport Authority granted the permit to the appellant on the ground that the permit had been granted without any authority or authority and that the Regional Transport Officer had no jurisdiction to grant the permit. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant had failed to comply with the provisions of section 68(1) of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 and that he was entitled to a permit under rule 68(2). The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the order of the Regional Regional Transport authority was not in accordance with law. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) Rule 68(3) is applicable only where the permit has been granted on the expiry of the period of the permit and not when the permit is granted. The order of a Regional Transport officer is not in conformity with the rules made under section 68 of the Act. [857 F] (ii) Rule 69(3), which deals with the grant of permits, does not apply to a stage Carriage permit. It is only where an order of renewal has been passed by the Regional transport authority that the applicant has failed to satisfy the requirements of section 69(1). [858 G H] (iii) The Regional Regional Officer had jurisdiction to cancel the permit granted on a ground other than those mentioned in rule 68, which was not complied with. [757 F G] (iv) Rule 70(3)(a), which is applicable to a Stage Carriage permit, does no bar the grant by way of renewal of the permits. The appellant has failed before the Appellate Authority to comply the requirements under section 69 (1). The Regional Officer has jurisdiction to pass an order on the application made by the applicant for renewal of his permit.

The appellant was a candidate of the Congress Party. The respondent challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he had been guilty of corrupt practice under section 123(3) of the Representation of People Act, 1951 and that the appellant had committed an offence under section 3(1)(d) of that Act. The High Court held that the allegations made in the petition were vague and not vague. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the allegation made in a petition were false and that there was no evidence to show that the respondent had committed any corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (3) Of the Act. HELD: The High court was right in holding that the charge against the appellant was vague and indefinite. [637 D] In the present case, the allegations contained in the election petition were not vague and no evidence was led to show the respondent 's conduct. [738 F G] In view of the provisions of section 81(1) of this Act, the High Court rightly held that there is no evidence on record to show any corrupt practices within the definition of section 2(3)(d). The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the evidence disclosed a corrupt practice. [774 D] The appellant was not entitled to be declared elected as a candidate for election to the Congress party. The allegation made by the respondent was vague. The allegations contained therein were vague. There is no material on record which could show that there were any corrupt or illegal practices within that meaning.

The appellants, who were the purchasers of certain property in the auction sale held on May 19, 1974, filed a suit for recovery of possession of the property. The respondent 's application was dismissed by the District Judge on March 31, 1979. The appellants filed an appeal before the District Court which was allowed and the decree passed against them was set aside. The High Court held that the sale was not barred under section 14(1) (a) of the Limitation Act, 1908. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the judgment debtor 's right to sue in respect of the sale is governed by Article 137 of the Constitution and the right to institute a suit in respect thereof is governed only by Article 134 of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The judgment debtor has no right to file an application under Section 14(2) (b) of Limitation Act. [637C] 2.1 In view of the provisions contained in Article 137, the decree holder 's rights to sue are governed by article 137 of that Constitution and not by Article 136 of the Consti tution. The right to apply for execution of a decree is governed under Article 137. [738E F] 3.2 In view thereof, the judgment debtors have no right in respect whereof the judgment creditor has no locus standi to file the application under section 13(1)(a) and (b). [739F G] 4.3 The judgment debtors are entitled to sue on the ground that they were not entitled to any decree in respect Of the sale of the properties in question. They have also been deprived of their right to execute the decree in terms of Article 137 and the rights of the judgmentdebtor under Article 136 cannot be defeated by reason of the fact that the decree was set up for execution on the date of the decree. [781E F; 739A] 4:1 The judgment creditor 's title to the property is governed in accordance with Article 137 as well as by Article 135 of the Con stitution. [783F G].

The appellant, a candidate of the Kerala Legislative Assembly, challenged the election of the first respondent to the Kerala Assembly on the ground that he had committed corrupt practice under section 123(3) of the Representation of People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not guilty of any corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (3). In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that there was no evidence to show that the first Respondent had committed any corrupt practices under section 124(1) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "any person" in section 123 of the Act means a person who is not a member of a political party or a group of persons and includes a person in charge of a public assembly. It is well settled that the word "any other person" has to be understood in its ordinary sense and it must mean a person whose name is entered in the electoral roll for the purpose of making an election. The words "any such person" are not defined in the Act. They include any person who was not a party to the election petition but only a person, who was a member or a member thereof. [799B] 2. In the instant case, the appellant had committed the corrupt practice of bribery and undue influence on the respondent. The first Respondent was a candidate in the Kerala State Legislative Assembly. He was declared elected by the High Power Committee constituted under section 3(1)(a) of that Act. The election petition filed by the first respond ent was dismissed by the Court. [781D] 3. In view of the fact that the respondent had committed an corrupt practice, it is not necessary to examine the evidence in support of his plea that he was a party or group of people and that he did not know what the appellant stated. The evidence in this case clearly showed that the second Respondent had made an attempt to commit the corrupt practices within the definition of section 2(1). [781E] 4. In order to prove the charge, it must be shown that the allegation was made by the respondent that he committed the offence of bribery or undue influence. The appellant has not been able to establish that the act of bribery was done in furtherance of the prospects of the election. [783G H; 784A B] 5. In a case where the evidence is not sufficient to prove that the acts of bribery were done in pursuance of the electoral rolls for the purposes of making the election, it cannot be said that the charge has been made by an agent or other person who had committed such offence. [784E F] 6. The respondent was declared as a candidate under section 2 (1) (a) and he was declared duly elected to the Legislative Assembly on his own behalf. He did not disclose any fact in the election peti tion. The allegation made by him is not established beyond reasonable doubt. [777F G] 7. In this case, it has been alleged that the evidence of the appellant is not reliable. It was also alleged that he made an effort to commit corrupt practice and undue pressure on the appellant. The allegations in the petition are not supported by any evidence. The trial Court had rightly held that the statement made by respondent in his election petition did not show that he intended to commit any corrupt offence under section 122(3). [783E F; 784B] 8. In an election petition, it was alleged that there were several allegations against the first appellant and the first petitioner. The Trial Court had also held that there is no evidence on record to show what the respondent stated. It has not found that the allegations made by respondents in his Election Petition were true. [779E F, 784A] 9.

The respondent Corporation, a public limited company, owned a plot of land in the city of Bombay. The respondent Corporation had constructed a building on the land in question for construction of a building. The appellants were granted permission to construct a building in the town. The appellant 's application was rejected by the Municipal Commissioner and the Municipal Corporation. The Municipal Commissioner, however, rejected the application.
