The writ petition filed by the appellants was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent Corporation was not entitled to exemption under section 4(1) (a) of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Act, 1961 as it had no power to grant permission to the respondent to construct the building in question. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the Municipal Committee had no jurisdiction to grant the permission to a respondent to build a building for construction purposes and that the permission granted by the Corporation was valid. [630B] 2. The Corporation has not been able to establish that the land was required for construction purpose and that it was not necessary for the respondent, to construct any building in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [731C D] 3. The State Government had no authority to grant sanction to a building which was required by the Act to be constructed on the plot of the land. It is well settled that the Corporation has power to refuse permission to build the building for the construction purposes, and that in any event it cannot be said that the development of the city was not bona fide. [781E] 4. The Government had not given any reasons for refusing permission to erect a building or to construct it on the site. It was also not open to the Corporation to refuse the permission.

The appellant company was a registered industrial concern engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling products. The workmen were employed by the appellant company for the purpose of manufacturing, selling and selling goods. The workers were employed on the same day. The employees were not paid wages for the period they had been working as such. The management filed complaints against the workmen under section 33(2) of the Act before the Industrial Court alleging that the workmen had committed breach of the provisions of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948. The Industrial Court dismissed the applications holding that the workers had committed violation of the principles of natural justice and that the employees were guilty of misconduct. The appellant company filed appeals to this Court. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The workmen have been guilty of breach of conditions of service and they are not entitled to any relief under section 10(2)(b) of Act. [782B] 2.2 The employer has a right to terminate the services of an employee if he is found guilty of any misconduct or contravention of the terms of employment. It is only when the employer makes a report that the employee has committed breach, it will be open to the employer to take appropriate action against the workman for breach of such conditions. [771C] 2:3 The employer is entitled to terminate an employee on the ground that he has been guilty or contravention thereof. If the employer does not comply with the requirements of section 10 (2)(a) of that Act, it is open to him to take recourse to the provisions contained in section 10 of the said Act. The employer may be justified in terminating the services without giving an opportunity to the workman to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. [761C D] 2 :4 The employer can terminate the service of a workman if he has committed any breach of his conditions of employment or is found to have committed breach thereof. It may be that the employer has failed to comply with this requirement and the employer is liable to pay wages for such period as may be specified in the order. [751C E] 2.(a) The employer must show cause within a reasonable time, why he shall not be removed from service or if he fails to comply within the stipulated time. If he has failed, he will be entitled to take action against him under section 25(2). [764F G] (b) The management is directed to reinstate the workmen in service with full back wages and allowances for the remaining period of their service. If it is found that the workman has committed an offence or contravention, it shall be open for the employer either to terminate or suspend the services. [741E F] 2(a) In the instant case, the employer had failed to show any cause why the workmen should not take action under section 20(2), and if they fail to comply the requirements, they will be liable to be dismissed. The Labour Court has rightly held that the closure of the factory was illegal. [731E G] 2 (b). The employer 's failure to comply this requirement is a breach of condition of service. It cannot be said that the termination of services of the workmen was illegal because it was not in accordance with law. [ 741F H] 3(c) The closure of a factory is illegal and unjustified. The closure must be held to have been illegal. The retrenchment is therefore, illegal. If there is breach of any condition of employment, the closure must necessarily be held illegal. It would be open under section 19(2A) to terminate a service of an employer if it is not in compliance with the provisions. [ 751F G; 751E] 4 (d).

The assessee company was a registered dealer in the Indian Mills. The assessee company sold shares to its shareholders and the company sold them to the assessee company on the ground that it had no business or interest in the shares of the company. The Income tax Officer held that the shares were not liable to be taxed under section 10(2) of the Act, but the assessee was entitled to a deduction of Rs. 1,50,000 as the value of the shares sold by it was not assessable to income tax. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Appellate Tribunal and held that there was no evidence on record to show that the sale proceeds were not received by the assessee in the course of its business or business. The High Court, however, held that in view of the provisions of section 10 (2) the assessee had no right to claim deduction under section 11(2). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the finding of the Appellate Tribunal that the sales were not assessable under section 12(2), was erroneous and that the High Court was wrong in holding that the assessee 's shares were liable to income Tax, and that there could be no question of any evidence on the record. HELD: (i) The finding of fact recorded by the Appellate Tribu nal was correct and must be set aside. [637 D] (ii) In view of section 12 (2), the High Courts should not interfere with the findings of the Tribunal unless there is a clear finding that the transactions were not in the nature of trade or business, but only one conclusion is reached by the Tribunal on the basis of which it can be said that the transaction was in the character of trade. [737 D E] (iii) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere with findings of fact arrived at by the authorities below.

The appellant was appointed as a District Munsif in the Madras State. He was promoted to the post of District Munsif on December 1, 1953. The appellant was confirmed in the service of the Government of India. On November 2, 1953, he was reverted to his substantive rank and was later confirmed in that post. In 1952, he filed a suit against the Government servant for a declaration that he had been guilty of misconduct and for a direction to the Government to reinstate him with full back wages. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had been dismissed from service on December 2, 1954. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Rule 3 of the Madras Civil Services Rules, 1950, which was framed under article 309 of the Constitution, provides that no person shall be deemed to have been dismissed or removed from service except with the previous sanction of the State Government. The words "any person who is in the employment of a District Judge" in r. 3(1) of the Rules are not intended to include a person who has been dismissed, removed or removed by an order of dismissal passed against him. (ii) Rule 4 of the rules framed under the Act does not provide for any appeal from the orders of dismissal made against him except with previous sanction. The word "any other authority" in the rule means a person appointed to the service and includes a person holding a post in the Government or a local authority. (iii) Rule 5 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1954, which is framed under r. 4(1), provides that where an order passed against a Government servant has been made by the State Govern ment to any other authority, it shall be final and conclusive. (iv) Rule 6 of the said rules does not contemplate any appeal against the order of removal or removal from service. The rule is intended to provide for appeals against orders of suspension or removal of the government servant against orders passed against them. (v) Rule 7 of the Mysore Civil Services Act, 1950 provides that the Government servants who were dismissed or suspended shall be entitled to be reinstated in service except on the ground that they had been removed from the service by an authority subordinate to it. The rules do not contemplate a appeal against orders made against them and the order was passed without giving him any opportunity of being heard. (vi) Rule 8 does not prescribe any procedure for the enquiry or trial of a person, who is dismissed or removal in accordance with the provisions of r. 7. (vii) Rule 9 provides that if an order has been passed by the Government under r . 3(2), it shall have effect as if it were made by an officer subordinate to him and shall be liable to be punished for misconduct. (viii) Rule 10 does not require any enquiry or enquiry in respect of a Government employee who is removed from his service, but only provides that such dismissal or removal should be made by way of punishment. (ix) Rule 11 provides that when the Government Servant has been removed or dismissed from the Service by an appellate authority, he shall be reinstated with full wages and allowances. (x) Rule 12 provides that a Government Servant who is found guilty of any misconduct under r, 3(3) shall be dismissed or remove him from service if he had not been dismissed for misconduct under rr. 5 and 6. (xi) The rule does not say that the dismissal or reduction in rank should be set aside by an inferior authority. Rule 12 lays down that no order shall be made except with a previous sanction in writing of the Governor. Rule 13 provides that any person who was dismissed or dismissed or removing him from his Service shall be given one month 's notice in writing to such authority and shall not be entitled for any period of three months 's pay.

The respondent was a shareholder of the appellant company. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the deceased to tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the shares in the shares were not liable to tax as they had been transferred by the assessee to his share holders and that the share holders were entitled to the benefit of section 10 (2). On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner but restored the order. The High Court held that there was no transfer of shares in favour of the respondent and that there could be no transfer by the appellant to his shareholder. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the expression "any person" in section 10 of the Act means a person who is not a member of the family of which he has been appointed or authorised by the Central Government under the provisions of the Income tax (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947. HELD: The word "person" in the context of the definition of "person", in the sense in which it occurs, includes a person whose share holders are appointed or permitted to be appointed or appointed by the appropriate Government under section 3(1). [723 B] In the present case, the shares of the company were transferred by him to his brother. The transfer was made by the deceased and the share holder was not liable for tax as he had been appointed and authorised by that Act.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Madhya Pradesh. He had been in possession of certain lands belonging to him and his ancestors. The appellant 's father, who was a resident of the former State, was assessed to income tax under the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, on the ground that he was not an Ruler of a State. He claimed that he had been assessed to agricultural income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The High Court held that the appellant was not a Ruler within the meaning of article 31(1)(a) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant was an Ruler within his meaning as defined in article 31A of the Constitu tion. He was not entitled to any protection under article 31 A of the constitution. [657 H] (ii) The definition of 'estate ' in article 366(22) of Constitution is wide enough to include a person who has been assessed by him to agricultural land tax for that year. It does not mean that he could be assessed to land tax only if he had paid the amount of rent or revenue to the State Government. [757 H; 758 A] (iii) The word 'estate" in article 2(22)(a), means a person whose land is held by him as an Ruler and includes a person holding land in excess of the ceiling limit prescribed by article 31.

The respondent, a retired employee of the appellant Bank, was transferred to the Central Administrative Tribunal under Rule 10 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The respondent filed an application before the Central Government for transfer of her husband from the Central Public Works Department, but the same was rejected by the Central Govt. on the ground that the transfer order was not in accordance with the rules and regulations. The Tribunal held that the respondent had no power to transfer the husband from his parent department to another department. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the order of transfer was in violation of the principles of natural justice. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of the Tribunal is not sustainable in law and is liable to be quashed. [702D] 2.2 In the instant case, the respondent has been transferred from his own department to the parent department. He has been posted at the place where he was working. He had no other choice but to transfer him to another place. The order does not indicate that the wife is in a position to accommodate the respondent. [781E] 2:3 In the absence of any specific provision in the rules or regulations, it cannot be said that the impugned order has been passed mala fide. [783G] 3:4 The order is set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal for fresh consideration. [784F] 4:5 The respondent shall be entitled to transfer her husband to another post from his original place to his parent Department.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to life imprisonment for the offence of murder and also under Section 304 Part II IPC. The High Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that they had committed the murder of one P.W.1, who was a member of the unlawful assembly. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the conviction of the appel lants is not sustainable in law because the evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 is consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and that they were liable to be convicted under section 302 I .P.c. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that the appellants had committed an offence punishable under Section 201 IPC. [630B] (2) In view of the evidence on record, it is clear that the accused were guilty of the murder and they were rightly convicted for the same offence. [730C] (3) The conviction of all the appellants under Section 307 I. P.C. is set aside. [781E F] (4) The sentence of imprisonment for life is maintained. [783G H] (5) In the instant case, the appellants were rightly sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of two years and they are entitled to be released on bail.

The respondents, who were partners of the appellant firm, filed a suit for recovery of certain sums due from them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage was not a mortgage within the meaning of section 2(1)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh General Clauses Act, 1904 and that the suit was barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the definition of 'person ' in section 2 (1) (c) is wide enough to include a person who has been declared as a limited company under the provisions of the Act, and that it would be an association of persons or persons for the purpose of carrying on business within the State. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The definition of "person" in section 3(1) of Andhra Pradesh Act is wide and it includes all persons who are declared as limited company. It is not necessary that a person should be deemed to have been a limited limited company for the purposes of carrying out the provisions or the rules made thereunder. [703B C] 2. The word "person ' has been defined in section 4(1). In the definition it includes only persons who have been declared a limited Company under the Act. It means all persons whose assets are held by the Central Government or State Governments and which are not subject to any law made by Parliament. [774C D] 3. The expression "person", in section 5(2) of that Act, has been used in the context of the definition. In the context it is clear that the word 'person" has been given a wide meaning and it is not possible to say that the expression "other person" has to be construed in its popular sense. [764C] 4. The words "other persons" in the definition are wide enough, but they have been used only in the sense of the term. It includes all those who are deemed to be a limited firm and not those who were declared a company under section 3 (1). [775G H; 776A B] 5. The question whether a person is a limited bank or not has to depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. [754F G] 6. In view of the provisions contained in section 6(2), it cannot be said that the appellant was a limited banking company within the definition as given in section 1 (c). The High Courts have rightly held that the respondents were not entitled to claim any relief under the Andhra General Clauses Acts, 1904. [ 776C D; 771A B].

The petitioners who were dealers in sugar, challenged the validity of the notification under section 3(1) of the Bihar Sugar (Control of Trade and Commerce) Order, 1955. The Central Government issued a notification under the Act on March 31, 1956, fixing the price at which the sugar was sold to the petitioners. The petitioners contended that the notification was ultra vires the provisions of article 19(1)(g) of Constitution as it contravened articles 14 and 19 (1)(f) of Part III of the Constitution and that the impugned notification was violative of article 14 inasmuch as it violated articles 14, 19 (2) and 19(3) of that article. The contention was rejected by the Central Government on the ground that the notifications were ultra vires article 19 (5) and (6) of article 31. Held, that the provisions Of section 3 (1) (g) are not violative of articles 14 or 19 (6). The notification under article 19 is in contravention of article 301 inasmuch as the notification issued under section 4(1), which provides for the fixation of price at the rate of Rs. 1/ per quintal and the notification thereunder was ultravires the Constitution. The notification issued by the Government under section 5(2) of Act is not violative Of articles 14 & 19 (3). The impugned notification is therefore void as it contravenes article 19. Held further, that there is no violation of article 20 inasmuch as there is a contravention of articles 19 and 19 of the constitution. The impugned notifications are ultra vires articles 14and 19 (4) and 31 (5).

The appellant company was a statutory company and its employees were governed by the West Bengal Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1956. The Industrial Tribunal held that the workmen had no right to claim bonus under section 10(2)(b) of the Act. The Tribunal held in favour of the workmen. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the reference made by the Tribunal was incompetent as it did not contain any provision for the determination of the question whether the workmen were entitled to claim the bonus under the Act, and that the award was bad because the reference was made in accordance with the provisions of section 10 (2)(a) of that Act. HELD : The reference made under section 33(1) of , is not a reference within the meaning of section 2(b) Of the Act and must be held to have been made in conformity with the principles laid down by this Court in Associated Cement Companies Ltd. vs Their Workmen, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 869, followed. The reference was incompetent because it did contain any specific provision for determination of bonus under that section. It is not open to the Tribunal to make a reference under section 3(b). [868 H; 867 A B] In the instant case, the Tribunal had made an award in accordance therewith and the award made by it was bad as it was made after the award had been made. The award was therefore bad because it was not made in compliance with the requirements of section 33 (1) Of that Act and the reference to the Industrial Tribunal was competent.

The appellant was a Hindu Religious Trust. He was appointed as the Chairman of the Board of Trustees under the Madras Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950. The appellant was appointed by the Board to manage his affairs and to exercise all powers conferred on him by the Act. On the same day he was appointed in the year 1952. In 1951, the appellant made a representation to the Government for approval of the scheme. The Government rejected the said representation but the Government did not consider it necessary to make any order under section 3(1) of the Act and passed an order on the same date as the scheme was framed. The Board thereafter issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court held that the scheme had been validly framed and the appellant was entitled to the protection of article 19(1)(f) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The scheme was not validly framed but it was only after the Act came into force. It was therefore not open to the Board under section 16(2) to make a fresh scheme in accordance with the provisions of the Madras Act and the rules made thereunder. [657 D] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant had no locus standi to challenge the validity on the ground that it contravened article 19 (1)(g) of . The High court was wrong in holding, that the impugned order was invalid because it violated articles 14 and 19(2). [658 G] (iii) The impugned order did not contravene article 19. It could not be said that the Act had been passed by the Government under section 17(1), but it did not infringe article 19 of the Constitution. [757 F H] (iv) The appellant 's contention that the Board was competent to make an order under the Act, was not correct. The scheme did not violate article 19 and was therefore void because it contravened articles 14 or 19(3).

The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the State of Orissa on March 1, 1984. He was appointed to the post of Principal of the school. The appellant was confirmed in the post on March 31, 1984 and he was confirmed on March 30, 1984 on the ground that he had been continuously working for more than three years. The order of termination was challenged by the appellant before the High Court which held that the appellant was not entitled to any salary for the period of his probation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the termination of service of the appellant amounted to a termination simpliciter and that the services of the teachers were terminated on March 15, 1984 without giving him an opportunity of being heard. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order terminating the services is not a punishment but a punishment for misconduct. [782B] 2.2 The termination of services of a teacher is not one of punishment and it is only when the employee has been appointed to a post in the same capacity as Principal. The termination is not an act of misconduct. It is only where the employee is appointed to another post or if he has been continuously in service for more years, he will be entitled to salary for that period. [77C] 3.1 In the instant case, the appellant had been appointed on March 16, 1984 as Principal of a school and was confirmed by the State Government on March 29, 1984 when he was appointed on April 15, 1985. The services of him were terminated by the order dated March 31. 1984. The appointment of the teacher was not made in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [76G H] 2:2 The appellant had no right to claim any salary from the date of his appointment. The management has been given a right to continue in service till he is appointed on that post. The right to be appointed to an office in the school was not taken away by the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. [75G H; 77A] 3:2 In the absence of any statutory provision or statutory rules, the termination is illegal. [78F G] 4:3 The appellant has been working as Principal on March 14, 1984 for more over three years and he has not been appointed in accordance therewith. He has been denied salary for a period of two years. His appointment was made in violation of the provisions contained in the Act by the management. The Act provides for the termination by the authority competent to terminate his services. [79G H, 77A B] 4.3 In the present case, there is no provision or any statutory rule providing for termination of the service of a teachers on March 17, 1984 but the appellant has not given him an option to continue the post till he was selected in accordance of the Rules. The question whether the appellant is entitled to the salary for this period is not relevant. [ 77A C] 4 :4 The appellant is not entitled for any salary as he had already been appointed by the Government on April 1, 1985 and he cannot claim any right to remain in service until he has retired from service. [ 78B] 5:5 The appellant being a teacher of a private school, is entitled for salary for all purposes including his salary.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the Punjab State. He was declared elected as a member of the Panchayat Samiti. The respondent challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he had been disqualified for being chosen as a candidate for election to the State Legislative Assembly and that his nomination paper was improperly rejected by the Returning Officer. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any salary for the period he was elected as member of Panchayat Samiti, but dismissed the petition holding that the respondent was not qualified to be chosen as an elector for election under section 7(1) (b) of the Punjab Panchayat Raj Act, 1961. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the High Court had erred in law in holding that a candidate who was elected under section 8(1)(b) could not be declared elected to any other office under the Punjab Government Act, and that the nomination paper could not have been rejected by him. HELD : (i) The appellant was entitled to the salary for his election as member. [707 D] (ii) The High Courts had erred on the facts of this case in holding the respondent guilty of corrupt practice. [771 C E] (iii) The finding of fact that the charge of corrupt practices was proved by the evidence led by the appellant, was not correct. [762 B] (iv) The question whether a candidate is entitled to salary for any period during which he was declared as an elected member under section 3(3)(b), is a mixed question of law and fact.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents tenant on the ground that the building was constructed by the respondent and that the construction was not bona fide. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the constructions were bona fide, and that there was no need to make any alteration in the structure. The High Court held that the buildings were bona bonafide and that they had been constructed by a tenant without the permission of the landlord. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the courts below had not properly appreciated the evidence adduced by the parties, and therefore the finding recorded by the courts in the impugned judgment was perverse. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The construction was bona fide and the building could not be constructed without the consent of the tenant. [703B] 2. The building was a part of the building and it was not necessary for the landlord to make alterations in the structures. The use of the word 'building ' is not a mere alteration of the structure, but a change of user of the site by itself does not amount to alteration of structure. [774C] 3. The courts below have rightly found that the structure was bona bonafide. The finding recorded on the basis of the evidence led by the respondents in the case is perverse and the High Court has rightly held that there were no need for making alterations in it. [764F] 4. In the instant case, the construction had been made without the sanction of the competent authority. There was no question of alteration of any structure. It was not disputed that the structures were bona bona fide or bona fide as the building had been built by a landlord without the written permission of his landlord. The Courts below have concurrently found that there is no need in the premises to make alteration of its structure. In view of the concurrent findings of fact, the courts have rightly held the construction to be bona fide on the part of both the parties. [754G] 5. The question whether the building is bona fide is not one of law and facts. [744C D] 6. The Court has also found that in the absence of a written permission by the landlord, the structure cannot be constructed as a whole or a part thereof. [734F G] 7. In this case, there was a clear finding on the question whether there was any need for the building to make it bona fide for the purpose of making alterations. The findings recorded by both the courts are not perverse and they are liable to be set aside.

The appellant company was a firm carrying on business in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The respondent company filed an application under Order 21 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree against the appellant company and for setting up of a new firm. The appellant company resisted the application on the ground that the summons were not served on the appellant as required by section 7 of the Act, and that the respondent was not a 'person interested in the business of the company. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the appellant had no locus standi to file the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in setting aside an ex parte order against the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in setting up a new company and not in setting out the facts of the case. [782B] 2.2 In view of the provisions contained in Order 21, Rule 10, the High court erred in holding that it was not necessary to set aside an order against a company. [774C D] 3. The High court was right when it held that the application under section 7 was not maintainable. [764F G] 4. In view thereof, the appeal must be dismissed. [754G H] 5.1 In the instant case, the appellant was a 'Person interested in a company and was not an 'person aggrieved '. The suit was filed on behalf of the respondent company for setting out its facts. It was alleged that the company had been carrying on the business in a particular manner and that it had been doing business in another company. It is also alleged that there was no evidence to show that the Company was carrying on any business in other companies. The application under order 21 Rule 9 was not properly made.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 120B, I.P.C., for having committed offences punishable under sections 323 and 506 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, on the allegation that he had taken possession of the land in dispute from the respondents. The Magistrate passed an order directing the appellant to hand over possession of land to the respondents within a period of six months. The appellant filed a petition under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the order of the Magistrate and directing the Magistrate to take cognizance of the offence on the ground that he was not in lawful possession of any land. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take action against the respondents, but directed the Magistrate not to proceed with the case. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the order passed by the Magistrate was without jurisdiction and that the High Court was in error in quashing the proceedings on the basis of the evidence adduced before him and that there was no illegality in the order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed under section 145(1) Cr. P.C. is not a nullity because it is an order made by the police to take possession of a land which is not lawful or illegal. [782B C] 2. In the instant case, the Magistrate did not have jurisdiction to proceed further with the complaint on the grounds that there were no materials before him to show that the appellant had taken any steps in the matter. The fact that the proceedings were pending before him was a mere irregularity and it could not be said that he acted mala fide or that he exercised his powers under section 144(1). [785C] 3. In view of the fact that there is no material to show whether the Magistrate has jurisdiction to deal with the matter, the order made under section 146(1)(a) Cr., P. C. would not be sustainable in law. [774E F] 4. The question as to whether the order was without authority or not does not arise for consideration in this case.

The appellant company was carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton yarn. The assessee sold its yarn to the respondent company and sold it to the appellant company. The Income tax Officer held that the sale of the yarn was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but held that there was no evidence on record to show that the goods were sold by the assessee to the assessee. The Tribunal held that it was not open to the Tribunal to go into the question whether the sales were in fact a sale or not and that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to go behind the finding of the Tribunal. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the sales did not amount to sale within section 2 (6) Of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961, because the Tribunal was not justified in taking into consideration the evidence on which it could come to its conclusion and the Tribunal acted beyond its jurisdiction in coming to its own conclusion. The question whether there was a sale of yarn or not is a question of fact depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Held further, that where the Tribunal has found that the assessee had failed to prove that the transactions were in reality a sale, it must be held that a sale was not an sale within that meaning. The High Court could not go into that question because the finding is based on no evidence. It is open to it to examine whether there is any evidence on the record to determine whether there has been a sale and whether there had been a sales in reality the sale was a trade or not. Held also, further,that the Tribunal did not go behind its finding on the question of law. The decision of the High court is based upon no evidence and it cannot be said that there has not been any evidence to show what was sold by it to it.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business as a dealer in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee had been paid remuneration for the services rendered by him to his wife and children. He, however, held that he was entitled to receive remuneration at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. In appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the Tribunal held that there was no evidence on record to show that the expenditure was incurred in connection with the business of the assessee. The High Court, on a reference, held in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee, but, on appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The expenditure was not incurred in the course of his business as an agent or employee of the firm. It is not necessary that the remuneration should be paid to the wife and child children. [419 F] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the amount of remuneration paid by the assessee to his son was not expenditure within the meaning of section 2(15)(vi) of the Income tax Act, 1922. [520 H] (iii) The Tribunal had rightly held that it was incurred for the purpose of carrying on the business as such and that the expenses were incurred in relation to the business. [619 F G] (iv) The assessee was entitled only to receive the remuneration at his own expense. [720 A C] (v) The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner had not applied its mind to the question whether the expenditure is incurred for carrying on of the business or not.

The appellant company was a textile mill. The appellant company had been carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cloth. It was alleged that the appellant company did not carry on its business as a result of which the appellant was compelled to work in the factory. The company filed an application under section 33C(2) of the , for setting aside the order of dismissal passed by the Industrial Tribunal, Patna, which was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order was bad because the appellant had not been given a hearing before the Tribunal and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to pass an order of reinstatement in service. HELD: (i) The order of the Tribunal is bad because it was made without giving any opportunity to the appellant to show cause why the appellant should not be dismissed from service. [408 D] (ii) The Tribunal has no power to dismiss a workman on the ground that he had been given an opportunity to show his case before the Industrial tribunal. It is only when the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the dispute was one of fact and the Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide it. If the Tribunal finds that there is a dispute between the appellant and the respondent, it would be open to the Tribunal to pass such order as it thinks fit. [414 D] The Tribunal had not given any opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action. It could not have made an order for reinstatement in the absence of a written statement or oral representation. [416 E F] (iii) The appellant was entitled to be heard before the tribunal and that he should be heard on merits.

The appellants were the tenants of a house in which they were living. The respondent filed an application for setting aside the decree and for setting up a new family. The appellants contended that the decree was not executable as the appellants had no right to sue for their eviction. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the appellants were not entitled to the benefit of section 14(1) (a) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Held, that the High Court was in error in holding that the order of the trial court was not appealable under r. 5 of the Limitation Act and that the appeal must be dismissed on the grounds that the appellant had no locus standi to file the appeal. The order of dismissal passed by the trial Court was a nullity and the appellants could not be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 15(1). The High Court in appeal did not interfere with the decree of the appellate court, because it was not open to the appellants to file an appeal under r . 5 of Order XLIII of the Civil Procedure Code. The High Courts were right in holding the order as a nullity. The appeal must therefore be dismissed. Held further, that in view of the provision contained in section 14 (1) of Order XXXVII of the C.P.C., the appellants cannot be allowed the benefit under r, 5 of order XLIII. The decree passed by a High Court is not appealable and the High Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal on the basis that it was barred by limitation.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that he had been in possession of the premises under the lease. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that the lease was not valid and the tenant had no right to remain in possession after the expiry of the period of lease. In appeal, the High Court held that the landlord had failed to prove that the lessee had been inducted into possession by the appellant on the date of the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Rent Control Tribunal was right in holding that there was no subsisting lease and the tenancy was not terminated after the expiration of the term of the lease, and that the tenant was entitled to remain at the time of the termination of the tenancy. [775B] In the instant case, the appellant had failed before the Rent Controller that he was in possession on the expiry Of the period for which the lease had been terminated. The landlord had not proved that the appellant was in occupation of the demised premises. The tenant had not produced any evidence to show that the tenancy had been determined by the Rent Control Court. [771C] In view of the provisions of section 106, the Rent control Tribunal could not have held that there has been a subsisting lease. [761F G] In order to determine whether the landlord was in actual possession of a demised premises, it must be shown that he has been inducted as a tenant on a monthly rent of Rs. 500 per month. The proviso to section 106 is intended to cover cases where the landlord has failed to establish that the lessor had been let out for more than three years and has not paid any rent in lieu thereof. [751G] In this case, there was nothing to show whether the tenant has been in actual physical possession of any premises or has not been inducted by him on a yearly rent of about Rs. 1000 per month, and the landlord having failed to produce any evidence that he is in actual occupation of any such premises, the tenant cannot be evicted from the demised property. [741G H] In considering whether the lease has been terminated after expiry of three years, it would be necessary to consider whether the tenancy has been determined on a regular rent or not. The question whether the lessee has been let into possession for more or less than three months is a question of fact and law.

The Governor of Assam, by an order dated March 3, 1964, directed the Governor to hold a departmental enquiry against the appellant and to submit his explanation within one month from the date of receipt of the order. The Governor further directed that the appellant should be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of the charges framed against him. On July 7, 1964 the Governor passed an order under article 311(2) of the Constitution directing the Governor not to hold any departmental enquiry and to make a fresh order on the basis of the report of the Commission. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Governor had no power to hold an inquiry against the appellants and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Governor has not been given a right to hold the enquiry against a person who is found guilty of misconduct or inefficiency or is guilty of any misconduct or misbehaviour but only to make an order on his own behalf. [775 G] (2) The power conferred by article 311 is discretionary and it is not necessary that the Government should have given a hearing to the person concerned. It is not essential that the authority must give a hearing in respect thereof. But, if the Government has given a notice of the proposed action it may be open to the Governor either to hold such inquiry or to make any order on its own behalf and to pass an order thereon. [771 C D] (3) The procedure for holding an enquiry against an officer is not mandatory. It does not require that the person should have been given an opportunity of making a representation against the proposed order. If the Government is satisfied that it is necessary or expedient so to do, it may pass such orders thereon as it thinks fit. [781 C] (4) The requirement of article 311 (2), is mandatory and not directory. It must be held that in the absence of any express provision in article 309, the Governor has no power under article 309 to hold that the procedure prescribed by article 309 is directory.

The petitioners, who were members of the Hindu religion, filed a suit for declaration that they had been in possession of certain properties belonging to them and that they were entitled to be registered as members of their religious institutions. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the respondents were not members of a Hindu religion and that the provisions of section 3(1) (a) of the U.P. Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951 were applicable to the case. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned order was bad in law as it had been passed without jurisdiction and that there was no violation of any fundamental right under article 19(1)(g) of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned order is not a nullity because it has been passed by the District Magistrate or the Board of Revenue or the Collector of the district concerned in exercise of his powers under section 3 (1) of Act No. XIV of 1951 and that it was not a valid order. [782B C] 2. The respondents were members in the Hindu religious institutions and they had no right to be admitted as members thereof. They had been registered as owners of certain property belonging to the Hindu community. There is no violation or violation of the fundamental rights under article 14 of the constitution. [781D E] 3. The petitioners are not members in any religious institution nor were they members of any religious institutions, and they have been denied the right to claim any relief on the ground that they belonged to a Hindu religious institution. They have no right or title to the property belonging thereto. They are entitled to claim the relief under section 4 (1)(a) read with section 3 of Act XIV of 1952. [783D] 4. The District Magistrate and the Board are directed to take steps for the removal of the respondents from the office of the Board. [784E F] 5. The Board is directed to consider the objections of the members of such religious institutions in accordance with law and after giving an opportunity to them to lead evidence, if any, to prove their case.

The assessee company was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of shares and securities. The Income tax Officer held that the loss suffered by it was not a capital loss but a loss of Rs. 1,00,000/ . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that there was no loss in the business as such and that the losses were not capital loss within the meaning of section 2(15) of the Act. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High Court had erred in holding that the profits were capital loss under section 2 (15) (a) of Income tax Act, 1922. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The assessee company had a right to claim deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of that Act and not under section 11(1). [775B] 2. The High Court was in error in holding the loss as capital loss. The loss suffered was a capital asset within the definition of section 3 (15). The loss was a revenue loss within section 2 of the 1922 Act. The income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the loss under s.10(2) (xv) and that it was a loss in respect of which the loss was incurred. [776C] 3. The Appellate Tribunal was right in holding, that the assessee company could not claim deduction on the ground that it had failed to establish that the capital loss was suffered by the company as such. [77F G] 4. The question whether the loss should be allowed under section 12(1) (b) of 1922 Act is a question of fact and not one of law. [76G H; 77A] 5. In view of the provisions of s.11(2), it was clear that the income tax officer had no power to assess or reassess the loss in any particular year. The Tribunal had rightly held that it could not be said that there had been a loss incurred by the appellant as such, and that there were no loss incurred in the previous year.

The appellant was appointed as a Research Assistant in the Defence Research Organisation. He was promoted to the post of Research Assistant on 1.1.1984. The respondent joined service as Research Assistant with effect from 1.4.1985 and continued to be in service till 31.3.1985. On 1.6.1985, he was promoted as Research Assistants with effectfrom 1.7.1985 to 31.12.1985 with effect therefrom. He retired on 30.9.1985 on attaining the age of superannuation. The appellant filed a writ petition before the Central Administrative Tribunal challenging the validity of the order dated 1.3.,1985 and the consequential orders dated 1st April, 1985. The Tribunal held that the respondent was entitled to be treated as having been appointed as Research Officer with effect on 1st July, 1985 and that he was entitled for all benefits including pension and gratuity. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled only to the benefit of the service rendered by him in the Military Engineering Service (Fixation of Ceiling on Land Holdings) Rules, 1961. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants were entitled to the benefits of the Service rendered by them in the military Engineering Service and that they were entitled for the benefit under the service rules. [603B C] 2.1 The respondent was not entitled to any benefit of service rules as he had been appointed on 1/7th July, 1984. He had been promoted as a research Assistant with retrospective effect from 31st March, 1985, and that his service rendered in the Army Engineering Service was liable to be counted for computing the period of qualifying service for determining the period for which he was appointed. [599B C; G] 2:2 The respondent is entitled to all benefits of service including pension, gratuity and other benefits as are admissible to him under the Rules. [600C D] 3:1 The appellants are entitled to claim the benefit in terms of the said service rules on the ground that they had been continuously working for more than three years. They have not been denied the benefit. [625F G] 3.2 The Tribunal has held that since the respondent had been granted the benefit, he would be entitled to get all benefits under the Service Rules. The order of the Tribunal is set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal for fresh disposal in accordance with law.

The appellant was elected to the Municipal Council of Greater Bombay. The election petition was filed in the High Court on the ground that the appellant had not been duly elected and that he had failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the election petition had been properly presented and that the petition was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition on the grounds of delay, laches or acquiescence. HELD : (i) The High court has not committed any error in dismissing the petition. [637 D] (ii) The election petitioner had failed in proving his case within reasonable time and that there was a failure on the part of the appellant to prove the allegation beyond reasonable time. [738 F G] (iii) The appellant had failed before the High Courts to establish his case. The order of dismissal passed by the High Judge is set aside and the election petitioner shall be deemed to have been duly nominated. [779 E] (iv) In the present case, the appellant was not a party to the petition and he had not filed any affidavit in support of his allegations. He had not produced any evidence in support thereof. The appellant did not produce any evidence on record. The trial court had rightly rejected the election application. [777 A B] (v) In view of the fact that the petitioner was a party, it could not be said that he was not duly elected.

The petitioner company was a registered dealer under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on the turnover of its business in respect of which the sales tax was payable by it. The petitioner challenged the validity of the notification and contended that the notification issued by the State Government under section 3(2) of the Act was ultra vires the Constitution as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the sales were not liable to tax on turnover of business in the State, because, the sales had been effected outside the State. The High Court held that the sales effected outside India were intra vires and that the levy of sales tax under the Act could not be sustained. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the notification dated January 1, 1956, issued by State Government in exercise of its powers conferred on it by section 3 of the U P. Sales tax Act, 1947, was ultravires and void as it violated article 14; (ii) the notifications issued by it under section 4(2), were invalid because, in view of the provisions of the Sales Tax Acts, the notification could not have been validly issued under section 5 of the General Clauses Act, 1904, and (iii) the sales made outside India could not fall within the purview of article 14. HELD: The notification dated February 1, 1957, was valid as it did not contravene article 14 because, on the facts of this case, the Sales tax authorities were justified in holding that the notifications were ultra vires article 14 and that, therefore, the levy was invalid. [657 H] (a) The notification issued under the provisions Of section 3 was ultra ultra vires. It was not open to the petitioner to challenge the validity on the ground that it contravened articles 14 and 19 of the constitution. The notification did not violate article 14 as it infringed articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitu tion. [757 H; 758 A] (b) The notifications issued under sections 3 and 4 were ultravies and void. It could not therefore be said that the impugned notification was ultra est because, as the notification was issued in exercise Of its powers under section 6 of the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1956 it did no affect the validity or invalidity of the notifications. [858 A B] (c) The impugned notification dated March 1, 1955, issued under s.3 of the Uttar Pradesh General Clauses (Regulation and Development) Act 1948, was invalid because it contravened the provisions contained in section 3 and that it violated articles 14 & 19 of Part III of the Schedule to the Constitution. [958 A C] (d) The State Government had no power to issue a notification under section3 of that Act. It is not open for the petitioner, to challenge that notification on the grounds that it was ultra ves and that there was no violation of article 19 or 31 of Part IV of the schedule. [1058 A D] (e) The validity of a notification issued thereunder could not, therefore be challenged in any court of law.

The appellant was convicted under section 376 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the appellant had committed rape with a woman who had been subjected to sexual intercourse with her without any provocation or provocation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The offence of rape is not murder if the victim has been subjected for sexual intercourse. [630H; 730A] 2. The crime is not an offence but murder if it is committed by a woman in the course of her marriage with another woman. It is not necessary that the offender should be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to life. [730B] 3. The appellant has been convicted under sections 376 and 376 of Indian Penal code, and sentenced by the High Court. The sentence of imprisonment imposed on him is set aside. [781A B] 4. In the instant case, the appellant was not subjected for rape with her. He had been convicted for the offence of sexual intercourse without any premeditation or provocation and he has been sentenced to rigorous imprisonment. [783C D] 5. The conviction of the appellant under section 377 of the Code is set at naught. [784E F] 6. In view of the fact that the victim was subjected to rape, it is not possible to hold that she had been forced to commit sexual intercourse by her husband or his wife. [777F] 7. The appeal must be allowed.

The respondent company was a registered dealer under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed compensation for the land acquired by it from the Government of India in respect of certain lands which were acquired by the State Government. The claim was disallowed by the Assistant Collector on the ground that the compensation was not paid within the time allowed by rule of law and that the amount of compensation was payable only after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed under section 23(1) of the Act. The High Court held that the claim was barred by limitation as it had been made before the expiry Of the period prescribed in section 23 (1). In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the question whether the amount paid by the Government to the Government was a revenue receipt or not and that it was not liable to be included in the compensation for any other reason. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "any other sum" in section 24(1)(a) of that Act means a sum which is payable by the assessee to the State. [775G] 2. The amount paid under the head "income from property" has been included in compensation for an asset or liability incurred by the owner of the land and not as a revenue expenditure. It is not necessary that the money should be included within the expression "income" in the definition of "income". [776G] 3. The question whether a sum paid under a head "Income from property", is a revenue deduction, is a matter which must be determined on the facts and circumstances of each case. [771C D] 4. In the instant case, the amount was not included in any compensation for acquisition of the property but as a capital expenditure, it could not be said that the sum paid by it to the assessee was a capital receipt or liability. The fact that the payment was made to the owner did not make any difference. [761C] 5. In view of the fact that there was no question of limitation on the amount being included in a compensation for a particular asset, the High Court was right in holding that the assessee had incurred a capital loss and therefore, it should be held that it could be said to have been incurred by him. [751G] 6. The liability to pay compensation under section 24 (1) is not a revenue debt but a revenue liability.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were in possession of the premises in dispute and that they had been in possession thereof. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the decree was not executable as it was passed without notice to the parties. In appeal, the High Court held that the compromise was not binding on the parties and that the appellants were entitled to protection under section 13(1)(e) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1950. The High Court also held that there was no valid agreement between the parties in respect of the suit premises and dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the High court had erred in holding that there were no valid agreements between the respondents and the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The compromise was binding on both the parties but the decree passed without hearing the parties was not a nullity as it did not contain any provision for eviction under section 14(1). [630 B] (2) In view of the provisions of section 13 of the Act, the decree could not be executed in favour of the appellants and the respondents were entitled only to protection of section 14. [632 C D] (3) The High court was right in holding the compromise as a nullity. [730 B C] (4) In the instant case, the compromise did not mention any specific agreement between them and the parties which was binding upon the appellants on the basis of the compromise. The compromise did contain any clause regarding the rights of the parties to the suit property. The respondents were in occupation of the same premises as they had already been in occupation thereof.

The assessee company was a public limited company carrying on business in the manufacture of textile goods. The Income tax Officer held that the loss suffered by it was not a capital loss but a revenue loss. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer and held that there was no loss to the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The loss suffered in the company is a capital asset and must be regarded as a capital receipt. [632 D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the losses suffered by the company were not a revenue expenditure. [733 C] (iii) The assessee company had no power to make any provision for the payment of dividend or loss arising out of the business of the company. It is not necessary that the profits should be regarded in the hands of the assessee and it must be shown that they were incurred by the assessee in carrying on the business. [781 D] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. Bengal Immunity Co., Ltd. , followed. (iv) The losses suffered in a company are not capital gains but are capital gains. [783 E F] Commissioner Of Income tax, West Bengal vs M. P. Roy & Sons, ; , referred to. (v) The profits of the companies must be treated as capital gains and must therefore be regarded for the purpose of section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. [784 D] In the present case, the loss was a revenue receipt and not a trading loss. The High Courts were right in taking the view that the assessee company could not be said to have incurred any expenditure on the capital gains because it had incurred a capital gain. [777 E F]. Commissioner of Incometax vs Moreshwar Sugar Mills Ltd., , followed, (vi) The Tribunal was right when the profits are made by the companies and the loss is a revenue asset.

The appellants were the tenants of village U.P. The land in dispute was acquired by the State Government under section 4(1) of the U. P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The appellants filed objections to the award on the ground that the award was not a valid one and therefore the award could not be set aside. The District Judge dismissed the objection holding that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to make an award under section 6(1). On appeal by the appellants, the High Court held that the order of the District Judge was not in accordance with law and that the District judge was not competent to make the award. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had no power to make a reference under section 18(1)(b) of U. p. (2) of Act II of 1956, to the District Court as the arbitrator was not appointed by the Government and therefore he could not make an order under section 17(3). HELD: The award is not in conformity with law. It is well settled that a reference made under section 19(1), is not a nullity because it is made under the Act. [757 H] In the present case, the District court had jurisdiction to pass the award under the provisions of the Act and therefore there was no question of any jurisdiction in the matter. The High Court was right in holding that section 18 (3) of Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Rules, 1950, did not apply to the proceedings before the District Arbitrator.

The petitioner was appointed as a temporary employee in the respondent Corporation. He was promoted to the post of Executive Engineer on ad hoc basis. The respondent Corporation, however, did not appoint him as Executive Engineer. The petitioner challenged the validity of the resolution by filing a writ petition before the High Court which held that the respondent was entitled to be considered for promotion to the cadre of Executive Engineers and that the petitioner was entitled only to be promoted to that post. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the impugned resolution was not valid, and quashed the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High court had erred in law in holding that since the respondent had been appointed as Executive Engineers on ad temporary basis, he could not be considered to have been promoted to a cadre of Superintending Engineer. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned resolution is valid and legal and is liable to be quashed. [795B] 2.1 The High court was right in holding the respondent 's promotion to that cadre. [774C D] 2:2 The High Courts were wrong in holding so because the respondent could not have been considered for selection to the posts of Executive Engi neer. [764F G] 3:3 The High courts had erred by holding that there was no statutory rule or regulation governing the promotion of the respondent to the said cadre. The rules do not provide any guidance for the exercise of the power under section 33 of the Act. [754G H; 771A B] 4:4 The High Powered Corporation is a body corporate and it has its own head, and it is an authority which can be exercised by the corporation to regulate the promotion and promotion of officers and servants in the cadre. It is not necessary that the rules should be framed for the purpose of determining the seniority of officers, servants and servants. [784C] 5:5 The High power under Section 33 of Act is a statutory power and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. [794F H; 781A C] 6:6 The High 'Court was right when it held that there were no statutory rules governing the recruitment, promotion and appointment of officers. [ 771B D] 7:7 The High Commis sioner had not considered the question whether the respondent is entitled to any promotion or appointment in the said post.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Judges of the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. The Chief Justice of India, by his order dated 15th September, 1987, directed that the appointment of the petitioners shall be made on the basis of merit and suitability. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court contending that the Chief Justice had no power to appoint a Judge of the High Courts as he was not a judge of the Court. The High Court rejected the contention of the peti tioners and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Commis sioner had no jurisdiction to appoint any Judge of a High Court as he had been appointed in the High tact of the Chief Minister. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The appointment of a Judge is not an act of the State but an act which is done by the Chief Ministers and is not subject to judicial review. It is only when the Chief Secretary or the Chief Secretaries are appointed in that behalf that he has been appointed as such. [703B] 2. The power to make appointments is not a matter of course within the meaning of Article 32. The Court cannot be said to have acted arbitrarily or capriciously or capricically or capricously or caprically or capricately. It must be exercised in accordance with the principles laid down by this Court in the case of Union of India vs M.L. Sharma, ; , referred to. In the instant case, the Chief Justices had no authority to appoint the petitioners as Judges. The appointments were made on a purely administrative basis and they were not subject matter of judicial review, nor were they made on any extraneous consideration. [781C] 3. The question whether the Chief justice was a judge or not is not one of fact. It has been held by this court in the decision reported in 1987 (Supp.) SCC 491 that the appointments made on behalf by the High Judges should be made only on administrative basis. [783D E] 4. The Constitution Bench had no jurisdic tion to make appointment of Judges and not on any irrelevant consideration. The President has also been given a right to appoint an ad hoc Judge as a Judge or a Judge. [784G H; 784A B] 5. The constitutional validity of Article 323 A is not challenged in the present case, because it is only in the context of the scheme of the Act that the power to appointment of an ad interim Judge is limited to administrative functions and not to judicial functions. It cannot be disputed that the President has been given the power under Article 323A. [777E] 6. The expression "any other matter" in Article 323 B means a matter which is not within the competence of the President, but which is outside the competence or authority of the Union. [779C D] 7. The word "court" in article 323 A has been used in the Constitution as a whole and it cannot be interpreted to mean a judicial function. It can only mean a matter that is not covered by any of the clauses of Article 341. [773D E; 784B C] 8. The scope of Article 324 A is limited only to administrative acts and not merely to administrative or quasi judicial functions, but also to administrative and quasi judicial bodies. [771F G] 9. The term "court ' has been defined in the Act to mean the judicial and quasi administrative functions. The words "any matter" are used in Article 324 of the Constitu tion. It may be a judicial or quasi administrative function. The expressions "other matters" in the definition of "court", have been used as a word of judicial or judicial function, but they are not exhaustive.

The respondent was appointed as a clerk in the appellant Bank. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Director, and he was later confirmed as an officer in the Bank. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of dismissal passed by the disciplinary authority. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the enquiry held against him was vitiated because of the absence of any evidence to show that he had been appointed as an Assistant Director and that he was not entitled to any relief in respect of his appointment as a Manager. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in interfering with the order passed by disciplinary authority, and that the order was vitiated by misdirection. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court had rightly held that the respondent was not competent to hold an enquiry against him. [730B] 2.2 In the instant case, the respondent had been compulsorily retired from service on the ground of his being a clerk and was not in a position to discharge his duties as a Branch Manager. He had been denied any right to continue in the post till he attained the age of superannuation. The order of compulsory retirement was passed by an authority competent to do so. [774C] 2:1 The respondent was compulsorily retired on the basis of the report of the Enquiry Officer and his appointment was made in accordance with law. He could not be said to have been appointed in a substantive capacity as a Head Clerk. He did not hold any post till his retirement. He continued in service till he attaining the age Of superannuation. He, therefore, had no right to remain in the service till his superannuation. [764C D] 2 :2 The High Courts were wrong in holding that since the respondent 's appointment was terminated by an order of termination, he could not have been denied the benefit of any statutory right. [754F G] 3:3 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that the disciplinary authorities had taken into consideration the report submitted by the Enquiry officer and the report made by the enquiry officer. The disciplinary authority was therefore justified in interfering in the order. [784C E] 4:1 It is not possible to hold that the appellant was appointed in substantive capacity till he retired on attaining the superannuation of 58 years. The appellant had been rightly denied the benefits of any service. [794F H; 774G H; 78A B] 2.(a) In the absence Of any evidence, it could not reasonably be said that the impugned order was passed mala fide or was in a manner prejudicial to public interest. [ 774C G] (b) The High courts were wrong when they had taken the view that the findings of the enquiry officers were vitiated because the respondent did not have any right of continue in service until he attained superannuation. It is also not possible for this Court to interfere with the finding of the disciplinary authori ty. [ 784C F] (c) The order passed on the appellant 's representation was not justified as it was made without affording him an opportunity of being heard. [ 764F] 2(a) The respondent had no locus standi to challenge the order in question because he was a clerk, and was entitled to be appointed in his substantive capacity. He has been denied all the benefits which were available to him under the relevant rules. [744G] (d) In view of the fact that the Enquiry Committee had taken note of the findings recorded by the Inquiry Officer and the recommendations made by it, the High Courts are not justified in holding the respondent guilty of misconduct.

The appellant Corporation, a public limited company, was formed by the Delhi Development Authority under section 3 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957. The appellant Corporation applied to the High Court for permission to construct buildings on the site and to grant sanction to construct building on the land. The High Court granted permission to the appellant Corporation to construct a building on it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The permission was not necessary in view of section 3(2)(a) of the Act. [408 D] (2) The High Courts have no power to grant permission under section 4(2). The permission is not necessary for the purpose of construction of buildings on a site. [509 F] (3) The sanction is necessary in order to enable the Corporation to make an application to the Government for sanction of the building. The Government has to consider whether the building is required for the purposes of construction or for the development of the land, and if so, what is the nature of the permission. [609 G] (4) The power under section 5(2) is not a discretionary power but it is a discretionary one. It is only when the Government has made an order that the building should be used for the construction of a building or for any other purpose. If the Government makes an order, it will be open to the Corporation either to make such an order or to refuse to grant the permission under sub section (2).

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 120B and 120 B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that the appellant had committed a breach of trust in respect of which he was charged. The Sessions Judge convicted him on the ground that the evidence of the witnesses were not reliable, and that the statements made by the witnesses did not amount to any confession or threat from the appellant. On appeal the High Court held that the statement made by them did not constitute a confession or inducement. Held, that the conviction was based on the evidence which was produced before the Magistrate and the Sessions Judge had no jurisdiction to try the case. The High Court was in error in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant could not be convicted for an offence under section 120B of the Penal Code, because he was a police officer within the meaning of section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. Held further, that there was no evidence to show that the witnesses had been examined by the prosecution and were not examined by him. The conviction was therefore based on a mere statement made before the police officer. The fact that the witness was examined by a police officers does not make any difference in the circumstances of the case and the High Courts were right in holding the appellant guilty of an offence punishable under section 5 (1) (a) of Prevention of Anti Corruption Act. The order of conviction passed against the appellant was therefore, set aside. The appeal must be allowed.

The respondent was charged under section 323 I.P.C. for having committed the offence of causing grievous hurt to one Ram Singh, a Sub Inspector of Police and was dismissed from service by the Additional District Judge, Amritsar on the ground that he had been convicted for having caused simple hurt to him. The trial court held that the respondent was guilty of having committed an offence under section 325 I. P.C., and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court in appeal affirmed the order of dismissal passed by the trial court. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the finding recorded by the first appellate court was erroneous and that the findings recorded by both the courts below were not based on any evidence and that there was no error apparent on the face of the record. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The finding recorded in the first appeal is not based upon any evidence or on any other material. [742D] 2. In the instant case, the High court had erred by holding that there were two charges against the respondent and the trial was vitiated by the error apparent from the face. [781E F] 3. The findings recorded in first appeal are not based merely on any material which could be said to have been established beyond reasonable doubt.
