It is well settled that the appellate court has no power to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by two courts below and it cannot interfere with such findings unless there is a manifest error apparent or patent error apparent upon the face or the record in support of the findings. [783E F].

The assessee, a private limited company, was carrying on business in tea and tea. The assessee had purchased the tea from one of its partners, who were the agents of the latter. In the assessment year 1959 60, the Income tax Officer held that the goods sold by the assessee were not taxable under section 2(g) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer and held that there was no evidence to show that the sales were made in the course of inter state trade or commerce. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the sale was not a sale within the meaning of section 2 (g) and therefore the sale could not be said to be an adventure in the nature of trade or business within the definition of 'business ' as defined in section 2 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Courts were right in holding that the transaction was a sale of goods within the scope of the definition. [615 F] In the instant case, the sales made by the appellant to the agents were not inter state transactions and therefore they were not liable to be taxed under section 4(1)(g) read with section 2. The sale was in the process of inter State trade or trade. It was therefore a transaction within the ambit of section 5(1). [616 F] Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal vs M/s. Swastik Mills Ltd., ; , referred to.

The appellant was a candidate for election to the Legislative Assembly of Punjab. The Returning Officer rejected his nomination paper on the ground that he had not been duly elected and that the nomination paper was improperly rejected. The appellant filed an appeal to the Election Tribunal which held that the Returning Officer had no jurisdiction to reject the nomination. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the expression "may" in section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, means a person who has been duly nominated and that he must be deemed to have been duly duly elected. Held, that the word "may ' in section 124(3), is wide enough to include a person whose nomination paper is improperly rejected under the provisions of the Act. The words "shall" in the context of the expression are not defined in the Act but only those words are used in the statute which are intended to be used in a statute. The word "shall ' in the section must be construed strictly and it must be interpreted in its ordinary sense as meaning a person appearing before the Returning officer. The use of the word 'may" is not restricted by the context in which it occurs. The expression "shall " in section 122(3)(a) means a statement made by the candidate to the Returning authority or his proposer and the proposer and his proposer are not required to be present at the time of making the nomination, but must be read as including a statement recorded by him to the effect that he has been improperly rejected and that is why the word used in section 127(3A) should be construed in its popular sense. The meaning of the words "may". in section 128(3 A) means that the candidate who has made the nomination must have been given an opportunity to make his nomination.

The appellants, who were workmen of the respondent company, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notices dated December 1, 1972 and January 31, 1972. The said notice was served on the appellants on May 3, 1972, but the appellants did not appear before the Labour Commissioner on July 7, 1972 when the matter came up for hearing. On August 11, 1972 the appellants filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the notices issued by the respondent Company and also the notices terminating their services. The appellants contended that the notice was bad as it had been served on them only on May 2, 1972; that the notices were not served on each of them on May 4, 1972 at the time when the notices had been issued and that the appellants had no locus standi to file the present appeal; that since the notices did not contain any specific provision in the Act for the termination of their services, they could not be said to have been served with a notice terminating their service. The Labour Commissioner rejected the contention of the appellants and held that the services of the workmen were terminated on May 1, 1971 at the instance of the Company and that they had no right to file any appeal; and that since there was no specific provision for the dismissal of their service, the notices could not have been issued in the present case. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the termination was bad because it was not a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Act and that there was nothing to show that the workmen had any right to be heard before the said notices were served on all the appellants. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the impugned notices were bad as they did not mention the names of the employees in the notice dated December 2, 1971 and that their services were terminated at the behest of the company and that no opportunity had been given to them to show cause against the said notice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notices issued under section 3(1) (d) are not vague and they do not mention any particular date in which the notices have been sent. [703B C] 2. The notice dated January 31 1972 was served upon all the workmen on May 5, 1972 but it did not specify any particular dates in which they were employed. It is only when the notice is served on any of the parties that the said service was terminated at any time before the date of the notice. [774C] 3. The services of a workman are terminated at an early stage and the workmen have no right or title to the said post. [764F G] 4. The termination of service is not a matter of course within the contemplation of section 3 (1) of that Act. [754G H; 77A B] 5. The expression "any person" in section 2 (1)(e) means any person who has been dismissed or removed from service by reason of his dismissal or removal, and includes any person whose services are terminated on the ground of misconduct or misconduct. [784F] 6. The word "any other person" is not defined in the statute as meaning a person who is dismissed or removal from service. It means a person whose service has been terminated at a time when he was dismissed or remove from service, and it includes any other person whose period of suspension has expired. [794F H; 78A B C] 7. The definition of "any workman" in the definition of 'workman" in Section 2(2) (e) is not restricted to persons who have been dismissed, removed or removed or reduced from service and it does not include any person employed in connection with the affairs of the companies.

The appellant, a trustee of the respondent, filed an application under section 47(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the sale was not valid and the sale had been validly made. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that a sale could be set aside under section 48(1). HELD: (i) The High Court erred in holding the sale void because the sale did not amount to a sale within the meaning of section 48. [601 B] (ii) The decision of the High court is final and binding on the parties. [702 C] (iii) In the present case, the appellant had made an application for setting out the sale in his favour under section 49(1), but he did not do so. He did not file any application for set aside the order of the trial court. The High court was right in holding on the basis that the appellant was a trustee and not a trustee. [783 C] In the instant case, there is no evidence to show that the respondent had made any application under r. 47(2) for setting up the sale of his property. The appellant did not make an application within the period prescribed by r. 48(2). [783 D F] (iv) The question whether a sale was valid or not does not arise in the present appeal.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Postal Service. He retired from service on 31st March, 1971. The respondent was compulsorily retired from the post of Superintendent in the Postal Department. On his retirement he was compulsorily retire under Rule 5(2) of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972. The appellant challenged the validity of the order of compulsory retirement by filing a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same on the ground that it violated Article 14 of the Constitution and that the impugned order was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 5 (2) provides for compulsory retirement of Government servants who are retired from Government service after attaining the age of 55 years. The rule is in consonance with Article 311(2). [630F] 2.2 Rule 5 provides for a compulsory retirement on attaining the prescribed age of superannuation. The proviso to Rule 5 lays down that compulsory retirement shall be made by the authority competent to retire a Government servant on attaining 60 years of age. The requirement of Rule 5 is that the authority concerned should have been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. [631F] 3.3 Rule 5 prescribes for compulsory retiring a government servant on reaching the age specified in Rule 5. The power to compulsorily retire a government employee is not absolute and it has no application to the case of compulsory retiring Government servant. It is only when the authority has given an option to retire the government servant, that is, after giving him an opportunity of showing cause against his proposed action, that the order should be made in accordance with the provisions of Rule 6. [731F G] 4.4 The power under Rule 6(2)(a) is not discretionary and it is only where the authority is satisfied that the government has given a reasonable opportunity to the servant to showcause against the action proposed to be taken, that discretion should be exercised judicially.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton fabrics. The assessee claimed that the profits earned by it were not taxable under section 4(1)(b) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and held that the losses suffered by the assessee were not liable to be taxed under section 5(2)(a). On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the loss suffered by it was a trading loss within the meaning of section 4 (1) (b) and that the profit earned by the company was not taxable in the hands of the business carried on by it, and that since the profits were not assessable under section 6(2), the losses could be taxed only if the profits had been actually received. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the assessee was liable to pay tax under section 7(1) of Act, and therefore, the loss incurred by it in carrying on the business was taxable under the provisions of section 5 (3)(a) of 1922. [417 D] In the present case, the losses were not chargeable under section 3(2) of that Act. The profits were assessable under the Indian Incometax Act, but the profits could be assessed only if they were actually received by the business. [416 E F] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. P. C. & Co., , referred to.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for appointment to the post of Assistant Engineer in the Kerala Public Works Department. The Public Service Commis sioner was appointed as Assistant Engineer on the basis of merit and suitability. The Government issued a notification dated July 1, 1979 fixing the inter se seniority of the candidates who had been selected by the Public Service Service Commission. The petitioners challenged the said order before the High Court contending that the Public Services Commission had no power to appoint the Public service Commission as Assistant Engineers on the ground that the Government had no authority to appoint Public Service Commissions. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State Government had not acted in accordance with the directions of the High court and that the appointment of Public Service commission was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government has power to make rules for recruitment to the posts of Assistant Engineers. It is well settled that the appointments made by Public Service Commissioners are subject to the approval of the Government. [601B] 2. The Commission has no power under section 3(1) of the Kerala Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1957 to appoint a Public Service Tribunal as Assistant Engi sioners on the recommendation of the Public Commission. It does not mean that the Commission has power under rule 4(2). [602D] 3. The appointment of the public service Commission is subject to approval of Government. The appointments made in accordance therewith are subject only to the final decision of the State Public Service Commissioner.

The respondent, a partnership firm, was incorporated in the year 1979. The partnership deed provided that the partners shall be entitled to claim the share of the profits and gains of the business. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the partnership deed was not binding on him as it was not executed by him. The High Court held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly held that there was no valid ground for interference with the order of the Income tax officer. [775B] 2.2 The High court has rightly held in favour of the respondent. [774C D] 3.3 The High courts have rightly found that the plaintiff had not filed any written statement and had not been able to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. [764F G] 4.4 In view of the fact that the defendant had filed a written statement, the High Court was right in holding that the plaint was barred under section 7(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. [754C] 5.4 The HighCourt has rightly found the plaintiff guilty of fraud and collusion between the parties. [784F] In view thereof, the order passed by the High court is set aside and the suit is remanded to the trial Court for deciding the question whether the plaintiff was entitled to the share in the profits or gains of business. [794C E] 5:5 The High 'Court has correctly held that it is not open to the High Courts to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the courts below.

The appellants are manufacturers of industrial products. They were manufacturing industrial products and they had been selling industrial products in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The State Government issued a notification dated March 31, 1983 exempting the industrial units from payment of sales tax on the ground that they were not entitled to exemption under the Act. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification by filing writ petitions before the High Court contending that the notification was ultra vires and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the exemption granted to them by the State Government was not in accordance with law and, therefore, the exemption could not be said to be in conformity with the provisions of the Act and that the Notification dated March 1, 1983 was ultravires tive. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: The notification dated April 31, 1984 is ultra vires as it is beyond the competence of the State Govern ment to exempt the industrial unit from payment tax on sales tax in respect of which exemption has been granted under the notification. [703B] In the instant case, the notification dated May 31, 1982 was issued by the Government of Madhya Bharat and the Notification was issued in exercise of its power under section 3(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Sales Tax Act, 1948. The notification did not contain any provision for exemption from payment or exemption. The Notification dated April 1, 1984 clearly provided that the benefit of exemption shall be available to the industrial establishment only if the exemption is granted by the Central Government in respect thereof. [781B] The notification was issued on March 31. 1983 and it was issued after the expiry of the period of exemption. It was not open to the State to contend that the concession given by the notification in question was ultra est. The exemption was not available to any industrial establishment even if the concession had been granted by a Government in favour of the industrial establishments. [783C] The exemption granted under section 4(1)(a) of Madhya Nadu Sales Tax Rules, 1948 is in accordance only with the conditions laid down therein and the exemption was subject to the condition that the industrial undertaking should be exempted from payment. [784G H; 784A B] The Notification issued by Government of India dated April 19, 1983 clearly provided for exemption of sales Tax on sales of industrial units. The benefit of the exemption had been given to industrial establishments only if it were not exempted from tax.

The Delhi High Court Rules, 1961 framed under the Delhi Judicial Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, provided that the seniority of a member of the service shall be determined by the State Government on the basis of length of service. Rule 3(b)(ii) provides that the members of the Service who are appointed to the service in accordance with the rules shall be entitled to seniority from the date of their appointment. Rule 4(b) provides for the method of recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to a service by direct recruitment. Rule 5(c)(iii) provides inter alia that the number of vacancies to be filled by direct recruits shall be fixed by the Government in consultation with the High Court. Rule 6(a)(ii), however, provides that seniority of members of a service shall not be determined on the date on which they are appointed. Rule 7(b), however provides that if any vacancy arises in the cadre of a District Judge or a District judge, the vacancies to which the direct recruits may be appointed shall be filled in by direct recruit and the remaining vacancies shall be reserved for the members belonging to the Service. Rule 8(a) provides as follows: "The seniority of the members shall be regulated by the rules made under this rule". Rule 7 (b)(iii), however empowers the High Courts to make rules for recruitment to the posts in the service of the Union Territory of Delhi, and the rules framed thereunder, provided for the mode of recruitment. The Rules further provides that in the case of direct recruits appointed to any service by promotion from the cadre to which they were appointed, the seniority shall be governed by the Rules made under the rules. Rule 9(a), however provided that if the vacancies are filled by promotion, the members who have been appointed to such service shall rank senior to them in accordance therewith. The High Court also directed that the vacancies shall not exceed the number prescribed for direct recruits. The respondents filed a writ petition in the Delhi High court challenging the validity of Rule 7 and the Rules framed thereunder. The Delhi High Courts (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules were amended by the Act of 1976 which provided that seniority shall not count for any period longer than the number fixed for direct recruitment to a post in the Service, but shall be counted for the purpose of determining seniority. The writ petition was allowed by the High court holding that Rule 7 was ultra vires and void as it violated Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the Rules were ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as the rules did not provide for the manner in which the vacancies were to be reserved, and that the rules were ultravires the Constitution and that they contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The rules framed under Rule 3 (b) (ii) are ultra vires Articles 14, 16 and 16. [799B C] 2. The rule is ultra vires Article 14 and is void as being violative of Articles 14 or 19(2)(g). [701C D] 3. The recruitment to posts in a service under the Union Territories of Delhi and Delhi and Haryana are governed by Rule 7 of the Rules. The appointments to the post in question are made by direct Recruitment and Promotion Rules, which are framed under Article 309 of the Constitu tion. The quota for direct recruit is fixed on the dates of their initial appointment. The seniority of direct recruit shall be reckoned from the dates on which he was appointed to that service. [781B C; 701C] 4. Rule 10(a ) (ii), therefore, provides for recruitment by direct direct recruitment and promotion to the cadre in accordancewith the rules and conditions laid down in Rule 3.

The appellant firm was a Hindu undivided family. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the firm to tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income from the firm was not taxable in view of the provisions of section 12(1)(a) and (b). On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner held that there was no provision for the assessment of the income to tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The Income Tax Officer had jurisdiction to assess the income under section 12 (1)(c) and not to assess a firm on the ground that he had no power to assess or reassess the income. [657 D] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. Ram Kishan & Co., ; , followed. In the present case, the Income Tax officer had jurisdiction in respect of the assessment year 1948 49. The High Court was right in holding that the Income tax officer had no jurisdiction to make a reference under section 18(1) (a). [658 G] Commissioner Of Income tax, Punjab vs M. P. Singh & Co. ; , referred to. In view of this decision, the High Court could not have made any reference under s.10(2)(b) and the Appellate Tribunal had jurisdiction. The order of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner was set aside by the High court.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the adopted son of one M. A. Pillai, who had been appointed as a sole arbitrator to decide his disputes relating to the properties in dispute. The appellant claimed that he had no right to file any suit for partition and possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit as it did not decide the question whether the appellant was entitled to claim partition or possession of properties in suit. HELD: (i) The High Court had no jurisdiction to try the suit and the High Courts were right in holding that the appellant had no locus standi to file the suit. [637 B C] (ii) The appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 9(1)(b) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950. [738 D] (iii) The question whether a suit for possession of immovable property in dispute is a matter of law and must be decided by the High courts within the meaning of article 136 of the Constitution. [781 B C]. (iv) The jurisdiction of the High ' Court under section 8(1) (b) is not limited to the jurisdiction of a civil court. It is only when it decides the question as to whether a particular case is one which is covered by the Act and the jurisdiction is limited to that of a Civil Court.

The appellant, a public limited company, was granted permission to construct a building on the land in question. The respondent No. 1, a local authority, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the sanction and the sanction accorded by the Municipal Committee. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the construction was not a 'public limited company ' within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the permission granted by the Chief Executive Officer was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The construction was a 'Public limited company within the definition of `public limited Company ' as defined under section 2 (1) (a) of Delhi Municipal Act, 1911. [730B] 2. The purpose of the construction is to ensure that the building is constructed on the site and not on any other site. It is also necessary that the owner or occupier of a building should have a right to construct the building on such land. The use of the building for the purpose of constructing a building would be sufficient if it was in accordance therewith. [781B] 3. The provisions of section 1(1)(a) and (b) of Act are not intended to be construed as laying down the procedure for construction of buildings. It does not mean that the owners or occupier should have an right to erect a building within the ambit of the statute. [783C D] 4. The object of the provision is to provide a machinery for construction and to ensure the safety of the buildings, and to provide for the safe custody of the premises in question, to enable the owner to construct it on the same site. [784E F] 5. The Court has to see whether the construction of a buildings is a 'private limited company" within the scope of the provisions contained in section 1 (1)(b) or not. [830C D; 830A B] 6. The question for consideration is whether the building was constructed on a plot of land and not a public street. [777E F, 830F G] 7. The court has to examine the provisions in the Act, and the Rules framed thereunder, and if it is found that there are no rules or regulations governing the construction, it would be open to the owner of the site to make an application for permission to erect the building within a period of one month from the date of the order. [779E F; 831A B C] 7 The Court should examine the scheme and the provisions made in the statute, and take into account the surrounding circumstances and the surrounding factors including the nature of the constructions, the purpose for which the construction has been constructed, the nature and extent of the proposed construction, the extent of its impact on the building, the location and the extent to which it is proposed to be erected. [773E F]. The Court cannot ignore the provisions or the rules made thereunder.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in the business of manufacturing liquor. The respondent, who was a partner in the firm, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his business business. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff had no right to sue for partition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the suit had been instituted in the year 1946, and that the decree passed by the trial court was not a nullity because the suit did not contain any provision for the institution of the suit. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was no provision for institution of a suit which could be filed in the years 1946, 1946 and 1946. [757 H] (ii) In view of the provisions of section 7(1)(b) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, the suit must be dismissed on the ground that it was barred under the provisions Of section 7 of the Limitation Act. The High Courts were right in not holding that a suit could be instituted in a year in which the cause of action arose. [781 B] (iii) In the present case the suit for dissolution was filed in 1946 and the suit having been instituted, it was not barred by time. [783 C D] (iv) The suit was not maintainable because the plaintiff was not entitled to sue in a particular year.

The appellant was a factory in Bombay. The factory was situated in the State of Bombay and it was used for the purpose of manufacturing and selling goods. The appellant was prosecuted under section 5(1) (a) of the Bombay Factories Act, 1948 on the ground that the factory was not a factory within the meaning of the Act. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 7 of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the word " factory" in section 2(1)(d) of that Act means any factory which is used for any purpose other than the manufacture or sale of goods and includes any building, machinery, plant, apparatus, apparatus or apparatus which is capable of being used for such purpose. Held, that the words " factory " are not defined in the Act but defined in section 3(1). The word " factories" in the definition of " factory means any building or machinery which is intended to be used for a purpose other as the manufacture of goods or for the sale of any goods or of any process incidental thereto. The word ' factory" has been used in the context in which it occurs and the words used are not capable of use. The expression " factories " means any premises which is meant for the manufacture, sale or sale. The definition of the word ' Factories ' in section 7(1), therefore, must be read as a whole. The meaning of that word has to be given to it in its ordinary sense and not in its popular sense. It is well settled that the expression " factory includes any machinery, equipment, apparatus etc., used in connection with the manufacture and sale of which is not capable or being used in relation to any process ancillary thereto. In the present case the word was used in section 10(1); it was not intended to include a building or plant which is for the use of the factory. The words " factories includes any premises" in that section, but were meant only for the purposes of the manufacture.

The respondent was appointed as a Junior Engineer in the State of Mysore on January 1, 1956. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Director (Civil) in the year 1957. The respondent was promoted as Assistant Director on January 31, 1956 and he was confirmed in that post on January 2, 1956, on the basis of his seniority in the cadre of Junior Engineer. On January 3, 1956 he was reverted to the higher post of Junior Engineers. He challenged the order of reversion by a writ petition in the High Court which allowed him to continue in service as Assistant Secretary on January 3. 1956. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to be absorbed in the post on the date he became permanent and that his seniority should be determined with reference to the date of his confirmation. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the order was not justified because the respondent had been promoted as Junior Engineer on January 4, 1956 when he was appointed on January 14, 1956; and that the High court erred in holding that the seniority of the respondent could be determined only with referenceto his date of confirmation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was right in holding the respondent 's claim to be permanent and not with reference thereto. [657 D] In the instant case, the respondent did not have any grievance against the order dated January 3,. 1956. His seniority could not be determined on the ground that he had been appointed on December 1, 1957 when he became temporary. The fact that he was promoted on January 15, 1956 was not a circumstance which would justify his claim for absorption in the higher posts.

The petitioner, a resident of the State of West Bengal, was born in the United States of America. The petitioner applied for a writ of mandamus to the respondents to appoint a guardian of a child on the ground that he had been a minor and that the child was not a minor at the time of his birth. The Court, however, directed the petitioner to submit a report to the Court within three weeks from the date of receipt of the report. The writ petition filed by the petitioner was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the mother of the child had been in a position to make an application for appointment of guardian of the minor, and that since the mother had not made any such application within three months from the receipt of report, the Court could not have directed the State Government to appoint another guardian. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The mother of a minor is entitled to be appointed as guardian of an child on his own behalf and not as a guardian for the minor. [703 B] 2. The father of a person who has been in custody of a foreign State, is entitled only to be a minor if he is found to be in a fit mental condition to make a application within two months from such date. [771 D E] 3. The power conferred on the Court by section 12 of the Act is not confined to the power of appointment of a guardian but only to the powers of an agency appointed under the Act. It is only when the Court has made an order that the guardian should be appointed in accordance with the provisions of the statute, it cannot be said that the father of the person who is in custody or is not a child within the meaning of section 12. [761 D] 4. The court must have regard to the nature and extent of the power conferred by the Act and the manner in which the power is conferred. It should not be confined only to such powers as are conferred on it by the statute. [752 F G] 5. The jurisdiction of the Court under section 12 is limited to the discretion of the court to appoint guardian for a minor, if he has been found to have been in any fit mental or physical condition to provide for the custody and control of the children. It cannot be confined to such power as are vested in the Court. [741 F G; 771 A] 6. The question whether an application under section 11 is maintainable is not one of fact. The discretion conferred on a court by section 13 is limited only to those powers which are conferred by it. If the court has made the order, it would be open to the court in exercise of its power under section 13 to appoint an guardian for such minor if it thinks fit. [781 F] 7. The provisions of section 13 are not confined merely to the jurisdiction of a court to make the order. It does not mean that the power to appoint or appoint a child is limited by the power given to it by section 11. If there is no provision in the Act for the appointment of an guardian, the court would be justified in directing the State Governments to appoint such a guardian if it considers necessary so to do. [791 F H] 8. The scheme of the law is that the Court should have regard only to matters which are specified in section 13 and not to matters specified in sections 14 and 15. If it thinks necessary, it may be desirable to make such provision for the purpose of making an order. [802 A B] 9. The courts must be satisfied that the court is satisfied that there has been a conflict between the provisions contained in section 12 and the provisions in the statute are not inconsistent with the scheme of law.

The appellant company was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of textiles. The company had paid bonus to its employees for the years 1964 65 and 1965 66. The workmen claimed that the bonus payable by it was not a capital expenditure within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the , as it was a capital receipt within the definition of 'industry ' under the . The Tribunal held that the claim made by the appellant company to the extent of Rs. 1,50,000 was not justified and dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the amount paid by it to its workmen for the year 1964 65 was a revenue receipt within section 2 (1)(c) of , as the bonus was a part of the capital expenditure, and that the deduction made by it from the bonus paid to its workers for the period 1964 65 to 1965 66 was not correct. HELD : The Tribunal had wrongly held that there was no evidence on record to show that the workmen were entitled to the bonus under section 2 of the . [417 D] In the instant case, the Tribunal has erred in treating the amount as a capital asset within the scope of section 3(1) (d) and not the bonus which it had paid. The Tribunal has rightly held that it was an allowable deduction under section 10(2)(c). [418 E F] The Tribunal was right in holding, that the amounts paid by the workmen for their year 1964 66 were a capital loss within the ambit of section 10 (2) (b) and therefore, the claim for bonus could not be sustained.

The appellant was appointed as a Sales Tax Officer in the Tamil Nadu State. He was promoted to the post of Sales Tax officer on March 31, 1962. The appellant was confirmed in the post on March 1, 1963. On March 2, 1968, he was reverted to the rank of Sales tax Officer. In his report dated December 7, 1969, the Government stated that the appellant had been promoted as Sales Tax Officers on March 3, 1970 and that he should be deemed to have been confirmed in that post. The Government further stated that he was not given any opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. On April 2, 1969 the Government issued a notice under Rule 8(1) of the Tamil Pradesh General Sales Tax Rules, 1957 for the recovery of Rs. 1,000/ from him. The said notice was challenged by the appellant in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of reversion was not justified and quashed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government had no power to cancel the order, and that the impugned order was bad in law because the appellant was a Sales tax officer and he was entitled to be considered for promotion as Sales tax Officers. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the Government is not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of it. [795B] 2. The impugned order is set aside and the matter remanded to the Government for fresh consideration. [774C D] 3. In the instant case, the appellant has been promoted to a higher post in the State. His promotion was not based on any rule or order which could be made applicable to him. He had been given an opportunity of showing cause against his proposed action and he should also be considered considered for the promotion as sales tax Officers on the ground that he had been confirmed by the Government. [764C] 4. The State Government has not taken into consideration any rule in the matter of promotion. It is true that the said rule does not apply to a case where the Government has given an order of promotion, but it is only when the Government makes a recommendation for the same. But if the Government considers that the promotion should be ordered, it would be open to the government to consider the representation of the employee concerned and take into consideration the relevant rules in the light of the relevant Rules.

The appellants, who were plying stage carriages in the State of Andhra Pradesh, challenged the validity of the scheme on the grounds that (1) the scheme was not a scheme for nationalisation of stage carriages; and (2) the schemes were not approved by the Government. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the scheme did not contain any provision for nationalisation under section 68(1)(b) of the Act, and that the schemes had been approved by it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The scheme was a scheme which was approved by Government and not a stage carriage. It is not necessary that the State should have taken into consideration the scheme in question before it. [630 B] (ii) The schemes were approved by government and not by the State Government. [730 C D] (iii) The Regional Transport Authority had no power to approve the scheme, and the scheme could be approved by a competent authority. [781 G H] (iv) The Scheme was approved in accordance with the provisions of section 68 (1)(a). The scheme did contain any specific provision for the nationalisation of the stage carriages. It was not necessary to have the scheme approved by that Government. There is no provision for such nationalisation. [783 C D, F G] (v) The State Government had no authority to approve or modify the scheme. The scheme could not be approved in view of the provisions contained in section 68. [784 A B] In the present case, the scheme itself was approved and published by the Transport Department. There was no provision in the Act for nationalisation. It did not provide for nationalisation in stage carriages under section 57(1) (b). The Regional transport Authority had not given any reasons for its approval. [777 C D; 784 A B].

The appellant company was a dealer in the State of Orissa. The Sales Tax Officer issued notices to the respondents under section 8(1) of the Act on the ground that they were not dealers within the meaning of the expression "dealer" in section 2(e)(i) of that Act and that the sales tax authorities had no jurisdiction to issue a notice under section 9(1). The appellant filed an application before the Sales Tax officer for exemption from payment of tax. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the application on the grounds that the appellant was not a dealer within the definition of "dealer". The High Court held that the words "dealer", in section 3(e) of Act were wide enough to include a dealer who had been registered under the Act and therefore the exemption could be granted only if the dealer had been issued a certificate of fitness. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The word "dealer " in section 8 (1) means a person who has been registered as a dealer under the . [408 D] (ii) The words "any dealer" in the proviso to section 9 (1), are wide enough and must be construed strictly. In the present case, the appellant had not produced any certificate of registration from the Sales tax Officer. The certificate was issued by the Sales Officer on the basis that the certificate was not issued by him. [409 D] Commissioner of Sales Tax vs M/s. Bengal Immunity Co., Ltd. , followed. (iii) The certificate issued by a dealer is not a certificate under section 3 (e)(ii). The certificate is not an essential condition for the grant of exemption. It is only when the certificate is issued that the dealer has been granted a certificate.

The petitioners were convicted for offences under sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code. The Sessions Judge, Patna rejected their applications on the ground that they had not been produced before the court and that the trial was vitiated by non application of mind. The State Government filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the order of detention. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Court had no jurisdiction to pass an order of release on bail, that the petitioners were not entitled to be released on bail because they were not produced before court and were not given any opportunity to produce their evidence before the trial court. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High court is set aside and the case remanded to the Sessions Judge for disposal according to law. [775G] 2. In the instant case, the petitioners have been produced by the State Government before the High Courts and they were produced before this Court. They are directed to be produced before a trial court on the same day. The petitioners shall be released forthwith if not required in any other case. [771C D] 3. The High Court should dispose of the writ petitions as expeditiously as possible, preferably within six months from the date of receipt of the copy of this order. [762F G] 4. In view of the fact that the State has filed a petition for special leave to appeal against the order passed by the High. Court, it is directed that the case be listed on the next day.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he was in possession of certain lands and that the tenant had not been given an opportunity to show cause why the tenancy should not be terminated. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the tenancy was not terminated by the landlord, but the tenant could not be evicted under section 14(1)(a) of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1948. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the notice terminating the tenancy had been given only after the expiry of the period of three years from the date of termination and that no notice terminating his tenancy was given by him within the meaning of section 14 (1)(b) of that Act. Held, that the provisions of section 15(1) (a) are not applicable to a case where the tenant has been given a reasonable opportunity to prove his case. The proviso to sub section (2) of section 16 is intended to give an opportunity of showing cause against the termination of tenancy and it does not apply to a situation where the landlord had been afforded an opportunity for showing cause why he should not have been given notice terminating tenancy. The words "any person aggrieved by any order" in sub section(1), are wide enough to include a tenant who has been evicted under the Act. The language of the proviso is clear and unambiguous and it cannot be said that the landlord was in occupation of the land after the termination. The word "tenant" in the context of the words "in possession of any land" in section 14, means a person who has become an owner of the lands or has been ejected under the provisions mentioned in sub sections (1) and (2).

The petitioners were the owners of certain property in Pakistan. The Custodian issued a notice under section 8 of the , calling upon them to show cause why they should not be evicted from their properties. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notice on the ground that it was barred by limitation as the petitioners had no locus standi to file the petition and that the Custodian had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition. Held, that the order of the Custodian was bad because the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under section 9 of the Act. The order of dismissal passed against them was not a nullity. The petition must be dismissed. The orders of the authorities are set aside and the Custodian is directed to proceed with the case in accordance with law. The notice issued by the Custodian under section 7 of the was valid and the petitioners shall be entitled to the relief under that section. The respondents were not given any opportunity to show their cause against the order. The notices issued by them were invalid because they had no right to file their petition. The authorities could not have proceeded with the proceedings in accordance therewith. Held further, that there was no valid notice under sections 8 and 9 of Act. There was no reason why the petitioners should be given an opportunity to prove their case. The fact that the petitioners did not file their written statement would not make them a party to the petition for special leave to appeal against the orders of dismissal. Held also, further,that the order passed by the authorities under section 10 of the is bad because it was made in accordancewith law and the proceedings were therefore liable to be quashed. The proceedings were not barred by time as they had not been proceeded with.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The assessee company carried on the business of manufacturing sugar and its sales were effected by the assessee company in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The Income tax Officer held that the profits of the assessee were not taxable under section 2(1)(xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner but reduced the amount to Rs. 1,50,000/ and directed the assessee to pay a sum of Rs. 3,00,000 as compensation for loss of profits. The Tribunal held that there was no evidence on record to show that the profit of the company was not taxable in view of section 2 (1)(xiv) of Act, 1961. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court held that it was a case of an agreement between the assessee and its employees for the purpose of carrying on the trade or business of selling sugar and that the assessee had no right to carry on the same business as the assessee was not liable to pay any amount under section 10(2) (xv). In appeal by special leave, the question for consideration was whether the profits were taxable in the hands of the assesses. HELD: The High Court was wrong in holding that the loss of profit of a company is not taxable because it is an agreement which has been entered into between the parties and the assessee. [775F] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. P.M. Pulp & Paper Mills Ltd., ; , followed.

The assessee company was a private limited company carrying on business in the manufacture of textile goods. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee company had not been assessed to income tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 and that the application for rectification of the mistake was barred by limitation. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application under section 66(1) of that Act, and that in view of the decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. P.M. Pulp & Paper Mills Ltd., , the application was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the applications for rectification were barred by time. [630H; 730A] (ii) The application for amendment of the application filed under section 33(1)(a) of Income Tax Act, 1961 is not maintainable because the application is not made within the period prescribed by section 10 of the Act. [730B] (iii) The question whether the application should be rejected on the ground that the applicant was entitled to relief under section 34(2). [731C D] (iv) The expression "any other person" in section 2(a) means a person who has been assessed or assessed to tax under the Act, but does not include a person whose income is assessed or chargeable to tax. [771B C] (v) The word "any person" used in section 10 (2) means any person who is assessed and assessed to pay tax under that Act. In order to attract the applicability of section 10, the expression "other person", in section 12(3), must be given a restricted meaning. [761C] (vi) The words "any one" in the context of the word "person" are wide enough to include a party who has not been subjected or assessed and is liable to pay any tax under this Act. The expression 'other person" is used in the sense that it includes only a person which has been subjected to tax by reason of the omission or failure on his part to make an application for the rectification of mistake, but must include a "person who has already been assessed and has not filed any application for such rectification".

The plaintiff, a Hindu, was the owner of certain lands in the suit. The defendants claimed that they were entitled to possession of the lands on the ground that they had been granted a lease for a period of ten years from the date of the grant of the lease. The trial court held that the defendants were not entitled to any relief under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and that the plaintiff was entitled to the benefit of section 92. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the defendants had not been able to prove their title to the lands in question. Held, that the trial court was right in holding that the plaintiffs were entitled only to the relief under the Act. The plaintiff was not entitled for any relief because he had not proved his title to those lands and had not produced any evidence to show that they did not produce any evidence of their title. The suit was therefore barred by time as the suit had been filed in the Court of Civil Judge, Calcutta. Held further, that a suit for possession of certain properties was barred under section 91 of the Act because it was based on a presumption which could be rebutted by the defendants. The presumption must be rebutted only by evidence of title and not by proof of title. It is not necessary to prove that the defendant had produced any documentary evidence to establish his title. In the present case, the defendants did not adduce any evidence in support of their claim that they was entitled for the benefit under section 93 of the Indian Evidence Act.

The appellant was the owner of a agricultural land in Bombay. The respondent purchased the suit land from one M/s. P.D. Patel and another. The appellant filed an application under section 9 of the Maharashtra Tenancy Act, 1948 for setting aside the sale on the ground that the land was not liable to be sold by the State Government as required by section 39(1) of the Bombay Tenancy Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff had no locus standi to file a suit in respect of the land and that the suit was barred by limitation. The High Court held that the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit on the basis of the provisions of the Act and that it could not have entertained the suit as it was filed within time. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to try the suit in view of section 39 (1) (a) of Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1939, which was applicable only to a civil court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The civil court has jurisdiction to decide the question whether the plaintiff was entitled to the relief claimed by him or not. [782B] 2. The Civil Court has no jurisdiction in respect thereof. It is not open to the Civil Courts to entertain a suit as there are two distinct classes of suits, one class of suits and another class of cases. The first class of suit is one which is governed by the Bombay Act. In the present case, the plaintiff has not filed any suit within time and therefore he cannot be said to have been in possession of the suit property. [771C] 3. The plaintiff had not filed a suit within the prescribed period of limitation. He was not entitled to any relief as prayed for by him. The suit was not barred by time. The jurisdiction of the Civil court is limited to the civil courts and it cannot be held that there are three distinct classes, namely, suits and other proceedings. [761C D] 4. In view of the fact that the defendant had filed a civil suit in the Bombay Court, the Civil Judge was not competent to entertain such a suit. The decision of the civil Court is final and binding on the parties. [753F G] 5. The question whether a civil Court has jurisdiction under section 39 of the said Act is one of fact and not one which can be decided by the Civil courts. [741G H; 74A B] 6. In order to decide whether a suit is barred by the provisions contained in section 39, it must be shown that the dispute between the plaintiff and the defendant was one which could be decided on its own merits. The Court has to determine whether the civil or revenue court had no power to entertain any suit as the civil jurisdiction of a civil nature is not excluded from the purview of the Code of Civil Procedure. [731G] 7. In deciding whether a particular civil court can entertain a claim for relief, it is necessary to examine the question as to whether a person has been in actual possession or not and whether he has been dispossessed by the authority concerned. The dispute between a person who has been evicted by the authorities concerned is one relating to the jurisdiction of civil courts. It may be that the jurisdiction which the civil Courts are empowered to entertain is not barred under section 38 of the Tenancy Act but it is only when the civil and revenue court exercises jurisdiction, that the authority has no power or jurisdiction to adjudicate upon such a dispute. [ 741G G] 8. The provisions contained therein are in pari materia with sections 39(2) and 39 of Bombay Act which are applicable to suits and proceedings under the Tenancy Acts.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of steel products. The assessee company carried on the business of manufacturing steel products and sold them to its customers. For the assessment year 1959 60, the assessee claimed exemption under section 10(2) (xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim for exemption but held that the assessee was entitled to exemption under the provisions of section 10 (2). On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Tribunal and held that it was not a business carried on by the company in the course of its business. In the appeals before this Court, it was contended for the Revenue that the expression "business carried on" in section 2(xv) means an activity carried on in or in connection with the business carried upon by the Company in the carrying on of any business of the assessee and not an activity which is carried on under the control of the company. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The word "business" in the context of the expression used in section 10 of the Act means a business carrying on or in relation to the carrying of any trade or business carried by the undertaking. It does not mean that the activity carried upon is an activity carrying on by or in furtherance of the object of the business. [782B C] 2. The expression "any other purpose" in sub section (1) of section 2 of the 1922 Act means an act which is engaged in the business and includes a business which is not carried on for profit. It is only when the activity is carried upon, that activity is an industry carried on with or in pursuance of any of the provisions contained in sub s.(2) of s.10(2). [785C] 3. The definition of "business carrying on" is wide enough to include a business engaged in or incidental to the business which has been carried on, and not merely an activity that is carried out by or under the management of the undertaking, but also when the business is carried with or without the consent of the parties. [783C] 4. The term "business carries on" does not include a carrying on any business. It includes a carrying out of the activity which has come to an end in the process of carrying on the activity. [784E F] 5. The question whether a business is engaged or carried on must be determined on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case. [885F G] 6. The High Court was right in holding that the word "reserve" in s.2(xv)(xv) should be construed as an activity for carrying on a trade or commerce. [781D E] 7. In view of the fact that the business has been set up by the appellant company, it is not possible to hold that the activities carried on were incidental to its business and that the undertaking was not an industry carrying on in the same manner as the business was carried on. [777E F; 784A B] 8. The Tribunal was right when the assessee company has carried on any activity for profit, but it is only where the business carries on a business that is engaged by or with the consent or connivance of the partners of the firm. [779F G].

The appellants were the descendants of a Hindu Religious Endowments. The respondents filed a suit for possession of certain lands in their favour on the ground that they were not hereditary tenants and that they had no right to hold the lands as hereditary tenants. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs were hereditary tenants, but the High Court held that the defendants were hereditary holders of the inam lands and that the appellants were entitled to the protection of section 3(1) (a) of the Madras Estates Abolition Act, 1954. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was barred by limitation as the plaintiffs had not been able to establish their right to the land in question. HELD : The High Court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show that the inam was hereditary tenants or that they did not hold the land as hereditary tenant. [630 B] (a). The suit was therefore barred by time as the appellants had not established their right of occupancy under section 3 (1) of Act, 1955. [730 C] (b) The High court was wrong on the view that the Inam was hereditary and the plaintiffs did not establish their rights to the lands in question, because they were hereditary occupants. [781 D F] (c) The suit is barred by the limitation as provided under section 4(1)(a). [731 C] In the present case the inam had been granted for a period of five years and the appellants did not prove their right.

The appellant Municipal Corporation of Indore, was assessed to tax under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1950. The respondents filed a suit for recovery of certain amounts from the appellant Municipality on the ground that they were not liable to pay any tax under section 3(1) (a) of the Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the assessment made by the Municipal Corporation was invalid and the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal, the High Court held that the levy of the tax was valid and the appellant was entitled to recover the amount from the respondents. On appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The levy of a tax under a statute is not valid unless it is shown that the tax has been levied in accordance with the provisions of the statute. [657 F] (2) The imposition of a fee is valid if it is found that the taxes are imposed on the basis of the annual value of the property and the annual rent is not liable for any tax. [757 A B] (3) The tax is levied in conformity with the rules made under section 4(1)(a) and (b). If the tax is imposed on a building or land, it cannot be said that the imposition was invalid because it is not a tax which has been imposed on it. [781 D F] In the present case, the Municipal Committee had no power to levy any tax in accordance therewith. The Municipal Committee was therefore competent to levy the tax under s 3(2) (b) of Act. [783 A B].

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The assessee company sold its products to a third party, who sold it to another person. The sale price was fixed at Rs. 1,50,000 and the balance was paid by the company as a result of which the sale price had been arrived at Rs, 2,50. The sales tax authorities held that the sale prices were not taxable under section 10(2) (xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, but the High Court in appeal reversed the finding of the Tribunal and held that there was no evidence to show that the sales were made by a third person. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the transaction was not one for sale within the meaning of section 10 (2) of Act 2 of 1922, because, in the present case, the sale was effected by a single person and the sale proceeds were sold at Rs 2,00,000. HELD : The sale was not a sale within section 10 of the Act. It was not an sale within that definition. The transaction was one for the purpose of carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. [417 D] In the present ease, there is no evidence that the assessee had sold its goods to another third person and it was only when the sale took place, that the price was arrived at by a separate person. It is not correct to say that the transactions were made in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The fact that the business was carried on by a company does not make any difference. [414 D] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. P. C. & Co., , referred to.
